## #3962 — userspace-dp: buildScreenSnapshots iterates zones in map (unsorted) order → nondeterministic wire byte-order defeats the content-hash dedup → the dataplane re-applies the screen config on every reconcile (fable-161 F-074) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, perf/churn — spurious dataplane re-apply):** `buildScreenSnapshots` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace` — grep buildScreenSnapshots) iterates the per-zone screen config by ranging over a Go MAP (zone→screen), which has NONDETERMINISTIC iteration order. So the serialized screen snapshot's byte order VARIES run-to-run even when the screen config is UNCHANGED. The reconcile uses a CONTENT HASH to skip re-applying an unchanged snapshot — but because the bytes differ each build, the hash differs → the dedup MISSES → the dataplane RE-APPLIES the entire screen config on EVERY reconcile (every commit, every periodic sync). Re-applying the screen snapshot is unnecessary control-socket + dataplane work (and, depending on the apply, can briefly reset screen counters / re-arm the SYN-cookie state). At scale (many zones, frequent reconciles) this is wasted churn + can mask a real screen-config change.

**Fix:** iterate the zones in a DETERMINISTIC (sorted) order when building the screen snapshot — sort the zone keys (by stable zone id or name) before ranging, so the serialized bytes are identical for an unchanged config → the content-hash dedup works → the reconcile SKIPS an unchanged screen snapshot. Audit the OTHER snapshot builders for the same map-iteration-nondeterminism (the same content-hash-dedup-defeat class — e.g. any build that ranges a map into a wire buffer). Fix buildScreenSnapshots here; note siblings.

**RED-on-revert:** building the screen snapshot twice from the SAME config yields IDENTICAL bytes (goes RED — nondeterministic byte order — on revert); the content hash is stable → a second reconcile with an unchanged config SKIPS the re-apply. Unit-test: two builds of the same multi-zone config produce byte-identical (and equal-hash) snapshots.

Provenance: fable-161 F-074, go-obs/dataplane module.

---

## #3965 — observability/perf: ReadPolicyCounters is O(P·(P+C)) and holds the policy mutex for the whole Prometheus scrape → scrape stall + mutex starvation at scale (fable-161 F-073) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, perf/scalability — scrape stall):** `ReadPolicyCounters` (grep ReadPolicyCounters — the policy hit/byte counter read on the Prometheus/gRPC path) is O(P·(P+C)) — for each of P policies it does a linear scan over the policy list (and C counters) — and it holds the policy MUTEX for the ENTIRE read. On a firewall with many policies (hundreds–thousands), every Prometheus scrape (default 15s, sometimes more frequent) walks this quadratic loop UNDER the lock → (a) the scrape itself stalls (seconds), and (b) the held mutex STARVES every other policy-mutex user for the duration — including the commit/apply path and session classification if they share the lock. So a large-policy-set firewall under active Prometheus scraping periodically stalls config commits + degrades the control plane.

**Fix:** (a) make the counter read O(P+C) — build an index/map (policy-id → counter) ONCE per read instead of a nested linear scan; (b) DON'T hold the policy mutex for the whole read — either snapshot the counters under a brief lock then format outside the lock, or use per-counter atomics so the read is lock-free. The scrape must not block commits. Verify the read is O(P+C) + the mutex hold is bounded (snapshot-and-release), not held across the whole serialization.

**RED-on-revert:** a benchmark/test with N=1000 policies shows ReadPolicyCounters completes in O(P+C) time + the mutex is held only briefly (goes RED — O(P²) + mutex held across the whole read — on revert); correctness of the counters is unchanged. Unit-test the counter-read correctness + a benchmark asserting the complexity/lock-hold improvement (or a test that a concurrent commit isn't blocked during a read).

Provenance: fable-161 F-073, go-obs/perf module.

---

## #3967 — snmp: SNMP agent / trap-groups configured after boot are inert until restart (day-2 config not reconciled) (fable-161 F-059) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config-lifecycle — day-2 SNMP config inert):** the SNMP agent / trap-groups are initialized/bound ONCE at daemon BOOT (grep the SNMP subsystem start — the agent listener + trap-group setup). A config change to SNMP (enable the agent, add/modify a community, add/modify a trap-group or its targets) applied AFTER boot via `commit` is NOT reconciled into the RUNNING SNMP subsystem — the change sits in the config but is INERT until the daemon restarts. So an operator who enables SNMP (or adds a trap target) on a running firewall sees NO effect (the agent doesn't start listening / traps don't go to the new target) until a restart → a silent config-doesn't-take-effect surprise (and a monitoring gap: the new trap target never receives traps).

**Fix:** reconcile the SNMP subsystem on EVERY commit/apply, not just at boot — on a config change touching `snmp`, (re)start/stop the agent listener to match the new enabled state + community/port, and rebuild the trap-group targets. Follow the daemon's reconcile pattern (the way other subsystems — networkd, ipsec, frr — are re-applied on commit). Make the SNMP apply idempotent (no-op when unchanged, restart the listener only when the bind params actually change). Verify: enabling SNMP on a running daemon starts the agent; adding a trap target starts sending traps to it — both WITHOUT a restart.

**RED-on-revert:** enabling SNMP (or adding a trap-group target) via a day-2 commit reconciles into the running subsystem — the agent starts listening / traps flow to the new target (goes RED — inert until restart — on revert); an unchanged SNMP config is a no-op (no listener bounce). Unit-test the SNMP reconcile-on-commit (the apply path re-invokes the SNMP setup with the new config).

Provenance: fable-161 F-059, go-obs/snmp module. Sibling class of the boot-gated-reconcile bugs.

## #3968 — userspace-dp CoS: build_cos_batch never clears pop_snapshot_stack across invocations → unbounded scratch growth (and/or a stale-entry panic) on the shaper hot path (fable-161 F-078) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, Rust dataplane — scratch stack never cleared):** `build_cos_batch` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp` — grep build_cos_batch / pop_snapshot_stack) reuses a scratch `pop_snapshot_stack` (a Vec used to hold the per-batch scheduler pop snapshot) but does NOT `.clear()` it at the START (or end) of each invocation. So entries from the PREVIOUS batch remain in the Vec and either (a) accumulate across batches → the Vec grows without bound (memory growth on the shaper hot path, called per-batch), or (b) the stale entries are re-read as if they belong to the current batch → wrong scheduler pop / a stale-index panic (out-of-bounds or a wrong queue drained). Either way the CoS/shaper batch build is corrupted after the first batch.

**Fix:** `pop_snapshot_stack.clear()` at the start of `build_cos_batch` (before pushing this batch's entries) — OR at the end after draining — so each invocation starts from an empty scratch. Verify the Vec's `len()` is bounded (returns to 0 between batches) and that no stale entry from a prior batch is ever read. Audit any OTHER reused scratch Vecs in the same function/hot path for the same missing-clear (the reused-scratch-not-cleared class). Match the existing scratch-reuse convention (the codebase reuses scratch Vecs with an explicit clear-at-start — mirror it).

**RED-on-revert:** call build_cos_batch twice with different inputs → the second call's pop_snapshot_stack contains ONLY the second batch's entries (len bounded, no first-batch residue) (goes RED — stale first-batch entries persist / len grows — on revert); a single call is correct. Rust unit test asserting the scratch is empty/correct at the start of the 2nd batch (or that two sequential batches produce independent correct results). FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-078, rs-dataplane/CoS module. RUST (cargo).

---

## #3970 — control-socket: fwdstatus Sampler does a redundant 1Hz control-socket poll on top of the status poll → violates the >1/s control-socket budget, starves session installs during bulk sync (fable-161 F-070) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, control-socket contention):** the forwarding-status (fwdstatus) Sampler issues its OWN periodic ~1Hz request to the userspace-dp control socket (grep the fwdstatus Sampler / forwarding-status poll), SEPARATE from and REDUNDANT with the existing 1/s status poll that already fetches the same (or overlapping) forwarding state. The project's control-socket budget (CLAUDE.md "Control socket contention"): the helper control socket is shared by status poll (1/s), HA sync, session installs, snapshot sync, and forwarding sync — "Adding a new control socket request at >1/s will starve session installs during bulk sync." The redundant fwdstatus 1Hz poll DOUBLES the status-poll rate on the shared socket → during bulk session sync (failover/failback), session installs are starved → slower convergence, and the fwdstatus data it fetches is already available from the primary status poll.

**Fix:** eliminate the redundant poll — have the fwdstatus Sampler CONSUME the forwarding state already fetched by the existing 1/s status poll (share the cached status result / subscribe to it) instead of issuing its own control-socket request. If fwdstatus genuinely needs a field the status poll doesn't fetch, ADD that field to the SINGLE status poll rather than adding a second poll. Net control-socket request rate for status must stay at 1/s, not 2/s. Verify no second periodic control-socket request originates from the fwdstatus path.

**RED-on-revert:** the fwdstatus Sampler makes NO independent control-socket request (it reads the shared status-poll result) — the control-socket status request rate stays 1/s (goes RED — a 2nd redundant 1Hz request, 2/s total — on revert); the fwdstatus data is still populated (from the shared poll). Unit-test that the Sampler doesn't issue its own control-socket call (mock/count the control-socket requests over N seconds).

Provenance: fable-161 F-070, control-socket-budget / go-obs module. CLAUDE.md control-socket contention rule.

## #3972 — config: one invalid port-mirroring entry (duplicate ingress / negative rate) fail-closes the WHOLE mirror table with only a Warn → all mirroring silently lost (fable-161 F-072) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, robustness — one bad entry drops all mirroring):** the port-mirroring / forwarding-options analyzer compilation (grep port-mirror / analyzer / mirror in the compiler) fail-CLOSES the ENTIRE mirror table when ANY single entry is invalid (a DUPLICATE ingress source, a NEGATIVE / zero sampling rate, or a malformed ratio) — it emits only a WARN and drops the whole set rather than rejecting just the bad entry (or hard-failing the commit). So an operator with 3 valid mirror sessions + 1 typo'd 4th loses ALL 4 mirror sessions (traffic analysis / IDS feed / packet capture silently stops for the good sessions too) with only a log warning they may not see. This is the WRONG fail mode: either (a) the bad entry should be a hard commit-reject (so the operator fixes it) OR (b) only the bad entry is dropped and the valid ones are kept — NOT "one typo silently disables all mirroring."

**Fix:** decide the correct fail mode and implement it. Preferred: HARD-REJECT the commit on an invalid port-mirror entry (duplicate ingress, negative/zero rate, malformed ratio) with a specific error naming the bad entry — consistent with how other config errors fail the commit (a typo shouldn't commit-green then silently drop). Do NOT fail-close the whole table on a warn. If per-entry salvage is preferred instead, drop ONLY the invalid entry + keep the valid ones + warn about the specific dropped entry. Match the project's config-validation posture (strict commit-reject for malformed leaves). Verify a valid mirror config is unaffected + an invalid entry produces a specific error (or a scoped drop), not a whole-table wipe.

**RED-on-revert:** a config with 3 valid mirror entries + 1 invalid (dup ingress or negative rate) → the commit is REJECTED with a specific error (OR only the bad entry is dropped + 3 kept) (goes RED — whole table fail-closed, 0 kept, only a warn — on revert); an all-valid config compiles all entries. Unit-test the mixed valid+invalid port-mirror config.

Provenance: fable-161 F-072, robustness/config module.

## #3975 — config: deactivate on a bracketed multi-value leaf mishandles it (setInactiveAtPath lacks the #2419 multi-value handling deletePath got in #3848) (fable-161 F-034) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config-mode parity):** `setInactiveAtPath` (the `deactivate`/`activate` config-mode edit — `pkg/config/ast_edit.go`) does NOT handle the bracketed multi-value leaf shape (#2419) the way `deletePath` now does (deletePath got the multi-value handling in #3848/#3846). Per the #2419 class: a `multi: true` leaf collapses a bracketed list `[ a b c ]` onto ONE leaf's Keys (`Keys=["field","a","b","c"]`) plus child Nodes. `deactivate <path> <field>` on such a leaf currently only matches/inactivates the first value (Keys[1]) — it fails to `deactivate` a specific member of a multi-value list, or mis-targets the wrong node, because it reads only Keys[1] and ignores Keys[2:]/Children (the exact #2419 read bug). So `deactivate` on a multi-value leaf (e.g. `deactivate ... from protocol [ tcp udp ]`, or a multi-value next-hop / proposal list) is a no-op or partial → the operator's deactivate silently doesn't take effect for all-but-first value.

**Fix:** mirror the #3848/#3846 deletePath multi-value handling in `setInactiveAtPath` (and the activate path) — when the target leaf is `multi: true`, match across `Keys[1:]` AND `Children` (use the same accumulation helper deletePath uses, e.g. firewallMatchValues / the member-match logic) so `deactivate`/`activate` correctly targets the whole multi-value leaf (or a specified member, matching deletePath's member-vs-whole semantics). Keep the args==1 whole-leaf vs member-delete gate consistent with #3846/#3879. Verify deactivate on a bracketed multi-value leaf inactivates it correctly (round-trips through show + commit).

**RED-on-revert:** `deactivate` on a bracketed multi-value leaf (`[ a b c ]`) marks the whole leaf (or the named member) inactive — round-trips + the compiler sees it inactive (goes RED — only the first value handled / no-op — on revert); a single-value leaf deactivate is unchanged; activate reverses it. Unit-test via ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath + the deactivate edit (NOT NewParser — per CLAUDE.md).

Provenance: fable-161 F-034, config-parity module. Same #2419 multi-value class as #3846/#3848/#3879; deletePath already fixed, deactivate path not.

## #3976 — userspace-dp: non-TCP 'then reject' sources the ICMP-reject reply from the physical PARENT ifindex instead of the VLAN sub-interface → reject drops / wrong-source on a VLAN sub-if (fable-161 F-188) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, Rust dataplane — reject broken on VLAN sub-if):** the non-TCP `then reject` path (the ICMP unreachable / reject reply generation — grep reject / icmp_unreachable in userspace-dp for the non-TCP branch) builds the reject reply using the PHYSICAL PARENT interface's ifindex / addressing rather than the VLAN SUB-INTERFACE the packet actually arrived on. So for traffic on a VLAN sub-interface (e.g. reth0.80), a `then reject` action generates an ICMP-unreachable that is sourced from / sent via the physical parent (reth0) ifindex — WITHOUT the VLAN tag / with the wrong source address → the reject packet is dropped (untagged on a tagged link) or has an invalid source → the sender never receives the reject (it sees a silent drop, not a reject) → `then reject` degrades to `then discard` on every VLAN sub-interface. (Contrast the TCP reject path, which may handle the ingress ifindex correctly; the non-TCP ICMP-reject branch does not.)

**Fix:** the non-TCP reject reply must be built for + emitted on the INGRESS sub-interface the packet arrived on (its ifindex, its VLAN tag, its source address) — not the physical parent. Use the packet's actual ingress ifindex / the VLAN-aware egress path (the same one normal forwarded/replied packets on a VLAN sub-if use — mirror how the TCP reject or the generated-reply path resolves the egress interface + VLAN tag). Verify a `then reject` on a VLAN sub-interface produces a correctly-tagged, correctly-sourced ICMP unreachable that reaches the sender.

**RED-on-revert:** a non-TCP packet on a VLAN sub-interface hitting `then reject` produces an ICMP-unreachable with the correct ingress-sub-if source + VLAN tag (goes RED — sourced from the physical parent ifindex, untagged/wrong-source, dropped — on revert); reject on a non-VLAN interface is unchanged. Rust unit test constructing a VLAN-sub-if ingress + a reject rule, asserting the reply's source ifindex/VLAN. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-188, rs-dataplane/forwarding module. RUST (cargo).

## #3979 — config-mode: 'configure exclusive' lock is never released on session exit (exclusiveHolder checked but configHolder cleared) → config permanently locked out (fable-161 F-049) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, availability — stuck exclusive config lock):** `configure exclusive` takes an exclusive configuration lock, but the release path on session exit checks/clears the WRONG holder field — it clears `configHolder` (the shared/private-mode holder) while the exclusive lock is tracked in a separate `exclusiveHolder` (grep configure exclusive / exclusiveHolder / configHolder in pkg/cli + pkg/configstore). So when the operator who holds the exclusive lock disconnects (or exits configure mode), the `exclusiveHolder` is NOT cleared → the exclusive lock persists with no live holder → EVERY subsequent `configure` / `configure exclusive` / `configure private` is REJECTED ("configuration database locked by <gone session>") → the firewall's config is PERMANENTLY LOCKED until a daemon restart. A single operator using `configure exclusive` then disconnecting bricks all future config edits.

**Fix:** the exclusive-lock release path must clear `exclusiveHolder` (the field the exclusive lock actually set), not `configHolder` — on session exit / configure-mode exit / disconnect, release whichever lock THIS session holds (match the holder field to the lock type taken). Ideally also add a stale-holder reclaim (a lock held by a session that no longer exists is reclaimable). Verify: `configure exclusive` + disconnect → the next `configure` succeeds (lock released).

**RED-on-revert:** session A `configure exclusive` then disconnects → session B `configure` succeeds (the exclusive lock was released) (goes RED — lock stuck, B rejected, permanent lockout — on revert); a live exclusive holder still blocks B; private/shared mode unaffected. Unit-test the exclusive-lock acquire→release→reacquire cycle across sessions.

Provenance: fable-161 F-049, CLI/RBAC / configstore module.

## #3980 — config display: 'show configuration' / 'show | display set' renders only the FIRST occurrence of a repeated keyword statement → repeated config (multiple ntp servers, static routes, etc.) shown incompletely (fable-161 F-037) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config-display fidelity):** the config renderer (`show configuration` hierarchical + `show | display set`) emits only the FIRST occurrence when a hierarchy level has MULTIPLE statements with the same leading keyword (grep the show-config / display-set renderer — the node-walk that de-dups or first-only-matches on a keyword). So a config with repeated same-keyword statements — e.g. multiple `system ntp server <ip>`, several static `route` entries under one destination, repeated `archive-sites`, multiple same-keyed items — renders only the FIRST, HIDING the rest. The operator's `show configuration` (and the `show | display set` used for backup/replication + the #3975 deactivate round-trip) does NOT faithfully reflect the committed config → a config backup taken via display-set is INCOMPLETE → restoring it loses the hidden statements (data loss on backup/restore).

**Fix:** the renderer must emit ALL occurrences at a hierarchy level, not first-only — walk ALL sibling nodes matching a keyword (FindChildren, not FindChild-first) and render each. This is the display-side sibling of the #3842 (compiler dup-block accumulate) + #2419 (multi-value) class: read across ALL siblings. Verify a config with N repeated same-keyword statements renders all N in both hierarchical + display-set output, and a display-set round-trip (show | display set → re-apply) reproduces all N.

**RED-on-revert:** a config with 3 `system ntp server` (or 3 repeated statements) renders all 3 in `show configuration` + `show | display set` (goes RED — only the first shown — on revert); a single statement is unchanged; the display-set round-trip reproduces all 3. Unit-test the renderer with a multi-occurrence config.

Provenance: fable-161 F-037, config-parity / display module. Sibling of #3842 dup-block + #2419 multi-value class.

## #3982 — config-mode: 'rename' of a non-first same-keyword sibling fails (matches only the first sibling) → cannot rename the 2nd+ of a repeated statement (fable-161 F-036) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config-mode edit):** the config-mode `rename <old> to <new>` edit (`pkg/config/ast_edit.go` — grep rename / renamePath) resolves the target by matching only the FIRST sibling at a hierarchy level with the given keyword/identity — so when there are MULTIPLE same-keyword siblings and the operator renames a NON-FIRST one (e.g. the 2nd of several `policy <name>`, `term <name>`, or a repeated statement), the rename either fails ("not found") or renames the WRONG (first) node. The operator cannot rename the 2nd+ occurrence → they must delete + re-add (losing ordering / sub-config). This is the config-edit sibling of the #3842 (dup-block) / #2419 (multi-value) / #3975 (deactivate) / #3980 (show-config) read-all-siblings class — the rename path matches first-only instead of matching the SPECIFIC named sibling.

**Fix:** `renamePath` must resolve the target by its FULL identity (the named-key, e.g. `term <name>` / `policy <name>`), matching the SPECIFIC sibling — not the first keyword match. Walk all siblings (FindChildren), select the one whose identity matches `<old>`, rename it. Guard against the new name colliding with an existing sibling (reject a rename that would create a duplicate identity). Verify renaming the 2nd of N same-keyword siblings renames the correct one, leaving the others untouched.

**RED-on-revert:** with 3 `policy A/B/C` (or 3 same-keyword siblings), `rename policy B to B2` renames exactly the B node (A + C untouched, order preserved) (goes RED — first-only match renames A or errors — on revert); renaming the first still works; renaming to a colliding name is rejected. Unit-test via ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath (build multi-sibling) + the rename edit (NOT NewParser — per CLAUDE.md).

## #3984 — config: keyed-list leaves 'system ntp server' / 'archive-sites' are non-multi {args:1,children:nil} → SetPath single-value-replace collapses them to the LAST on flat-set/load-set replay (2nd deletes 1st) (fable-161 F-041) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701); PRECISELY DIAGNOSED by the #3980 engineer during the F-037 fix.

**Defect (MEDIUM, config data loss — repeated keyed-list statement collapses to last):** the keyed-list LEAVES `system ntp server <ip>`, `system archive-sites <url>` (and siblings of that shape) are declared in `setSchema` as `{args:1, children:nil}` and are NOT `multi: true`. So `SetPath`'s single-value-REPLACE branch (`pkg/config/ast_edit.go`) treats a SECOND `set system ntp server 2.2.2.2` as a REPLACEMENT of the first (`server 1.1.1.1`) rather than an addition → on a flat-set / `load set` / display-set round-trip replay of a multi-server config, all but the LAST server are DROPPED. The COMPILER already reads all of them via `FindChildren` (`compiler_system.go:65,163`) — so the config is internally multi-value, but the SET-path edit collapses it. Net: an operator with 3 NTP servers who does a `load set` (or whose config is round-tripped through display-set for backup/HA-config-sync) LOSES 2 of the 3 servers silently.

**Fix:** mark these keyed-list leaves `multi: true` in `setSchema` (`pkg/config/schema.go` / schema_system) so SetPath ADDS each occurrence as a distinct sibling instead of replacing, and ensure the compiler read stays `FindChildren`-based (already is). Mirror the #2419 multi-value handling for these keyed leaves. Audit the OTHER `{args:1,children:nil}` leaves that the compiler reads via FindChildren (the SetPath-collapse-vs-compiler-FindChildren mismatch class) — e.g. any repeated keyed statement — and mark them multi too. Verify: `set ... server A` + `set ... server B` + `set ... server C` → all 3 present after SetPath, round-trip through display-set reproduces all 3.

**RED-on-revert:** 3 `set system ntp server` via ParseSetCommand + SetPath → all 3 sibling nodes present (goes RED — collapsed to the last, 1 present — on revert); a single server unchanged; a display-set round-trip (F-037 #3980 now renders all 3, this fix makes the re-apply KEEP all 3). Unit-test via ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath (NOT NewParser). Coordinate with #3980 (the display side, merged) — this is the SET side of the same repeated-keyed-list class.

Provenance: fable-161 F-041, config-parity module. SET-side sibling of #3980 (F-037 display) + the #2419/#3842 read-all-siblings class. Confirmed by the #3980 engineer's scoped-out finding.

## #3985 — cli: 'monitor interface' leaves a stdin-reading goroutine alive after exit → it steals keystrokes from the next command (fable-161 F-021) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, CLI UX — leaked stdin goroutine steals input):** the `monitor interface <if>` command (the live-refresh interface monitor — grep monitor interface / the goroutine that reads stdin for the quit key 'q') spawns a goroutine to read stdin (to detect the quit keystroke) but does NOT terminate that goroutine when the monitor exits (on 'q' / Ctrl-C / the refresh loop ending). So after `monitor interface` returns, the leaked goroutine is STILL blocked reading os.Stdin → it STEALS the first keystroke(s) of the operator's NEXT command (the char goes to the dead monitor's reader, not the CLI prompt) → the operator's next command is corrupted/eaten. Repeated `monitor interface` invocations leak a goroutine each, and each competes for stdin.

**Fix:** the stdin-reader goroutine must be STOPPED when the monitor exits — use a context/done channel the monitor cancels on exit, and ensure the goroutine returns (don't leave it blocked in a bare os.Stdin read). A blocking os.Stdin.Read can't be cancelled mid-read, so structure it so the goroutine checks the done signal (e.g. read with a cancellable reader, or restore the terminal + drain, or use the CLI's existing input mux instead of a raw stdin read). Ensure exactly ONE stdin consumer is active after the monitor exits (the CLI prompt). Verify no goroutine leak + no stolen keystroke after `monitor interface` exits.

**RED-on-revert:** after `monitor interface` exits, no monitor stdin-reader goroutine remains + the next command's first keystroke reaches the CLI prompt (goes RED — leaked goroutine steals the keystroke — on revert); the monitor still responds to 'q'. Unit-test the goroutine lifecycle (the reader goroutine returns on monitor exit — assert via a done signal / goroutine-count, or a seam counting active stdin readers).

Provenance: fable-161 F-021, CLI/RBAC module.

## #3988 — config: scheduler start/stop date-time parsed as UTC (or wrong TZ) instead of the system local time → schedulers activate/deactivate at the wrong wall-clock time (fable-161 F-052) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config correctness — scheduler fires at wrong time):** the `schedulers scheduler <name>` start-date / stop-date (and daily start-time/stop-time) parsing (grep scheduler / start-date / ParseInLocation / time.Parse in pkg/config or the scheduler compiler) parses the operator-supplied date-time as UTC (uses `time.Parse` which defaults to UTC, or a fixed TZ) rather than the SYSTEM LOCAL time zone. Junos scheduler times are LOCAL wall-clock (the operator writes `start-date 2026-07-01.09:00` meaning 09:00 local). Parsing it as UTC shifts every scheduler by the local UTC offset (e.g. -7h for PDT) → a firewall policy scheduled to activate at 09:00 local activates at 16:00 local (09:00 UTC) → the time-based policy (a maintenance-window allow, a business-hours block) is active at the WRONG hours → a security/availability window is wrong by the UTC offset.

**Fix:** parse scheduler date-times in the SYSTEM LOCAL time zone — use `time.ParseInLocation(layout, value, time.Local)` (not `time.Parse`) so the wall-clock the operator wrote is interpreted as local time. Verify a scheduler `start-time 09:00` activates at 09:00 LOCAL, not 09:00 UTC. Audit the stop-date + the recurring daily-time parsing for the same UTC default. (If the design intent is explicitly UTC, document it — but Junos convention is local; match Junos.)

**RED-on-revert:** a scheduler with `start-date <date>.09:00` in a non-UTC local TZ activates at 09:00 LOCAL (the parsed time equals the local wall-clock) (goes RED — parsed as UTC → shifted by the offset — on revert); a UTC-local system (offset 0) is unchanged. Unit-test the parse with a fixed non-UTC time.Local (or inject the location) asserting the resulting instant matches local wall-clock.

Provenance: fable-161 F-052, config-parity / scheduler module.

## #3992 — userspace-dp WireGuard: wg_encap resolves the outer (underlay) route TWICE per encapsulated packet → redundant per-packet route lookup on the WG TX hot path (fable-161 F-088) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, Rust dataplane perf — redundant per-packet route lookup):** the WireGuard encapsulation TX path (`wg_encap` — grep wg_encap / the WG outer/underlay route resolution in userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg) resolves the OUTER (underlay) route for the encapsulated UDP packet TWICE per packet — once to determine the egress interface / next-hop, and again (redundantly) when building the outer IP header / for the source address (or a second FIB/neighbor lookup that repeats the first). Route/FIB resolution is a non-trivial per-packet cost (LPM lookup + neighbor resolve); doing it twice on every WG-encapped packet is wasted work on the encryption hot path — at line rate over a WG tunnel this is a measurable per-packet overhead (2× the route-lookup cost).

**Fix:** resolve the outer route ONCE per packet and reuse the result (egress ifindex, next-hop, source address, neighbor MAC) for both the egress decision AND the outer-header construction. Cache the single lookup's result in a local and thread it through, rather than re-resolving. Verify the outer header + egress are built from the single lookup (identical result, one FIB/neighbor call per packet). Mirror how the non-WG forward path resolves the route once.

**RED-on-revert:** instrument/count the outer-route (FIB/neighbor) resolutions per wg_encap call → exactly 1 (goes RED — 2 per packet — on revert); the encapsulated packet's outer header + egress are unchanged (same next-hop/source/MAC). Rust unit test counting the route-resolution calls per encap (mock/count the FIB lookup seam), asserting 1 not 2, + asserting the outer header is byte-identical to before. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-088, rs-dataplane/wg perf module. RUST (cargo).

## #3993 — config CoS: a rewrite-rule term with an inline loss-priority drops the loss-priority (only the code-point/forwarding-class kept) → DSCP/802.1p rewrite loses the drop-precedence marking (fable-161 F-027) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, CoS config-parity):** the class-of-service rewrite-rule compilation (grep rewrite-rule / rewriteRule / loss-priority in the CoS compiler) drops the INLINE `loss-priority` from a rewrite-rule term — it keeps the forwarding-class + code-point but ignores the `loss-priority <low|medium-low|medium-high|high>` qualifier on the same term. A Junos CoS rewrite-rule maps `(forwarding-class, loss-priority) → code-point` — the loss-priority is part of the MATCH key (a term rewrites the DSCP/802.1p bits for a specific forwarding-class AT a specific loss-priority). Dropping the inline loss-priority means the rewrite is applied to ALL loss-priorities of that forwarding-class (or the wrong one) → the drop-precedence-specific DSCP/802.1p marking is wrong → downstream routers/switches see the wrong drop-precedence codepoint → WRED/policing decisions in the rest of the network misbehave for that traffic.

**Fix:** the rewrite-rule term compiler must read the inline `loss-priority` and include it in the rewrite mapping key — `(forwarding-class, loss-priority) → (code-point)` — so each (FC, loss-priority) pair rewrites to its configured code-point. Mirror how the classifier (the reverse direction) keys on (code-point) → (FC, loss-priority). Verify a rewrite-rule with 2 terms differing only in loss-priority produces 2 distinct mappings (not one that overwrites/drops).

**RED-on-revert:** a rewrite-rule with `forwarding-class X loss-priority low code-point A` + `forwarding-class X loss-priority high code-point B` compiles to TWO distinct mappings (low→A, high→B) (goes RED — loss-priority dropped, one mapping / wrong code-point — on revert); a term without loss-priority is unchanged. Unit-test the rewrite-rule compile with per-loss-priority terms (ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath, NOT NewParser).

Provenance: fable-161 F-027, config-parity / CoS module.

## #3994 — config IKE: dead-peer-detection with a bare 'dead-peer-detection;' statement (or interval-only) is misinterpreted — the bare-stmt/interval-only DPD mode is not compiled correctly (fable-161 F-038) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verified STILL-LIVE on current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, IPsec config-parity):** the IKE `dead-peer-detection` (DPD) compilation (grep dead-peer-detection / dpd in the IKE/ipsec compiler + schema) mishandles the BARE statement form. Junos DPD can be configured as: (a) a bare `dead-peer-detection;` (enable DPD with defaults), (b) `dead-peer-detection interval <n>;` / `threshold <n>;` (enable + tune), (c) `dead-peer-detection always-send;` / `optimized;` / `probe-idle-tunnel;` (mode). The compiler treats the bare statement as DISABLED (or requires a sub-field to enable), OR the interval-only form doesn't set the enable flag / mode — so `set security ike gateway <g> dead-peer-detection` alone does NOT enable DPD in the generated strongSwan config, OR the mode (always-send/optimized) is dropped. Result: an operator who configures DPD (to detect a dead IKE peer + tear down / re-establish the tunnel) gets NO DPD (or the wrong mode) → a dead peer's tunnel is not detected → traffic blackholes over the stale SA until it expires.

**Fix:** the DPD compiler must handle all forms — a bare `dead-peer-detection` ENABLES DPD with the strongSwan defaults (dpd_delay / dpd_action); `interval`/`threshold` tune it; the mode (always-send/optimized/probe-idle-tunnel) maps to the strongSwan dpd_action / charon settings. Generate the correct swanctl `dpd_delay` + `dpd_timeout` + action for each form. Verify a bare `dead-peer-detection` produces a DPD-enabled gateway config. Mirror the Junos DPD semantics.

**RED-on-revert:** `set security ike gateway G dead-peer-detection` (bare) → the generated swanctl config has DPD enabled (dpd_delay set) (goes RED — DPD not enabled / disabled — on revert); `dead-peer-detection interval 10` sets the interval; the always-send/optimized mode maps correctly; no DPD stanza → no dpd. Unit-test the DPD compile across the forms (ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath).

Provenance: fable-161 F-038, config-parity / ipsec module.

## #3995 — userspace-dp CoS: DSCP/802.1p rewrite-rule does not MATCH on loss-priority at apply time → per-loss-priority rewrite mappings collapse to forwarding-class-only (documented gap, compiler_validate_warn.go:739) (fable-161 F-027 residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-06)

Split out from #3993 (F-027). The Go compiler correctly compiles + wires per-(forwarding-class, loss-priority) DSCP rewrite entries (verified: compiler_class_of_service.go:225, wire at cos.go:146/protocol.go:360). But the RUST userspace dataplane does NOT yet match the rewrite on loss-priority when applying it — it applies the rewrite by forwarding-class only. This is a KNOWN, WARNED gap: `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go:739` emits "class-of-service dscp rewrite-rule loss-priority is accepted for compatibility but not yet enforced by the userspace dataplane."

**Impact:** two rewrite terms differing only in loss-priority (e.g. voice/low→af11, voice/high→ef) both compile + reach the dataplane, but the dataplane applies ONE of them (the FC-matched one) regardless of the packet's actual drop-precedence → the drop-precedence-specific DSCP marking is not applied → downstream WRED/policing keyed on the codepoint sees the wrong drop-precedence for that traffic.

**Design question (route via /research):** does the userspace-dp rewrite-apply path have the packet's LOSS-PRIORITY available at rewrite time (from the classifier / the CoS metadata), so it can select the (FC, loss-priority)-specific rewrite entry? If yes → a driveable dataplane change (add loss-priority to the rewrite match key in the apply path, mirroring the classifier). If the loss-priority isn't tracked per-packet through to rewrite, that's a larger CoS-metadata-plumbing design decision. Converge a PLAN before implementing.

**Deferral rationale:** this is a documented, warned-about feature gap (not a regression). The Go half is correct; the enforcement is a Rust dataplane feature. Tracked here for /research → /engineer when prioritized.

Provenance: fable-161 F-027 residual (the enforcement half), rs-dataplane/CoS. RUST (cargo).

## #4000 — config commit: a bare 'commit' while a 'commit confirmed' window is pending silently DROPS newly-staged candidate edits (confirms the pending config + returns success without applying the new edits) (fable-161 F-047) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs the current commit-confirmed path — this area was recently touched by #3861/#3865, so confirm the behavior against current origin/master before fixing).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config-session correctness — silent edit loss):** while a `commit confirmed <N>` rollback window is PENDING, if the operator makes ADDITIONAL candidate edits and then runs a bare `commit` (no args), the bare commit CONFIRMS the pending config (clears the rollback timer, per the #3861 behavior) but does NOT APPLY the new staged candidate edits — it returns SUCCESS. So the operator believes their new edits committed (commit returned OK) but they were silently DROPPED (only the previously-pending config is now active). This happens across gRPC / REST / CLI. Junos semantics: a `commit` during a confirm window should confirm the pending config AND commit any new candidate edits (a fresh commit that also confirms) — the new edits must not be silently lost.

**Fix (verify-first — #3861/#3865 recently changed this path):** determine the current behavior with a test: (1) `commit confirmed`, (2) stage a new candidate edit, (3) bare `commit` → check whether the new edit is in the active config. If it's dropped: the bare-commit-during-confirm-window path must APPLY the new candidate (a normal commit of the current candidate) in addition to clearing the confirm timer — NOT just confirm-and-discard. If the candidate is UNCHANGED since the pending commit, a bare commit confirms (no-op apply). If the candidate has NEW edits, commit them (and confirm the window). Return an accurate result (committed the new edits). Coordinate with the #3861 commit-confirmed logic (don't regress the timer-clear). IF already-correct (the new edits DO apply) → report already-correct with file:line, no PR.

**RED-on-revert:** `commit confirmed 5` → stage `set system host-name X` → bare `commit` → the active config has host-name X (the new edit committed) + the confirm window cleared (goes RED — new edit dropped, host-name unchanged, but commit returned success — on revert); an unchanged candidate bare-commit just confirms. Unit-test the commit-confirmed-then-edit-then-commit sequence (configstore).

Provenance: fable-161 F-047, CLI/RBAC / configstore module. Interacts with #3861/#3865 (commit-confirmed) — verify-first.

## #4001 — proxy-arp: proxyARPReassertLoop re-installs responders without the apply semaphore → races a concurrent commit reconcile that just removed them (re-adds a just-deleted proxy-ARP responder) (fable-161 F-170) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verify vs CURRENT origin/master — check adjacency with OPEN #2197).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA/config race — stale proxy-ARP responder re-added):** the proxy-ARP periodic reassert loop (`proxyARPReassertLoop` — grep proxyARPReassertLoop / the proxy-arp responder reassert) re-installs the configured proxy-ARP responders on a timer WITHOUT holding the apply semaphore (`applySem` / the reconcile lock) that the commit/config-reconcile path uses. So if a `commit` REMOVES a proxy-ARP entry (or a VIP move removes a responder) and the reassert loop fires concurrently (or just after), the reassert loop RE-INSTALLS the just-removed responder from its stale cached set → the removed proxy-ARP responder comes back → the firewall answers ARP for an address it should no longer proxy (a stale VIP / a decommissioned address) → traffic is mis-attracted to this node (an HA blackhole/mis-steer if the VIP moved to the peer). The reassert loop's cached responder set is not synchronized with the commit reconcile.

**Fix:** the proxyARPReassertLoop must acquire the apply semaphore (the same `applySem` / reconcile mutex the commit path holds) before re-installing responders, so a reassert cannot interleave with a commit reconcile — the reassert always sees the CURRENT (post-commit) responder set, never a stale one. Alternatively, drive the reassert from the reconcile's authoritative current set (re-read the live config under the lock) rather than a cached snapshot. Ensure a commit that removes a responder is not undone by a subsequent reassert. Coordinate with #2197 (verify this isn't already covered / is the same root cause — dedup if so).

**RED-on-revert:** a commit removes a proxy-ARP responder; a concurrent/subsequent reassert does NOT re-add it (the reassert sees the current set under the lock) (goes RED — reassert re-installs the removed responder from a stale cache — on revert); a reassert with no concurrent commit still refreshes the current responders. Unit-test the commit-remove + reassert race (inject the reassert to fire against a post-removal reconcile, assert the removed responder stays gone).

Provenance: fable-161 F-170, proxy-arp / HA-race module. Adjacent to #2197.

## #4002 — userspace-dp CoS: residual-surplus admission uses a per-worker split of a shared atomic → each of N workers admits the FULL surplus → total admitted is Nworkers× the intended surplus (#2955 over-admission class) (fable-161 F-194) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master + #2955).

**Defect (MEDIUM, Rust dataplane — CoS shaper over-admission):** the CoS scheduler's residual-surplus admission (the leftover bandwidth budget redistributed after each class takes its guaranteed share — grep residual / surplus / admit in userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos) reads/decrements a SHARED surplus atomic in a way that lets EACH of the N worker threads admit the FULL residual surplus independently (a split/per-worker read without a single authoritative CAS-decrement of the shared pool). So instead of the total admitted-from-surplus across all workers summing to the surplus S, each of N workers admits up to S → total ≈ N×S admitted → the CoS classes collectively OVER-ADMIT by ~Nworkers× the intended surplus → shaped classes exceed their configured rate under multi-worker load (the shaping ceiling is breached), defeating the CoS guarantee. This is the #2955 over-admission class (a per-worker split of a pool that should be atomically shared).

**Fix (verify-first):** make the residual-surplus admission draw from the shared pool via a single authoritative atomic CAS-decrement (fetch_sub / compare-exchange loop) so the TOTAL admitted across all workers == S, not N×S. Each worker admits only up to what it atomically claims from the shared surplus; when the pool is exhausted, further admissions are denied. Mirror the #2955 fix pattern (the correct shared-pool CAS). Verify under N-worker concurrency the total surplus-admitted == S (not N×S). Watch for the memory ordering (the CAS needs at least Acquire/Release for the pool visibility).

**RED-on-revert:** a concurrency test with N workers each attempting to admit from a shared surplus S → total admitted == S (goes RED — total == N×S, over-admit — on revert); a single worker admits up to S. Rust test (loom or a deterministic N-thread harness) asserting the shared CAS bounds the total. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-194, rs-dataplane/CoS module. #2955 over-admission class. RUST (cargo).

## #4005 — cli: 'monitor traffic matching "<filter>"' truncates the pcap filter to the FIRST token → a multi-token filter (tcp port 80) captures on just 'tcp' (fable-161 F-022) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verify vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, CLI — wrong packet capture filter):** the `monitor traffic ... matching <filter>` command (the tcpdump/pcap-style live capture — grep monitor traffic / matching / the pcap filter arg in pkg/cli) truncates the `matching` filter expression to its FIRST whitespace-delimited TOKEN. So an operator running `monitor traffic interface geX matching "tcp port 80"` gets a capture filtered on just `tcp` (the `port 80` is dropped) → far more traffic than intended is captured/displayed (or the wrong filter entirely), and a multi-token BPF filter (`host 10.0.0.1 and port 443`, `udp and not port 53`) is silently reduced to its first token. The operator's diagnostic capture is wrong — they see traffic they didn't ask for (or miss the narrowing), making live troubleshooting misleading.

**Fix:** pass the ENTIRE `matching` filter expression (all tokens, the full quoted string) to the pcap/tcpdump filter, not just the first token. The command parser must capture the whole remainder (or the quoted argument) as the filter string. Preserve quoting/spaces. Verify a multi-token filter (`tcp port 80`) is applied verbatim to the capture. Mirror how tcpdump/libpcap takes a full filter expression.

**RED-on-revert:** `monitor traffic ... matching "tcp port 80"` applies the full `tcp port 80` BPF filter (goes RED — truncated to `tcp` — on revert); a single-token filter (`icmp`) unchanged; a filter with `and`/`or`/`not` is preserved. Unit-test the filter-arg parse (assert the full multi-token filter string reaches the pcap/tcpdump invocation).

Provenance: fable-161 F-022, CLI module.

## #4006 — build/test: 'make test' runs only the Go suite, never the Rust userspace-dp cargo suite → a Rust dataplane regression passes 'make test' clean (fable-161 F-091) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verify vs current Makefile).

**Defect (MEDIUM, test-infra gap — Rust regressions invisible to `make test`):** the `make test` target runs `go test ./...` (the Go suite) but does NOT run the Rust `userspace-dp` cargo test suite. Since the Rust AF_XDP userspace dataplane is the ONLY runtime forwarding path (the eBPF path is retired, #1373/#1476), a Rust dataplane regression (a forwarding bug, a CoS/NAT/session correctness break) passes `make test` completely green → a developer running `make test` before a commit/PR gets a false all-clear for the most critical code. The 3000+ cargo tests (the primary correctness gate for forwarding) are only run manually.

**Fix:** add the Rust cargo suite to `make test` (or a `make test-all` that `make test` depends on) — run `cargo test --release` (with the pinned toolchain / the documented `--test-threads=1` to dodge the __skb_wait_for_more_packets socket-test hang) for `userspace-dp` (and the retained shim) as part of the standard test target. Gate it so a Rust test failure fails `make test`. If the full cargo suite is too slow for the default `make test`, at minimum add a `make test-rust` target + wire it into CI / the pre-merge gate + document that `make test` alone is insufficient for dataplane changes. Prefer making `make test` comprehensive (Go + Rust) so the single command is a real gate.

**RED-on-revert:** `make test` runs BOTH the Go suite AND the cargo suite (a deliberately-broken Rust test makes `make test` FAIL) (goes RED — make test passes despite the Rust failure — on revert). Verify by temporarily breaking a Rust test + running `make test` (must fail). This is a Makefile/build change; the "test" is that `make test` exit code reflects a Rust failure.

Provenance: fable-161 F-091, test/build module.

## #4008 — appid: an application/term with an explicit 'protocol 0' (or protocol omitted defaulting to 0) matches BOTH TCP and UDP instead of the intended single protocol → over-broad application match (fable-161 F-164) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master — verify whether the fan-out is in the Go appid compiler or the Rust dataplane match).

**Defect (MEDIUM, appid matching — over-broad protocol match):** the application-identification catalog compile (grep appid / ProtocolNumber / the application/term protocol field in pkg/appid or the compiler) treats an application term whose `protocol` is 0 — either EXPLICITLY `protocol 0` OR OMITTED (defaulting the field to the zero value 0) — as a WILDCARD that fans out to match BOTH TCP (6) AND UDP (17) (or all protocols). But a term with protocol omitted should either be an error / a specific default, and `protocol 0` (HOPOPT) is a specific protocol number, NOT a wildcard. The `(protocol=0, present=true)` case vs `(protocol omitted)` case are conflated. Result: an application term intended to match a single protocol (or a genuinely protocol-0 match) instead matches BOTH TCP and UDP → a policy referencing that application permits/matches more traffic than intended (a TCP-only app-match now also matches the UDP flow on the same port) → an over-permit (security) or an over-broad classification.

**Fix (verify-first — determine if the fan-out is Go-compile or Rust-match):** distinguish `protocol` PRESENT-and-0 from ABSENT. An absent protocol should follow the documented default (match-any only if that's the intended semantics, else require it / inherit from the app); an explicit `protocol 0` should match protocol 0 only. Do NOT fan a 0 into {TCP, UDP}. If the intent is "protocol unspecified = match the app's other terms", encode that explicitly rather than a 0→{TCP,UDP} fan-out. Mirror Junos application semantics (an application term specifies protocol + port; protocol is normally required). Verify a TCP-only term matches only TCP.

**RED-on-revert:** an application term with `protocol tcp` (6) matches only TCP; a term with an omitted/0 protocol does NOT silently match both TCP and UDP (goes RED — 0 fans to TCP+UDP over-match — on revert). Unit-test the appid term compile/match for the protocol-0 / omitted cases (assert no TCP+UDP fan-out). If the fan-out is in the Rust dataplane match (not the Go compile), REPORT that + re-scope to Rust.

Provenance: fable-161 F-164, appid / config-parity module.

## #4009 — test/cluster-deploy: the secondary-node detection grep never matches → cluster-deploy stops the PRIMARY node first ~50% of the time → a spurious failover mid-deploy (masks real failover regressions) (fable-161 F-093) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verify vs current test/incus/cluster-setup.sh).

**Defect (MEDIUM, test-infra — deploy triggers a spurious failover):** the cluster deploy script (`test/incus/cluster-setup.sh` — grep the secondary/primary detection in the deploy target) tries to detect which node is the SECONDARY (so it can deploy/restart the secondary first, keeping the primary serving), but the detection grep NEVER MATCHES (a stale pattern — the `show chassis cluster status` output format changed, or the grep targets the wrong field/case). So the script falls back to a fixed order and stops/restarts the node that happens to be the PRIMARY first ~50% of the time (whenever node0 is primary and the script restarts node0 first) → a spurious FAILOVER happens DURING the deploy (the primary goes down → the secondary takes over) → (a) the deploy churns the cluster state unnecessarily, and (b) it MASKS real failover behavior: a test-failover run right after a deploy-that-already-failed-over starts from an unexpected primary, and the "which node is primary" assumption in downstream smoke (apply-cos-config, test-failover) is wrong ~50% of the time — exactly the flakiness this campaign worked around with the force-node0-primary gate (haval-fable*.sh).

**Fix:** fix the secondary-detection grep to match the CURRENT `show chassis cluster status` output (verify the actual field/format — RG0 primary/secondary per node) so cluster-deploy reliably deploys the SECONDARY first (restart the non-primary node first, then the primary), avoiding a mid-deploy failover. OR make the deploy order deterministic + explicitly re-assert the intended primary after deploy (the force-node0-primary pattern). Verify a deploy does not flip the primary (the same node is primary before + after deploy).

**RED-on-revert:** after a cluster-deploy, the node that was RG0 primary before is still primary after (no spurious failover) (goes RED — deploy stops the primary first → failover → primary flips — on revert / with the broken grep); the secondary is restarted first. Test by asserting the pre/post-deploy primary is stable (or unit-test the detection grep against a captured `show chassis cluster status` sample).

Provenance: fable-161 F-093, test/build module. Root cause of the force-node0-primary workaround in the HA batch-tf scripts.

## #4011 — userspace-dp test: tx_latency_hist_cross_thread_snapshot_skew_within_bound is a load-sensitive cross-thread timing flake → now that 'make test' runs the Rust suite (#4006), it makes the gate itself flaky (fable-161 F-091 residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Surfaced by #4006 (F-091, which wired the Rust cargo suite into `make test`). During the full cargo run under load (4 concurrent qemu VMs + agy), `tx_latency_hist_cross_thread_snapshot_skew_within_bound` FAILED (3463 passed / 1 failed); it passed 3/3 in isolation under lower load. Its own comment warns of scheduler-jitter flakiness.

**Problem:** Now that #4006 makes `make test` run the Rust suite (the intended reliable dataplane gate), this load-sensitive cross-thread timing test will INTERMITTENTLY fail `make test` on a busy dev box / CI — undermining the whole point of F-091 (a trustworthy single-command gate). A flaky gate trains developers to ignore failures.

**Fix (make the test robust or exclude it from the default gate):** options —
1. RELAX the skew bound so scheduler jitter under load doesn't trip it (widen the acceptable cross-thread snapshot skew to a value that holds under realistic contention, keeping it a meaningful assertion — it's checking the histogram snapshot doesn't skew UNBOUNDEDLY, not a tight timing bound).
2. Make it deterministic — remove the wall-clock timing dependency (inject a clock, or assert the invariant structurally rather than via a timing window).
3. If it's genuinely a perf/timing gate that can't be made deterministic, mark it `#[ignore]` by default (run it only in a dedicated perf target, like the criterion benches #4006 excluded) so it doesn't flake the correctness gate.
Prefer (1) or (2) — keep the assertion in `make test` but make it robust. Verify it passes reliably under simulated load (a loop / a stress harness) — not just in isolation.

**RED-on-revert / validation:** the test passes reliably under contention (a repeated-run harness, e.g. 20× under a `stress`-loaded box or a tight loop, all green) — where the current version flakes. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-091 residual (the flake exposed by wiring Rust into make test). RUST (cargo). HIGH-adjacent priority — a flaky make test defeats #4006.

## #4013 — snmp: an ifTable GETBULK walk does a live netlink LinkList (RTM_GETLINK) TWICE per returned varbind → an O(interfaces²) RTM_GETLINK storm on the kernel during an SNMP walk (fable-161 F-180) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verify vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, perf/DoS — netlink storm during SNMP walk):** the SNMP ifTable GETBULK/GETNEXT handler (grep the SNMP ifTable / GETBULK / LinkList in pkg/snmp) issues a LIVE netlink `LinkList` (RTM_GETLINK dump) TWICE for EACH returned varbind (once to resolve the interface for the current OID, once for the next-OID lookup) instead of snapshotting the interface list ONCE per PDU. An SNMP GETBULK walk of the ifTable over N interfaces returns O(N) varbinds, each triggering 2× a full RTM_GETLINK dump → O(N) (or O(N²) with the per-column repetition) full kernel interface dumps per single SNMP walk. On a box with many interfaces (or a monitoring system polling the ifTable frequently), this floods the kernel with RTM_GETLINK requests → high CPU in the netlink path + slow SNMP responses + contention with other netlink users (the interface reconcile, VRRP). A malicious/aggressive SNMP poller can amplify a single GETBULK into a netlink DoS.

**Fix:** snapshot the interface list ONCE at the start of the GETBULK/walk PDU (a single LinkList) and serve all varbinds in that PDU from the cached snapshot — do NOT re-dump per varbind or per next-OID lookup. Cache the LinkList result for the duration of the PDU (or a short TTL). Verify a GETBULK over N interfaces does 1 (or O(1)) LinkList, not O(N)/O(N²). Mirror how other high-frequency callers snapshot (the >1/s control-socket budget discipline in CLAUDE.md is the analogous rule for netlink here).

**RED-on-revert:** a GETBULK walk over N interfaces triggers O(1) LinkList dumps, not O(N) (goes RED — 2N dumps — on revert); the ifTable values are still correct (served from the snapshot). Unit-test by counting the LinkList/netlink invocations per GETBULK PDU (mock/count the netlink seam), asserting it's bounded (1 per PDU, not per varbind).

Provenance: fable-161 F-180, robustness/DoS / snmp module.

## #4015 — df-bit set/clear action is inverted → 'set df-bit clear' clears nothing (sets DF) and 'set df-bit set' sets nothing → wrong Don't-Fragment marking on tunneled/forwarded packets (fable-161 F-066) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST + determine Go-compile vs Rust-apply).

**Defect (MEDIUM, forwarding correctness — inverted DF marking):** the `df-bit set` / `df-bit clear` action (the Don't-Fragment bit control on a tunnel / firewall-filter / forwarding action — grep df-bit / DfBit / DontFragment in the compiler + dataplane) is INVERTED — a config that says `df-bit clear` (clear the DF bit, ALLOW fragmentation) actually SETS the DF bit (or vice versa). So the DF bit on the affected tunneled/forwarded packets is the OPPOSITE of what the operator configured. Impact: `df-bit clear` (intended to allow fragmentation of oversized packets, e.g. into a tunnel) instead sets DF → oversized packets are DROPPED with a PMTUD "fragmentation needed" instead of being fragmented → a blackhole for large packets over the tunnel; conversely `df-bit set` (intended to force DF for PMTUD) instead clears it → packets that should trigger PMTUD get silently fragmented. Either way the operator's DF policy is reversed → PMTUD/fragmentation misbehavior.

**Fix (verify-first — is the inversion in the Go compiler mapping or the Rust dataplane application?):** trace the df-bit action from config → compiled value → dataplane application. Find where set↔clear is mapped to the actual DF-bit write (set DF = write the IP DF flag = 1; clear DF = write 0). Correct the inversion at the single point where it's flipped. Do NOT double-invert (fix it in ONE place). If the inversion is in the Go compiler → Go fix; if in the Rust dataplane DF-write → REPORT "genuine but Rust-scoped: <file:line>" + STOP (no Go PR; re-dispatch as Rust). Verify `df-bit set` results in DF=1 on the wire and `df-bit clear` in DF=0.

**RED-on-revert:** `df-bit set` → the forwarded/tunneled packet has IP DF=1; `df-bit clear` → DF=0 (goes RED — inverted, set→0 / clear→1 — on revert). Unit-test the df-bit action → the actual DF bit written (Go: the compiled DF value; Rust: the IP header DF flag on the emitted frame). If Rust-scoped, report it.

Provenance: fable-161 F-066, config-parity / forwarding module. Verify Go-vs-Rust.

## #4017 — image bake: bake.py signs the appliance image BEFORE the validation gate → a FAILED/invalid image is signed and publishable (fable-161 F-092) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, re-verify vs current scripts/image/bake.py).

**Defect (MEDIUM, build/supply-chain — a failed image gets signed):** the appliance image bake (`scripts/image/bake.py` — grep the sign step + the validation/verify gate) performs the image SIGNING step BEFORE (or independently of) the VALIDATION gate that checks the image is well-formed / boots / passes its checks. So if the validation FAILS, the image has already been SIGNED — a signed-but-invalid image exists and is publishable (a downstream publish/upload step, or an operator, may ship the signed artifact assuming the signature implies validity). A signature on a broken image is worse than no signature: it conveys false trust (the #1864 verify-dataplane / secure-boot chain assumes a signed image is a validated one). A bake that fails validation must NOT leave a signed artifact.

**Fix:** reorder the bake so VALIDATION runs BEFORE signing — sign the image ONLY after all validation gates pass. If validation fails, abort the bake WITHOUT signing (and clean up / do not leave a signed partial artifact). Alternatively, gate the publish step on both signed AND validated. Ensure the exit code / artifact state reflects a failed validation (no signed output). Verify: a bake whose validation fails produces NO signed image (and exits non-zero); a passing bake signs after validation.

**RED-on-revert:** a bake with an injected validation failure produces NO signed artifact + exits non-zero (goes RED — a signed image exists despite the validation failure — on revert); a passing bake signs after validation. Test by injecting a validation failure into the bake flow (mock the validate step to fail) + asserting no sign step ran / no signed output. This is a scripts/image/bake.py ordering fix; the test can be a Python unit test of the bake step ordering (assert sign is called only after validate succeeds).

Provenance: fable-161 F-092, test/build / supply-chain module. Adjacent to the #1864/#1930 secure-boot + verify-dataplane chain.

## #4020 — test: destructive HA smoke targets (test-failover / test-ha-crash reboot the SHARED loss cluster) do NOT take the #1875 cluster lock → can collide with a concurrent agent's deploy/smoke (fable-161 F-090) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current Makefile + test/incus).

**Defect (MEDIUM, test-safety — destructive smoke races the shared cluster):** the DESTRUCTIVE HA smoke targets (`make test-failover`, `make test-ha-crash`, `test-double-failover`, `test-stress-failover` — the ones that REBOOT / force-stop a node on the SHARED loss cluster `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1`) do NOT take the #1875 cluster lock (`/tmp/xpf-cluster.lock`) that deploys + `apply-cos-config.sh` self-lock. Per CLAUDE.md #1875: the loss cluster is SHARED between agents; deploys self-lock so they queue rather than collide. But a `test-failover` that REBOOTS fw0 mid-iperf is FAR more destructive than a deploy, and it takes NO lock → if another agent is mid-deploy (or mid-smoke) on the cluster, the reboot collides → both operations corrupt each other's cluster state (a deploy pushing binaries while a node reboots → half-deployed node; a concurrent test-failover measuring loss while another reboots → garbage results). This campaign's batch-tf scripts (haval-fable*.sh) run test-failover on the shared cluster and would collide with another agent's deploy.

**Fix (verify-first):** wrap the destructive smoke targets in the #1875 lock — the same self-lock / `with-cluster.sh` mechanism deploys use, so a test-failover QUEUES behind (or blocks) a concurrent deploy/smoke instead of colliding. Confirm the current lock mechanism (test/incus/with-cluster.sh + the lock file /tmp/xpf-cluster.lock) and route the destructive Makefile targets through it (or document that callers MUST wrap them in `with-cluster.sh`). Do NOT weaken the existing deploy/apply-cos lock. Verify a test-failover acquires the lock (queues behind a held lock, doesn't collide). If the destructive targets ALREADY take the lock → report already-correct.

**RED-on-revert:** a `make test-failover` invocation acquires the #1875 cluster lock before rebooting (blocks/queues if held) (goes RED — reboots without the lock, collides with a concurrent deploy — on revert). Test by asserting the target's recipe routes through with-cluster.sh / takes the lock (a Makefile/script inspection test, since a live run needs the cluster).

Provenance: fable-161 F-090, test/build module. CLAUDE.md #1875 shared-cluster-lock discipline.

## #4021 — config CoS: interface-level class-of-service (applied at the physical interface, no unit) is dropped → only per-unit CoS is compiled (fable-161 F-028) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master — CoS-parity findings have a mixed track record; F-027 was already-correct).

**Defect (MEDIUM, CoS config-parity — interface-level CoS lost):** the class-of-service interface binding compilation (grep the CoS interface / scheduler-map / rewrite-rule / classifier binding in the CoS compiler) reads the CoS config only from the per-UNIT level (`interfaces geX unit N class-of-service ...` / `... unit N scheduler-map`) and DROPS a CoS binding applied at the physical INTERFACE level (`interfaces geX class-of-service ...` / `class-of-service interfaces geX { scheduler-map M }` with no unit). In Junos, CoS can be bound at the interface level (applies to the whole port) OR per-unit. If the compiler only reads the unit level, an operator who applies a scheduler-map / classifier / rewrite-rule at the interface level (a common config for a single-unit port) gets NO CoS on that interface → the shaping/classification/marking silently doesn't apply.

**Fix (verify-first — confirm the interface-level binding is actually dropped):** the CoS binding compiler must read BOTH the interface-level AND the per-unit CoS bindings, applying the interface-level binding to the port (or to unit 0 / all units per Junos inheritance semantics) when present. Determine the correct Junos precedence (unit-level overrides interface-level, or interface-level applies to all units). If interface-level CoS is ALREADY compiled → report already-correct with file:line. Verify an interface-level scheduler-map produces a live CoS binding.

## #4024 — userspace-dp: a flowless (session-less) non-first-fragment with a MissingNeighbor result is FIB-reinjected as transit, BYPASSING the zone security policy → deny-all is bypassed for flowless-frag transit (fable-161 F-259) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST — security fail-open, verify the exact path).

**Defect (MEDIUM, security fail-open — deny-all bypassed):** on the flowless (session-less) forwarding path in userspace-dp, a packet that (a) has no established session (flowless — e.g. a non-first fragment that can't be classified to a flow, or a first-packet before session install) AND (b) resolves to a `MissingNeighbor` forwarding result, is FIB-REINJECTED (handed back to the kernel for transit forwarding) WITHOUT first passing the ZONE SECURITY POLICY check. So under a deny-all (or a restrictive) zone policy, this flowless-fragment transit traffic is FORWARDED by the kernel reinject path even though the policy would DENY it → a policy bypass. An attacker sending non-first fragments (or exploiting the missing-neighbor window) to a destination the firewall should DENY can get the traffic transited via the FIB reinject → the deny-all is not enforced for this class. grep the flowless / MissingNeighbor / FIB-reinject / XDP_PASS path in userspace-dp/src/afxdp (the forwarding decision for a session-less packet with an unresolved neighbor).

**Fix (verify-first):** a flowless packet must pass the zone security policy BEFORE being FIB-reinjected — evaluate the zone policy (or at minimum the deny/permit decision for the src/dst zones) on the flowless path, and only reinject/transit if PERMITTED. A MissingNeighbor result should NOT be a policy-bypass escape hatch (missing neighbor = the next-hop MAC isn't resolved yet, which is orthogonal to whether the policy permits the flow). If the packet is denied by policy, DROP it (don't reinject). Handle the non-first-fragment case (a non-first frag that can't be classified should be handled per the fragment-handling policy, not blindly reinjected). Mirror how the normal (session) path enforces the zone policy before forwarding. Fail-CLOSED: if the flowless packet can't be policy-evaluated, DROP (don't reinject).

**RED-on-revert:** under a deny-all policy, a flowless packet (non-first frag / pre-session) with a MissingNeighbor result is DROPPED (not FIB-reinjected/transited) (goes RED — reinjected, deny-all bypassed — on revert); under a permit policy it's forwarded normally; a normal session packet unaffected. Rust unit test constructing a flowless + MissingNeighbor + deny-all scenario, asserting DROP not reinject. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-259, security fail-open / rs-dataplane module. RUST (cargo). Adjacent to the flowless-frag session-gate class.

## #4027 — config: an 'interfaces interface-range' definition creates a phantom interface entry that is brought admin-down (the range name itself is treated as an interface) → member interfaces mis-managed (fable-161 F-029) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master — config-parity findings mixed track record).

**Defect (MEDIUM, config-parity — interface-range mishandled):** an `interfaces interface-range <name> { member <if>; ... }` definition (a Junos construct that applies a common config to a SET of member interfaces) is mis-compiled — the RANGE NAME itself (`<name>`, e.g. `range-uplinks`) is treated as a real interface, producing a PHANTOM interface entry that is then brought ADMIN-DOWN (marked ActivationPolicy=always-down / down) by the unmanaged-interface reconcile, because no kernel NIC matches the range name. Meanwhile the range's config may not be correctly applied to the actual MEMBER interfaces. So `interface-range` either (a) creates a bogus admin-down phantom (harmless-looking but wrong config state + a confusing `show interfaces`), or (b) fails to apply the range's config to its members (the members don't get the shared config). grep interface-range / interfaceRange in the compiler + the networkd/reconcile.

**Fix (verify-first — confirm the phantom + the member-application behavior):** the compiler must EXPAND an interface-range into its MEMBER interfaces (apply the range's config to each member), and must NOT treat the range name as a physical interface (no phantom entry, no admin-down of the range name). Members get the range's shared config (merged with their own per-interface config). Verify: `interface-range R { member geX; member geY; <shared cfg> }` applies <shared cfg> to geX + geY, and R itself is not a managed/admin-down interface. If interface-range is ALREADY expanded correctly (no phantom) → report already-correct with file:line.

**RED-on-revert:** an interface-range with 2 members applies its shared config to both members + creates NO phantom admin-down interface for the range name (goes RED — phantom range-name interface / members not configured — on revert); a normal interface unchanged. Unit-test the interface-range compile (ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath) asserting member expansion + no phantom.

Provenance: fable-161 F-029, config-parity module. VERIFY-FIRST.

## #4028 — cluster: handleEventStreamFullResync hardcodes RG 0..15 → a cluster with redundancy-group >= 16 never re-exports those RGs' sessions on a full resync (session-sync gap) (fable-161 F-166) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA session-sync — high RG numbers never resync):** `handleEventStreamFullResync` (the full session-resync handler on the HA event-stream path — grep handleEventStreamFullResync / the RG iteration in pkg/cluster or pkg/daemon) iterates redundancy groups with a HARDCODED range `0..15` (or a fixed 16-element loop). If the cluster config defines a redundancy-group with an id >= 16, that RG's owned sessions are NEVER re-exported during a full resync (the resync loop skips it) → on a reconnect / full-resync event, the standby never receives the sessions for RG>=16 → those sessions are missing on the standby → on a failover of RG>=16, the connections are dropped (no synced session state). Junos redundancy-group ids can exceed 16 (up to ~255 / the configured max), so a cluster with high RG ids has a silent session-sync hole.

**Fix (verify-first):** iterate the ACTUAL configured redundancy groups (the RG ids from the live cluster config) in handleEventStreamFullResync, not a hardcoded 0..15 range. Derive the RG set from the config (the same source the rest of the cluster code uses for RG enumeration — e.g. currentRedundancyGroups() / the config's cluster.redundancy-groups). So every configured RG is re-exported on a full resync regardless of its id. Mirror how the incremental sync / the RG-ownership code enumerates RGs. Verify a cluster with an RG id >= 16 re-exports that RG's sessions on a full resync.

**RED-on-revert:** a full resync with a configured RG id=20 (or >15) re-exports that RG's sessions (goes RED — RG 20 skipped, sessions not resynced — on revert); RGs 0..15 still resync; the RG set follows the config. Unit-test the full-resync RG enumeration with a high-id RG (assert it's included). test-failover WARRANTED (HA session-sync) — batch-validate.

Provenance: fable-161 F-166, HA session-sync module.

## #4031 — cluster: monitorFabricState exits + leaks a sibling netlink socket when its subscription channel closes (no resubscribe) → fabric link-state monitoring dies permanently (fable-161 F-167) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA robustness — fabric monitoring dies + fd leak):** `monitorFabricState` (the fabric-link-state monitor goroutine — grep monitorFabricState in pkg/cluster or pkg/daemon) EXITS PERMANENTLY when its netlink subscription channel CLOSES (an ENOBUFS overflow / a transient netlink error closes the update channel, like the #3950 monitorLinkState / neighbor-listener class), and it LEAKS a sibling netlink socket (a second subscription / a fd opened alongside that isn't closed on the exit path). After that, fabric link-state changes are no longer detected → the fabric-up/down transitions that drive HA fabric forwarding + failover decisions stop being observed → a fabric link event (a fabric-down that should trigger a failover / a fabric-up that should resume cross-chassis forwarding) is missed → HA mis-behaves (a stale fabric-up assumption → blackhole, or a missed fabric-down → no failover). Plus the leaked netlink fd accumulates.

**Fix (verify-first — mirror the #3950 monitorLinkState resilient-resubscribe fix):** on the subscription channel close (ENOBUFS / recoverable error), do NOT exit + do NOT leak — CLOSE the current subscription cleanly (release the netlink socket/fd), LOG a warning, RE-SYNC the current fabric state (a full read to catch up on missed transitions), and RE-SUBSCRIBE (continue the loop). Only exit on context-cancel. Ensure the sibling netlink socket is closed on every exit/resubscribe path (no fd leak) — use defer / a cleanup. Mirror the #3950 runLinkStateSubscription pattern (resubscribe + catch-up) exactly. Verify a transient channel close keeps the fabric monitor alive + no fd leak.

**RED-on-revert:** inject a subscription channel close → the fabric monitor re-subscribes + continues (delivers a subsequent fabric event) + the sibling netlink socket is closed (no leak) (goes RED — exits permanently + leaks the fd — on revert); context-cancel exits cleanly (closing the socket). Unit-test the resubscribe + fd-cleanup (inject the subscription seam; assert the goroutine survives + the socket count returns to baseline). test-failover WARRANTED (HA fabric) — batch-validate.

Provenance: fable-161 F-167, HA-fabric robustness module. Sibling of #3950 (monitorLinkState ENOBUFS).
