## #4033 — cluster: heartbeat retry loop ignores commsCtx (doesn't stop on cancel) + StartHeartbeat overwrites a running heartbeat without stopping the old one → goroutine leak + duplicate heartbeats (fable-161 F-168) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA robustness — heartbeat goroutine leak + double-fire):** two coupled issues in the cluster heartbeat (grep StartHeartbeat / the heartbeat retry loop / commsCtx in pkg/cluster):
1. The heartbeat SEND/retry loop ignores `commsCtx` (the cluster-comms context) — on a comms restart / context cancel it does NOT stop; the loop keeps running (a bind-retry / send loop that only checks its own timer, not `<-commsCtx.Done()`) → a stale heartbeat goroutine survives past the comms teardown.
2. `StartHeartbeat` OVERWRITES the running heartbeat (reassigns the heartbeat goroutine / channel) WITHOUT first STOPPING the previous one → on a reconnect / comms restart, a NEW heartbeat goroutine is started while the OLD one is still running → TWO heartbeat goroutines fire concurrently (goroutine leak + duplicate heartbeats → the peer sees double the heartbeat rate, and the leaked goroutine may send stale state / hold a socket).
Result: repeated comms restarts (a flapping fabric / repeated reconnects) LEAK heartbeat goroutines (one per restart) + send duplicate/stale heartbeats → resource growth + confusing peer-side heartbeat accounting (the 200ms/threshold-5 detection could mis-fire).

**Fix (verify-first):** (1) the heartbeat loop must select on `commsCtx.Done()` (or the appropriate cancel) and EXIT when the comms context is cancelled — every retry/bind/send iteration checks the ctx. (2) `StartHeartbeat` must STOP the previous heartbeat (cancel its ctx + join/wait) BEFORE starting a new one — idempotent start (a running heartbeat is torn down first). Ensure exactly ONE heartbeat goroutine at a time. Mirror the StartHeartbeat/stop discipline (a stored cancel func + wait). Verify: a comms restart stops the old heartbeat + starts one new (not two); a ctx cancel stops the loop.

**RED-on-revert:** N sequential StartHeartbeat calls (simulating N comms restarts) leave exactly 1 heartbeat goroutine running (goes RED — N goroutines leaked / the loop ignores ctx-cancel — on revert); a ctx cancel stops the heartbeat. Unit-test the StartHeartbeat-stops-previous + the ctx-cancel-exits (goroutine-count / a done-signal seam). test-failover WARRANTED (HA heartbeat) — batch-validate.

Provenance: fable-161 F-168, HA robustness module.

## #4034 — cluster: a non-fatal error in the tail of the config apply path skips syncConfigToPeer → the standby never receives the config (stays stale) after a partially-successful commit (fable-161 F-169) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA config divergence):** in the config apply path on the primary, `syncConfigToPeer` (the push of the committed config to the standby) is called at the TAIL of the apply, AFTER a series of subsystem applies (grep the apply path — daemon_apply.go / commitAndApply → the ordered subsystem applies → syncConfigToPeer). If one of the tail subsystem applies returns a NON-FATAL error (a subsystem that logs+continues, e.g. a best-effort apply that fails but doesn't abort the commit — the config is committed + active locally), the error handling RETURNS/short-circuits BEFORE reaching `syncConfigToPeer` → the standby is NEVER sent the new config → the standby stays on the OLD config → the two nodes DIVERGE. So a commit that succeeds locally (with a non-fatal subsystem hiccup) does NOT propagate to the standby → on failover, the standby serves the stale config. The config-sync is skipped precisely when the local apply had a (recoverable) problem — the worst time to skip sync.

**Fix (verify-first):** ensure `syncConfigToPeer` runs even when a tail subsystem apply returns a non-fatal error — the config IS committed + active locally, so the standby MUST get it regardless of a best-effort subsystem hiccup. Move `syncConfigToPeer` so it runs unconditionally after the config is committed (a `defer` or a guaranteed call), OR don't let a non-fatal subsystem error short-circuit before the sync. Distinguish a FATAL apply error (the commit should roll back → no sync) from a NON-FATAL one (commit succeeds → MUST sync). If the commit succeeded locally, the standby gets the config. Verify a commit with a non-fatal tail-subsystem error still syncs to the peer.

**RED-on-revert:** a commit where a tail subsystem apply returns a non-fatal error still calls syncConfigToPeer (the standby receives the new config) (goes RED — sync skipped, standby stale — on revert); a clean commit syncs; a fatal error rolls back (no sync). Unit-test the apply path with an injected non-fatal tail error, asserting syncConfigToPeer is still called. test-failover WARRANTED (HA config-sync) — batch-validate.

Provenance: fable-161 F-169, HA config-sync module.

## #4036 — control-socket: a fixed 3s read deadline is too short for a large (up to 64MB) apply_snapshot → a big dynamic-feed / large-config apply times out + reports FAILED while the dataplane actually applied it live (fable-161 F-182) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, robustness — false apply-failure on large payloads):** the userspace-dp control socket uses a FIXED ~3s read/response deadline (grep the control-socket deadline / SetDeadline / timeout in pkg/dataplane/userspace), but an `apply_snapshot` request can be up to the MaxControlRequestBytes cap (~64MB, #2744) — a large dynamic-address feed, a big policy/NAT config, or a full session snapshot. Transferring + applying 64MB over the control socket can take LONGER than the fixed 3s deadline → the Go side times out on the read and REPORTS the apply as FAILED, even though the Rust helper actually RECEIVED + APPLIED the snapshot successfully (the dataplane IS live with the new config). So a large-config commit reports a spurious failure (the operator sees "dataplane apply failed" / the commit errors) while the dataplane is correctly forwarding with the new config → confusing + can trigger a needless rollback / retry / a false HA dp-failure.

**Fix (verify-first):** the control-socket deadline for a large payload must SCALE with the payload size (or the apply type) — a fixed 3s is wrong for a 64MB apply. Options: (a) size the deadline to the payload (a base timeout + a per-MB allowance, up to a sane max); (b) for the large apply_snapshot request specifically, use a longer deadline than the 1/s status poll. Ensure the deadline is generous enough that a legitimate 64MB apply completes without a false timeout, while a genuinely-hung helper still eventually times out. Verify a large apply_snapshot (near the 64MB cap) does NOT report a false failure. Coordinate with the #182 control-socket-contention discipline (don't hold the socket forever).

**RED-on-revert:** a large apply_snapshot (a payload that takes > 3s) completes + reports SUCCESS (goes RED — times out at 3s, reports FAILED while the dp applied it — on revert); a normal small apply is unchanged; a genuinely-hung helper still times out (at the larger deadline). Unit-test the deadline sizing (a mock control socket with a slow-but-successful large apply asserting no false timeout).

Provenance: fable-161 F-182, robustness / control-socket module. #2744 (64MB cap) + #182 (control-socket contention).

## #4038 — cluster: a single fabricRefreshCh is consumed by ONE fabric goroutine → in a dual-fabric (fab0+fab1) cluster the second fabric's refresh events are lost (fable-161 F-053) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA dual-fabric — second fabric's events lost):** the fabric refresh mechanism uses a SINGLE shared `fabricRefreshCh` channel that is consumed by ONE fabric goroutine/consumer (grep fabricRefreshCh / the fabric refresh consumer in pkg/cluster or pkg/daemon). In a DUAL-FABRIC cluster (fab0 + fab1 — two fabric links for redundancy), both fabrics feed refresh events into the single channel but only ONE consumer reads it (or one fabric's producer wins the channel) → the SECOND fabric's refresh events are LOST / not acted on → fab1's state transitions (a fab1 up/down, a fab1-triggered forwarding refresh) are missed → the dual-fabric redundancy is degraded (a fab1 event that should drive a forwarding-table refresh / a failover decision is dropped). So a cluster configured with two fabric links doesn't correctly handle the second fabric.

**Fix (verify-first — confirm dual-fabric is supported + the channel is genuinely shared/single-consumer):** give each fabric its own refresh channel/consumer, OR fan-out the single channel to all fabric consumers (so both fab0 + fab1 events are processed), OR make the single consumer fabric-aware (process events tagged per-fabric). Ensure every configured fabric's refresh events are acted on. If dual-fabric isn't supported (single-fabric only by design) → report that (lower severity / deliberate). Verify a fab1 refresh event drives its refresh in a dual-fabric config.

**RED-on-revert:** in a dual-fabric config, a fab1 refresh event is processed (drives the fab1 forwarding refresh) (goes RED — fab1 events dropped, only fab0 processed — on revert); single-fabric unchanged. Unit-test the dual-fabric refresh routing (inject a fab1 event, assert it's consumed). test-failover WARRANTED if dual-fabric is testable — else note lab-deferred. 

Provenance: fable-161 F-053, HA-fabric module.

## #4041 — userspace-dp: the debug-log direct-TX path double-pushes tx_offset on a tuple-mismatch → duplicate free-list entry aliases an in-flight TX frame (on-wire corruption / double-free, debug-log build) (fable-161 F-079) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master — this is the debug-log-gated build; verify the path).

**Defect (MEDIUM, Rust dataplane — TX frame aliasing on the debug-log path):** on the DEBUG-LOG direct-TX path (the build with debug-log TX tracing enabled — grep the debug-log direct-TX / tx_offset push / the tuple-mismatch branch in userspace-dp/src/afxdp), when a TX descriptor's tuple does NOT match the expected (a tuple-mismatch diagnostic branch), the code pushes the `tx_offset` (the UMEM frame offset) onto the free-list / recycle stack TWICE (a double-push — once on the mismatch branch, once on the normal completion) → the SAME UMEM frame offset appears twice in the free list → it's handed out twice for a future TX → two TX descriptors point at the SAME frame → the frame is aliased while still in-flight on the wire → on-wire corruption (the second writer overwrites the first frame's bytes before it's transmitted) OR a double-free (the frame is recycled twice). This is on the DEBUG-LOG build (the debug-log-direct-TX feature), so it doesn't affect the release build — but a debug-log deployment (used for diagnostics) corrupts TX / crashes.

**Fix (verify-first):** the tuple-mismatch diagnostic branch must NOT push the tx_offset a second time — the frame is recycled exactly ONCE (either on the mismatch branch OR the normal path, not both). Restructure so the recycle/free-list push happens exactly once per frame regardless of the tuple-match diagnostic. Verify (via a debug-log-build test) that a tuple-mismatch frame is pushed to the free-list exactly once (no duplicate offset). If the double-push is already guarded / not reachable → report already-correct.

**RED-on-revert:** on the debug-log path, a tuple-mismatch TX frame's offset appears in the free-list/recycle exactly ONCE (goes RED — pushed twice, duplicate offset — on revert); a matching tuple is unchanged. Rust unit test (under the debug-log cfg) asserting the recycle-count == 1 per frame / no duplicate offset. FULL cargo test --release (+ the debug-log build if separately gated).

Provenance: fable-161 F-079, rs-dataplane debug-log TX module. RUST (cargo).

## #4043 — lldp: received LLDP TLV strings (system-name / port-description / system-description) are logged + displayed without sanitizing control chars → ANSI-escape / log injection via a crafted LLDP frame (fable-161 F-178) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master — NOTE there may be uncommitted lldp.go WIP in the maintainer's checkout; the worktree bases off clean origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, security — log/terminal injection via LLDP):** LLDP neighbor TLV strings received from the wire — system-name, port-description, system-description, port-id (grep the LLDP TLV parse / neighbor-table store / the show-lldp-neighbors display in pkg/lldp) — are stored + LOGGED + DISPLAYED (in `show lldp neighbors` + any syslog/event log) WITHOUT sanitizing control characters. LLDP is an L2 protocol; ANY device on the local L2 segment (or an attacker with L2 access) can send an LLDP frame with a crafted TLV containing ANSI escape sequences, newlines, carriage returns, or other control chars. When the firewall LOGS or DISPLAYS the neighbor's name/description: (a) ANSI escapes injected into an operator's terminal (`show lldp neighbors`) can move the cursor / clear the screen / spoof output / (in some terminals) trigger actions; (b) newlines/CR injected into a syslog line forge log entries (log injection — a fake log line, or splitting one entry into two). This is the same control-char-sanitization class as the #1798 annotation-text + #3905 defense. A neighbor is untrusted input.

**Fix:** sanitize LLDP-received TLV strings before storing/logging/displaying — strip or escape control characters (C0/C1, ANSI ESC sequences, CR/LF, other non-printable) from system-name/port-desc/system-desc/port-id (and any other operator-visible received string). Mirror the #1798/#3905 SanitizeControlChars / the annotation-text sanitizer. Keep the display readable (replace control chars with a safe placeholder or strip). Verify a crafted LLDP TLV with ANSI/CRLF is neutralized in both the log line and the show output.

**RED-on-revert:** an LLDP neighbor with a system-name containing ESC/CRLF/control chars is sanitized (no raw ESC/CR/LF reaches the log or the show output) (goes RED — raw control chars pass through to the terminal/log — on revert); a normal ASCII name is unchanged. Unit-test the TLV-string sanitization (feed a crafted TLV, assert the stored/displayed string is control-char-free).

Provenance: fable-161 F-178, security / lldp module. #1798/#3905 control-char-sanitization class.

## #4044 — lldp: the received-neighbor table is unbounded → an LLDP frame flood (many spoofed chassis/port ids) grows it without limit → memory exhaustion / OOM (L2 DoS) (fable-161 F-177) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master — NOTE possible uncommitted lldp.go WIP in the maintainer's checkout; worktree bases off clean origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, DoS — unbounded LLDP neighbor table):** the LLDP received-neighbor table (grep the neighbor store / map keyed by chassis-id+port-id in pkg/lldp) has NO SIZE CAP and NO per-port limit. LLDP is an L2 protocol; any device on the local segment can send LLDP frames with arbitrary (spoofed) chassis-id / port-id values. An attacker (or a misbehaving/looped switch) flooding LLDP frames with many DISTINCT chassis/port ids causes the neighbor table to GROW WITHOUT BOUND (one entry per distinct id) → memory exhaustion → OOM → the daemon is killed (an L2-local DoS: whoever can put frames on the segment can OOM the firewall). Even without malice, an L2 loop can multiply neighbor entries.

**Fix:** bound the LLDP neighbor table — (a) a per-interface (and/or global) MAX neighbor count (a sane limit — a real switch port sees 1, maybe a handful, of LLDP neighbors; cap at e.g. 16-64 per port); when the cap is hit, either drop new neighbors (with a rate-limited warn) or evict the oldest/least-recently-seen (LRU); (b) ensure aged-out neighbors (past their TTL) are reaped so stale entries don't accumulate. Prefer a per-port cap + TTL reaping. Verify a flood of distinct-id LLDP frames does NOT grow the table past the cap. Mirror any existing bounded-table pattern (the conntrack/session table has GC; LLDP should too).

**RED-on-revert:** feeding N > cap distinct-id LLDP frames on one port leaves the neighbor table bounded at the cap (goes RED — grows unbounded to N — on revert); normal (few-neighbor) operation unchanged; aged neighbors are reaped. Unit-test the cap + reaping (feed > cap neighbors, assert bounded; advance time past TTL, assert reaped).

Provenance: fable-161 F-177, robustness/DoS / lldp module.

## #4047 — web-management: the REST/config API binds to a non-loopback address without requiring api-auth → unauthenticated mutating REST + /metrics from the network (fable-161 F-155) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-06)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM/HIGH-adjacent, security — unauthenticated network REST):** when `system services web-management` (or the config/REST API) is configured to bind to a NON-LOOPBACK address (a management interface / 0.0.0.0), the HTTP REST server (`pkg/api` — grep the bind address + the auth middleware) does NOT require api-auth (an API key / credential) for the MUTATING endpoints (config set/commit/rollback) or /metrics → ANY host that can reach the management address can issue mutating config changes + read /metrics WITHOUT authentication. The REST API on 127.0.0.1:8080 is loopback-safe by default, but a non-loopback bind exposes the same unauthenticated endpoints to the network. So an operator who binds web-management to a mgmt interface (a normal deployment) unknowingly exposes an unauthenticated config-mutation surface → a network attacker can reconfigure the firewall / read metrics.

**Design question (route via /research — the correct auth posture is a design decision):** the fix needs a design decision on the auth model:
- (a) REQUIRE api-auth (an API key / token, or client-cert) for ANY non-loopback bind — reject the config at commit if web-management binds non-loopback without an auth method configured (fail-closed: no auth → loopback only);
- (b) enforce auth in the REST middleware for all mutating endpoints when the bind is non-loopback (401 without a valid credential);
- (c) restrict /metrics + mutating endpoints separately (metrics may be intentionally network-exposed for Prometheus, but MUTATING must always require auth on non-loopback).
Converge a PLAN: which endpoints require auth, what auth mechanism (API key / cert / the existing user model), and whether a non-loopback-without-auth config is a hard commit-reject vs a runtime 401. Coordinate with any existing api-auth / RBAC in pkg/api + the #3199 system-services posture.

**Verify-first:** confirm the current behavior — does a non-loopback web-management bind ALREADY require auth (middleware / config gate)? If auth is already enforced → report already-correct. If unauth → this is genuine; converge the design plan.

**RED-on-revert / validation (once the plan converges):** an unauthenticated mutating REST request to a non-loopback bind is REJECTED (401 / the config is commit-rejected); a loopback request or an authenticated request succeeds. ## #4049 — lldp: LLDP fails to start on Junos slash-named interfaces (ge-0/0/0) — net.InterfaceByName is called with the Junos name instead of the Linux kernel name (ge-0-0-0) → no socket, no LLDP on renamed ports (fable-161 F-068) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master, which includes #4045/#4046 lldp.go changes).

**Defect (MEDIUM, LLDP broken on renamed interfaces):** the LLDP manager opens its AF_PACKET socket / resolves the interface via `net.InterfaceByName(<name>)` (grep InterfaceByName / the socket-open path in pkg/lldp) using the JUNOS-style slash name (`ge-0/0/0`, `reth0.50`) rather than the LINUX KERNEL name (`ge-0-0-0` — xpf renames kernel interfaces to dash-form vSRX names via .link files, and the Junos display name uses slashes). `net.InterfaceByName("ge-0/0/0")` FAILS (no kernel interface has a slash in its name — the kernel name is `ge-0-0-0`) → the LLDP socket is never opened on that interface → LLDP does NOT run on any renamed (dash-named) port → no LLDP TX/RX on the actual data interfaces. So LLDP silently doesn't work on exactly the interfaces an operator cares about (the renamed ge-*/reth* ports), only (maybe) on non-renamed ones.

**Fix (verify-first):** convert the Junos slash name to the Linux kernel name (the dash form / the actual kernel ifname) before `net.InterfaceByName` — use the project's existing name-conversion helper (grep LinuxIfName / the slash→dash conversion used elsewhere, e.g. the CoS/firewall-filter LinuxIfName the #3972/#4009 work referenced). Resolve the kernel name from the Junos name (via the interface config / the networkd rename map) so the LLDP socket opens on the correct kernel interface. Verify LLDP starts on a `ge-0/0/0`-configured (kernel `ge-0-0-0`) interface. If LLDP ALREADY converts the name → report already-correct with file:line.

**RED-on-revert:** LLDP opens its socket on the kernel interface for a Junos-slash-named config interface (goes RED — InterfaceByName fails on the slash name, no socket — on revert); a non-renamed interface unchanged. Unit-test the name resolution (assert the slash name maps to the kernel dash name before InterfaceByName; mock the interface-lookup seam).

Provenance: fable-161 F-068, LLDP module. LinuxIfName conversion class.

## #4051 — config API: raw-AST render paths (REST show/export/search/rollback + gRPC ShowConfig) emit cleartext PSK / auth-key / SNMP community — #2053 only redacted the typed-struct path (fable-161 F-020) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM/HIGH-adjacent, security — secret exposure in config output):** the RAW-AST config render paths — the REST `show config` / `export` / `search` / `rollback` endpoints + the gRPC `ShowConfig` (grep the AST-format / FormatSet / the config-render used by these endpoints in pkg/api + pkg/grpcapi) — emit the config by walking the AST and printing leaf values VERBATIM, including SECRET leaves: IKE/IPsec pre-shared-keys, WireGuard/auth keys, SNMP community strings, BGP/OSPF auth-keys, RADIUS/TACACS secrets. #2053 added redaction ONLY on the TYPED-STRUCT render path (the compiled-config display), NOT on the raw-AST paths. So a REST `GET /config` (or export/search/rollback-diff) or a gRPC ShowConfig returns the secrets IN CLEARTEXT to whoever can call the API → secret leakage (esp. combined with F-155's unauthenticated non-loopback REST — an attacker reads all PSKs/keys). Junos redacts secrets in `show configuration` (SECRET-DATA / ##SECRET-DATA##) — xpf's raw-AST paths do not.

**Fix:** apply secret redaction on the RAW-AST render paths too — identify the SECRET leaves (the schema knows which leaves are secret-typed — grep the schema secret/encrypted-password markers, the config.Secret type the #2053 work used) and redact/mask them (replace with `##SECRET-DATA##` / a placeholder, or the encrypted form) in the AST render used by REST show/export/search/rollback + gRPC ShowConfig. Reuse the #2053 secret-leaf identification (the typed-struct path already knows the secret set — apply the same set to the AST walk). Keep the config structurally valid (a redacted secret still round-trips as a placeholder, or is clearly marked). Verify a config with a PSK/community renders the secret REDACTED on every AST-render endpoint.

**RED-on-revert:** a REST show/export + gRPC ShowConfig of a config with an IKE PSK + SNMP community returns the secrets REDACTED (no cleartext PSK/community in the output) (goes RED — cleartext secrets in the raw-AST output — on revert); a non-secret config unchanged. Unit-test the AST render with a secret-bearing config across the endpoints.

**Design note / verify-first:** confirm which render function backs each endpoint (REST show/export/search/rollback + gRPC ShowConfig) and whether ANY already redact. If all raw-AST paths are already redacted → report already-correct. If the secret-leaf set is ambiguous (which leaves are secret) → that's the design question; else it's a driveable /engineer fix reusing #2053's secret set.

Provenance: fable-161 F-020, security / config-API module. #2053 typed-struct-only redaction.

## #4052 — test: test-failover.sh preflight session-count check is racy — asserts >= MIN_SESSIONS the instant iperf3 -P8 starts (before the 8 handshakes complete) → false FAIL (fable-161 batch-tf false-alarm) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Surfaced during the fable-161 HA-2nd-tier batch validation. `test/incus/test-failover.sh` (~line 165-171) runs, IMMEDIATELY after starting `iperf3 -P8 -t120`, a preflight check:
`fw0_sessions = show security flow session destination-prefix <target> | grep -c "Session State: Valid"; assert >= MIN_SESSIONS(4)`.

**Defect (test-quality — false FAIL):** the 8 TCP streams take a short time to complete their 3-way handshakes; the check runs with NO settle-wait, so at that instant fw0 may have only 0-3 established sessions → the assertion FAILS even though forwarding + establishment are healthy. Confirmed empirically: on a CLEAN settled cluster the same query returns 25 sessions at 23.4 Gbps / 0 retr — the failure is purely the racy timing (the check caught the sub-second establishment window). Passed by luck in a prior run; failed 2/2 in the batch run. This is a FALSE ALARM that masks the real (healthy) failover result and can waste an investigation.

**Fix:** poll-with-timeout the session count instead of a single immediate assert — loop `for i in $(seq 1 N); do cnt=$(...); [[ $cnt -ge $MIN_SESSIONS ]] && break; sleep 0.5; done` (a few seconds max), then assert. The real failover assertions (survive-reboot, sync-count, manual-failover) already have their own waits; only this preflight count lacks one. Verify the check passes reliably once the streams establish.

**RED-on-revert:** the preflight session-count check passes on a healthy cluster (polls until >= MIN_SESSIONS or a short timeout) — the single-immediate-assert version flakes. Test-infra only.

Provenance: fable-161 HA-batch-tf false-alarm. Adjacent to the #4009/#4020 test-infra hardening.

## #4053 — observability: 'show security flow session' per-session Pkts/Bytes counters read 0 on the AF_XDP fast path despite heavy traffic (40.9 GB / 23.4 Gbps observed with all sessions at Bytes: 0) (fable-161 obs-gap) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Surfaced during the fable-161 HA-batch validation (VERIFY-FIRST whether pre-existing vs a campaign regression).

**Observation (MEDIUM, observability — session byte/pkt counters not surfaced):** on the loss userspace cluster at 23.4 Gbps sustained iperf3, every `show security flow session` entry shows `Pkts: 0, Bytes: 0` on BOTH In and Out directions, even though 40.9 GB flowed through the AF_XDP fast path. The session COUNT is correct (25 valid sessions), and forwarding is full-rate — but the per-session packet/byte counters displayed by `show security flow session` (+ `destination-prefix`) are stuck at 0. So an operator can't see per-session traffic volume, and any tooling/test keying on per-session bytes (e.g. a throughput-per-session check) sees 0.

**Fix (verify-first — is this pre-existing or a regression? and are the counters even mirrored?):** the AF_XDP fast-path forwards without necessarily updating the per-session Pkts/Bytes fields that the display reads (the dataplane may count in a different structure, or the mirror to the show path doesn't carry the counters). Determine: (a) does the userspace-dp helper maintain per-session byte/pkt counters, and are they published in the conntrack mirror / the session snapshot the show path reads? (b) if the counters exist in the dataplane but aren't mirrored → wire them to the show path (like F-051 did for SessionCount). Sibling of F-051 (GC stats / SessionCount were 0 on the userspace path — the per-session Pkts/Bytes may be the same class of "counter not surfaced from the userspace dataplane"). If it's a KNOWN pre-existing gap (never surfaced on AF_XDP) → this is a feature (wire the counters), not a regression. If a recent merge broke a previously-working counter → a regression to fix.

**RED-on-revert / validation:** a session carrying N bytes of iperf traffic shows Bytes >= N (goes RED — Bytes: 0 — currently); the counters track traffic. First VERIFY whether it ever worked (check an older build's session-byte display, or the helper's per-session counter publication).

Provenance: fable-161 obs-gap (surfaced during batch validation). Sibling of F-051 userspace-counter class.

## #4054 — userspace-dp: export_all_sessions runs push_delta_lossless / frame serialization UNDER the global lock → a large session export blocks the worker → the control plane sees a false dataplane-failure → needless helper restart (fable-161 F-086) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA availability — false dp-failure restart under session-export load):** the bulk session export path (`export_all_sessions` / the owner-RG bulk export — grep export_all_sessions / push_delta_lossless / the frame serialization in userspace-dp/src/afxdp/event_stream or ha) performs the potentially-large work (iterating the whole session table + `push_delta_lossless` + frame serialization) WHILE HOLDING the GLOBAL lock (the coordinator/worker lock that the status poll + the forwarding path also need). On a firewall with many sessions (a bulk export at failover / a full-resync), this serialization can take long enough that the worker appears UNRESPONSIVE to the control plane's health check (the status poll can't acquire the lock / the worker misses its liveness deadline) → the control plane concludes the dataplane has FAILED → it RESTARTS the helper (a needless restart that DROPS all sessions + flaps forwarding) — exactly when a bulk export is happening (a failover), the worst time to restart. So a large session export self-inflicts a dp-failure-restart.

**Fix (verify-first):** move the expensive export work (the table iteration + push_delta_lossless + frame serialization) OUT of the global-lock critical section — take a SNAPSHOT of the session set under a brief lock, release the lock, then serialize/push OUTSIDE the lock. The lock must be held only long enough to copy the references/needed data, not for the whole export. So a large export doesn't block the worker's liveness / the status poll → no false dp-failure. Mirror the snapshot-and-release pattern (like the #3965 policy-counter fix did on the Go side). Verify a large export doesn't starve the status poll / trip the liveness deadline. If the export is ALREADY off the global lock (snapshot-then-serialize) → report already-correct.

**RED-on-revert:** a large session export completes without holding the global lock across the serialization (a concurrent status-poll / liveness check is NOT starved during the export) (goes RED — export holds the lock across the whole serialization → liveness starved → false dp-failure — on revert); a small export is unchanged. Rust test/benchmark asserting the lock-hold during export is bounded (snapshot-and-release), or that a concurrent lock-acquirer isn't blocked for the export duration. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-086, HA availability / rs-dataplane module. RUST (cargo). Sibling of #3965 (Go policy-counter snapshot-and-release).

## #4056 — config store: rollback slots / archive files / rescue.conf write the FULL config (incl IKE PSK, keys, community) as 0644 plaintext → secrets readable by any local user, defeating master-password encryption (fable-161 F-050) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-06)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST vs current origin/master).

**Defect (MEDIUM/HIGH-adjacent, security — secrets at rest in plaintext, world-readable):** the config store's rollback slots, config archive files, and rescue.conf (grep the rollback-slot / archive / rescue.conf WRITE path in pkg/configstore — store_commit.go and adjacent) write the FULL committed config — INCLUDING secret leaves (IKE/IPsec PSKs, WireGuard/auth keys, SNMP community, BGP/OSPF auth) — as CLEARTEXT to files created with mode 0644 (world-readable). So any local user (or a compromised low-priv process) can read all firewall secrets from the rollback/archive/rescue files on disk. This DEFEATS the master-password encryption (`system master-password` / the encrypted-secret feature): even if the active config encrypts secrets, the rollback/archive copies persist them in cleartext at 0644. Junos stores config archives with restricted perms + supports encrypted secrets throughout.

**Fix (verify-first — determine current perms + whether secrets are encrypted in these files):** (1) restrict the file mode to 0600 (owner-only) for rollback slots + archives + rescue.conf (grep the os.WriteFile / os.OpenFile perms — they should be 0600, not 0644, for files containing secrets); (2) if the master-password / encrypted-secret feature is configured, the secrets in the rollback/archive copies should be ENCRYPTED (or redacted) the same as the active config — don't persist cleartext secrets to a rollback/archive when encryption is enabled. Minimum viable: 0600 perms. Better: encrypt/redact secrets in the persisted copies consistently with the active-config encryption. Reuse the #2053 secret-leaf set + the master-password encryption path. Verify the rollback/archive/rescue files are 0600 + (if encryption on) don't contain cleartext PSKs.

**RED-on-revert:** a rollback slot / archive / rescue.conf containing an IKE PSK is written 0600 (not 0644) + (if master-password set) the PSK is not cleartext (goes RED — 0644 world-readable + cleartext PSK — on revert); a config without secrets unaffected. Unit-test the file mode + (if applicable) the secret handling of the persisted copies.

**Design note (verify-first → /engineer if perms-only is the fix, /research if the encryption-in-rollback needs a design decision):** the 0600 perms fix is DRIVEABLE. Whether to ENCRYPT secrets in rollback/archive (vs just restrict perms) is a design decision (round-trip: an encrypted rollback must decrypt to restore) — if that's needed, converge a plan; else ship the 0600 perms fix.

Provenance: fable-161 F-050, security / configstore module. #2053 secret-set + master-password encryption.

## #4059 — security policy: a to-zone junos-host DENY/REJECT policy is not enforced for DIRECT host-bound traffic (host-inbound service admission mirrors only, not the zone deny) → traffic destined to the firewall itself bypasses an explicit junos-host deny (fable-161 F-193) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701, VERIFY-FIRST — security, verify the current enforcement).

**Defect (MEDIUM, security — junos-host deny not enforced):** a security policy with `to-zone junos-host` (the special zone for traffic destined to the FIREWALL ITSELF — management, protocols, services) that DENIES or REJECTS is NOT enforced for direct host-bound traffic. The dataplane / kernel-chain setup mirrors only the host-inbound SERVICE ADMISSION (which services/ports are allowed inbound per `host-inbound-traffic`), NOT the zone POLICY deny. So an operator who writes `policy ... from-zone X to-zone junos-host ... then deny/reject` to block traffic to the firewall from zone X does NOT get that traffic blocked — it's admitted if the host-inbound service allows the port (or reaches the host regardless). grep the junos-host zone handling / the host-inbound admission vs the to-zone-junos-host policy evaluation in userspace/zones.go + the kernel-chain / host-inbound setup.

**Design question (route via /research — the enforcement mechanism is a design decision):** enforcing a to-zone-junos-host policy deny requires evaluating the zone policy for host-bound traffic (traffic terminating at the firewall), which currently goes through the host-inbound admission (a service allowlist), not the full policy engine. The design:
- Where to enforce the to-zone-junos-host policy? (a nftables input-chain rule derived from the policy? the userspace host-inbound path evaluating the zone policy before admitting?)
- How does it compose with host-inbound-traffic (the service allowlist) — is the policy deny an ADDITIONAL gate (deny wins), or does it REPLACE the service allowlist?
- The #3611-adjacent host-inbound work is relevant.
Converge a PLAN: the enforcement point, the compose semantics (deny-wins), and the fail-closed posture. Verify-first: does xpf ALREADY enforce a to-zone-junos-host deny anywhere (a kernel input-chain rule / a policy check on the host path)? If enforced → report already-correct. If only the service allowlist gates host-bound → genuine, converge the plan.

**RED-on-revert / validation (once plan converges):** traffic from zone X to the firewall's own address, matched by a `to-zone junos-host ... deny` policy, is DROPPED (goes RED — admitted via the service allowlist despite the deny — currently); an allow policy + host-inbound service admits normally. Provenance: fable-161 F-193, security / host-inbound module. /RESEARCH (design). Go+Rust.

## #4060 — config commit: reject the ##SECRET-DATA## redaction placeholder on commit-ingest (mirror errRedactedSecretIngest) → re-applying a redacted REST export shouldn't silently commit the placeholder as a literal secret (fable-161 F-020 follow-up) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Follow-up to #4051/#4057 (raw-AST secret redaction, merged). The new `SecretDataPlaceholder = ##SECRET-DATA##` (used by RedactedClone for REST show/export + gRPC ShowConfig) has NO symmetric commit-ingest guard, UNLIKE the existing `SecretRedacted` (`<redacted>`) which is rejected on ingest via `errRedactedSecretIngest`.

**Hazard:** an operator who does a REST `export` (now secret-redacted per #4051) and then re-applies that config (a `load`/commit of the exported text) would silently commit `##SECRET-DATA##` as a LITERAL secret value for every secret leaf → the IKE PSK / key / community becomes the literal string `##SECRET-DATA##` → the tunnel/auth breaks with a nonsense secret (and the operator doesn't realize the export wasn't restorable). The cleartext DR archive is the restorable backup, but a hand-rolled re-apply of a redacted export is a foot-gun.

**Fix:** on commit-ingest (the same path that rejects `<redacted>` via errRedactedSecretIngest — grep errRedactedSecretIngest / the ingest validation in pkg/configstore or pkg/config), also REJECT a secret leaf whose value is exactly `##SECRET-DATA##` (the SecretDataPlaceholder) with a clear error ("config contains the redaction placeholder ##SECRET-DATA## — this is a redacted export, not a restorable config; restore from the DR archive or re-enter the secret"). Mirror the errRedactedSecretIngest pattern + the secret-leaf set. So a redacted export can't be silently committed with placeholder secrets.

**RED-on-revert:** committing a config with a secret leaf == ##SECRET-DATA## is REJECTED with a specific error (goes RED — silently committed as a literal secret — on revert); a normal secret commits. Unit-test the ingest-reject for the placeholder.

Also (doc): add an operator-doc line noting REST `export` is secret-redacted (not a full-fidelity restorable backup — use the DR archive / `request system configuration rescue` for restore).

Provenance: fable-161 F-020 follow-up (from the #4057 hostile review MINOR-1). Go.

## #4061 — VRRP: a BACKUP does not adopt the MASTER's advertised interval (Master_Adver_Interval) → uses its own configured interval for Master_Down_Interval per RFC 5798 §6.1/§6.4.2 → failover-timing mismatch when master/backup intervals differ (fable-161 F-076) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master NOT the stale local checkout; several fable-161 VRRP/host findings have proven already-correct).

**Defect (MEDIUM, VRRP correctness — RFC 5798 interval adoption):** RFC 5798 §6.1 defines `Master_Down_Interval = (3 × Master_Adver_Interval) + Skew_Time`, where `Master_Adver_Interval` is the interval ADVERTISED BY THE CURRENT MASTER (learned from the received advertisement's Max Adver Int field), NOT the backup's own locally-configured interval. §6.4.2 (Backup state, on receiving an advertisement) says the backup MUST set `Master_Adver_Interval` to the Adver Interval in the received packet and recompute `Master_Down_Interval` + `Skew_Time` from it. If xpf's VRRP state machine (pkg/vrrp) computes `Master_Down_Interval` from its OWN configured `AdvertiseInterval` instead of the master's advertised interval, then a cluster where the master + backup have DIFFERENT configured intervals (a misconfig, or a rolling change) gets a wrong master-down timer → premature or delayed failover detection → a failover-timing bug (a backup with a shorter local interval than the master fails over too early → flapping; a longer one detects master-down too late → traffic loss). Note xpf uses 30ms RETH intervals; a mismatch is the risk.

**Fix (verify-first):** in the BACKUP state's advertisement-receive handler (grep the Master_Down / masterDownInterval / AdvertiseInterval usage in pkg/vrrp), learn `Master_Adver_Interval` from the RECEIVED advertisement (the Max Adver Int field, centiseconds on the wire per RFC 5798) and compute `Master_Down_Interval` + `Skew_Time` from THAT, not from the local config. Verify: a backup receiving a master advertising interval Y computes master-down from Y, regardless of the backup's own configured interval. If xpf ALREADY learns the master's interval from the received advert → report already-correct with file:line (check the advert parse — does it read + use the Max Adver Int?).

**RED-on-revert:** a backup receiving a master advert with interval Y (!= the backup's local interval) computes Master_Down_Interval from Y (goes RED — uses the local configured interval — on revert); matching intervals unchanged. Unit-test the master-down computation from a received advert (inject an advert with a specific Max Adver Int, assert the timer).

Provenance: fable-161 F-076, VRRP / RFC 5798 §6.1/§6.4.2. /RESEARCH-or-/ENGINEER (verify-first; if the fix is a clear 'read the advert interval' it's driveable).

## #4065 — userspace-dp: a GRE/IPIP packet whose OUTER header is unparseable is handled inconsistently with #2410's malformed-tunnel fail-closed posture — verify the drop-vs-pass + logging behavior (fable-161 F-185) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master, NOT the stale local checkout; several fable-161 dataplane findings proved already-correct).

**Claimed defect (MEDIUM, dataplane robustness/security — malformed-tunnel handling):** the GRE/IPIP decap path (grep the GRE/IPIP outer-header parse in userspace-dp/src/afxdp — the tunnel decap / gre.rs / ipip) handles a packet whose OUTER (encapsulating) header is UNPARSEABLE (a truncated/malformed GRE or IPIP header) INCONSISTENTLY with the #2410 malformed-tunnel fail-closed posture. #2410 established that a malformed/unparseable tunnel packet should be handled fail-CLOSED (dropped + counted/logged, not silently passed or silently dropped in a way that hides an attack). The current path may: (a) silently DROP the packet without a screen/counter (so a malformed-tunnel flood is invisible — no observability), OR (b) fall through to a path that PASSES/reinjects it (fail-open — a crafted malformed tunnel bypasses inspection). VERIFY-FIRST which it is.

**Fix (verify-first — determine the actual behavior vs #2410):** trace the GRE/IPIP outer-parse failure path. Compare to #2410 (grep 2410 — the malformed-tunnel handling it added). Determine: on an unparseable outer, does the code (i) drop + increment a malformed-tunnel/screen counter + optionally log (the correct fail-closed + observable behavior), (ii) drop SILENTLY (no counter — an observability gap), or (iii) pass/reinject (a fail-open bypass)? If it ALREADY matches #2410 (fail-closed + counted) → REPORT "already-correct: <file:line>" + STOP (no PR). If (ii) silent-drop → add the malformed-tunnel counter/screen (observability). If (iii) fail-open pass → make it fail-CLOSED (drop + count), matching #2410. Reuse the #2410 malformed-tunnel counter/screen mechanism. Verify a crafted unparseable-outer GRE/IPIP packet is dropped + counted (not passed, not silently swallowed).

**RED-on-revert:** an unparseable-outer GRE/IPIP packet is dropped + the malformed-tunnel counter increments (goes RED — passed/reinjected [fail-open] OR silently dropped with no counter — on revert); a valid GRE/IPIP packet decaps normally. Rust unit test constructing a truncated/malformed GRE + IPIP outer, asserting drop + counter. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-185, dataplane robustness / rs-dataplane module. #2410 malformed-tunnel fail-closed. RUST (cargo). VERIFY-FIRST (drop-vs-pass ambiguous in the finding text).

## #4067 — RBAC: a read-only / config-viewer login-class user can run 'monitor traffic' (which spawns a root tcpdump on a data interface) → privilege escalation / packet capture by an unprivileged role (fable-161 F-023) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master; several fable-161 RBAC/CLI findings may be already-correct).

**Defect (MEDIUM, security/RBAC — unprivileged packet capture):** the `monitor traffic` operational command (which spawns a root `tcpdump` on a data interface to capture packets — grep monitor traffic / the RBAC/login-class permission check for it in pkg/cli) is available to a READ-ONLY or config-viewer login-class user (a role intended to only VIEW config/status, not capture traffic). So an unprivileged operator role can run a live packet capture on the firewall's interfaces (via the root tcpdump the command spawns) → they can see traffic they shouldn't (other users' traffic, credentials in cleartext protocols) AND it runs tcpdump as ROOT (a spawned-root-process surface). This is a privilege/authorization gap — packet capture should require an operator/super-user class, not read-only. Junos gates `monitor traffic` behind the `maintenance`/`view-configuration`-plus permission, not plain read-only.

**Fix (verify-first — confirm the current RBAC gate):** gate `monitor traffic` (and any other command that spawns a privileged capture/exec — `monitor interface` raw, request commands that shell out) behind the appropriate login-class permission (operator/maintenance/super-user), NOT read-only/config-viewer. Grep the login-class / permission model (pkg/cli RBAC — the command-permission map / the class-to-command gate) + where monitor traffic is dispatched. If it ALREADY requires an elevated class → report already-correct with file:line. If read-only can run it → add the permission gate (deny for read-only/config-viewer; require the capture/maintenance permission). Verify a read-only user is denied `monitor traffic` while an operator/super-user is allowed.

**RED-on-revert:** a read-only login-class user running `monitor traffic` is DENIED (permission error) (goes RED — allowed to spawn the root tcpdump — on revert); an operator/super-user is allowed; other read-only commands (show) unaffected. Unit-test the RBAC gate for monitor traffic across login classes.

Provenance: fable-161 F-023, security / CLI-RBAC module. VERIFY-FIRST.

## #4069 — userspace-dp HA: the RG-activation reverse-prewarm uses O(N·M) Vec::contains (linear membership per session) → slow failover prewarm with many sessions (fable-161 F-192) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master; several fable-161 dataplane findings proved already-correct).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA failover perf — O(N·M) prewarm):** on RG activation (a failover — this node becomes primary for a redundancy group), the reverse-session prewarm (the code that pre-installs / warms the reverse-direction session entries for the RG's synced sessions — grep the RG-activation prewarm / reverse-prewarm / RefreshOwnerRGs in userspace-dp/src/afxdp) checks membership via a linear `Vec::contains` INSIDE a per-session loop → O(N × M) where N = sessions to prewarm and M = the Vec being scanned. On a failover with many synced sessions (a busy cluster — thousands of sessions), this quadratic prewarm makes the failover SLOWER (the prewarm is on the failover critical path — the ~60ms/~130ms failover budget), delaying when the newly-primary node fully forwards. So a high-session-count cluster has a slower failover than necessary.

**Fix (verify-first):** replace the O(N·M) `Vec::contains` membership check with an O(1) HashSet/FxHashSet lookup (build the set once, O(M), then per-session O(1) membership → O(N+M) total). Grep the exact `Vec::contains` in the prewarm loop; confirm it's on the failover/RG-activation path. If it's already a HashSet / already O(N+M) → report already-correct with file:line. Preserve the prewarm semantics (same sessions prewarmed, same result — only the data structure changes). Verify with a large-N benchmark or a complexity assertion.

**RED-on-revert:** the RG-activation prewarm membership check is O(1)-per-session (HashSet) not O(M) (Vec::contains) — a large-N prewarm completes in O(N+M) (goes RED — O(N·M) Vec::contains — on revert); the prewarmed set is identical. Rust benchmark/test asserting the complexity improvement (e.g. a large N prewarm doesn't scale quadratically) + the prewarmed-set correctness. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-192, HA failover perf / rs-dataplane module. RUST (cargo). VERIFY-FIRST.

**RED-on-revert:** a stanza inheriting from a group that defines a leaf-list gets the group's list values (goes RED — the inherited leaf-list is dropped/suppressed — on revert); a stanza with its own explicit list overrides per Junos; a non-list leaf inherits normally. - the interval/threshold semantics (N missed → down).

## #4073 — routing: next-table inter-VRF routes are installed WITHOUT the ip-rule needed to reach the target table, and the global lookup rule (pref 100) precedes l3mdev (pref 1000) → next-table leaking silently fails / VRF traffic mis-routed (fable-161 F-174) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Result: (a) a next-table route pointing at another VRF's table is never consulted because no ip-rule routes the lookup there, OR (b) the global rule at pref 100 wins over the per-VRF l3mdev rule at pref 1000 → traffic that should follow the VRF's table follows the global/main table instead → inter-VRF next-table leaking silently fails or VRF traffic is mis-routed (leaks to the wrong table). grep the ip rule (netlink RuleAdd) priorities + the l3mdev rule + the next-table install in pkg/routing.

**Fix (verify-first — routing/netlink rule ordering is subtle):** (a) ensure a next-table leak installs BOTH the route in the target table AND the ip-rule that reaches it (or that the l3mdev rule + the route suffice); (b) fix the rule PRIORITY ordering so the per-VRF l3mdev rule (pref 1000) is consulted BEFORE any global lookup rule that would shortcut it — the global rule at pref 100 must NOT preempt the VRF's own table lookup for VRF-bound traffic (or the global rule's scope must exclude VRF traffic). Determine the correct netlink rule priorities for the VRF + next-table topology (l3mdev l3mdev-table + the leaked-route table + the global rule). If next-table ALREADY installs the rule + the priorities are correct → report already-correct with file:line. This is subtle netlink rule-ordering; verify against the actual `ip rule` output the daemon produces.

**RED-on-revert:** a next-table leak from VRF-A to VRF-B's table is reachable (traffic in VRF-A destined to a VRF-B-leaked prefix follows the leaked route) + the l3mdev rule (pref 1000) isn't preempted by a global pref-100 rule (goes RED — the leak isn't consulted / global preempts VRF — on revert); a non-VRF route unchanged. Test the rule install + priorities (unit-test the netlink RuleAdd calls / the rule set the daemon produces for a next-table + VRF config).

Provenance: fable-161 F-174, routing / VRF / next-table module. VERIFY-FIRST (netlink rule ordering subtle). /RESEARCH-or-/ENGINEER.

## #4074 — userspace-dp NAT: pool source-NAT (PAT) does not translate the ICMP query id for ICMP echo/query traffic (RFC 5508 §3.1) → multiple internal hosts pinging the same target through a pool collide on the query-id → replies mis-associated (fable-161 F-186) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master; several fable-161 NAT/dataplane findings proved already-correct).

**Defect (MEDIUM, NAT correctness — ICMP query-id not translated, RFC 5508):** pool source-NAT (PAT — port/address translation via a NAT pool) translates the L4 PORT for TCP/UDP, but for ICMP ECHO / query traffic it does NOT translate the ICMP QUERY IDENTIFIER (the Identifier field in an ICMP Echo Request/Reply, which for ICMP acts as the "port" for NAT demux — RFC 5508 §3.1 "ICMP Query Mappings"). grep the pool SNAT / PAT translation + the ICMP handling in userspace-dp/src/nat (source.rs / the ICMP-query NAT). RFC 5508 requires a NAT to translate the ICMP Query Id (and rewrite the ICMP checksum) so the (translated-source, query-id) tuple is unique. If xpf's pool SNAT leaves the query-id UNtranslated: two internal hosts A and B both pinging the same external target T through the pool, both using query-id 0x1234, get SNAT'd to the same pool address (or different addresses) but the SAME query-id → the return ICMP Echo Replies can't be demuxed back to A vs B (the conntrack reverse lookup collides on (pool-addr, 0x1234)) → replies mis-associated / dropped → ICMP (ping, PMTUD, traceroute) through pool SNAT is unreliable for concurrent flows.

**Fix (verify-first):** pool SNAT must translate the ICMP query-id for ICMP echo/query traffic — allocate a unique query-id (like a port) from the pool's id space so (translated-source, translated-query-id) is unique, rewrite the ICMP Identifier + fix the ICMP checksum, and key the conntrack reverse entry on the translated query-id. RFC 5508 §3.1. If pool SNAT ALREADY translates the query-id (grep the ICMP-id NAT / the query-id allocation) → report already-correct with file:line. Note: interface-SNAT / a single-address may or may not have the same gap — check both. Mirror the TCP/UDP port-allocation mechanism for the ICMP id.

**RED-on-revert:** two concurrent ICMP echo flows (same query-id, same target) through pool SNAT get DISTINCT translated query-ids (or are otherwise demuxable) → both replies return to the correct host (goes RED — same query-id, replies mis-associated — on revert); a single ICMP flow unchanged; TCP/UDP unaffected. Rust unit test: two ICMP echoes with the same id through pool SNAT, assert distinct translated ids + correct reverse demux. FULL cargo test --release.

Provenance: fable-161 F-186, NAT / RFC 5508 §3.1. RUST (cargo). VERIFY-FIRST.

## #4076 — routing: anchor-path keepalive should bump linkGen on a transient-lookup-error + device-vanished recreate (parity with the legacy branch's default:return F7 guard) (fable-161 F-063 follow-up) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Follow-up to #4071/#4075 (GRE keepalive on the anchor path, merged). Non-blocking MINOR from the #4075 review.

**Edge (astronomically-unreachable, hardening):** in applyAnchorLocked's reconcile, a TRANSIENT (non-not-found) lookup error keeps willRecreate=false → the code falls through to the LinkAdd-EEXIST-adopt idiom. In the overwhelming common sub-case the device exists → EEXIST → adopt-in-place → runner retained (correct). But there's one effectively-unreachable sub-case: a transient (non-not-found) lookup error AND the device simultaneously vanished so LinkAdd SUCCEEDS (created=true) → linkGen is NOT bumped despite a genuinely NEW device → a µs window before startKeepalive drains the outgoing runner where a stale keepalive tick could LinkSet* the new device (the gen guard wouldn't catch it, since the gen wasn't bumped).

This is effectively unreachable (an absent device reports not-found, not a transient transport error; the tick interval is >=1s vs a µs window) and is strictly better than the pre-#4075 state (no keepalive at all). But for exact parity with the legacy branch's F7 discipline (which handles a transient non-not-found lookup error with `default: return`, aborting the apply), the anchor path should either:
- mirror the legacy `default: return` on a transient non-not-found lookup error, OR
- bump linkGen whenever `created` ends true (a new device always gets a fresh generation).

Prefer bumping linkGen when created=true (simpler, covers the case without aborting the apply). One-line hardening. Add a test for the transient-error + device-vanished-so-LinkAdd-created path asserting linkGen is bumped.

Provenance: fable-161 F-063 follow-up (from the #4075 review MINOR). Go.

## #4083 — cluster HA: the fallback full BulkSync (when incremental session sync falls behind / on reconnect) may race with concurrent incremental delta application → sessions double-applied or lost during the bulk-vs-delta overlap window (fable-161 F-258) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master; several fable-161 HA session-sync findings proved already-correct — weight-verify hard).

**Defect (MEDIUM, HA session-sync — bulk-vs-delta race):** the fallback full BulkSync (the mechanism that does a FULL session-table resync when incremental delta sync falls behind, on reconnect, or on a sequence gap — grep BulkSync / bulkSync / fallback / the full-resync path in pkg/cluster) may RACE with concurrent INCREMENTAL delta application. During the window where a full BulkSync is in flight (streaming the whole session table) AND incremental deltas continue arriving (new sessions installed / sessions torn down), the two paths can interleave such that: (a) a session created AFTER the bulk snapshot but delivered by an incremental delta BEFORE the bulk stream finishes is OVERWRITTEN by the (older, absent) bulk state → the session is LOST; or (b) a session appears in BOTH the bulk stream and an incremental delta → DOUBLE-APPLIED (benign if idempotent, but a torn-down-then-bulk-readded session RESURRECTS). VERIFY-FIRST: confirm the bulk sync + incremental delta paths can overlap without a barrier / generation guard / ordering.

**Fix (verify-first — the correct fix depends on the current sync architecture):** the bulk-vs-delta overlap needs a consistency guard — e.g. (a) a generation/epoch: the bulk snapshot is tagged with a generation; an incremental delta with a NEWER generation wins over the bulk state (so a post-snapshot delta isn't overwritten by the bulk); or (b) a barrier: hold incremental application until the bulk completes, then replay the buffered deltas in order; or (c) the bulk is applied ADDITIVELY (never deletes a session the bulk didn't see, only adds/updates) + a separate reconcile GC. Grep how the existing incremental sync orders vs the bulk (the #2874/#3878 producer_seq / the sync sequence). If there's ALREADY a generation/barrier that prevents the race → report already-correct with file:line. If the paths can overlap unguarded → this is a design decision (the guard mechanism) → converge a plan. Mirror the existing sync-hold / gen-guard patterns (the #2082 sync-hold, the #3075 gen-guard).

## #4088 — userspace-dp NAT: pool SNAT misclassifies an ICMP echo with identifier 0 as flowless → id==0 reintroduces the (pool_addr, 0) reverse-tuple collision (fable-161 F-186 follow-up) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Follow-up to #4074/#4086 (pool-SNAT ICMP-id translation, RFC 5508, merged). Copilot finding on #4086, deferred per the moderate plumbing cost.

**Edge:** nat/source.rs `icmp_query = matches!(protocol, PROTO_ICMP|PROTO_ICMPV6) && src_port != 0` misclassifies an identifier-bearing ICMP query whose identifier == 0 (a valid on-wire id) as flowless: parse_flow_ports (inspect.rs:1034) returns Some((ident, 0)) for a query even when ident==0, and None for non-query ICMP — both flatten to src_port=0, so `src_port != 0` can't distinguish an id==0 query from a non-query. An id==0 echo therefore takes the address-only path (no id translation) → two id==0 flows behind one pool address collide on (pool_addr, 0) — the exact bug #4074 fixed, residual for id==0.

**Severity:** narrow. Standard ping uses a nonzero PID/process id; id==0 is uncommon on-wire. Behavior is strictly better than pre-#4074 (pre: ALL ids collided; now: only id==0). Not a regression — a residual edge.

**Fix (the plumbing #4086 deferred):** base icmp_query on whether the tuple came from an identifier-bearing ICMP QUERY (parse_flow_ports returned Some for an ICMP protocol), not on src_port != 0. The clean signal (Some-vs-None) isn't preserved past SessionFlow today. Two options assessed in #4086:
- a new field on SessionFlow (a hot per-packet struct — 83 construction literals), OR
- a new bool param on match_source_nat_result_for_tuple (28 call sites, 25 in tests) sourced from a new signal at the poll_descriptor call site.
Either threads an "icmp_identifier_present" / "flow_has_ports" bool from the frame parser into the NAT match. Prefer the least-invasive (likely the poll_descriptor→match param, or reuse an existing has-ports signal if one is already plumbed). Update the tests that assume src_port==0 means non-identifier.

**RED-on-revert:** two ICMP echoes with identifier 0 (same target) through pool SNAT get DISTINCT translated ids (demuxable) (goes RED — both address-only, (pool,0) collision — currently); a nonzero-id flow unchanged; non-query ICMP still address-only. Rust unit test. FULL cargo.

Provenance: fable-161 F-186 follow-up (#4086 Copilot finding 2). RUST (cargo). Low priority (narrow edge).

## #4092 — WireGuard: verify the handshake TAI64N timestamp handling (monotonic per-peer replay-protection greatest-timestamp check + the TAI64N encoding) per the Noise/WireGuard spec (fable-161 F-190) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-161 (base ddf9f58701 — VERIFY-FIRST against origin/master; MANY fable-161 findings proved already-correct or premise-wrong. Weight-verify HARD.)

The WireGuard protocol (Noise IK + the WG-specific timestamp) embeds a TAI64N timestamp in the handshake initiation, and the RESPONDER must track the GREATEST timestamp seen per peer and REJECT an initiation whose timestamp is <= the stored greatest (monotonic replay protection — a replayed or reordered initiation is dropped). The finding claims either (a) the TAI64N ENCODING is wrong (TAI64N = 8-byte seconds-since-TAI-epoch + 4-byte nanoseconds, big-endian, with the TAI offset), or (b) the greatest-timestamp replay check is missing/wrong (not stored per-peer, or the comparison is wrong, or it's not persisted so a restart resets it). VERIFY-FIRST which, if any.

**VERIFY-FIRST:** grep the WG handshake initiation processing + the timestamp field. Determine: (a) is the TAI64N correctly encoded/decoded (the epoch offset, big-endian, nanoseconds)? (b) is there a per-peer greatest-timestamp store + a reject-if-<=stored check (replay protection)? Trace an initiation's timestamp validation. If xpf uses an EXISTING WG crate (boringtun / a Rust WG impl) that handles the handshake + timestamp → the timestamp logic is the crate's, likely correct → REPORT already-correct (crate-handled) with file:line. If xpf hand-rolls the handshake + the timestamp check is missing/wrong → confirm the gap.

**IMPORTANT — likely crate-handled or already-correct:** xpf's WG (grep wg / wireguard / boringtun in userspace-dp) — if it delegates the handshake to a maintained crate, the TAI64N + replay check are the crate's responsibility (correct). Only a hand-rolled handshake would have this gap. Determine which.

**Fix (only if a genuine hand-rolled gap):** implement/fix the per-peer greatest-timestamp replay check (reject initiation timestamp <= stored greatest) + correct TAI64N encoding. Persist the greatest timestamp if the peer state persists across restart (or accept the restart-reset tradeoff per the WG spec — the spec allows a bounded reset). 

**RED-on-revert (if genuine):** a replayed WG initiation (timestamp <= the stored greatest) is REJECTED (goes RED — accepted, replay succeeds — on revert); a fresh initiation (greater timestamp) accepted. Rust unit test. FULL cargo.

Provenance: fable-161 F-190, WireGuard handshake / Noise-spec. RUST. VERIFY-FIRST (likely crate-handled / already-correct).

## #4097 — security: FRR community-list members and as-path regexes are rendered into frr.conf verbatim (bypassing sanitizeFRRValue) — an embedded newline injects arbitrary router bgp/neighbor commands into the managed section (fable-163 F2) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-163 (base 20480f5175 == origin/master). HIGH security, config-injection into the root FRR daemon. VERIFY-FIRST at HEAD then fix.

**Defect:** pkg/frr/policy_render.go:1309 (community-list `member`) and :1325 (`ap.Regex` as-path) render the value VERBATIM with bare %s, while every OTHER free-text FRR field the module defends (neighbor description :673, BGP password :679, OSPF/RIP/IS-IS auth) is routed through `sanitizeFRRValue` (:38, strips C0/DEL incl newline). The commit-time strict gate `validateFRRAuthValuesStrict`/`frrTokenUnsafeIndex` (compiler_validate_strict.go:1179/1216) applies to AUTH SECRETS ONLY; the community/as-path validators (:1108) check only that a REFERENCE is defined, never member/regex content. The lexer `readString` (pkg/config/lexer.go:207) turns `\n` in a quoted value into a real newline byte.

**Exploit:** `set policy-options as-path evil "^1$\n router bgp 65000\n neighbor 6.6.6.6 remote-as 65000"` (or the same via HA config-sync / rollback reload / lenient load, which re-parse stored values) → the lexer yields ap.Regex with literal newlines → `generatePolicyOptions` renders it verbatim at :1325 into the xpf-managed section of /etc/frr/frr.conf → frr-reload.py applies it → the injected `router bgp`/`neighbor` lines execute as real FRR config → rogue BGP session / redistribution → traffic redirection or exfiltration. Converts `policy-options`-scoped config-write (a scope a Junos RBAC regex can grant while denying `protocols bgp`) into arbitrary routing-daemon control. Also breaks the #1960 lenient-load 'stored bad value stays inert at render' invariant (which sanitizeFRRValue enforces for auth/description but not these two).

**Fix:** (1) route `member` and `ap.Regex` through `sanitizeFRRValue` at render (parity with the auth/description fields); (2) add a commit-time newline/CR (ideally full frrTokenUnsafeIndex) gate over community members + as-path regexes, lenient-downgraded on load/peer-sync (per the #1960 doctrine — strict on operator commit, warn on load/sync). Sibling F20 (as-path regex has no Junos→FRR syntax translation) is in the same file — can fold.

**RED-on-revert:** an as-path regex / community member containing a newline is (a) rejected on strict operator commit, and (b) render-sanitized (the newline stripped) on the lenient/load/sync path so no injected line reaches frr.conf (goes RED — verbatim newline reaches the managed section — on revert). Unit-test the render (sanitizeFRRValue applied) + the strict validator (ParseSetCommand + tree.SetPath).

Provenance: fable-163 F2, security/frr/config-injection. Not in the 528-title dedup corpus (closest F-035 annotation-injection = different surface; #2643 community KIND work added no content sanitization). Go.

## #4098 — security: IPsec local_ts/remote_ts traffic selectors are rendered into swanctl.conf unsanitized + uncommit-validated — config-injection into the root charon keying daemon (updown → root RCE) (fable-163 F4) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-163 (base 20480f5175 == origin/master). HIGH security, config-injection → root RCE. VERIFY-FIRST at HEAD then fix.

**Defect:** pkg/ipsec/policy.go:176-182 renders LocalTS/RemoteTS with bare %s, UNLIKE the sibling child.Name on :175 which uses `sanitizeSwanctlValue`:
    fmt.Fprintf(&b, "      %s {\n", sanitizeSwanctlValue(child.Name))
    if child.LocalTS != "" { fmt.Fprintf(&b, "        local_ts = %s\n", child.LocalTS) }   // RAW
    if child.RemoteTS != "" { fmt.Fprintf(&b, "        remote_ts = %s\n", child.RemoteTS) } // RAW
`effectiveTrafficSelectors` (policy.go:341-381) sources these from `traffic-selector local-ip/remote-ip` (+ identity fallbacks). grep of compiler_validate*strict*.go for the source leaves shows NO commit validation; lexer.go:207 materializes `\n` in a quoted value.

**Exploit:** `set security ipsec vpn v1 traffic-selector ts1 local-ip "10.0.0.0/24\n        updown = /tmp/x.sh"` → renderConfig writes a real newline + `updown = /tmp/x.sh` into the swanctl children{ts1{...}} block; no strict validator rejects it → charon (running as ROOT) executes the updown script on tunnel up/down → root RCE. Alternatively inject esp_proposals/mode/mark_* to silently alter crypto posture. Reachable on the normal commit path AND via HA reverse-sync / `load override` / a restricted RBAC author who can set selectors but not updown/proposals directly (privilege escalation within the grammar). The module already treats swanctl interpolation as an injection surface (#1798/#2126 sanitize name/id/cert/PSK) — traffic selectors were missed + have zero commit validation.

**Fix:** (1) run LocalTS/RemoteTS through `sanitizeSwanctlValue` at render (parity with child.Name); (2) add a strict validator parsing each as a CIDR/range list and rejecting control chars, lenient-downgraded on load/sync per #1960.

**RED-on-revert:** a traffic-selector local-ip/remote-ip containing a newline (or a non-CIDR/range token) is rejected on strict commit + render-sanitized on load/sync so no injected `updown=`/`esp_proposals=` line reaches swanctl.conf (goes RED — verbatim reaches the children block — on revert). Unit-test the render + the strict validator.

Provenance: fable-163 F4, security/ipsec/injection/rce. Distinct from F-035/F-005/F-020; the specific render-omission + validation-absence for local_ts/remote_ts. Go.

## #4099 — security: local interactive CLI 'show configuration' is not secret-redacted — a read-only / config-viewer login class prints IKE PSKs, SNMP communities, auth-keys in cleartext (CLI residual of F-020/#4051) (fable-163 F3) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-163 (base 20480f5175 == origin/master). HIGH security, secret disclosure to a view-only class. VERIFY-FIRST at HEAD.

**Defect:** pkg/cli/cli_show.go (case "configuration") calls the NON-redacted store renderers — ShowActive()/ShowActiveSet()/ShowActiveJSON()/ShowActiveXML()/ShowActiveInheritance()/ShowActivePath* — which return active.Format()/FormatSet()/... with no masking (store_format.go:31-36). The REDACTED variants EXIST (ShowActiveRedacted/ShowActiveSetRedacted/... store_format.go:319-351) and are correctly used by gRPC (server_config.go:279) + REST (api/config.go:184) after #4051/F-020 — the local CLI was never wired to them.

**Exploit:** a user with login class `read-only` or `config-viewer` (both = PermView, types_system.go:558) SSHes into the CLI → `show configuration` → checkPermission(["show","configuration"]) → PermView → allowed (permissions.go:63) → ShowActiveSet() → active.FormatSet() prints every `security ike ... pre-shared-key`, `snmp community`, `system ... authentication-key` in CLEARTEXT. Junos shows only the $9$/##SECRET-DATA form to these classes; a view-only operator can harvest every firewall secret at HEAD.

**Design note (the #4051/#4057 scope decision):** #4057's scope note deliberately left the on-box CLI cleartext ('operator-reads-own-secrets, Junos parity, root has DB access'). BUT that rationale applies to super-user/operator — NOT to read-only/config-viewer (a VIEW-only class that should never see secrets, matching Junos which shows $9$-encrypted to everyone). Route via /research if the redaction should apply to ALL CLI classes vs only the non-privileged (read-only/config-viewer) classes; the DRIVEABLE minimum is to redact for the view-only classes. Recommend: redact for read-only/config-viewer (and likely all non-super-user), keep the existing *Redacted store methods.

**Fix:** route cli_show.go (and the cli_config.go candidate / `compare rollback` show paths with the same gap under PermConfig) through the *Redacted store methods already implemented for gRPC/REST, gated on login class (redact for read-only/config-viewer at minimum).

**RED-on-revert:** a read-only login class running `show configuration` sees ##SECRET-DATA## (not the cleartext PSK) (goes RED — cleartext — on revert); a non-secret leaf unaffected. Unit-test the CLI show path per login class.

Provenance: fable-163 F3, security/secret-redaction/cli/vsrx-parity. The CLI residual of F-020 (#4051 fixed only REST+gRPC ShowConfig). Go.

## #4100 — VRRP: IPv4 VRRPv3 advertisement checksum omits the RFC 5798 §5.2.8 IPv4 pseudo-header (IPv6 leg has it) → total advert rejection + split-brain in a mixed xpf↔vSRX/Cisco cluster (fable-163 F10) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-163 (base 20480f5175 == origin/master). MEDIUM, vsrx-interop/HA. VERIFY-FIRST at HEAD.

**Defect:** pkg/vrrp/packet.go:74-81 (marshal) + :133-137 (parse) compute/verify the IPv4 VRRP checksum over the VRRP payload ONLY (onesComplementChecksum, no pseudo-header), while the IPv6 path (vrrpIPv6Checksum :176-205) correctly prepends the src/dst/length/next-header pseudo-header. `Marshal(isIPv6, srcIP, dstIP)` receives the addresses but DISCARDS them on the IPv4 leg. RFC 5798 §5.2.8 requires the checksum over the VRRP message PLUS an IPv4-or-IPv6 pseudo-header (upper-layer src/dst, VRRP length, next-header 112) for BOTH families (a change from VRRPv2, which for IPv4 had no pseudo-header). vSRX/Cisco/keepalived-v3 do IPv4 the RFC 5798 way.

**Impact:** a mixed cluster (xpf ↔ real vSRX, or xpf joining an existing IPv4 VRRP group) — a conformant peer verifies with the pseudo-header → nonzero residual → discards xpf's IPv4 advert; symmetrically xpf's ParseVRRPPacket rejects the conformant peer's advert → mutual timeout → dual-master split-brain on the IPv4 VIP (duplicate MAC/IP, asymmetric forwarding). A pure-xpf cluster is self-consistent (both wrong the same way) → LATENT until interop (staged vSRX migration).

**Fix:** add the IPv4 pseudo-header (src 4B, dst 4B, zero, protocol 112, VRRP length 2B) to BOTH marshal + parse, mirroring vrrpIPv6Checksum. NOTE: this changes the wire checksum — a rolling upgrade of a pure-xpf cluster will have a transient window where old (no-pseudo-header) and new (pseudo-header) nodes reject each other's adverts → coordinate as a both-sides change or gate on a capability. Consider back-compat (accept BOTH the pseudo-header and the legacy no-pseudo-header checksum on parse during a migration window?) — flag if this needs a design decision.

**RED-on-revert:** a canonical RFC-5798 IPv4 advert (checksummed WITH the pseudo-header) is ACCEPTED by xpf's parse, and xpf's marshalled IPv4 advert validates under the pseudo-header algorithm (goes RED — rejected / no-pseudo-header residual — on revert). Unit-test the IPv4 checksum vs a known-good RFC-5798 vector + a round-trip.

Provenance: fable-163 F10, vsrx-parity/interop/rfc-conformance/ha. Not in the 528-title corpus (F-076 #4061 = master-down-timing, different). Go.

## #4101 — security: DHCPv4 client installs YourIP/0 on-link when a rogue/broken server sends a zero or non-contiguous subnet mask → connected 0.0.0.0/0 route blackholes/hijacks all IPv4 forwarding (fable-163 F6) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-04)

Found by fable-review-163 (base 20480f5175 == origin/master). MEDIUM security, untrusted-input. VERIFY-FIRST at HEAD.

**Defect:** pkg/dhcp/dhcp.go:922-939 guards only `mask == nil`; a present-but-DEGENERATE mask is not checked:
    mask := ack.SubnetMask()
    if mask == nil { mask = net.CIDRMask(24, 32) }
    ones, _ := net.IPMask(mask).Size()   // 0.0.0.0 → (0,32); non-contiguous 255.255.0.255 → (0,0)
    ...
    Address: netip.PrefixFrom(addr, ones),   // ones==0 → addr/0
The apply path (dhcp.go:1549-1555) does AddrReplace(link, addr) with the resulting YourIP/0.

**Exploit:** xpf runs DHCPv4 on an uplink/mgmt interface (fxp0 bootstrap default) → a rogue/buggy server ACKs with option 1 = 0.0.0.0 (or a non-contiguous mask) → net.IPMask.Size() returns ones=0 → lease becomes YourIP/0 → the kernel installs a connected route for 0.0.0.0/0 on that interface → all IPv4 forwarding blackholed/hijacked until the lease is replaced. A single crafted ACK, no operator action. vSRX rejects a mask yielding no host bits.

**Fix:** after .Size(), reject/clamp when ones==0 OR bits!=32 (non-contiguous mask → Size() returns (0,0)); enforce 0 < ones <= 32 (a /32 lease is arguably valid — decide the floor; at minimum reject ones==0 and non-contiguous). On rejection, decline the lease / fall back / log (don't install YourIP/0).

**RED-on-revert:** a DHCP ACK with subnet mask 0.0.0.0 (ones=0) or a non-contiguous mask is REJECTED (no YourIP/0 installed) (goes RED — YourIP/0 → 0.0.0.0/0 connected route — on revert); a normal /24 ACK installs normally. Unit-test leaseFromACKv4 with a degenerate mask.

Provenance: fable-163 F6, security/correctness/dhcp/untrusted-input. No corpus DHCP finding on mask validation. Go.
