## #4718 — userspace-dp: NAT reconciliation silently drops rules on unparseable IP/prefix (no diagnostic) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
Three NAT snapshot reconcilers in `userspace-dp` skip a rule/prefix on a parse
failure via a bare `continue`/`{}` with no warning log, so an operator debugging
a config/sync drift gets zero signal that a NAT rule was dropped.

## Provenance
From gemini-review-041 findings Low-3, Low-4, Low-5 (a tight near-identical LOW
cohort — grouped into one issue per triage rule). All verified GENUINE.

## Evidence (origin/master `cae466c7b`)
- `userspace-dp/src/nat/destination.rs` `DnatTable::from_snapshots`: `Err(_) => continue`
  on unparseable destination (:324, :330) and `pool_address` (:343) — silent.
- `userspace-dp/src/nat/static_nat.rs` `StaticNatTable::from_snapshots`:
  `parse_nat_prefix(...) None => continue` for `external_ip` (:357) / `internal_ip` (:361) — silent.
- `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs` `parse_match_prefix` (:1360): both parse
  failures hit `Err(_) => {}` (:1375) — silently drops the prefix.

## Fix
Emit a warning (`eprintln!("xpf-dp: ...")` / logging framework) on each skip,
naming the rule and the malformed field. These run during control-plane
reconciliation, not the packet hot path, so logging adds no forwarding latency.

## Severity — Low (observability-gap)
- Behavior is fail-closed (dropped rule matches nothing), so no security bypass;
  the gap is purely operational transparency — silent NAT omissions are very hard
  to troubleshoot in production.

## #4719 — dataplane: ClearAllSessions deletes sessions one syscall per key (blocks controller, no yield) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
`ClearAllSessions` deletes v4/v6 sessions with a per-key `DeleteSession` /
`DeleteSessionV6` loop — one syscall per key, no batching and no
`runtime.Gosched()`. A `clear security flow session all` against a large table
(up to 10M sessions) blocks the controller goroutine for the full key count,
which can trip the HA peer watchdog.

## Provenance
From gemini-review-041 finding Low-11 (verified GENUINE; severity Low-Med).

## Evidence (origin/master `cae466c7b`)
`pkg/dataplane/maps_session.go:352` `ClearAllSessions`: per-key `m.DeleteSession(key)`
(:372) and `m.DeleteSessionV6(key)` (:396). Batch APIs already exist in the same
file but are unused here — `BatchDeleteSessions` (:282), `BatchDeleteSessionsV6`
(:295); the `BatchIterate*` paths (:249, :278) already call `runtime.Gosched()`.

## Fix
Chunk-delete via `BatchDeleteSessions`/`BatchDeleteSessionsV6` (e.g. 256 keys per
syscall) and `runtime.Gosched()` between chunks — reuse the established yield
pattern.

## Severity — Low-Medium (performance / HA-safety)
- Blast radius: a bulk clear stalls the controller for seconds→minutes at 10M
  sessions, risking an HA watchdog timeout / split-brain failover.
- Why not higher: only fires on an explicit operator bulk-clear at extreme scale.
  Why not dismissed: a real controller stall with an existing batch API left
  unused.

## #4731 — cli: `show ... | match/except` still buffers entire output via io.ReadAll (streamable like #4709) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
#4709 (PR #4730) made the interactive **pager** stream `show` output incrementally
(bounded memory). Its sibling `dispatchWithPipe` (`show ... | match|except|count|last`,
pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go) still does `io.ReadAll` on the command output, buffering the
ENTIRE output in memory before filtering — the same OOM class #4709 fixed, for a large
`show route | match ...` / `show security flow session | match ...`.

## Scope
- `| match` and `| except` are line-oriented grep-like filters — they can stream
  line-by-line with bounded memory (reuse the `lineSource` seam #4709 added).
- `| count` and `| last N` inherently need the full stream (count all lines / show the
  last N), so leave them buffered (or stream `count` as a running tally; `last` needs a
  bounded ring buffer of N, not the whole output).

## Fix
Apply the `lineSource` (bufio.Reader + 1-line lookahead) streaming from #4709 to the
`match`/`except` arms of `dispatchWithPipe`, filtering and writing each line as it is
read rather than `io.ReadAll` + `strings.Split`. Optionally convert `count` to a running
counter and `last` to an N-line ring buffer to bound their memory too.

## Provenance
Flagged during #4709 / PR #4730 (the pager-streaming fix) as an explicit related
residual, out of that PR's scope. Severity: Low (memory-efficiency; only triggers with
very large piped output on a RAM-constrained firewall). Fail-mode: OOM under large output,
not a correctness bug.

## #4743 — observability: userspace-dp NoRoute/martian + IPv6-ext-header-denied drop counters (from #4373 dataplane residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
Split out from #4373 (config/Go/doc scope closed there). The Rust AF_XDP dataplane
(userspace-dp) lacks visible drop counters for two silent-drop classes, so a
firewall-filter `accept` log can have NO matching visible drop when the packet is
later dropped for a routing/header reason — the "reject/filter/PBR log confusion"
#4373 called out, dataplane half.

## Gaps (from #4373 E4/H2/H7 + E6)
1. **NoRoute / martian drop counter** (E4/H2/H7): when a packet is admitted by a
   filter `accept` but then dropped because there is no route (NoRoute) or it is a
   martian (multicast/broadcast/unspecified/loopback dst that policy-match's
   `RouteDropNote` advisory already flags at simulate-time), the userspace-dp path
   drops it with no counter/log. Add a live drop counter (+ optional rate-limited
   log) so the drop is observable and correlates with the filter-accept log.
2. **IPv6 extension-header fail-closed drop counter** (E6): the userspace-dp
   fail-closed drop on an unparseable/over-limit IPv6 extension-header chain has no
   counter — add one so these fail-closed drops are visible (relates to the
   MAX_IPV6_EXT_HEADERS handling; see #4555).

## Fix
Add per-class atomic drop counters in userspace-dp (mirror the existing dataplane
counter pattern) incremented at the NoRoute/martian and ext-header-denied drop
sites, and surface them through the control plane (the per-zone/global counter
readout path, e.g. alongside the #3651 counters). Optional: a rate-limited log at
each site. Bounded userspace-dp change (helper, not the verifier-gated shim).

## Test
RED-on-revert: a NoRoute/martian packet and an ext-header-over-limit packet each
bump their counter; a normally-forwarded packet does not. Revert → counter stays 0.

## Provenance
#4373 dataplane residual (E4/H2/H7 NoRoute + E6 ext-header), identified during the
#4373 verify-first (the config/Go/doc side landed via #4625/#4504/#3615/#2513/#3610).
Minor residuals also noted on #4373: H1/H4/H6 test-coverage gaps, E2/E5/E7 low nits.
Severity: Low (observability gap; drops are correct, just not counted).

## #4752 — observability: NAT pool-utilization alarm skips deterministic (CGNAT) pools — no per-subscriber block-exhaustion metric [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
Split from #4559 (deterministic CGNAT NAT is now fully enforced — allocator + fail-closed
+ advisory + docs). Residual gap: the NAT pool-utilization alarm (#2079, now closed) keys
off pool-wide `UsedPorts`, but a DETERMINISTIC pool's capacity is per-subscriber (each
subscriber owns a fixed contiguous block). So the pool-utilization alarm SKIPS deterministic
pools (feature-gaps.md:292), and there is no signal when a deterministic pool is running out
of SUBSCRIBER BLOCKS (block-exhaustion) — even though a subscriber whose IP falls outside the
provisioned range is already fail-closed at the dataplane (`DeterministicSubscriberOutOfRange`).

## Gap
- Deterministic pools have no utilization/exhaustion observability: an operator can't see how
  many subscriber blocks are allocated vs the pool's block capacity, nor get an alarm as the
  pool approaches block exhaustion.
- The pool-wide `UsedPorts` metric is meaningless for a deterministic pool (ports are
  pre-partitioned into per-subscriber blocks, not round-robin allocated).

## Fix
Add a deterministic-pool-aware utilization metric/alarm: report allocated-blocks /
total-blocks (block capacity = floor(port-range / block-size)), and alarm as it approaches
capacity — mirroring the #2079 pool-utilization-alarm mechanism but keyed on block-occupancy
instead of `UsedPorts`. Surface via the existing pool-utilization Prometheus/alarm path.

## Provenance
Identified during the #4559 verify-first (which found #4559 fully implemented). Severity: Low
(observability nicety — deterministic pools already fail CLOSED at the dataplane on
out-of-range subscribers, so this is a capacity-planning signal, not a security/compliance gap).
#2079 is closed, so this is tracked separately.

## #4759 — observability: per-type ICMP/ND host-inbound accept counters (split the global nft accept rules) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

the host-inbound ICMP-error and ND (neighbor-discovery) accept rules in the kernel nftables

focused PR (not bundled with the metrics-only batch).

Those accept rules are GLOBAL (not per-zone), so this yields AGGREGATE ICMP-error / ND accept
counts, not per-zone. A per-zone breakdown would need per-zone rule splitting (a larger

## #4785 — userspace-dp: implement IPIP (proto-4/41) tunnel decap/encap — currently REJECTED at commit (#4785 half 2) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

**Provenance:** surfaced by the #4478 `/research` (branch `research/4478-ipip-decap-zone`, converged `59ab9ff661f5`). #4478 itself was PLAN-KILLED — its *security* framing (a fail-**open**) is invalid: in the userspace dataplane (the only supported runtime) every tunnel is `AnchorOnly=true` → a `netlink.Tuntap` routing anchor, never a kernel `Iptun`/`Ip6tnl` decapper (`daemon_run.go:120,153,163` → `tunnel.go:459` `applyAnchorLocked`; confirmed by `tunnel_anchor_test.go`). So there is **no kernel IPIP decap** and inbound proto-4 is **dropped (fail-closed)**, not forwarded into a zone.

**This issue is the fail-closed residual, not a security bug.** IPIP (`set …tunnel … mode ipip`) is accepted at commit, the TUN anchor is created, and the endpoint reaches the dataplane snapshot — but there is **no userspace IPIP decap primitive** (unlike GRE, which has the `GRE_DECAP_INGRESS_FLAG` userspace decap-ingress stage in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/mod.rs`). An inbound proto-4 outer frame to the firewall's tunnel-source hits `is_local_destination` → kernel INPUT → no `IPPROTO_IPIP` handler → dropped. **Net: IPIP inbound tunnels do not pass traffic** — a vSRX parity gap (Junos supports `ip-in-ip`).

**Severity:** LOW/feature-completeness. Fail-closed (no bypass), synthetic surface today (no operator relies on IPIP inbound since it never worked). Distinct from the GRE path (which is fully implemented).

**Design already exists:** the #4478 plan §5 retains a **Path B** design (static `USERSPACE_SESSIONS` steering + a userspace-dp IPIP decap stage mirroring GRE: new `TunnelKind::Ipip`, decap-ingress flag, re-zone stage) and notes **Path C** (a `native_ipip` shim redirect) is cleaner but **blocked by #1864** (the shim verifier-gate toolchain). Start from `docs/research/4478-ipip-decap-zone/plan.md` on the research branch.

**Scope:** implement userspace-dp IPIP inbound decap + tunnel-zone re-application, mirroring the GRE decap-ingress architecture. Needs `/triple-review` (hot-path forwarding + a new decap stage). Verify with a loss-cluster IPIP tunnel: inbound inner traffic must be zone-policy-enforced (a deny policy on the inner zone must DROP).

## #4788 — config: commit-time advisory for silently-dead 'mode ipip' tunnel (from #4785 research) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

**Provenance:** near-term recommendation from the #4785 `/research` (PLAN-DEFER, branch `research/4785-ipip-inbound-decap`, converged `e80f4627d`). #4785 (full IPIP encap+decap+steering) is PLAN-DEFERred as demand-gated, but the research surfaced a cheap, valuable interim mitigation.

**Problem:** `set …tunnel … mode ipip` is accepted at commit and creates a Tuntap anchor, but IPIP is **non-functional in both directions** in the userspace dataplane — there is no userspace IPIP encap or decap stage (unlike GRE). Egress inner packets routed to the IPIP anchor resolve `tunnel_endpoint_id != 0` → the egress dispatcher (`frame/mod.rs` ~L399) classifies `TunnelKind::Unknown` → **drop**; inbound proto-4 is fail-closed-dropped (no kernel Iptun under anchor-only). So an operator configuring `mode ipip` gets a **silently dead tunnel** with no signal.

**Fix (cheap, WARN-only, zero dataplane surface):** a commit-time advisory (sibling of the #4455 Component B `validateHostInboundManagedRoutingMismatch` / #3226 / #4454 pattern in `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go`) that WARNs when a tunnel `mode ipip` is configured — stating IPIP is not yet implemented in the userspace dataplane (#4785) and the tunnel will not pass traffic, so the operator is not silently misled. Mirrors the accepted-only advisory doctrine; honors #1960 lenient-load. Test: a config with `mode ipip` warns; `mode gre`/`mode wireguard` do not.

Small Go-only follow-up. The full IPIP implementation remains #4785 (deferred, Path B ready via `/engineer 4785` if demand appears).

## #4790 — SECURITY: 'monitor traffic matching <filter>' option injection → arbitrary file write / RCE (escapes restricted CLI) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

**Provenance:** gemini-review-042 Critical #1, verified genuine on current master (b4f2ddb2f).

`pkg/cli/cli_request.go` `handleMonitorTraffic` builds the tcpdump argv `["tcpdump","-i",iface,"-n","-l"]`, appends `-c <count>` if given, then appends the user-supplied `matching <filter>` token **directly as a positional arg** (`cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, filter)`) with **no `--` separator**, and runs `exec.CommandContext(ctx, cmdArgs[0], cmdArgs[1:]...)`.

tcpdump parses options anywhere on its command line (getopt). A `matching` value that begins with `-` is therefore parsed as a tcpdump **option**, not a BPF filter:
- `matching "-w/path/to/file"` → tcpdump `-w` writes the capture to an arbitrary file (arbitrary file write as the daemon user).
- `matching "-z<cmd>"` (with a rotation option) → tcpdump `-z` runs a postrotate command (RCE).

The command is gated on `PermControl`, but the CLI is a **restricted Junos-like shell** — control-level admins are explicitly NOT supposed to have host file/shell access. This is a privilege-escalation / restricted-shell-escape. No shell is involved (argv exec), so this is *option* injection, not shell injection — but the impact (arbitrary file write, potential RCE) is equivalent.

**Fix (small, driveable now):** pass the filter after a `--` sentinel so tcpdump's getopt treats everything after it as the BPF expression, never an option: `cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "--", filter)`. Also validate `iface` does not begin with `-` and `count` is numeric (defense in depth). Extract the argv build into a testable `buildMonitorTrafficArgs` helper with unit tests asserting a `-w…`/`-z…` filter lands after `--` and cannot be an option.

---

## #4791 — address-set bracket-list members silently dropped (only first value compiled) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Defect

`address-set` member bracket-lists silently drop all but the first value, causing
a security under-enforcement (or a fail-open bypass for excluded addresses).

`parseAddressBookEntries` in `pkg/config/compiler_security_addressbook.go`
(current master `pkg/config/compiler_security_addressbook.go:254-266`) iterates
the children of an `address-set` node and appends only `member.Keys[1]` for the
`address` / `address-set` member cases:

```go
for _, member := range child.Children {
    switch member.Name() {
    case "address":

            as.AddressSets = append(as.AddressSets, member.Keys[1])
        }
    }
}
```

A bracketed member list collapses onto ONE leaf. Per the multi-value-leaf
contract (#2419), a config such as:

```

```

parses to a single leaf `Keys = ["address", "10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"]` (the lexer
strips `[`/`]`; `schema_security.go` marks `address`/`address-set` under
`address-set` as `multi: true`). Reading only `member.Keys[1]` captures
`10.0.0.1` and silently drops `10.0.0.2` (and any further members). The config
commits cleanly with no error/warning.

ingress interface from that single-valued map:

Operators troubleshooting or evicting sessions on a specific interface get

## #4793 — config DB decrypt panics (daemon boot loop) on wrong-length GCM nonce [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Defect

`maybeDecryptTreeJSON` decrypts the config DB with an on-disk GCM nonce but
never validates the nonce length before calling `gcm.Open`. Go's
`crypto/cipher` GCM `Open` PANICS (not errors) when the nonce length does not
match `gcm.NonceSize()`:

    panic("crypto/cipher: incorrect nonce length given to GCM")

So a corrupted/truncated nonce in the encrypted config envelope turns a
recoverable read error into an unrecoverable daemon panic at boot.

Current master `pkg/configstore/crypto.go:130-147`:

```go
nonce, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(env.Nonce)
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode nonce: %w", err)
}
...
gcm, err := cipher.NewGCM(block)
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("create GCM: %w", err)
}
plaintext, err := gcm.Open(nil, nonce, ciphertext, nil)   // panics if len(nonce) != gcm.NonceSize()
```

The base64 decode only validates encoding, not the decoded byte length. A
short/long nonce (bit-rot in `/etc/xpf/.configdb/active.json`, a truncated
write, a hand-edited/restored backup) decodes fine, then panics inside the Go
stdlib.

## Impact

File corruption or a malformed restored envelope crashes the daemon at
`Store.Load()` on boot -> restart loop, defeating the intended fail-closed path
that should surface a recoverable error (e.g. `ErrConfigDBUnreadable`) so
recovery CLI actions can run. This is a reliability / self-inflicted-DoS gap.

## #4795 — getOriginalKernelName appends f0 for single-function PCI (wrong .link OriginalName) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Defect

`getOriginalKernelName` reconstructs a systemd predictable interface name from
the PCI address but unconditionally appends the function suffix `f%d`. For a
single-function PCI device (function 0) systemd's predictable name is `enpXsY`
with NO `f0`, so the reconstructed name is wrong (`enpXsYf0`).

Current master `pkg/dataplane/compiler.go:1634-1680`:

```go
fn, err := strconv.ParseUint(sf[1], 10, 8)   // NB: base-10
if err != nil {
    return ""
}
return fmt.Sprintf("enp%ds%df%d", bus, slot, fn)   // always appends fN
```

The sibling helper `pciAddrToEnp` in `pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go:112-137` handles
this correctly and demonstrates the intended behavior:

```go
fn, err := strconv.ParseUint(sf[1], 16, 8)   // base-16
...
if fn > 0 {
    return fmt.Sprintf("enp%ds%df%d", bus, slot, fn)
}
return fmt.Sprintf("enp%ds%d", bus, slot)     // single-function: no fN
```

Two divergences: (1) `getOriginalKernelName` omits the `fn > 0` gate, and
(2) it parses the function in base-10 instead of base-16 (harmless for
functions 0-7, wrong for ARI multi-function >= 0x8).

## Impact

`getOriginalKernelName` feeds the `.link` `OriginalName=` used to match RETH
member interfaces (which match by PCI kernel name because their MAC alternates).
A wrong reconstructed name (`enpXsYf0` for a single-function NIC) fails to match,
so the RETH member is not renamed/managed on reboot.

## #4800 — userspace-dp: per-new-flow session-publish + N-way sibling-replication locks serialize every transit install — build a connection-rate generator + measure the new-flow ceiling [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-12)

## Summary

Build a **connection-rate (new-flows/sec) generator + a loss-cluster new-flow-ceiling harness** for the userspace dataplane, and measure the sustained NEW pool-mode-SNAT flow rate at which cross-worker synchronization on the new-flow install path (NAT allocator `live` mutex, `publish_shared_session`, `replicate_session_upsert`) becomes the aggregate bottleneck.

## Why

The `perf-test` skill measures **bulk throughput** (elephant flows), which puts near-zero load on the per-NEW-flow install path. Several design decisions (notably #2852 Phase-2 SNAT-allocator sharding — see the converged research at `docs/research/2852-portalloc-phase2/plan.md`) are gated on a **connection-rate** measurement that no current harness can produce. Without it, per-new-flow scaling work is speculative.

## Scope

- A traffic generator that opens many **distinct, short-lived** connections/sec (distinct sources × many distinct destinations) through the firewall on the loss userspace cluster (`loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1`), with a pool-mode SNAT rule on the WAN egress path.
- Instrument the sustained new-flow rate via `PortAllocatorSnapshot.allocations_total` delta/sec + per-core `perf` (is the allocate/publish/replicate path single-core-bound?).
- Report which of {NAT allocator mutex, `publish_shared_session` mutex, `replicate_session_upsert` queues, per-worker session install, RX queue, NIC} saturates first.

## Follow-on

If — and only if — this measurement shows the new-flow install path is lock-bound and the residual NAT allocator mutex is a material contributor, reopen the #2852 Phase-2 design (`docs/research/2852-portalloc-phase2/plan.md` §5, Option A), correctly re-scoped as "shard ALL per-new-flow cross-worker state (publish + replication + NAT)", since NAT-allocator sharding **alone** is architecturally insufficient (the publish + N-way replication locks serialize every new flow regardless). See #2852 for the full analysis.

## #4807 — config: interface-range member-range with a huge trailing integer panics the compiler (int64 overflow bypasses interfaceRangeMaxMembers guard) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`expandMemberRange` in `pkg/config/compiler_interface_range.go:250-273` computes the member count as `en-sn+1` (plain `int`, 64-bit on amd64) both for the `interfaceRangeMaxMembers` cap check AND for the slice capacity passed to `make`. A `member-range` whose end value is near `math.MaxInt64` overflows that subtraction to a large negative number, which:

1. Passes the guard `if en-sn+1 > interfaceRangeMaxMembers` (a negative number is never `> 4096`), silently bypassing the intended 4096-member cap.
2. Reaches `make([]string, 0, en-sn+1)` with a **negative capacity**, which panics at runtime (`runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range`).

## Current code (origin/master @ cbf1ee3ce), pkg/config/compiler_interface_range.go:250-273

```go
func expandMemberRange(rangeName string, toks []string) ([]string, []string) {
	if len(toks) != 3 || toks[1] != "to" {
		return nil, []string{...}
	}
	start, end := toks[0], toks[2]
	sp, sn, ok1 := splitTrailingInt(start)
	ep, en, ok2 := splitTrailingInt(end)
	if !ok1 || !ok2 || sp != ep || sn > en {
		return nil, []string{...}
	}
	if en-sn+1 > interfaceRangeMaxMembers {      // overflow bypasses this
		return nil, []string{...}
	}
	out := make([]string, 0, en-sn+1)            // panics: negative cap
	for i := sn; i <= en; i++ {
		out = append(out, fmt.Sprintf("%s%d", sp, i))
	}
	return out, nil
}
```

`splitTrailingInt` (same file, line 280) uses `strconv.Atoi(s[i:])`, i.e. `ParseInt(s, 10, 0)` — bit size 0 means native `int`, which is 64-bit on the amd64 targets this project ships to. So a value like `9223372036854775807` (`math.MaxInt64`) parses successfully as `en`.

## Trace

1. Config contains: `set interfaces interface-range R member-range ge-0/0/0 to ge-0/0/9223372036854775807`.
2. `splitTrailingInt("ge-0/0/0")` → `sn = 0`. `splitTrailingInt("ge-0/0/9223372036854775807")` → `en = 9223372036854775807` (parses fine as a 64-bit `int`).
3. `en - sn + 1` = `9223372036854775807 + 1` → signed 64-bit overflow → wraps to `math.MinInt64` (`-9223372036854775808`).
4. `-9223372036854775808 > 4096` is `false` — the `interfaceRangeMaxMembers` guard is bypassed.
5. `make([]string, 0, -9223372036854775808)` panics: `runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range`.

## #4810 — configstore: loadRollbackHistory skips an unreadable intermediate rollback slot (continue), shifting every older `rollback N` index → silently restores the WRONG historical config [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`Store.loadRollbackHistory()` (`pkg/configstore/store_commit.go:781`) reads
rollback text slots `xpf.conf.1..N` at boot. Per the deliberate #3441 L2 fix,
a **non-ENOENT** read error on an *intermediate* slot is logged and `continue`d
(rather than `break`ing) so later readable slots are not dropped. But the
history buffer is **purely positional** — `HistoryEntry` carries no slot/generation
tag — so skipping an intermediate slot shifts every older slot's user-facing
`rollback N` index down by one. `rollback N` then silently restores the config
that actually lived in slot `N+1`.

`pkg/configstore/store_commit.go:781` (`loadRollbackHistory`):
```go

    path := s.rollbackPath(i)
    data, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {

## #4816 — config: duplicate hierarchical security-zone blocks overwrite instead of merge (compileZones) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`compileZones` (`pkg/config/compiler_security_zones.go:81-136`) allocates a fresh `ZoneConfig{}` per `security-zone` AST instance returned by `namedInstances(node.FindChildren("security-zone"))` and does an unconditional `sec.Zones[inst.name] = zone`. If the same zone name appears as two separate sibling AST nodes, the second silently overwrites (does not merge with) the first, dropping the first block's `Interfaces`, `HostInboundTraffic`, `AddressBook`, etc.

## Reachability — refuting the review's claimed trigger, confirming the real one

The review claimed this is trivially reachable via two sequential `set` CLI commands, e.g.:
```
set security zones security-zone trust interfaces ge-0/0/0.0
set security zones security-zone trust host-inbound-traffic system-services ping
```
That is **refuted**: `ConfigTree.SetPath` (`pkg/config/ast_edit.go:211`, "container" path ~line 402) finds and *reuses* an existing node with matching `Keys` before creating a new one:
```go
found := false
for _, n := range *current {
    if !n.IsLeaf && keysEqual(n.Keys, nodeKeys) {
        current = &n.Children
        found = true
        break
    }
}
```
So two sequential `set security zones security-zone trust ...` commands merge into ONE `security-zone`/`trust` container with both children — `namedInstances` only ever sees one instance for that name via the normal CLI `set` workflow.

The bug IS reachable through the **hierarchical** parser (`Parser.parseStatements`, `pkg/config/parser.go:119-155`), which has no merge logic — it blindly appends every parsed block to `nodes`. That parser path is used by `load merge terminal` / `load override` / `load replace` (pasting or loading full hierarchical Junos-style config text). A config with the same `security-zone trust { ... }` name written as two separate blocks (e.g. an operator merges two hand-authored config fragments, or pastes a second `security-zone trust { ... }` block instead of editing the first) produces two literal sibling `security-zone` nodes named `trust`, and `compileZones` silently drops the first block's properties.

**Precedent — this is the same bug class already partially fixed under #4544.** The `interfaces`/`host-inbound-traffic` case in the SAME function was already hardened for exactly this scenario:
```go
// #4544: MERGE across ALL host-inbound-traffic blocks under
// this interface (Junos merge semantics), not FindChild
// (first-wins). A hand-authored `load override` config can
// carry two literal blocks under one interface; the
// hierarchical parser (parseStatements) keeps them as
// separate same-key siblings — it does NOT merge — so
// FindChild would read only the first and silently drop the
// rest. Iterate FindChildren and union their token sets.
```
That fix covers duplicate `host-inbound-traffic` blocks *within* one zone/interface. It does NOT cover duplicate `security-zone <name>` blocks at the outer level — `namedInstances(node.FindChildren("security-zone"))` still allocates-and-overwrites per instance with no merge.

## #4818 — config: load override with duplicate hierarchical security-zone blocks silently overwrites zone (drops interfaces/HIB/address-book) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`compileZones` (`pkg/config/compiler_security_zones.go:81-135`) allocates a fresh `ZoneConfig` and does `sec.Zones[inst.name] = zone` for every entry `namedInstances(node.FindChildren("security-zone"))` returns, with no check for an existing entry. `LoadOverride` (`pkg/configstore/store_command.go:220-241`) installs the raw hierarchical parse tree directly as the candidate with **no merge/dedup pass**, and the hierarchical parser (`pkg/config/parser.go` `parseStatements`) appends every parsed block as-is without merging same-name siblings. So a `load override` of a config file containing two literal `security-zone trust { ... }` blocks (e.g. from a copy-paste error, or concatenated config snippets/templates) silently drops the FIRST block's entire configuration — interfaces, screen profile, host-inbound-traffic, address-book, description, tcp-rst — with no warning, no error, and no indication at commit time.

## Correction to the reviewed trace

The reviewed trace (gemini-review-043) originally described this as reachable via two separate `set security zones security-zone trust ...` flat commands. That reproduction is **refuted**: `ConfigTree.SetPath` (`pkg/config/ast_edit.go:211-421`) find-or-creates same-key container nodes (`found := false; for _, n := range *current { if !n.IsLeaf && keysEqual(n.Keys, nodeKeys) { current = &n.Children; found = true; ... } }`), so two `set` lines targeting the same zone name always merge into ONE node's children — `namedInstances` only ever sees one "trust" entry from flat-set input, and `LoadMerge` of hierarchical text goes through the same SetPath-merging path (`LoadMerge` converts hierarchical input to flat commands and applies each via `applyEditLine`). The overwrite is real only via `LoadOverride`, which installs the parsed tree verbatim with true AST siblings intact.

## Evidence (origin/master @ cbf1ee3ce)

`pkg/config/compiler_security_zones.go:81-90`:
```go
func compileZones(node *Node, sec *SecurityConfig) error {
	for _, inst := range namedInstances(node.FindChildren("security-zone")) {
		zone := &ZoneConfig{Name: inst.name}
		for _, prop := range inst.node.Children {
			...
		}
		sec.Zones[inst.name] = zone   // unconditional overwrite
	}
	return nil
}
```
`pkg/configstore/store_command.go:220-234` (`LoadOverride`): `tree, errs := config.NewParser(content).Parse(); ...; s.candidate = tree` — no merge pass on the raw hierarchical tree.

This project already recognized and hardened the analogous inner-level hazard: `host-inbound-traffic` sub-blocks under a zone (or under an interface) are explicitly MERGED across `FindChildren` siblings rather than overwritten, per #4544/#3362 (see the comments at `compiler_security_zones.go:99-119`): *"A hand-authored `load override` config can carry two literal blocks under one interface; the hierarchical parser (parseStatements) keeps them as separate same-key siblings — it does NOT merge — so FindChild would read only the first and silently drop the rest."* The SAME hazard was not addressed at the outer `security-zone` instance level — `compileZones`'s per-instance loop is exactly the one-level-up case of the bug the project already fixed for HIB blocks.

## Fix

Mirror the #4544 pattern: instead of allocating a fresh `ZoneConfig` per raw AST instance, find-or-create by name and merge properties across all sibling instances (append `Interfaces`, merge `HostInboundTraffic`/`InterfaceHostInbound` via the existing `mergeHostInbound`, last-wins or first-wins for scalar fields with a doc note on which).

## Validation performed

Read `compileZones`, `namedInstances`, `SetPath`, `parseStatements`, `LoadOverride`, and `LoadMerge` on origin/master. Confirmed `LoadOverride` is the one candidate-install path that bypasses SetPath's container-merge logic and can carry true duplicate top-level `security-zone <name>` siblings into the compiler.

## Severity

HIGH — silent, undetected loss of a security zone's interface/host-inbound/address-book configuration from a supported operator workflow (`load override`) with no commit-time warning. Blast radius: packets on the dropped zone's interfaces lose zone association, causing either fail-closed drops or matching the wrong policy set, depending on default zone handling. Bounded by requiring a duplicate top-level block in the loaded file (not triggered by routine `set`/`load merge` usage).

## #4819 — config: duplicate hierarchical ssh-known-hosts host blocks overwrite instead of merge [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

The `ssh-known-hosts` case in `pkg/config/compiler_security.go:52-63` builds a fresh `keys []SSHKnownHostKey` slice per `host` AST instance from `namedInstances(child.FindChildren("host"))` and does an unconditional `sec.SSHKnownHosts[hostInst.name] = keys`. If the same host name appears as two sibling AST nodes (each with a different key type), the second overwrites the first, silently dropping the first block's key(s).

## Reachability

Same class of bug as #4816/#4817 — see #4816 for the full `SetPath`-merge vs. `parseStatements`-append analysis. The NORMAL, single-block Junos form for multiple key types on one host —
```
host h1 {
    ssh-rsa "AAAA...";
    ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 "AAAA...";
}
```
— is handled correctly today: both keys land as children of ONE `host`/`h1` node, and the `for _, kp := range hostInst.node.Children` loop collects both into `keys`. Two sequential `set security ssh-known-hosts host h1 ssh-rsa ...` / `set security ssh-known-hosts host h1 ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 ...` CLI commands also merge correctly via `ConfigTree.SetPath`'s container-reuse (`pkg/config/ast_edit.go:211`), refuting the review's literal claimed trigger.

The bug IS reachable via `load merge terminal` / `load override` with a hand-authored config containing two SEPARATE `host h1 { ... }` blocks (each with a different key type) — the hierarchical parser (`pkg/config/parser.go:119`) keeps them as distinct same-key siblings with no merge, and this compiler case has no dedup/merge logic.

## Trace

1. Operator `load merge`s a config where `host h1` is defined as two separate blocks (e.g. from merging two config fragments that each add a different key type for the same host):
   ```
   host h1 { ssh-rsa "AAAA..."; }
   host h1 { ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 "AAAA..."; }
   ```
2. `namedInstances` returns two `host` instances both named `h1`.
3. First iteration: `keys = [{ssh-rsa, ...}]`, stored at `sec.SSHKnownHosts["h1"]`.
4. Second iteration: fresh `keys = [{ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ...}]` overwrites `sec.SSHKnownHosts["h1"]` — the RSA key is silently dropped.
5. If the remote host later presents its RSA key (the dropped type) during an SSH-based connection (e.g. HA cluster config sync, automated SSH service) that xpf verifies against known-hosts, verification fails with no indication that a valid key was ever configured but lost.

## Fix direction

Append to the existing slice instead of replacing it:
```go
sec.SSHKnownHosts[hostInst.name] = append(sec.SSHKnownHosts[hostInst.name], keys...)
```

## Severity

LOW-MEDIUM (review labeled Medium; kept in that range) — not reachable via ordinary sequential `set` commands, only via `load merge`/`load override` with a hand-duplicated block. Impact when triggered is an availability/ops issue (SSH host-key verification failure for the dropped key type), not a silent security downgrade (a missing known-hosts entry causes verification to fail-closed, not accept an unverified host).

## Correction to the reviewed trace

The reviewed trace used two `set security ssh-known-hosts host h1 ...` commands. Refuted for the same reason as #4818/#4820 — `SetPath` merges same-key containers, so flat `set`/`load merge` cannot produce this. Only `LoadOverride` of hierarchical text with a genuine duplicate top-level `host` block reaches this path.

## Evidence (origin/master @ cbf1ee3ce)

`pkg/config/compiler_security.go:52-63`:
```go
case "ssh-known-hosts":
    sec.SSHKnownHosts = make(map[string][]SSHKnownHostKey)
    for _, hostInst := range namedInstances(child.FindChildren("host")) {
        var keys []SSHKnownHostKey
        for _, kp := range hostInst.node.Children {
            name := kp.Name()
            if v := nodeVal(kp); v != "" {
                keys = append(keys, SSHKnownHostKey{Type: name, Key: v})
            }
        }
        sec.SSHKnownHosts[hostInst.name] = keys
    }
```

## Fix

`sec.SSHKnownHosts[hostInst.name] = append(sec.SSHKnownHosts[hostInst.name], keys...)` instead of a plain assignment.

## Validation performed

Same pattern/reachability analysis as #4818 (security zones) and #4820 (RPM probes) — all three share the identical `namedInstances`-loop-overwrite root cause, only reachable via `LoadOverride`.

## Severity

MEDIUM — dropping a valid host key type causes SSH host-key verification failures for automated/HA-cluster SSH usage against that host when the server presents the dropped key type. Requires a `load override` with a duplicate top-level `host` block.

## Summary
`probePinManager.clear()` (`pkg/routing/probe_pin.go`) swallows the netlink
*list* errors from `RuleList` / `RouteListFiltered` with a bare `continue`
and then unconditionally `return nil`. The dump-failure case is therefore
invisible to the caller, and `clear()`'s wired-up error return is dead code.

## Evidence (origin/master)
`pkg/routing/probe_pin.go`, `clear()`:
```go
func (p *probePinManager) clear() error {
	for _, family := range []int{unix.AF_INET, unix.AF_INET6} {
		rules, err := p.ops.RuleList(family)
		if err != nil {
			continue            // <-- list failure swallowed
		}
		...
		routes, err := p.ops.RouteListFiltered(family, ...)
		if err != nil {
			continue            // <-- list failure swallowed
		}
		...
	}
	return nil                  // <-- always nil, even if every dump failed
}
```
The caller `Apply()` already contains error-handling plumbing that can never fire:
```go
func (p *probePinManager) Apply(pins []ProbePin) map[string]error {
	if err := p.clear(); err != nil {          // <-- clear() never returns non-nil
		slog.Warn("failed to clear probe pin band", "err", err)
	}
	...
```

## Failure trace
1. `Apply()` runs at daemon start / config apply and calls `clear()` to flush
   the reserved probe-pin rule band + probe tables before re-programming.
2. A transient dump failure (e.g. `ENOBUFS` during a rule/route dump) makes
   `RuleList` / `RouteListFiltered` return an error.
3. `clear()` `continue`s past the failed family/table and returns `nil`.

## #4827 — config: validateFirewallFilterFamilyCollisionsAST indexes afNode.Keys[0] without an empty-slice guard [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`validateFirewallFilterFamilyCollisionsAST` (`pkg/config/compiler_firewall.go:328-`) accesses `afNode.Keys[0]` (and conditionally `Keys[1]`) with no length check:

```go
af := afName
if af == "" {
    af = afNode.Keys[0]
    if len(afNode.Keys) >= 2 {
        af = afNode.Keys[1]
    }
}
```
(`compiler_firewall.go:365-368`)

## Reachability

Every `Node` produced by the live parser (`pkg/config/parser.go` `parseStatement`, which bails out before constructing a node when `len(keys)==0`) or by `ConfigTree.SetPath` (which always seeds `Keys` with at least the consumed keyword tokens) structurally guarantees `len(Keys) >= 1`. So this is **not reachable through normal config parsing** — the `af == ""` empty-keys branch (the "Set-command shape: family { inet { ... } inet6 { ... } }" case) only ever sees `afNode` values drawn from `familyNode.Children`, which are themselves parser/SetPath-constructed nodes.

The one path that bypasses those invariants is `pkg/configstore/db.go:276`, `json.Unmarshal(data, tree)` — the candidate/active `ConfigTree` is deserialized from the on-disk store with plain `encoding/json` and no `Node.UnmarshalJSON` validator. A corrupted or hand-edited on-disk DB file (disk corruption, manual tampering, or a future encoder bug) could produce a persisted `Node{Keys: []string{}, ...}` under a `firewall family { ... }` block, which would panic this function with an out-of-range index when that store is next loaded and re-validated.

## Fix

```go
af = afNode.Name()  // Name() safely returns "" for an empty Keys slice
if len(afNode.Keys) >= 2 {
    af = afNode.Keys[1]
}
```

## Validation performed

Traced every `Node` construction site in `pkg/config/parser.go` and `pkg/config/ast_edit.go` (`SetPath`) and confirmed both structurally guarantee `len(Keys) >= 1`, so this is not reachable via any parse of operator-supplied config text — only via `pkg/configstore/db.go`'s plain `json.Unmarshal` of a persisted (and potentially corrupted) `ConfigTree`.

## Severity

LOW — cheap defense-in-depth fix; the crash requires a corrupted/malformed on-disk config-store file, not attacker- or operator-reachable config text. Matches the project's fail-closed-on-load stance (#1960) that a bad persisted state should error, not panic.

## #4829 — configstore/journal: Log() holds the single mutex across synchronous fsync, blocking Tail() reads [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-11)

## Summary

`Journal.Log()` and `Journal.Tail()` (`pkg/configstore/journal/journal.go`) share a single `sync.Mutex` (`j.mu`, `journal.go:100`). `Log()` holds it across `f.Write` + a synchronous `f.Sync()` and, on rotation/creation, `fsatomic.SyncDir()` (`journal.go:157-224`). `Tail()` (`journal.go:262-284`) takes the same mutex purely to read already-written segment files. A commit/rollback/system-action append that's mid-`fsync` on a busy or slow disk blocks any concurrent `show system commit` / commit-history REST query for the full fsync duration (can be hundreds of ms).

## Evidence (origin/master @ cbf1ee3ce)

`pkg/configstore/journal/journal.go:157-159, 216-221`:
```go
func (j *Journal) Log(entry *Entry) error {
	j.mu.Lock()
	defer j.mu.Unlock()
	...
	if _, err := f.Write(buf); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write journal entry: %w", err)
	}
	if err := f.Sync(); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("sync journal: %w", err)
	}
	if created || rotated {
		if err := fsatomic.SyncDir(filepath.Dir(j.path)); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("sync journal dir: %w", err)
		}
	}
	return nil
}
```
`journal.go:262-264`:
```go
func (j *Journal) Tail(limit int) ([]*Entry, error) {
	j.mu.Lock()
	defer j.mu.Unlock()
	...
```

## Fix

A plain `RWMutex` is not a drop-in fix without care: the type's own doc comment notes readers must be serialized against segment rotation too ("a reader that opens the current segment while Log rotates it to '.1' would read the same inode under both names and duplicate entries"). A correct fix needs either (a) a dedicated rotation-state lock separate from the per-write fsync, so `Tail` only blocks on the (fast) rotation step and not the fsync, or (b) performing the `f.Sync()`/`SyncDir()` calls after releasing `j.mu` (the file itself is already fully written at that point; only the rotation bookkeeping needs the lock).

## #4830 — pkg/ra: time.After inside select in releaseDrain/waitConnReady leaves an unstopped timer scheduled [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

Two `select` blocks race a channel receive against `time.After(claimWaitTimeout)` (5s). When the channel case fires first, the `time.Timer` allocated by `time.After` is not stopped — it stays live in the runtime's timer heap for up to `claimWaitTimeout` before firing and being reclaimed. Standard Go footgun (`time.NewTimer` + deferred `Stop()` is the fix), here in two places:

`pkg/ra/ra.go:138-148` (`releaseDrain`):
```go
select {
case <-s.stopped:
case <-time.After(claimWaitTimeout):
    ...
}
```
`pkg/ra/sender.go:222-228` (`sender.waitConnReady`):
```go
select {
case <-s.connReady:
    return s.connOpened.Load()
case <-time.After(timeout):
    return false
}
```

## Fix

```go
t := time.NewTimer(claimWaitTimeout)
defer t.Stop()
select {
case <-s.stopped:
case <-t.C:
    ...
}
```

## Validation performed

Confirmed both current call sites on origin/master use `time.After` directly inside `select` with no `Stop()`/reuse.

## #4831 — dead code: userspaceSupportsSourceNAT (pkg/dataplane/userspace/capabilities.go) is unused and encodes stale pre-pool-SNAT logic [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

Triage of a no-evidence Gemini review finding ("Finding 15") against origin/master (fac171b1da42c99942de8ea4256fc8a5c746ac5b). The review gave only a title; evidence below was located and verified independently.

## What the code is

pkg/dataplane/userspace/capabilities.go:492
```go
func userspaceSupportsSourceNAT(ruleSets []*config.NATRuleSet) bool {
	for _, rs := range ruleSets {
		if rs == nil { continue }
		for _, rule := range rs.Rules {
			if rule == nil { continue }
			if rule.Then.Interface || rule.Then.Off { continue }
			return false   // any non-interface (i.e. pool) SNAT => "unsupported"
		}
	}
	return true
}
```

## Why it is dead + stale

- **Unused:** `git grep -n "userspaceSupportsSourceNAT" origin/master --` returns ONLY the definition at capabilities.go:492. No caller anywhere in the tree (prod or test). Because it is an unexported function, the compiler does not flag it (only unused *locals* are a compile error), so it sits silently.
- **Stale / conflicting logic:** the function reports pool-mode SNAT as unsupported (returns `false` for any rule whose `Then` is not `Interface`/`Off`). That contradicts the current design — the sibling comment in the same file (capabilities.go:73) states: *"Pool-mode source NAT is now implemented in the userspace dataplane"*. The live capability gate `userspaceConfigUsesPersistentSourceNAT` (capabilities.go:116, called at :87) is the one actually used. So this leftover encodes an obsolete "pool SNAT not supported" rule that would give a WRONG answer if anyone re-wired it.

## Impact

None at runtime today (dead). Risk is future drift: a reader could resurrect it as a capability check and silently regress pool-SNAT admission. Low severity, cleanup.

## Fix

Delete `userspaceSupportsSourceNAT` (and its now-unused imports if any). If a source-NAT capability gate is wanted, it should be derived from the current userspace SNAT support matrix, not this pre-pool-SNAT relic.

Severity: Low (dead code / hygiene). Origin: Gemini review-043 Finding 15 (no-evidence; verified in triage).

## #4832 — test-coverage gap: (*CLI).testRouting longest-prefix route lookup (pkg/cli/cli_request_testcmd.go) is untested [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-11)

Triage of a no-evidence Gemini review finding ("Finding 20") against origin/master (fac171b1da42c99942de8ea4256fc8a5c746ac5b). The review gave only a title; evidence below was located and verified independently.

## What is untested

`(*CLI).testRouting` at pkg/cli/cli_request_testcmd.go:226 backs `run test routing destination <ip-or-prefix> [instance <name>]`. It contains non-trivial logic that can regress silently:

- **CIDR normalization:** a bare address is padded to `/32` (v4) or `/128` (v6) before matching (cli_request_testcmd.go:265-272).
- **Longest-prefix match:** it walks all routes, `net.ParseCIDR`-parses each `Destination`, and keeps the most-specific `rNet.Contains(filterIP)` hit via `ones, _ := rNet.Mask.Size()` (cli_request_testcmd.go:280-294).
- **VRF vs global:** `instance != ""` routes through `GetVRFRoutes(instance)` else `GetRoutes()` (:254-258).
- v4/v6 handling and the `filterErr` fallback to `net.ParseIP`.

## Evidence of the gap

- `git grep -ln "testRouting\|GetVRFRoutes" origin/master -- pkg/cli/*_test.go cmd/cli/*_test.go` → no test file exercises `testRouting`.
- The sibling handler in the SAME file, `testSecurityZone`, IS covered (pkg/cli/host_inbound_display_3654_test.go:93,109), so the asymmetry is clear: the zone lookup has a regression test, the route lookup does not.

## Why it matters

LPM selection + CIDR normalization is exactly the kind of arithmetic that regresses without notice (e.g. a `>=` vs `>` on `ones`, a v6 default padding bug, or a VRF/global mixup). A table-driven test over a small synthetic route set would lock in: exact-host match, longest-prefix selection among overlapping routes, v6 default, VRF-instance path, and no-match.

## Fix

Add `pkg/cli/cli_request_testcmd_test.go` with a mock routing manager returning a fixed `[]routing.RouteEntry`, asserting the selected best route for several destinations (incl. v6 and instance cases) and the "No matching route found" path.

Severity: Low (test-coverage). Origin: Gemini review-043 Finding 20 (no-evidence; verified in triage).

## #4834 — config: no commit-time validation of SNMP community 'clients' prefixes — mistyped 'restrict' keyword silently flips a deny-except allowlist to allow-all (SNMP fail-open) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

The `snmp community <c> clients { <prefix> [restrict]; ... }` source-IP allowlist is not validated at commit time. Every token in the list is accepted as-is; an unparseable token is silently dropped at compile time (`compileClientNets`, inert). This is fail-closed for a mistyped *prefix* (good), but it is **fail-open** for a mistyped `restrict` keyword: the typo detaches `restrict` from a broad prefix, turning a `0.0.0.0/0 restrict` (deny-all-except) entry into a plain `0.0.0.0/0` allow entry, and the community becomes answerable from **any** source IP.

This is a residual gap in the same fail-closed doctrine established by #4289/#4711 (SNMP `clients` enforcement) — the enforcement itself is correct, but nothing stops a commit from producing a config the operator did not intend.

## Root cause

- Schema leaf accepts arbitrary tokens with no value typing:
  `pkg/config/schema_system.go:966`
  ```go
  "clients": {desc: "...", args: 1, multi: true, placeholder: "<prefix>", children: nil},
  ```
  No `valueType`, so `SchemaValidate` performs no prefix/keyword check.
- `parseSNMPClients` (`pkg/config/snmp_clients.go`) treats **any** token that is not the literal string `restrict` as a new prefix entry:
  ```go
  if t == "restrict" { out[len(out)-1].Restrict = true; continue }
  out = append(out, SNMPClient{Prefix: t})
  ```
  A mistyped `restric`/`restrictt` becomes a bogus prefix entry AND leaves the preceding broad prefix as a plain *allow*.
- `compileClientNets` (`pkg/config/snmp_clients.go`) silently skips the unparseable bogus token ("inert, never a silent allow-all") — but the detached broad prefix survives as an allow.
- `SNMPCommunity.AllowsSource` (`pkg/config/snmp_clients.go`) does longest-prefix match; `0.0.0.0/0` (ones=0, restrict=false) matches every source → allow.
- Enforcement is live on the real serving path: `pkg/snmp/agent.go:588` `if !comm.AllowsSource(srcIP)` with `srcIP` from the UDP `remoteAddr.IP` (`agent.go:490-494`).

## Concrete fail-open trace

Idiomatic Junos "deny all except the mgmt subnet":
```
set snmp community mon clients 0.0.0.0/0 restrict
set snmp community mon clients 10.0.0.0/8
```
`AllowsSource(8.8.8.8)`: `0.0.0.0/0 restrict` (ones=0, deny) is beaten only inside 10/8 → any outside source is **denied**. Correct.

Now the operator fat-fingers the keyword:
```
set snmp community mon clients 0.0.0.0/0 restric      # typo: "restric"
set snmp community mon clients 10.0.0.0/8
```
`parseSNMPClients` produces `{Prefix:"0.0.0.0/0"}`, `{Prefix:"restric"}`, `{Prefix:"10.0.0.0/8"}`. `compileClientNets` drops `restric`, keeps `0.0.0.0/0` as **allow** and `10.0.0.0/8` as allow. `AllowsSource(8.8.8.8)` now matches `0.0.0.0/0` (ones=0, allow) → **allow-all**. The community is answerable from the entire Internet with **no commit warning**. (Both AST shapes — flat-set/bracket and hierarchical block — reach the same result.)

## #4835 — EventStream.writeFrame releases es.mu before SetWriteDeadline+Write — concurrent callers (ackLoop vs Pause/Resume/RequestDrain) race on the same conn [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`EventStream.writeFrame` takes `es.mu` only long enough to read `es.conn`,
then releases it before calling `conn.SetWriteDeadline` and `conn.Write`.
Multiple goroutines call `writeFrame` independently — the periodic
`ackLoop` goroutine (100ms ticker) and the `Pause`/`Resume`/`RequestDrain`
call sites — so two callers can be inside the unlocked
`SetWriteDeadline`+`Write` section of the SAME connection at the same time,
with no mutual exclusion.

## Evidence (origin/master @ cbf1ee3ce)

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/eventstream.go:794-824`:

```go
func (es *EventStream) writeFrame(typ uint8, seq uint64, payload []byte) error {
	es.mu.Lock()
	conn := es.conn
	es.mu.Unlock()
	if conn == nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("event stream not connected")
	}
	...
	_ = conn.SetWriteDeadline(time.Now().Add(2 * time.Second))
	if len(payload) == 0 {
		_, err := conn.Write(hdr[:])
		...
	}
	...
	_, err := conn.Write(buf)
	...
}
```

Independent callers on independent goroutines:
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/eventstream.go:760-773` (`ackLoop`, its own
  goroutine on a 100ms ticker) → `sendAckIfNeeded` → `writeFrame(EventTypeAck, ...)`.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/eventstream.go:184,190,225` (`Pause`, `Resume`,
  `RequestDrain`) → `writeFrame(...)`, called from whatever goroutine
  drives HA/drain state transitions (a different call path than `ackLoop`).

## #4837 — config: DDNS forced-refresh / error-backoff-max silently ignore a malformed value (falls back to default with no commit error) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary

`system services dynamic-dns forced-refresh <value>` and `... error-backoff-max <value>` accept a Go duration string or a bare-seconds integer, but a value that parses as neither is silently discarded — the field is left unset (falls back to its downstream default) with no commit-time error or warning telling the operator their value was rejected.

## Evidence (origin/master @ cbf1ee3ce)

`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:599-610` (`parseDurationSeconds`):
```go
func parseDurationSeconds(v string) int {
	v = strings.TrimSpace(v)
	if v == "" {
		return 0
	}
	if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil {
		return n
	}
	if d, err := time.ParseDuration(v); err == nil {
		return int(d.Seconds())
	}
	return 0
}
```

`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:561-570` (`compileDDNSServices`):
```go
if v := ddnsServicesScalar(node, "forced-refresh"); v != "" {
	if s := parseDurationSeconds(v); s > 0 {
		cat.ForcedRefreshSeconds = s
	}
}
if v := ddnsServicesScalar(node, "error-backoff-max"); v != "" {
	if s := parseDurationSeconds(v); s > 0 {
		cat.ErrorBackoffMaxSeconds = s
	}
}
```

No caller of `compileDDNSServices` checks whether `v != ""` but `parseDurationSeconds(v) == 0` (i.e., a non-empty value that failed to parse) and emits a commit warning/error for that case — the schema validator file (`pkg/config/schema_validators_ddns.go`) only validates the hostname leaf, not these two tunables.

## #4839 — refactor: pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol.go — 3,064-LOC / 78-struct wire-protocol god file, split per domain [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-22)

From the gemini-review-044 defensive-refactor audit (base/current master `03a92b49c`). Triaged GENUINE and novel — not covered by the existing refactor backlog (#4404/#4407/#4408/#4409/#4421 do not mention `protocol.go`).

## Current master

- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol.go` — **3,064 LOC**, **78 `type … struct` definitions** in a single file. No `protocol_<domain>.go` split files exist today (only `protocol_test.go` siblings).
- Anchors: `ControlRequest` (L29), `ControlResponse` (L47), `ConfigSnapshot` (L54), `ZoneSnapshot` (L205), `ClassOfServiceSnapshot` (L317), `TunnelEndpointSnapshot` (L434), `SourceNATRuleSnapshot` (L531), `PolicyRuleSnapshot` (L1212), `RouteSnapshot` (L1292), `HAStateUpdateRequest` (L2166).

## Why it's over the modularity threshold

3,064 LOC is well past the project's ~2,000-production-LOC modularity bar, and this is the single file every developer touches when adding a field to *any* subsystem's control-plane wire message (NAT, policy, CoS, HA, zones, tunnels, routes). That guarantees frequent merge conflicts and makes the serializable-types database hard to browse. This is the lowest-risk high-value cut on the list: pure compile-time type organization within one Go package.

## Suggested split (mechanical, same `userspace` package)

Move domain struct clusters into per-domain files, keep the core envelope types in `protocol.go`:
- `protocol_nat.go` — `SourceNATRuleSnapshot`, `StaticNATRuleSnapshot`, `DestinationNATRuleSnapshot`, `NAT64RuleSnapshot`, `Nptv6RuleSnapshot`, `NatPortRangeWire`, `NatAppTermWire`.
- `protocol_policies.go` — `PolicyRuleSnapshot`, `FirewallFilterSnapshot`, `FirewallTermSnapshot`, `FlexMatchSnapshot`, `PolicerSnapshot`, `ThreeColorPolicerSnapshot`.
- `protocol_cos.go` — `ClassOfServiceSnapshot` + CoS/DSCP/scheduler snapshots.
- `protocol_zones.go` — `ZoneSnapshot`, `ScreenProfileSnapshot`, `ScreenMissingProfileRef`.
- `protocol_tunnels.go` — `TunnelEndpointSnapshot`, `TunnelWgPeerWire`.
- `protocol_routes.go` — `RouteSnapshot`.
- `protocol_ha.go` — `HAStateUpdateRequest`, `SessionSyncRequest`, `SessionDeltaDrainRequest`, `SessionExportRequest`, `SessionDeltaInfo`.
- Keep `ControlRequest`/`ControlResponse`/`ConfigSnapshot`/`ProcessStatus`/`BindingStatus`/`WorkerRuntimeStatus` in `protocol.go`.

## Invariants / gate

- **Zero behavior change**: this is code-motion only. Every `json:"…"` tag MUST be preserved byte-identical — the Rust `userspace-dp` helper deserializes these structs, so a renamed/omitted tag is a wire break.
- No hot-path impact (Go control-plane serialization; struct layout unchanged).
- Gate: `go test ./pkg/dataplane/userspace/...` (incl. `protocol_test.go`, `protocol_failopen_2124_test.go`, `protocol_null_collections_2214_test.go`) + a JSON round-trip parity check against the Rust deserializer.

Driveable-now pure code-motion (class A / mechanical).

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tests.rs` — **8,342 LOC**

Both remain monolithic catch-alls even though their modules have *already* extracted many focused sibling test files:

## #4845 — refactor: pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go — 3,600-LOC warn-validator monolith, split per-domain (mirror the strict split) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-10)

## Summary

`pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go` is **3,600 prod LOC / 39 funcs** on current master (`0b5e9cb4c`), well past the `docs/engineering-style.md` modularity discipline (~2,000 LOC = split before next substantive change; ~3,000 = must split). It collapses ~16 cross-domain WARN validators into one file, all aggregated by `ValidateConfig` (line 85).

The **strict** counterpart was already split per-domain (#4405 CLOSED took `compiler_validate_strict.go` 6,997 → 478 LOC + per-domain files like `compiler_validate_strict_nat.go`). The **warn** side never followed and has kept growing.

## Evidence (current master `0b5e9cb4c`)

- File: `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go` — 3,600 LOC, 39 funcs.
- `ValidateConfig` — `:85` — aggregates all warn validators into one `[]string`.
- Domain-spread validators (all in this one file):
  - Host-inbound / policy-log: `validateHostInboundMulticastWarnings` `:1658`, `validateDefaultPolicyLogWarnings` `:2039`, `validatePolicyLogInertOnDenyWarnings` `:2095`, `validateJunosHostDirectDeliveryWarnings` `:2227`, `validatePreIDDefaultPolicyLogWarnings` `:2286`
  - Firewall/filter: `validateFilterLossPriorityWarnings` `:2314`, `validateFirewallInterfaceSpecificWarnings` `:2356`, `validateFilterNoCatchAllWarnings` `:2520`
  - DDNS: `validateDDNSBackendWarnings` `:2678`, `validateSurfaceADDNSWarnings` `:2939` (+ ddns* helpers)
  - Interface/DHCP: `validateDHCPRelayParityWarnings` `:1882`, `validateInterfaceParityWarnings` `:1925`
  - Routing: `validateRoutingRuleWindowWarnings` `:3272`, `validateRibGroupLeakWarnings` `:3336`
  - CoS: `validateCoSOversubscriptionWarnings` `:3409`, `classOfServiceClassifierQueueWarnings` `:3479`

## Why it is over threshold / matters

3,600 LOC in one file is the top merge-conflict surface in `pkg/config` alongside metrics descriptors; every warn-validator PR (across ~10 unrelated domains) touches the same file, and locating "where are the firewall warnings" requires grepping 3,600 lines. The strict validators were split for exactly this reason.

`pkg/config/compiler_nat.go` is **2,565 prod LOC / 37 funcs** on current master (`0b5e9cb4c`), over the `docs/engineering-style.md` ~2,000-LOC modularity threshold. It triply fuses three unrelated concerns in one file:

## #4857 — dhcp: ClearDUID derives state-file path from unvalidated interface name -> arbitrary root file unlink (path traversal) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
`Manager.ClearDUID` derives a state-file path directly from an unvalidated interface
string and passes it to `os.Remove`, allowing a control-plane caller to unlink an
arbitrary root-owned file via `..` traversal.

## Current master (29a046ec5)
- `pkg/dhcp/dhcp.go:613` `duidPath` joins the raw identifier:
  `return filepath.Join(m.stateDir, "dhcpv6-duid-"+ifaceName)`
- `pkg/dhcp/dhcp.go:527` `ClearDUID` calls `os.Remove(m.duidPath(ifaceName))` with no
  validation of `ifaceName`.
- `pkg/api/dhcp.go:95` forwards the REST `req.Interface` field verbatim:
  `s.dhcp.ClearDUID(req.Interface)`. The gRPC path is equivalent.

## Scenario (input -> wrong output)
A REST/gRPC request sets `interface` to `../../../../../etc/passwd`. The joined path is
`/var/lib/xpf/dhcpv6-duid-../../../../../etc/passwd`, which normalizes to `/etc/passwd`.
`xpfd` (root) then runs `os.Remove` on it. Any unlinkable root-owned file reachable by a
sufficiently deep traversal can be deleted. The fixed `dhcpv6-duid-` prefix only alters
the first `..` component.

## Fix
Reject anything that is not a canonical Linux interface name before all DUID path ops:
reject `/`, `\`, `.`/`..` components and NUL; verify the cleaned result stays under the
cleaned `stateDir`. Prefer a reversible filename encoding or a keyed map over embedding
the raw identifier. Add REST + gRPC traversal tests and a direct containment unit test.

## Severity justification
security. Trigger: single crafted `interface` value on the DHCP-DUID-clear RPC. Blast
radius: arbitrary root file unlink (DoS / weakened boot). Fail-open (no containment
check). Bounding: the control plane binds loopback only (127.0.0.1 REST/gRPC), so the
caller must already reach the local API — this is a privilege-boundary / defense-in-depth
break rather than a remote RCE, which is why it is a bug/security issue rather than
Critical.

Source: Codex review 175 finding C175-HC-020 (A10-b3), re-verified on current master.

## #4858 — cli: 'request system zeroize' never deletes /etc/xpf/.configdb -> config + master.key survive and re-activate on reboot (false factory reset) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
`request system zeroize` deletes only legacy `*.conf` / `rollback*` files under
`/etc/xpf` and never removes the authoritative config database `/etc/xpf/.configdb`
(active/candidate/rollback trees, `master.key`) or `.config.journal`. It reports
`System zeroized. Configuration erased.` and, on the next reboot, the daemon reloads the
"erased" configuration and secrets from the surviving DB.

## Current master (29a046ec5)
- `pkg/cli/cli_request_system.go:57` (`case "zeroize"`): the wipe loop at lines 69-74 only
  removes names ending `.conf` or beginning `rollback` in `/etc/xpf`, then
  `os.RemoveAll("/sys/fs/bpf/xpf")` and networkd files. No `.configdb` / `.config.journal`
  removal. All `ReadDir`/`Remove`/`systemctl` errors are discarded.
- `pkg/configstore/store.go:195` `New` opens `.configdb` with "no file-only fallback".
- `pkg/configstore/store_persist.go:18` `Load` reads the active tree from that DB on start.

## Scenario
Super-user confirms zeroize. `.configdb/{active,candidate,rollback.N}.json`, `master.key`,
and `.config.journal` survive. Command prints success and asks for reboot. On reboot
`configstore.New` + `Store.Load` restore the prior tenant's policy, credentials, and keys.

## Fix
Route zeroize through one shared, tested factory-reset primitive (shared with any RPC
path): stop mutators, `RemoveAll` the full `.configdb` directory + enumerated sibling
artifacts with checked errors, fsync parents, and report success only after verification.
Add a temp-dir test that commits a secret, runs the wipe, rebuilds a `Store`, and asserts
startup is empty.

## Severity justification
security / data-remanence. Trigger: normal `request system zeroize` on any box using the
`.configdb` store (the default). Fail-open: success reported while authoritative config +
encryption keys persist and re-activate after reboot. Blast radius: a decommissioned /
repurposed / handed-off appliance leaks the previous tenant's full config and secrets.
Distinct from indexed in-memory key-zeroization (F-038-031) and journaling (F8): this is
the on-disk DB not being deleted at all.

Source: Codex review 175 finding C175-HC-022 (A10-b2), re-verified on current master.

## #4859 — cli RBAC: operator can 'forwarding disarm' / queue-unregister / ISSU-drain — destructive dataplane verbs omitted from the PermMaint maintenance gate [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
The RBAC maintenance gate classifies only `request system {reboot,halt,power-off,zeroize}`
and `request chassis cluster failover` as `PermMaint`. The destructive dataplane-control
leaves `request chassis cluster data-plane userspace {forwarding disarm | queue ...
unregister/disarm | binding ... unregister/disarm}` and `software in-service-upgrade`
resolve to plain `PermControl`, which the predefined `operator` class holds. An operator
account can therefore take forwarding out of service or force RGs secondary.

## Current master (29a046ec5)
- `pkg/cli/permissions.go:175` `requestSubcommandIsMaintenance` returns true only for
  `system reboot/halt/power-off/zeroize` and `chassis cluster failover`; every other
  `request` verb falls through to `PermControl` (permissions.go:147/155).
- `pkg/cli/cli_request_chassis.go:180-206` dispatch: `forwarding`/`queue`/`binding` reach
  `provider.SetForwardingArmed(...)` / `SetQueueState(...)` / binding teardown with no
  second permission check or confirmation.
- `pkg/config/types_system.go` `LoginClassPermissions`: `operator = {PermView, PermClear,
  PermControl}`; maintenance is deliberately super-user-only.

## Scenario
`operator` runs `request chassis cluster data-plane userspace forwarding disarm`.
`checkPermission` maps it to `PermControl` (operator has it), dispatch calls
`SetForwardingArmed(false)`, and forwarding stops on the active node.

## Fix
Classify `request` verbs by resolved leaf + operation, not just the first three tokens.
Require `PermMaint` for forwarding/queue/binding `disarm|unregister`, ISSU ownership
drain, and packet injection if retained in production; keep read/status and restorative
`arm|register` at the lower level. Add positive/negative tests per leaf and abbreviation.

## Severity justification
security / authorization / availability. Trigger: one operator-class command. Fail-open:
a class explicitly denied maintenance can stop forwarding / force ownership away. Blast
radius: network outage across zones on the active firewall. Distinct residual of the
indexed F21 fix, which gated only reboot/halt/power-off/zeroize/failover — these userspace
control + ISSU leaves were never added.

Source: Codex review 175 finding C175-HC-014 (A10-b2), re-verified on current master.

## #4860 — cli: view-only 'show log <file>' reads any root-readable file under /var/log (no syslog allowlist) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
`show log <filename>` lets any class with only `PermView` read an arbitrary root-readable
file directly under `/var/log`. The root daemon runs `tail` against the caller-supplied
basename with no configured-syslog allowlist, returning content the CLI account could not
otherwise read.

## Current master (29a046ec5)
- `pkg/cli/cli_show_system.go` `showDaemonLog`: if `args[0]` is non-numeric it is treated
  as a filename; `logPath := filepath.Join("/var/log", filepath.Base(filename))` then
  `exec.Command("tail", "-n", ..., logPath).CombinedOutput()`.
- `pkg/cli/permissions.go:151` maps `show` to `PermView`.

## Scenario
A read-only / config-viewer account runs `show log auth.log`, `show log audit.log`,
`show log dpkg.log`, etc. `filepath.Base` blocks traversal but there is no allowlist, so
the daemon returns any root-readable child of `/var/log` (auth/audit/package/service logs
containing usernames, source addresses, tokens, operational detail).

## Fix
Restrict `show log <name>` to the configured syslog/event log file set (an allowlist),
or gate arbitrary host-log reads behind a higher permission than `PermView`. Reject names
not in the allowlist rather than shelling `tail` on any basename.

## Severity justification
security / information-disclosure. Trigger: one `show log <name>` from a view-only
account. Fail-open: privilege escalation of read scope (view-only -> host logs). Bounding:
confined to `/var/log` direct children (no traversal), and requires an authenticated CLI
account, which is why it is security/bug rather than Critical. Not covered by the secret
config-redaction findings.

Source: Codex review 175 finding C175-HC-099 (A10-b2), re-verified on current master.

## #4861 — ddns: credentialed HTTP backends accept plaintext http:// endpoints and follow HTTPS->HTTP redirect downgrades (credential exposure) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
Credentialed HTTP DDNS backends (dyndns2, DuckDNS, Cloudflare, Route53) accept plaintext
`http://` endpoints and follow HTTPS->HTTP redirect downgrades under the default client
policy, transmitting Basic credentials / query tokens / bearer tokens / SigV4 auth without
TLS.

## Current master (29a046ec5)
- `pkg/ddns/backend_dyndns2.go:109` / `:209`, `pkg/ddns/backend_cloudflare.go:54`,
  `pkg/ddns/backend_http.go:98`: build requests to the configured `server`/endpoint
  without enforcing `https` scheme, and the shared client does not block redirect
  downgrade to `http` for same-host sensitive headers/query credentials.

## Scenario
Configure `server http://...` (or an HTTPS endpoint that 30x-redirects to HTTP). The
provider credential is sent in cleartext; an on-path attacker recovers it, alters the
advertised firewall address, or replays updates. Route53/Cloudflare credentials often
have authority beyond a single hostname.

## Fix
Reject non-`https` endpoints for any backend that carries credentials (commit-time
validation), and set a `CheckRedirect` that refuses HTTPS->HTTP downgrade / strips
credentials on cross-scheme redirect. Add tests for plaintext-endpoint rejection and
redirect-downgrade credential stripping.

## Severity justification
security. Trigger: an operator configuring (or being redirected to) a plaintext endpoint.
Fail-open: credentials leave the box unencrypted. Blast radius: provider-account
compromise + DNS record tampering. Distinct from the fixed dyndns2 malformed host/scheme
validation (codex-review-157 M05): this is acceptance of valid-but-plaintext authenticated
endpoints across multiple backends.

Source: Codex review 175 finding C175-HC-074 (A10-b3), re-verified on current master.

## #4862 — config parser: top-level unmatched '}' stops parsing with zero errors and silently drops all trailing config (fail-open) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
`Parser.Parse()` never asserts the lexer reached EOF, and `parseStatements()` treats a top-level `TokenRBrace` identically to EOF. A single stray unmatched `}` at the top level of a hierarchical config makes the parser stop with **zero `ParseError`s** and silently drop every statement after the brace.

## Current-master evidence (90af98b9d)
- `pkg/config/parser.go:40-44` — `Parse()` calls `parseStatements()` once and returns `(tree, p.errors)` with no trailing-token / EOF check.
- `pkg/config/parser.go:145` — loop breaks on `if tok.Type == TokenEOF || tok.Type == TokenRBrace`. At the top level a `}` is not an error; the loop just returns the nodes collected so far.

## Failure scenario (input → wrong output)
Load-override / commit-check text such as:
```
system { host-name fw; } }        <-- stray unmatched brace
security { policies { ... deny ... } default-policy { deny-all; } }
```
1. `parseStatements()` collects the `system { ... }` node, then peeks `}`, and breaks.
2. `Parse()` returns the partial tree and **no errors**.
3. `LoadOverride`/`CheckText` only check `len(errs)==0`, so the truncated tree compiles/commits.
4. Everything after the stray `}` — including the `security` policy tail and default-policy — is silently discarded. The committed config is weaker than the authored file with no operator-visible warning.

This is a fail-open config-acceptance path: a single stray brace in an imported Junos config accepts a prefix and drops the security tail.

## Fix
Make a top-level `TokenRBrace` a parse error, OR have `Parse()` consume/verify the next token after `parseStatements()` and reject anything other than `TokenEOF`. Add tests for `system { ... } } security { ... }` proving a parse error and no tail drop.

## Severity justification
- **Exploitability/trigger:** low deliberate exploitability, but easily hit by accident when importing/pasting Junos config with an unbalanced brace.
- **Blast radius:** fail-OPEN — silently drops trailing security stanzas (deny/default-policy) with no error surfaced to the operator; the resulting firewall is weaker than authored.
- **Bounding factors:** requires the hierarchical (curly-brace) parse path; flat-`set` config is unaffected. The dropped tail must contain security-relevant statements to be dangerous.
- **Why not higher:** requires a malformed input rather than a normal one, and Junos operators typically review a commit diff. **Why not lower:** the total absence of any error on a structurally invalid config is the core danger — the system reports success while silently truncating policy.

Verified `pkg/config/parser.go` is unchanged since the review base (`git log 385f940b7..origin/master -- pkg/config/parser.go` is empty).

## #4863 — nat64: deterministic NAPT64 accepts IPv6 sources outside the configured subscriber prefix that share the subscriber word (wrong-tenant block + lying reverse map) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-09)

## Summary
Deterministic NAPT64 subscriber-index derivation checks only the 32-bit subscriber *word*, never the IPv6 prefix bytes **before** that word. A permitted IPv6 source in a **different** subscriber prefix that happens to share the same subscriber word is accepted and mapped into the in-prefix subscriber's fixed port block; the stateless reverse mapping then attributes it to the wrong (configured-base) subscriber.

## Current-master evidence (90af98b9d)
`userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs:291-323` `deterministic_indices_v6`:
```rust
let off = deterministic_v6_word_offset(params.host_prefix_len); // 4 for /32, 8 for /64
let src_word  = u32::from_be_bytes([src_octets[off..off+4]]);
let base_word = u32::from_be_bytes([params.host_base[off..off+4]]);
if src_word < base_word { return None; }
let sub_idx = src_word - base_word;
if sub_idx >= params.host_count { return None; }
```
There is **no** `src_octets[..off] == params.host_base[..off]` membership check. `reverse_deterministic_v6` (allocator.rs:334-370) reconstructs from `params.host_base`, so a wrong-prefix source is later reported as an in-prefix subscriber. `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs` `allocate_source` / `build_deterministic_v6` install no source-prefix predicate either.

## Failure scenario (input → wrong output)
Config: `deterministic_host_base_v6 = 2001:db8::`, `deterministic_host_prefix_len = 32`.
- In-prefix subscriber `2001:db8:0:5::` → `src_octets[4..8] = 00000005`, `sub_idx = 5`.
- Out-of-prefix source `2001:db9:0:5::` → also `src_octets[4..8] = 00000005`, `sub_idx = 5` → **accepted**, claims subscriber 5's deterministic block on `2001:db8::`.
- `reverse_deterministic_v6` maps the external `(IPv4,port)` back to `2001:db8:0:5::`, not the real `2001:db9:0:5::` source → the audit/reverse map lies.

## Fix
In `deterministic_indices_v6`, reject sources whose prefix bytes before the subscriber word differ from `params.host_base` (`src_octets[..off] != params.host_base[..off]` → `None`). Add red tests for /32 (`2001:db9:0:5::`) and /64 wrong-prefix/same-word fail-closed.

## Severity justification
- **Exploitability/trigger:** requires deterministic NAPT64 configured AND policy permitting the out-of-prefix source to reach the NAT64 destination prefix. In a normal CGN the subscriber prefix faces one interface, limiting reachability.
- **Blast radius:** correctness/isolation — deterministic CGN's whole value is stateless reverse mapping without per-flow logs; a lying reverse map defeats lawful-intercept/attribution, and a shared subscriber word lets one tenant/VRF consume/exhaust another's fixed block.
- **Bounding factors:** only sources sharing the same 32-bit subscriber word collide; forwarding still translates (not a forwarding bypass).
- **Why not higher:** no unauthenticated forwarding bypass; needs permit + colliding word. **Why not lower:** deterministic-NAT attribution is a compliance property, and the reverse map silently misidentifies the subscriber.

This is a bug in the #4559 deterministic-NAPT64 implementation (not a duplicate of #4559, which tracked the feature's dataplane enforcement). `allocator.rs` has no source-prefix fix since base.
