## #5753 — feeds/policy: nested-set static-alias binding with an unready feed still fails OPEN (nameRepresentability lacks the dynamic-binding guard #5751 added) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

PR #5751 (#5645, codex-182 M38) closed the composite-binding and top-level
static-alias partial-deny fail-opens for dynamic-address feed bindings. One
residual arm of the SAME class remains, verified during the hostile review of
#5751:

A dynamic-address binding name nested INSIDE an address-set that ALSO has a
static address-book alias, with an UNready feed, stays **fail-OPEN**. The
`nameRepresentability` walk (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/policies_lower.go`) is not
passed `cfg.Security.DynamicAddress.AddressBindings`, so when it recurses into a
nested address-set member it cannot tell that a member name is a DECLARED-but-
unresolved dynamic binding — it resolves the static alias instead, enforcing
only the partial static subset while the unready feed's prefixes go unmatched
(a `deny` under-matches = fail-open).

(A binding nested inside an address-set WITHOUT a static alias already fails
CLOSED via the undefined-reference path — this gap is specifically the
nested + static-alias coincidence.)

## Fix

Thread `cfg.Security.DynamicAddress.AddressBindings` into `nameRepresentability`
(mirroring the top-level `addrRepresentable` guard added in #5751): when a
nested member name is a declared dynamic binding ABSENT from the resolved feed
overlay, return unrepresentable (taint → `__unsupported_address__` → whole-
snapshot preflight reject) BEFORE resolving its static alias. Add a fail-on-
revert test: a `deny` referencing an address-set that contains a static-aliased
binding whose feed is unready must taint the side (whole-snapshot reject), not
enforce the partial static subset.

## Provenance

Verified real during the hostile review of PR #5751 (rev5751, bar 5). Out of the
four #5645 acceptance cases, so correctly deferred from #5751; this closes the
nested arm of the same fail-open class.

## #5754 — feeds/config: warn at commit when a policy references a dynamic-address binding whose feed name is unknown (silent whole-dataplane default-deny foot-gun) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-14)

## Summary

A firewall policy that references a dynamic-address feed binding whose feed name
is TYPO'd or otherwise never fetches (unknown feed, permanent fetch failure with
no persisted last-good) leaves that binding UNRESOLVED forever. Per the
established #5645/#3261 fail-closed contract (reinforced by #5751), an
unresolved feed-bound name referenced by any policy taints the dataplane
snapshot → `__unsupported_address__` → whole-snapshot preflight reject → the
node stays at fresh-boot **default-deny** (or retains previous-good on a running
box) indefinitely, with NO commit-time signal that a typo caused it.

This is fail-closed (safe — it denies rather than under-matches), but it's a
sharp operator foot-gun: a single mistyped feed name in one policy silently
holds the ENTIRE dataplane at default-deny on the next fresh boot, and the
operator gets no warning at commit time.

## Proposed fix

Add a **commit-time validation warning** (not a hard reject — the reference may
resolve once the feed fetches) when a policy references a dynamic-address
binding whose feed name(s) do not match any configured feed (`services feeds`)
— i.e. an unknown/unstartable feed that can never become ready. Surface it as a
config validation warning ("policy <x> references feed-binding <b> whose feed
<name> is not defined; the binding will be unresolved and its policy will fail
closed until the feed is configured and fetches"). This blunts the foot-gun
without changing the fail-closed runtime behavior.

## Provenance

Non-blocking caveat raised during the hostile review of PR #5751 (rev5751). The
runtime behavior is pre-existing and correct (fail-closed); this is a
usability/observability hardening so a typo is caught at commit rather than
discovered as a whole-dataplane default-deny after the next reboot.

## #5759 — daemon: cold-boot host-inbound fence sets hostInboundEnforced=true even when it emitted ZERO drops (addressless→addressed transition can fail-open) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

PR #5757 (#5644) added the cold-boot host-inbound fail-closed fence: on a
cold-boot `applyHostInboundFilter` failure with no prior table to retain, a
DENY-ALL fence is installed and `Daemon.hostInboundEnforced` is set true so a
LATER (day-2) failed install is covered by the atomic-load retention (no fresh
fence). Surfaced as a non-blocking note during the hostile review (rev5757b).

Edge case: in the exotic path where the ONLY host-inbound enforcement at cold
boot is a junos-host `programs` entry whose addresses are all DHCP-pending (zero
resolvable addresses), and the real install fails, the fence emits ZERO drop
rules but still `Store(true)`s `hostInboundEnforced`. If an address then appears
and the next apply ALSO fails, it is treated as day-2 (no fresh fence installed)
and that newly-appeared address fail-OPENs until a clean commit.

This is NOT a regression (pre-PR that path also fails open) and is a documented,
self-healing #3698 addressless window with NO exposure at cold boot (no address
⇒ no reachable host service ⇒ nothing to expose). So it does not warrant blocking
#5757. Filing the concrete hardening so it's tracked.

## Proposed fix

In `applyHostInboundFilter` / `installHostInboundColdBootFence`, skip
`d.hostInboundEnforced.Store(true)` when the fence emitted ZERO drop rules (no
scoped firewall-local address). Then if an address later appears and re-apply
fails, `hostInboundEnforced` is still false → a real (non-empty) fence is
installed for the now-addressed set, closing the fail-open. Add a test: a
cold-boot install failure with an all-DHCP-pending programs entry emits a
zero-drop fence and leaves `hostInboundEnforced==false`; a subsequent
address-appearance + failure installs a non-empty fence.

## Provenance

Non-blocking edge raised in the hostile review of PR #5757 (rev5757b, bar-1
minor note). Low priority — no cold-boot exposure — but a clean one-line-guard
hardening that closes the addressless→addressed transition.

## #5765 — [cohort] claude-spark-review-002 — Rust dataplane u16 length-cast defense-in-depth (4 currently-unreachable truncation sites) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

[cohort] claude-spark-review-002 low-materiality / defense-in-depth survivors —
Rust dataplane u16 length casts on packet/payload lengths.

Four `... as u16` casts on packet/segment/frame lengths in the AF_XDP dataplane
were flagged as potential integer-truncation (wrap for >64K). Verified vs
origin/master (bf3c57a7f): all four exist, none is exploitable today (the u16
truncation is UNREACHABLE), but they are worth pre-emptive hardening as
defense-in-depth — the codebase already uses validated narrowing newtypes
(VlanId/TunnelTtl/QueueId/InterfaceMtu) for exactly this class.

## Sites (all currently unreachable-for-wrap)

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/checksum.rs:357` — `checksum16_ipv4`
   `payload.len() as u16` (IPv4 pseudo-header length).
2. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/mod.rs:1631/1657/1712` — `segment.len() as u16`
   (IPv4 pseudo-header for TCP/UDP checksum verification).
3. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/inject.rs:73/142` — `frame_len.min(u16::MAX)`
   (saturating; already defensive — include only for consistency).
4. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tcp.rs:578/615` — SYN-cookie reply
   `total_len as u16` / `tcp_len as u16`.

## Why low-materiality (unreachable today)

AF_XDP processes individual frames from the UMEM, each ≤ the configured frame
size (~2-9 KB), so no single payload/segment reaches 64K. IPv4 `total_len` is
itself a u16 (≤65535) → an IPv4 L4 segment is ≤65515 < 65536 and cannot wrap.
An IPv6 jumbogram (>64K) cannot fit a single ≤9 KB frame and the dataplane does
not reassemble >64K datagrams. inject.rs already saturates via `.min(u16::MAX)`.

## Proposed hardening (defense-in-depth, when the cluster wall permits a dataplane change)

Replace the raw `as u16` casts with an explicit checked/saturating conversion
(`u16::try_from(len).unwrap_or(u16::MAX)` or a debug_assert on the bound), or a
validated length newtype mirroring the existing VlanId/TunnelTtl pattern, so a
future frame-size increase / GRO super-frame / IPv6-jumbogram reassembly cannot
silently wrap a checksum or length field. NOTE: this is a Rust userspace-dp
change → needs `cargo test --release` and (if it touches the forwarding path)
loss-cluster smoke, currently blocked by the shim-ABI wall — so it's hardening

## #5768 — zeroize: bound factory-reset deletion to xpf-OWNED artifacts (denylist residual — unlisted/subdir config roots still glob-delete siblings) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

PR #5767 (#5684) bounded `zeroize` (factory reset) with a lexical
`ValidateFactoryResetRoot` denylist (`FactoryResetForbiddenRoots`: /, /etc,
/var, /srv, /usr, /usr/local, /var/lib, /mnt, /opt, ...) so a custom `-config`
directly in a shared dir (`/etc/xpf.conf`→/etc) or dir-shaped (`/srv/x`→/srv)
no longer turns zeroize into a broad delete. That closes the realistic #5684
footgun and default `/etc/xpf` is safe.

Residual (surfaced by the hostile review of #5767, rev5767 Bar 2): a DENYLIST is
inherently incomplete on a wildcard-glob wipe. A custom `-config` in an UNLISTED
shared dir or a SUBDIR of a listed root still resolves the wipe root to an
unowned directory and glob-deletes siblings:
- `/data/xpf.conf` → `/data` (not on the denylist)
- `/mnt/backup/x.conf` → `/mnt/backup`, `/media/usb/x.conf` → `/media/usb`
  (subdirs of listed roots escape)
- `/opt/foo/x.conf` → `/opt/foo`
- notably `/etc/frr/x.conf` → `/etc/frr`, where the sweep would glob-delete
  xpf's OWN rendered `/etc/frr/frr.conf`.

Not a regression (strictly better than pre-#5767) — filing the long-term close.

## Proposed fix (ownership-scoped deletion, not a bigger denylist)

Stop the broad `*.conf` / `rollback*` glob + `RemoveAll(<root>/.configdb)` /
`RemoveAll(<root>/tls)` on a computed root. Instead delete ONLY the specific
artifacts the daemon itself created/owns:
- the exact config file path the daemon was started with (not a glob of the dir),
- the specific `.configdb` / `tls` / rollback / journal files the configstore
  wrote (track them, or keep them under a dedicated xpf-owned subdir that
  zeroize removes wholesale),
so a shared/unlisted config directory can never have unowned siblings removed.
An allowlist/denylist race is unwinnable on a wildcard wipe; ownership-scoped
deletion is the durable close.

## Provenance

Non-blocking residual from the hostile review of PR #5767 (rev5767 Bar 2). The
#5767 denylist ships as the immediate mitigation; this tracks the durable fix.

## Defect

`ClearSessions` drives full-table conntrack walks on BOTH the gRPC and REST
surfaces with no shared admission bound — the same CPU/per-bucket-BPF-map-lock
contention DoS class as #5708 (M35), but on the session-CLEAR path rather than
the session-LIST/SUMMARY path.

- gRPC: `ClearSessions` → `clearFilteredSessionsV4Rescan` → `IterateSessions`
  (+ v6) walks the whole table.
- REST: the equivalent clear handler is likewise ungated.

Because #5708 hoisted the session-walk limiter to a process-wide shared
singleton (`diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter`, cap 4) and gated the LIST/SUMMARY
scans (GetSessions/GetSessionSummary/GetZonePairSummary + their REST peers), the
CLEAR full-table walks now stand out as the remaining uncovered high-cost
table-walk surface: an unauthenticated-by-principal loopback caller (see the
RBAC gaps #5278/#5561) can issue unbounded concurrent ClearSessions rescans.

## Why a separate issue (not folded into #5708)

#5708's scope is the session LIST/SUMMARY read scans. ClearSessions is a
mutation path with its own filter/rescan semantics, and REST clear is *also*
ungated — so it's a consistent, distinct gap, not the asymmetry #5708 fixed.
Folding it would have widened #5708 past its stated boundary. Filed per the
one-issue-per-finding discipline.

## Fix direction

Gate both the gRPC `ClearSessions` full-table rescan and the REST clear handler
through the SAME shared `diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter` (fail-fast →
`codes.ResourceExhausted` / HTTP 429), mirroring #5708's acquire/defer pattern.
Add fail-on-revert bound tests for both surfaces. Confirm the rescan filter path
(clearFilteredSessionsV4Rescan) is the only walk entry and is gated before the
walk, released on every exit.

## Provenance

Surfaced during the hostile review of PR #5778 (#5708) — the reviewer noted
ClearSessions as an equivalent ungated full-table walk, consistent across both
surfaces, and recommended a follow-up rather than a scope expansion of #5708.

## #5784 — daemon: system archival transfer-interval (config-minutes) NewTicker lacks a ×time.Minute product-overflow clamp — same class as #5723, minutes-scoped/lenient-ingress-only [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-13)

## Defect

`system archival … transfer-interval` (daemon_archive_timer.go:119 →
`realArchiveTicker` → `time.NewTicker`) is a config-derived interval multiplied
by `time.Minute` with no product-side overflow clamp. This is the SAME bug CLASS
as #5723/#5705 (config-interval × time.Unit overflows int64-ns → a non-positive
`time.Duration` → `time.NewTicker` panics → xpfd crash), but MINUTES-scoped
rather than seconds.

At COMMIT it is safe: the schema bounds `transfer-interval` to
`ValidateInteger(1, 2880)` (2880 min ≪ the overflow threshold), so a normal
commit cannot reach the panic. The residual is ONLY the lenient ingress: a
deliberately-crafted on-disk `Store.Load` / peer-sync config carrying
`transfer-interval > ~1.5e8` minutes bypasses the strict SchemaValidate (same
lenient-load path #5723's runtime clamp defends), and the raw-int `<= 0` guards
in the archive-timer path inspect the seconds/minutes integer, NOT the
`× time.Minute` product — so the wrapped-negative Duration reaches `NewTicker`
and panics.

## Fix direction

Mirror the #5723 `clampRPMIntervalSeconds` / #5705 `clampKeepaliveIntervalSec`
two-layer shape, minutes-scoped: add a product-side clamp on the
`transfer-interval × time.Minute` before `time.NewTicker` in
daemon_archive_timer.go, so a pathological lenient-Load / peer-sync value clamps
to a positive bounded Duration instead of overflowing to non-positive. The
commit-time schema bound (1..2880) stays; the clamp is defense-in-depth for the
strict-validate-bypassing ingress. Add a fail-on-revert clamp test with a
pathological minutes value.

## Materiality

Low — requires a hand-crafted Load/peer-sync config with transfer-interval on the
order of 10^8 minutes (~285 years); a normal operator cannot trigger it (commit
rejects >2880). Filed to CLOSE the config-interval×time.Unit overflow class the
#5705/#5723 sweep established (seconds done; this is the minutes straggler).

Surfaced during the hostile review of PR #5781 (#5723) — the reviewer's repo-wide

## #5789 — host-inbound: retained nft generation does not cover newly appeared local addresses after failed rerender [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

`hostInboundEnforced=true` only says a real ruleset or a non-empty fallback was
loaded at some earlier generation. It does not prove that the retained nftables
generation covers the current desired destination-address set.

Two concrete paths remain after #5759's zero-drop fallback fix:

1. A previously addressed zone gains another static/DHCP/SLAAC address. The
   next real render fails, atomic nft retention keeps the old generation, and
   that generation has no destination-scoped default deny for the new address.
2. An addressless interface has a successful real install containing only an
   `iifname`-scoped `to-zone junos-host` program. That success stores
   `hostInboundEnforced=true`. An address later appears and a failed rerender
   skips the cold-boot fallback even though the retained program-only table has
   no coarse destination-scoped deny for the new address.

## Code paths

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft.go`: `applyHostInboundFilter`,
  `installHostInboundColdBootFence`, `buildHostInboundFencePayload`
- `pkg/daemon/daemon.go`: `hostInboundEnforced`
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/junos_host_deny.go`: address-independent interface
  program construction

## Security impact

A newly reachable local address can temporarily lack the intended host-inbound
default deny after a failed day-2 apply. Atomic replacement protects only rules
and destinations present in the retained generation; it cannot protect an
address that did not exist in that generation.

## Required design

Replace the sticky boolean as the sole day-2 discriminator with installed
generation/coverage state (or an interface-scoped fail-closed fence) that can
answer whether the currently installed table covers the exact desired
address/interface authority. On failed rerender, install a bounded fence for
newly uncovered destinations without weakening retained valid rules.

## #5790 — host-inbound: successful table teardown leaves hostInboundEnforced sticky true and can skip fresh-install fence [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

The no-enforcement branch of `applyHostInboundFilter` deletes
`inet xpf_hostinbound` but does not clear `d.hostInboundEnforced`. The flag can
therefore remain true after successful teardown even though no prior table is
present.

If a later configuration becomes enforceable and its first real nft load
fails, the stale true value takes the day-2 retention branch and skips the
cold-boot fallback. There is no retained table to protect the newly reachable
local addresses, so the failure can be fail-open.

## Code paths

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft.go`: early `!hasEnforceableView &&
  len(unzonedV4)==0 && len(unzonedV6)==0 && len(programs)==0` delete path and
  later real-load failure branch
- `pkg/daemon/daemon.go`: `hostInboundEnforced`

## Required fix

Make successful table teardown publish the corresponding false state, with a
state-machine contract that cannot race a later apply. A subsequent first
install failure must take the cold-boot/fresh-install fail-closed path.

## Acceptance criteria

- Successful real/fallback install sets the appropriate state.
- Successful no-enforcement teardown clears it.
- A later enforceable generation whose real load fails attempts a non-empty
  fallback rather than assuming a retained table.
- Teardown failure does not falsely clear state for a table that may still be
  installed.
- Tests cover install -> teardown -> failed reinstall ordering.

## Provenance

Found during the independent design review of #5759. Separate from #5759's
zero-drop fallback classification and safe to fix independently.

## Problem

`dhcpLeaseChangeRequiresRecompile` treats every configured `fxp*`, `fab*`, and

when all DHCP clients are in that set. Host-inbound lifeline classification is
narrower: standalone lifelines are `fxp0`, `em0`, and `fab*`; `fxp1` is
deliberately non-lifeline unless chassis-cluster role makes it one.

that would rebuild host-inbound protection for the newly reachable address.

- `pkg/config/lifeline.go`: host-inbound lifeline classification
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft.go`: host-inbound view/fence application

Do not use the broad management-VRF name class as a proxy for host-inbound
lifeline exemption. A DHCP lease change must trigger the full recompile when
the interface can participate in dataplane/zone host-inbound enforcement, even
if it is placed in the management VRF. Centralize or explicitly join the two
classification contracts so future names cannot drift silently.

## Acceptance criteria

- Standalone zoned DHCP `fxp1` triggers the full recompile/address callback and
  receives host-inbound protection after address acquisition.
- Actual lifelines (`fxp0`, `em0`, applicable `fab*`/control links) retain the
  intended management-only fast path.
- Chassis-cluster role-dependent cases are covered.
- Tests pin the classification boundary and the resulting host-inbound apply.

## #5794 — nat: expose deterministic source-NAT forward/reverse mapping lookup (vSRX parity) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-22)

## Summary

xpf enforces deterministic CGNAT/NAPT64 allocation, but the reverse-mapping helpers are test-only and no CLI, gRPC, or REST surface lets an operator resolve:

- internal subscriber -> translated IPv4 + assigned port block; or
- translated IPv4 + port -> internal subscriber.

That leaves the central compliance/forensics workflow unavailable even though current docs describe the mapping as reversible for CGN compliance.

## Current evidence (master `3821cd9d`)

- `userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs` defines `reverse_deterministic_v4` and `reverse_deterministic_v6`.
- Every call is in `userspace-dp/src/nat/tests_pool.rs`; `rg 'reverse_deterministic_v[46]('` finds no production caller.
- Forward allocation uses `deterministic_indices_v4/v6` and stateful return traffic uses reverse session entries.
- `docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md`, `docs/feature-gaps.md`, and `docs/vsrx-gaps.md` describe reversibility, but there is no operational command or API exposing it.
- #5660's O(N) performance report is therefore not a live datapath problem; it is this missing product surface.

## vSRX/Junos parity

Junos exposes `show security nat source deterministic` with filters for pool, internal host, and translated IP+port, and reports host IP, external IP, and port range:

https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/cli-reference/topics/ref/command/show-security-nat-source-deterministic.html

Juniper's deterministic NAT documentation identifies reverse mapping as the mechanism that removes per-flow translation-log dependence:

https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/interfaces-adaptive-services/topics/topic-map/deterministic-nat.html

This issue should carry the `vsrx-parity` label.

## Required design invariants

1. Provide a canonical domain query, not CLI-only arithmetic. CLI, gRPC, and REST must consume the same typed result.
2. Support both enforced modes:
   - IPv4 deterministic source NAT (mode 1);
   - IPv6 subscriber -> IPv4 deterministic NAPT64 (mode 2).
3. Query the **last successfully applied** NAT generation. Do not calculate from desired-but-unapplied config, and fail visibly when no applied view is available.
4. Forward query accepts pool + internal host and returns external IPv4, inclusive port range, block size, and applied generation.
5. Reverse query requires pool + external IPv4 + translated port and returns the internal IPv4/IPv6 subscriber plus applied generation.
6. Reject ambiguous queries when multiple deterministic pools contain the same external tuple unless the caller selects a pool. Never return the first map iteration match.
7. Keep the control query off packet processing paths. Do not add a persistent reverse hash index to the allocator solely for an operator request.

## #5795 — dhcp: fixed 30s T1 clamp schedules renewal after short leases expire [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Problem

`pkg/dhcp/renewalTimers` applies a fixed 30-second minimum to T1:

```go
t1 = leaseTime / 2
if t1 < 30*time.Second {
    t1 = 30 * time.Second
}
```

The current test suite explicitly pins:

- a 40-second lease to T1=30s instead of the RFC half-life (20s);
- a 2-second lease to T1=30s and T2Remaining=1s;
- a zero lease duration to the same 30s/1s schedule.

For every finite lease shorter than 60 seconds, the client waits past the RFC T1. For leases shorter than 30 seconds it does not attempt renewal until after the lease has expired. The run loop retains and may continue using the address while waiting, so a short-lease WAN can forward with an expired binding and then churn into re-acquisition instead of renewing on time.

This is distinct from closed #4526, which fixed duration overflow for the `0xFFFFFFFF`-second sentinel. No existing open or closed issue found for the short-lease clamp.

## Evidence on current master

Base: `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`

- `pkg/dhcp/commit.go:41-64`: fixed 30s T1 / 1s T2-remaining floors.
- `pkg/dhcp/commit_test.go:58-90`: `"t1 clamped to 30s"`, `"t2 remainder clamped to 1s"`, and `"zero lease time"` canonize the failure.
- `pkg/dhcp/renew.go` and the v4/v6 run loops consume these waits directly.
- The lease parser does not impose a >=60s server-lease floor.

## Required invariants

1. For a valid finite lease, T1 must occur before lease expiry.
2. T2 must occur after T1 and before lease expiry.
3. Normal leases keep RFC defaults (T1 ~= 0.5, T2 ~= 0.875) without a fixed floor that crosses the lease lifetime.
4. Very short but positive leases must not create a zero-duration retry loop; derive any safety floor proportionally and cap it below expiry.
5. Zero, negative, or otherwise invalid lease durations must fail closed into re-acquisition/error handling, not manufacture a 30-second lease state.
6. The `0xFFFFFFFF`-second sentinel remains overflow-safe and does not regress #4526.
7. IPv4 and IPv6 use the same timer semantics.
8. Tests cover boundary durations around 1s, 2s, 30s, 59s, 60s, and the infinite sentinel.

## #5796 — dhcpserver: one-file Kea memfile reads lose active leases across LFC rotation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

xpf treats `/var/lib/kea/kea-leases{4,6}.csv` as the complete Kea memfile database, but after Lease File Cleanup (LFC) begins that file is only the new append log. The active lease set spans Kea's LFC file set (`previous`, `input`, and the current file) until compaction completes.

Kea's own LFC contract says the DHCP server moves the current lease file to the LFC input file before invoking `kea-lfc`; the finished compacted result becomes the previous file. See the primary Kea documentation: https://kea.readthedocs.io/en/latest/arm/lfc.html#overview and lines describing `previous`, `input`, `output`, and `finish`.

Current xpf consumers open only the current path:

- `pkg/dhcpserver/ddns_leases.go:parseActiveLeases`
- `pkg/dhcpserver/dhcpserver.go:parseLeaseCSV` (operational lease display)
- `pkg/dhcpserver/lease_sync.go:readSyncLeasesViaMemfile` (HA fallback)

The generated Kea config does not disable LFC, so Kea's default periodic cleanup applies.

## Impact

1. **DDNS destructive reconciliation:** immediately after LFC rotates the current file, a valid header-only current file is treated as a trusted empty lease set. `pkg/ddns` may then delete every xpf-owned A/AAAA/PTR record for leases that still exist in Kea memory and in the LFC previous/input files.
2. **HA lease-sync fallback:** when the control socket is unavailable, the fallback can publish or pre-seed only the post-rotation delta, omitting live leases. On takeover this can permit duplicate allocation or lose reservations.
3. **Operational display:** `show dhcp server leases` can omit the compacted active set and show only leases changed since the last LFC.
4. A size/mtime check around one current-file read does not fix this: the current file can be perfectly stable and legitimately header-only while the active set lives in the other LFC files.

This sharpens the M3/M5 notes collected in #5672; it is a distinct, material correctness issue and should not be buried in that mixed hardening cohort.

## Evidence on current master

Base: `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`

- `pkg/dhcpserver/dhcpserver.go:114-115`: only canonical current paths are modeled.

## #5797 — system syslog: preserve per-facility severity selectors instead of first-facility/most-restrictive collapse [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

A Junos `system syslog host <destination>` can carry multiple independent `<facility> <severity>` selectors. xpf parses all of them, but the daemon collapses them into one `SyslogClient`:

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:853-856` chooses the **first** configured facility as the outgoing facility.
- `syslogHostMinSeverity` folds every selector into the **single most restrictive** severity.
- `pkg/logging.SyslogClient` has only one `Facility` and one `MinSeverity`.
- The logging README explicitly documents this lossy fold.

That is not equivalent to Junos selector semantics. For example:

```
system {
  syslog {
    host 192.0.2.10 {
      daemon info;
      authorization critical;
    }
  }
}
```

Junos forwards daemon records at info-or-higher and authorization records at critical-or-higher. xpf sends every forwarded record with the first facility and applies `critical` to all of them, silently dropping daemon notice/info events. Reversing the statement order changes the emitted facility even though the selector set is semantically the same. A `none` selector can suppress unrelated facilities entirely.

This is distinct from #5672, which only rejects misspelled facility keys, and from closed #5314, which completed severity-name parsing while deliberately retaining the one-client fold.

## Evidence on current master

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `pkg/config/compiler_system.go:309-347` preserves every host selector in `host.Facilities`.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:793-823` reduces all selector severities with `MoreRestrictiveMinSeverity`.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:853-856` uses only `host.Facilities[0].Facility`.
- `pkg/logging/syslog.go:88-98` exposes only scalar `Facility` and `MinSeverity`.
- `pkg/logging/syslog.go:766-789` documents the lossy merge as an implementation constraint.
- `pkg/daemon/syslog_severity_5314_test.go:60-73` currently locks in the most-restrictive cross-facility fold instead of Junos behavior.

Juniper's system-logging contract defines facility/severity pairs independently:
https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/network-mgmt/topics/topic-map/directing-system-log-messages-to-a-remote-destination.html

## #5798 — userspace-dp/NAT64: fragment-association hit is not ingress-domain scoped and bypasses input-filter/PBR/zone-policy enforcement [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Defect

`Nat64FragAssoc` authorizes a non-first IPv6 fragment from a cache key containing only `(address family, source, destination, fragment identification)`. It omits protocol, effective logical ingress interface, security zone, routing instance, fabric-origin identity, and direction.

`poll_descriptor` consults that cache before the ordinary flowless enforcement arm. On a hit it returns the cached `SessionDecision` directly, skipping the interface input filter, PBR, route/zone derivation, zone security policy, and host-bound gates that the miss path runs.

## Mechanically verified source (`3821cd9d2`)

- `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:329-339`: `Nat64FragKey` has only `addr_family`, `src`, `dst`, and `ident`.
- `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:392-458`: all workers share the Arc-backed cache; lookup refreshes and returns the first fragment's complete decision.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:99-124`: `nat64_consult_forward_fragment_assoc` returns that decision on a non-first IPv6 fragment.
- `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:3599-3630`: the cache-hit `else if` arm wins before the flowless enforcement branch.
- `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:3631-3909`: input filter, PBR, routing, zone policy, and local-delivery gates exist only in the miss branch.

## Security trace

1. A permitted first NAT64 fragment from security domain A installs an association and its resolved/NAT decision.
2. Within the ~2 second TTL, a non-first fragment carrying the same source, destination and 32-bit fragment ID arrives from domain B (or a different VRF/fabric origin).
3. The key aliases because no ingress authority is present.
4. Lookup returns the domain-A permit/egress/NAT decision.
5. The packet bypasses domain-B input filtering, PBR and zone-policy derivation and is forwarded under domain A's authority.

Fragment-ID guessing is not an authorization mechanism. The case is directly reachable with a coordinated/spoofing sender, mirrored traffic, interface migration, or duplicate address space across VRFs. The shared cross-worker cache makes the decision globally visible.

## Scope / duplicate check

This is distinct from:

- #5146: first-fragment association published before session commit;
- #5447: expired entries are not pruned before capacity eviction;
- #5624: associations survive config-generation replacement;
- #5689: ordinary same-family NAT/NPT non-first fragments have no association;
- #5467: flowless TX can bypass output-filter evaluation.

Those issues are adjacent and should coordinate on one fragment-association abstraction, but none owns ingress-security-domain aliasing plus the pre-enforcement hit placement.

## Required fix

1. Put the association in a modular `fragment_assoc/` component shared by NAT64 and ordinary NAT only after the relevant designs converge.
2. Key on safe fragment identity **and authority**: family, upper-layer protocol, source, destination, fragment ID, direction, effective logical ingress ifindex, effective ingress zone, routing instance/fabric origin, and the current config/FIB/HA authority stamp. Do not read payload bytes as L4.

## Durable architecture record

This issue is the source of record for the **Paladin codex-183 final-report content assembly architecture R8**. No implementation or final-report publication is authorized by this issue.

- Architect base: `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`
- Verdict: **IMPLEMENTATION-READY DESIGN; EXECUTION BLOCKED on the explicit material decisions and user authorizations in section 17.3**

- LF count: `4607`
- Embedded zero-form SHA-256: `ec22e2f0c01d1fccc967c8144edbb53a05c6489fb79421e03c706775162e5ffc`
- Detached sealed-byte SHA-256: `9006e087100022bdd95acb6826a82173a6bc3f6456ea28fad90b45be671f9590`
- Payload encoding: 11 ordered comment chunks, base64 of contiguous raw-byte ranges

### Disposition

R8 closes CDR7-F1 through CDR7-F6 in design while preserving the frozen arithmetic, artifact/hash DAGs, digest domains, successor conservation, and model-neutral T00 boundary. The design now includes typed lexical-key/generated-ID separation, a closed executable term/equation registry, descriptor-stable corpus retention, authenticated control and review facts, complete content/evidence/coordinator/filing schemas, anti-self-approval authority closure, byte-total report grammar, and exact publication/cleanup successor receipts.

Read only comments headed `Architecture payload chunk NN/11`, sort by NN, extract the single base64 code block from each, decode each independently, verify its declared raw offset/length/SHA-256, concatenate without separators, then verify the detached digest and byte/LF counts above. A final conformance comment contains the reopened GitHub comment manifest and reconstruction result.

## #5800 — userspace-dp/io_uring: retry exhaustion can release a packet buffer while an SQE still references it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

## Summary

`write_all()` submits an `io_uring` write whose SQE borrows the caller's Rust slice, but `reap_matching()` returns after 4,096 interrupted/transient waits without proving that the matching CQE was reaped or that the SQE was cancelled. The slow-path caller then drops the request and frees `req.bytes` even though the kernel may still dereference that address.

This is a live memory-lifetime violation in the userspace dataplane slow path.

## Evidence

Verified on `master` at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`.

- `userspace-dp/src/io_uring_write.rs:216-228` explicitly documents that the retry ceiling may return with the SQE outstanding and the buffer subsequently dropped.
- `userspace-dp/src/io_uring_write.rs:343-383` returns at `MAX_WAIT_RETRIES` for repeated `EINTR` or transient errors without CQE/cancellation proof.
- `userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:433-455` owns the bytes only in the loop-local `PacketRequest`; after the write error is recorded, that request is released.

The matching tag also starts at `1` in every `write_all()` call. An abandoned completion can therefore collide with a later call after the next call's pre-submit stale drain.

## Reachable failure trace

1. A slow-path packet is dequeued into `req.bytes`.
2. `opcode::Write` stores the slice's raw address in an SQE.
3. `submit_and_wait_one()` submits the SQE, then repeatedly returns `EINTR` or another transient error.
4. Retry 4,096 returns `WriteError::Transferred` without reaping the matching CQE.
5. The slow-path iteration records a drop and releases `req.bytes`.
6. The outstanding kernel operation may read memory that Rust has already freed or reused.

Potential effects include packet-data disclosure/corruption, helper crash, or undefined behavior under sustained signal/error pressure.

## Required invariants

- A function must never return while an in-flight SQE references caller-borrowed storage.
- Every submitted operation reaches one terminal state before its buffer owner is released: matching CQE reaped, cancellation CQE reaped, or ring teardown/drain proving no kernel references remain.
- `user_data` identities must be unique for the ring lifetime, not restart per call.
- Fatal-ring handling must retain all in-flight owned buffers until teardown/drain completes.
- The latency bound may stop a worker from waiting synchronously, but it may not weaken memory lifetime.

## Suggested design direction

Move submitted writes into a ring-owned in-flight registry containing owned packet bytes and a ring-global monotonically increasing ID. On retry-budget exhaustion, return control only after ownership has moved into that registry. Reap/cancel later, or tear down and drain the ring before releasing entries. Treat cancellation submission alone as insufficient; observe its completion and the target operation's terminal state.

## #5801 — userspace-dp/slowpath: day-2 MTU increases leave the persistent TUN at its startup ceiling [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-18)

## Summary

The userspace dataplane preserves `SlowPathReinjector` across snapshot reconciles. Its TUN MTU and immutable `mtu` field are programmed only when the reinjector is created. A valid day-2 configuration that raises a data-interface MTU therefore updates the accepted snapshot but does not update the live slow-path TUN. Reinjected packets above the old ceiling are persistently dropped until helper restart/recreation.

## Evidence

Verified on `master` at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`.

- `userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:294-335` stores the creation MTU as immutable state and exposes no reconcile/update operation.
- `userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:340-355` drops packets above `live_mtu`.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/reconcile/snapshot.rs:481-500` intentionally preserves the reinjector, prints a warning, and leaves the live TUN unchanged when `snapshot.slow_path_mtu()` changes.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/reconcile/snapshot.rs:501-508` applies the desired MTU only when constructing a new reinjector.

## Reachable failure trace

1. The helper starts while the largest configured data-interface MTU is 1,500.
2. `xpf-usp0` is created and programmed to 1,500.
3. An operator commits a valid day-2 change raising a data-interface MTU to 9,000.
4. Snapshot reconcile preserves the existing reinjector and only warns.
5. The accepted snapshot now requires jumbo handling while the live TUN remains at 1,500.
6. Firewall-local/control traffic requiring slow-path reinjection above 1,500 returns `MtuExceeded` indefinitely until restart.

This creates a configuration-convergence failure and a persistent availability blackhole after a routine committed change.

## Required invariant

A successful snapshot publication must not expose a configured slow-path MTU different from the live TUN's enforceable MTU. The reconcile must either:

- program the existing TUN to the new value and publish the new live state only after success; or
- transactionally replace the reinjector/TUN; or
- reject/roll back the snapshot if the required MTU cannot be installed.

A warning is not sufficient after the configuration has been accepted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Day-2 MTU increases and decreases converge the live TUN without process restart.
- [ ] Snapshot publication and live-TUN programming have explicit success/rollback ordering.
- [ ] A failed `SIOCSIFMTU` does not leave the new snapshot reported as fully applied.
- [ ] `mtu()`, `live_mtu`, degraded state, and enqueue admission agree after every reconcile.

## #5802 — userspace-dp/NAT: VLAN pre-routing scope uses physical parent instead of logical unit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Summary

The AF_XDP miss path resolves VLAN logical ingress identity for zone-policy enforcement, filters, CoS, and later routing, but the earlier DNAT/static-NAT/NPTv6 pre-routing scope lookup still uses the physical AF_XDP bind ifindex. On a trunk whose VLAN units have different zones, interface names, or routing instances, a packet can match (or miss) a NAT rule using the parent/first-unit identity instead of the logical unit that actually received it.

This can apply translation outside the configured `from zone`, `from interface`, or `from routing-instance` boundary before the correct logical zone policy runs.

## Evidence

Verified on current `master` at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`.

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1510-1550` derives `ingress_zone_name`, `ingress_ifname_dnat`, and `ingress_ri_dnat` from `meta.ingress_ifindex`.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1558-1582` passes those physical-parent values into scoped DNAT and static-NAT matching.
- NPTv6 inbound immediately reuses the same `ingress_zone_name`.
- The same path later calls `resolve_ingress_logical_ifindex(forwarding, physical_ifindex, ingress_vlan_id)` before resolving the zone pair (`poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1894-1915`), explicitly documenting that raw physical identity is wrong for co-parented VLAN units.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/interfaces.rs:70-95` maps both logical and physical ifindexes; the physical parent intentionally retains only one zone when units differ, so it cannot represent a per-packet VLAN unit.

No test references the three DNAT ingress-scope variables or covers scoped NAT across co-parented VLAN units.

## Reachable failure traces

### Wrong permit/translation

1. Physical `eth0` carries VLAN 10 (`ge-0/0/0.10`, zone trust, RI blue) and VLAN 20 (`ge-0/0/0.20`, zone guest, RI red).
2. A destination-NAT rule is scoped `from zone trust` or `from interface ge-0/0/0.10`.
3. A VLAN-20 packet arrives on physical ifindex `eth0`.
4. Pre-routing scope resolves the physical parent's retained zone/config identity, potentially `trust` / unit 10.
5. DNAT translates the guest packet under a rule that was not configured for guest.
6. Later zone policy correctly sees unit 20, but it evaluates the already-translated destination and cannot undo the out-of-scope NAT match.

### Wrong miss

The inverse parent mapping causes a valid unit-scoped DNAT/static-NAT/NPTv6 rule to miss, forwarding an untranslated packet or selecting a different route/policy target.

## Required invariant

Every pre-routing scope consumer for one packet must use one canonical logical ingress identity resolved from `(physical_ifindex, ingress_vlan_id)`:

- logical ifindex;
- logical config interface name;
- logical routing instance;

## #5803 — userspace-dp/CoS: parked low-rate queue can force O(elapsed ticks) worker stall [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-22)

## Summary

The CoS timer-wheel cold-start optimization snaps an over-horizon wheel only when **no queue is parked**. A valid very-low-rate queue can park tens of millions of 50-us ticks in the future. If the owning worker becomes idle and later resumes while that queue is still parked, `advance_cos_timer_wheel()` replays every elapsed tick synchronously on the packet worker.

At the documented 1 byte/s effective rate, one 1,500-byte packet can create roughly 30,000,000 iterations (about 25 minutes of logical ticks) in one call, stalling all packet processing owned by that worker.

## Evidence

Verified on current `master` at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`.

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/tx_completion.rs:249-266` performs one loop iteration per elapsed tick unless the over-horizon snap succeeds.
- `snap_cos_timer_wheel_over_horizon()` returns `false` when any queue is parked.
- The source comment at `tx_completion.rs:292-310` explicitly confirms wake ticks are uncapped, rates as low as 1 B/s are accepted, a 1,500-byte head can park about 30,000,000 ticks out, and an idle worker can re-enter the O(lag) loop.
- The existing fallback test proves the path is intentional/reachable but does not bound its wall-clock cost.

PR #1854 fixed the common no-park cold-start case for #1782. Its original claim that the parked fallback was naturally bounded was later retracted in source comments, but the residual parked-queue stall has no issue owner.

## Impact

A low transmit-rate configuration, or a control-plane/config-sync input that produces one, can cause a multi-second-to-minute packet-worker latency spike after idle. Because the timer wheel runs inline on the AF_XDP worker, unrelated queues, interfaces, sessions, HA heartbeats, and control traffic assigned to that worker stop making progress during catch-up.

This is a deterministic CPU-exhaustion/availability fault, not only a telemetry artifact.

## Required invariant

Advancing CoS scheduling state after arbitrary wall-clock idle must be bounded by the number of live queues/wheel slots, never by elapsed 50-us ticks. A parked queue's absolute wake deadline must remain correct across the jump: due queues wake once, future queues remain parked for their original deadline, and stale slot entries cannot fire early.

## Fix direction

Implement the previously deferred absolute-deadline rebase (plan option B) or an equivalent bounded scheduler:

- keep each parked queue's absolute `next_wakeup_tick` authoritative;
- on over-horizon lag, clear/rebuild wheel slots by iterating live parked queues once;
- wake queues whose deadline is `<= now_tick`;
- reinsert future queues relative to the snapped `current_tick` without changing their absolute deadline;
- preserve stale-entry generation/identity checks;
- cap work at O(number of queues + wheel slots), with no elapsed-tick loop.

A min-heap/calendar queue is also acceptable if it preserves deterministic fairness and adds no steady-state allocation or shared lock.

## #5804 — userspace-dp/GRE: implement key and call-ID session identity for gre-performance-acceleration [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Summary

`security flow gre-performance-acceleration` is accepted, compiled, shown, and copied into Rust `ForwardingState`, but no packet path reads it. All GRE traffic is keyed only by address family, protocol 47, outer source/destination IP, and zero L4 ports. Distinct keyed GRE/PPTP sessions between the same endpoints therefore alias one firewall session.

Closed #3360/PR #3454 deliberately chose the bounded config-truth fix and documented actual GRE key/call-ID extraction as a **separate deferred dataplane feature**. This issue owns that feature.

## Evidence

Verified on current `master` at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`.

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types/forwarding.rs:247-256` says `gre_acceleration` is not read and GRE flows remain 5-tuple-only.
- `userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs:10-18` has no tunnel discriminator.
- Flow parsing supplies `src_port=0,dst_port=0` for protocol 47, so every keyed GRE flow sharing the outer addresses hashes/equates identically.
- Native GRE encap/decap already understands the RFC 2890 Key Present field (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs`), but transit session classification does not extract it.

## Impact

When two GRE tunnels share outer endpoints:

1. The first packet creates one session/policy/NAT/timeout/accounting decision.
2. A packet carrying a different GRE key/call ID hits that same session.
3. It can inherit the first tunnel's permit, NAT state, routing resolution, counters, and timeout instead of receiving an independent policy decision.

This defeats the purpose of the advertised acceleration feature and can cross-associate logically distinct tunnels. PPTP enhanced-GRE call IDs add directional semantics that cannot be handled by blindly treating the field as an ordinary TCP/UDP port pair.

## Required design invariants

- When acceleration is disabled, behavior remains byte-for-byte 5-tuple compatible.
- When enabled, supported GRE discriminator formats form part of session identity before lookup/install/cache hashing.
- RFC 2890 32-bit keys retain all 32 bits; no truncation to one `u16`.
- Directionally symmetric keys reverse symmetrically rather than swapping arbitrary halves as TCP/UDP ports do.
- PPTP call-ID/request/response directionality is modeled explicitly; forward and reverse keys must meet on the same logical session without conflating other calls.
- Unkeyed GRE remains a distinct discriminator class from keyed value zero/malformed keyed headers.
- Truncated, fragmented, unsupported-version, checksum, sequence, and routing-present GRE headers fail closed for discriminator extraction without out-of-bounds reads.
- Session table, flow cache, NAT aliases, HA sync, event stream, clear/show filters, hashing, metrics, and persistence all use the same identity.
- Rolling upgrade cannot let an old peer/helper silently drop the discriminator and widen identity.

## Architecture questions to resolve before implementation

1. Extend `SessionKey` with a typed `TunnelDiscriminator`, or encode into existing ports? The latter needs an exact reversible 32-bit layout and protocol-specific reverse semantics and risks misleading every port consumer.

## #5805 — screen: per-destination ICMP/UDP flood sketches collapse sustained at-threshold traffic after the first second [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Defect

The #3607 token-bucket migration fixed the per-zone aggregate ICMP/UDP flood gates, but deliberately left the primary per-destination sketches on `RateCounter`. `RateCounter` retains the confirmed count-all/two-whole-second defect: after a destination sends exactly the configured threshold in one second, the first packet in the next second sees `prev_count == threshold`, increments `count`, and is over limit. Rejected packets continue incrementing, so a sustained at-threshold destination is then dropped nearly completely until a full idle second.

This means the primary Junos-compatible limits still do not implement the configured `N packets/second` contract:

- ICMP: per destination IP.
- UDP: per destination IP and destination port (or the documented per-IP fold for non-first fragments).

The secondary zone-wide token bucket is correct, but it is reached only after the primary sketch admits the packet, so it cannot repair the primary over-throttle.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `userspace-dp/src/screen/mod.rs:659-663`: `icmp_flood_drop` calls `icmp_dst_sketch.increment(..., now_secs, threshold)` first and returns drop immediately when over.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/mod.rs:708-716`: UDP does the same through `increment` / `increment_ip_port`.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/syn_rate.rs:198-206` and `:226-239`: every sketch cell is a `RateCounter` and every event, including rejected events, is charged.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/rate.rs:79-103`: previous whole-second count is retained with weight 1.0; current count always increments.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/rate_tests.rs:122-153`: the repository explicitly proves a full-threshold stream is admitted only for the first window and then over-throttled.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/mod.rs` comments explicitly say this per-destination migration was deferred from #3607.

Concrete trace for threshold 100:

1. second N: 100 packets to one destination pass; each row ends at `count=100`;
2. second N+1 first packet: `prev_count=100`, `count=1`, sum 101 -> drop;
3. the drop is counted, so all later packets in N+1 drop and end at `count=100`;
4. every active second repeats until a completely idle second clears the prior bucket.

## Impact

A legitimate service operating at its configured screen threshold can be reduced from the intended sustained rate to nearly zero after one second. This is firewall behavior and vSRX-parity drift, not merely telemetry: packets are discarded by the primary security-screen gate. Operators cannot tune the advertised threshold to a stable sustained ceiling.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.

## Deduplication

- #3607 diagnosed this primitive and migrated only the pure shaper/validation consumers. Its converged plan explicitly left the #3315 per-source/per-destination sketch unchanged for a separate fail-closed analysis; that issue is closed after the reduced-scope implementation.
- #4112 added ICMP/UDP per-destination sketch semantics, but retained `RateCounter`; it does not own or fix sustained-at-threshold behavior.
- No open or closed issue found that owns this deferred per-destination migration.

## #5806 — screen: tolerant load or HA sync of a dangling profile reference disables all checks for the zone [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Defect

Strict commit now rejects a zone that references an undefined screen profile, but tolerant startup/load and HA config-sync deliberately downgrade that invariant to a warning. The userspace dataplane receives the dangling reference as metadata, then both flow-present and flowless screen paths return `Pass` when no resolved profile exists. Every configured screen check for that zone is therefore disabled while the stale/malformed synchronized configuration remains active.

The runtime warning added by #3082/#3908 removes the silence but does not restore the security invariant. A peer upgrade, tolerant recovery, or HA synchronization event can leave a zone forwarding without LAND, fragment, source-route, SYN/ICMP/UDP flood, scan/sweep, or session-limit enforcement even though the active configuration says a screen is attached.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `pkg/config/compiler_uniformgates.go:245-258`: commit/commit-check is strict, but tolerant compilation downgrades the missing-reference error to a warning.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/screens.go:115-151`: unresolved zone/profile references are published separately because no `ScreenProfileSnapshot` is built.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/mod.rs` flow-present missing-profile branch calls `maybe_warn_missing_profile` and returns `Pass`.
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/mod.rs:1179-1193`: the flowless path does the same; comments explicitly identify fail-closed-vs-pass as deferred.
- `userspace-dp/src/protocol/security.rs:93-109`: the wire contract documents warning-only, fail-open behavior for older control planes and HA sync.

## Reachability

The strict user commit path is protected. The affected paths are still production-reachable:

1. loading an older or externally modified `active.json` through tolerant startup/recovery;
2. HA/config synchronization from a peer whose schema/config state is skewed;
3. rolling upgrade intervals where the producing side does not enforce the current reference invariant.

## Impact

This is a security-control disappearance, not only a diagnostic gap. The active config continues to claim a screen profile on the zone while the dataplane enforces none of it. Warning rate limiting cannot make forwarding fail closed and can be missed during failover noise.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.

## Deduplication

## #5807 — daemon: SIGTERM is not caught until after startup mutates managers and the dataplane [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Defect

`xpfd` enters `Daemon.Run(context.Background())`, performs config/bootstrap, interface naming, manager initialization, first config application, and dataplane setup, and only then installs `signal.NotifyContext`. A SIGTERM or daemon-mode SIGINT during phases 1-3 therefore takes the process default action: immediate process termination. Go defers and the daemon's ordered shutdown sequence do not run.

Startup has already begun mutating persistent and kernel/external state at that point. An operator or service manager stopping a slow/blocked startup can leave partially applied links/routes, FRR/IPsec/DHCP/HA/dataplane state, commit-confirm recovery work, and background workers without the cleanup/fencing path that steady-state shutdown relies on.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `cmd/xpfd/main.go:406-421`: constructs the daemon and calls `d.Run(context.Background())`; no signal is captured by `main`.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go:175-232`: `Run` starts loops, loads/bootstrap config, performs interface naming, initializes managers, applies config, and sets up the dataplane.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go:234-245`: signal notification is installed only after those mutations complete.
- Early-error defers cover only the policy scheduler and pin-retry loop; an uncaught signal does not execute even those defers because the process exits at the signal default action.

## Impact

This defeats the service manager's expectation that `systemctl stop/restart` receives an orderly, fenced shutdown even while startup is in progress. The highest-risk window is a startup blocked after HA/dataplane ownership or kernel state has changed but before Phase 4 installs the handler.

Severity: **High**. Confidence: **High**.

## Deduplication

No open or closed issue was found that owns signal installation before startup mutation. Existing shutdown/race issues, including #5681, address lifecycle joining after shutdown begins; they do not make an early SIGTERM observable to `Daemon.Run`.

## Required design

Install signal capture before the first externally visible mutation while preserving the intentional distinction between:

- the long-lived daemon parent context used by explicitly ordered services;
- the signal/apply-abort context used to stop or fence startup and later applies;
- interactive SIGINT ownership by the CLI versus SIGTERM ownership by the daemon.

The design must define the transactional result for a signal in each startup phase:

1. before config/bootstrap mutation;
2. during interface naming/lifeline setup;
3. during manager construction/first apply;
4. during dataplane setup after partial activation;
5. after normal service startup.

## #5808 — upgrade: unbounded systemctl is-active can strand post-flip cutover beyond rollback deadline [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Defect

The post-flip userspace-helper readiness gate is documented and called with a rollback deadline, but its first probe invokes `systemctl is-active` using `exec.Command(...).Output()` with no context or timeout. If systemd/DBus or the subprocess wedges, one probe can block indefinitely. The loop never gets back to its deadline check, so standalone auto-rollback and HA failure fencing do not execute within the promised window.

The same unbounded default also exists in the package-level legacy `unitActiveProbe`; production `cmd/xpfd` currently injects its own equally unbounded `defaultUpgradeUnitActive` into `HelperHealthProbe`.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `cmd/xpfd/upgrade.go:196-200`: `defaultUpgradeUnitActive` uses `exec.Command("systemctl", "is-active", ...).Output()` without `CommandContext`.
- `cmd/xpfd/upgrade.go:146-154`: that function is injected as `HelperHealthDeps.UnitActive` in the production upgrade system.
- `pkg/upgrade/helper_health.go:101-119`: the readiness loop computes `end`, calls `checkHelperReady`, and only tests the deadline *after* the call returns.
- `pkg/upgrade/helper_health.go:124-127`: `checkHelperReady` calls the unbounded `unitActive()` before the already-bounded control-socket probe.
- `pkg/upgrade/system_linux.go:142-151`: the package fallback probe has the same unbounded command shape.

A configured 30-second cutover deadline is therefore not an execution bound; it is only checked between probes.

## Impact

After the active symlink/version flip, the orchestrator can remain stuck indefinitely instead of rolling back or keeping the HA node fenced. The upgrade journal and rollback deadline no longer provide their stated recovery guarantee. A service-manager stop can then collide with a hung upgrade subprocess in an indeterminate post-cut state.

Severity: **High**. Confidence: **High**.

## Deduplication

#5286/its merged PR strengthened readiness from process-active to armed-forwarding target-binary identity, but retained this unbounded `is-active` primitive. No open or closed issue was found that owns end-to-end deadline enforcement for the readiness probe.

## Required fix

Make the deadline authoritative across every potentially blocking operation:

1. Pass a context or remaining-duration budget into the unit-active probe; use `exec.CommandContext`.
2. Bound the control-socket status timeout by the smaller of configured `StatusTimeout` and remaining overall time.
3. Do not sleep past the deadline; use a context-aware timer capped to remaining time.
4. Distinguish definitive inactive, command failure, and deadline/cancellation in the final wrapped error while retaining `errors.Is` for timeout/cancel causes.
5. Ensure the outer cutover/rollback code can proceed immediately after the probe returns and never waits on a leaked subprocess.
6. Reuse one bounded production primitive in `cmd/xpfd` and `pkg/upgrade`; do not leave two implementations with different timeout behavior.

## #5809 — xpfd: positional command after a daemon flag is ignored and starts the daemon [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Defect

Top-level command classification inspects only `argv[1]`. A leading daemon flag selects daemon mode. Go's global `flag.Parse` then stops at the first non-flag token, but the daemon path never checks `flag.Args()`/`flag.NArg()`. Consequently, invocations such as:

```sh
xpfd --debug cleanup
xpfd --config /tmp/xpf.conf version
xpfd --no-dataplane show system
```

silently ignore the positional command and start `xpfd` instead of rejecting the invocation. Flags after that first positional token are also left unparsed.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `cmd/xpfd/main.go:45-84`: `classifyCommand` treats any leading `-` token as `cmdDaemon` and does not scan later arguments.
- `cmd/xpfd/main.go:331-360`: daemon mode registers flags and calls the global `flag.Parse()`.
- The daemon path has no `flag.NArg()` or `flag.Args()` validation before constructing and running the daemon.
- Go's `flag` package stops parsing at the first non-flag argument, leaving it and the remaining tokens in `Args`.

## Impact

An operator trying to run a maintenance verb with global-looking flags can accidentally launch a second daemon or a config-only daemon. The command reports no usage error, and the requested cleanup/version/check operation never occurs. Under root/systemd tooling this can contend for sockets, pinned state, routes, or config locks.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.

## Deduplication

Existing command hardening rejects an unknown first positional token and validates leftover operands for individual verbs such as cleanup/upgrade. No open or closed issue was found that owns leftover positional arguments on the daemon-flag path.

## Required fix

Make top-level parsing unambiguous:

1. After daemon flag parsing, reject every positional remainder before logging setup, `daemon.New`, or any side effect.
2. Prefer a dedicated `FlagSet`/pure `parseDaemonArgs(args)` helper instead of the process-global flag set so tests can pin behavior without `os.Exit` or global state.
3. Emit a deterministic usage error naming all unexpected tokens and explaining that subcommands must be the first argument.
4. Do not reorder or reinterpret `xpfd --flag subcommand` as the subcommand unless a documented global-flag grammar is deliberately designed; silent reinterpretation could apply daemon-only flags to destructive verbs.

## #5810 — cluster failover: malformed optional node grammar can broaden into an untargeted RG failover [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Defect

The cluster-failover command/action grammar is parsed independently at three layers and is not closed over malformed or trailing tokens. Several malformed forms silently degrade to the broader untargeted `ManualFailover(rg)` operation instead of failing before side effects.

### Reproducible forms on current master

1. Remote CLI: `request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group 1 nod 0`

2. In-process CLI: `... redundancy-group 1 node` or `... redundancy-group 1 nod 0`

   - Missing or misspelled selector operands fall through to `ManualFailover(1)`.
3. gRPC loopback action: `cluster-failover:1:node`
   - the handler finds `:node`, sets `nodeStr` to empty, but then executes targeted parsing only when `nodeStr != ""`;
   - it falls through to the ordinary untargeted failover branch.

Both CLI parsers also accept trailing operands on otherwise valid reset/data/RG forms, creating additional grammar ambiguity.

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

## Impact

A truncated automation variable or typo in a privileged HA command can trigger a real redundancy-group failover with no target constraint. The intended operation may have been “make node N primary”; broadening it to an untargeted yield changes ownership in the opposite or unexpected direction. The loopback gRPC form remains reachable to trusted local clients even though the fabric interceptor rejects it.

#4883-C fixed only the remote CLI's exact bare-`node`/missing-value case. ## Defect

Most global-only `clear` handlers recognize only a prefix and discard every remaining token before issuing an unscoped mutation. A command that looks scoped to the operator can therefore report success while clearing the entire cache/counter/table.

Examples on current master include:

```text
clear arp 192.0.2.10
clear ipv6 neighbors interface ge-0-0-0
clear interfaces statistics ge-0-0-0
clear security nat statistics rule web
clear security nat source persistent-nat-table pool p1
clear security counters zone untrust
clear firewall all filter edge
clear system config-lock session 42
```

The remote and in-process CLIs have separate parsers and do not enforce identical exact arity. Some isolated paths were hardened previously, but the global rule is not systematic.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `cmd/cli/clear.go:18-90`: top-level `arp` discards all suffixes; `system`, `interfaces`, and `ipv6 neighbors` require only a prefix.
- `cmd/cli/clear.go:96-124,225-246`: NAT statistics/persistent table, security counters, and firewall all accept prefix matches with trailing operands.
- `pkg/cli/cli_clear.go:18-94,97-180,412-426`: the in-process CLI mirrors the same permissive shapes.
- The local `clear security policies hit-count` branch still uses `len(args) >= 2`, while the remote branch was hardened to exact arity by #5570.

All named backends are global-only; the discarded suffix is not carried into the mutation.

During incident response or troubleshooting, an operator can believe they cleared one neighbor, interface, policy/rule, zone, or session owner and instead erase all corresponding state or evidence. The command's success output reinforces the false scope. ARP/neighbor flushes can cause a broad forwarding disturbance; counter clears destroy diagnostic evidence.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.

- #5570 fixed exact arity only for the remote `clear security policies hit-count` path.
- #4883-E fixed malformed DHCP DUID selectors.

## #5812 — remote CLI: configuration-mode exit discards release failure and loses immediate retry state [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Defect

When an operator explicitly enters `exit` or `quit` in remote configuration mode, the CLI discards any `ExitConfigure` RPC error and unconditionally clears its local configuration-mode state, edit path, and prompt. A transport timeout/disconnect before the release reaches the daemon can leave the server-side configuration lock and candidate owned by that session, while the client has thrown away the only immediate in-process retry path.

This is distinct from process teardown/EOF cleanup, where best-effort bounded release is reasonable because the client is exiting.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `cmd/cli/shared.go:517-527`: explicit `exit`/`quit` executes `_, _ = c.client.ExitConfigure(...)`, then always stores `configMode=false`, clears `editPath`, resets the prompt, and returns success.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go:49-53`: the RPC is idempotent from the client's perspective and always returns success when reached; it invokes `ExitConfigureSession`.
- `pkg/configstore/store_lock.go:227-241`: release is session-holder-gated and clears candidate/lock state only when the request reaches the owning server session.
- `cmd/cli/main.go` separately has bounded best-effort release for terminal teardown; that path has no interactive recovery and should remain separate.

## Impact

A transient RPC failure can leave the configuration lock held until disconnect cleanup or lease reclamation while the current CLI claims it exited successfully. The operator loses the candidate context/edit path and cannot simply retry `exit`; another session may be blocked and the candidate's disposition becomes unclear.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.

## Deduplication

#5053 bounds best-effort release during CLI process teardown and signal handling. It does not cover an explicit interactive `exit` command that should report failure and preserve retry state. No other issue was found for this state transition.

## Required fix

Treat explicit exit as a transactional client state change:

1. Issue `ExitConfigure` with the command context/bounded timeout.
2. On any RPC error, return the error and retain `configMode`, `editPath`, and configuration prompt exactly so the operator can retry or inspect the candidate.
3. Only clear local configuration state after a successful RPC response.
4. Preserve idempotence for the response-lost case: a retry after the server already released must still return success and let the client transition to operational mode.
5. Keep EOF/process-exit cleanup bounded and best-effort; do not make CLI shutdown wait indefinitely for a release response.

## Acceptance criteria

- A fake client returning timeout/unavailable leaves all local config-mode state and prompt unchanged and surfaces an error.
- Retrying with success clears state exactly once and prints the exit message once.
- A fake server that releases then returns a simulated lost-response error followed by idempotent success is recoverable.

## #5813 — CLI session display: tolerated nil interface or unit entries panic the in-process daemon [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Defect

The tolerant/load/HA-sync compiler permits present-but-nil `InterfaceConfig` map values and nil `InterfaceUnit` entries. The `show security flow session` display path builds an egress ifindex/VLAN-to-name map without guarding either pointer. A matching host interface causes a nil dereference inside the in-process CLI, and `CLI.Run` has no panic recovery, so an operator display command can terminate `xpfd`.

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `pkg/cli/cli_show_flow.go:259`: every session display builds this map before printing entries.
- `pkg/cli/cli_show_interfaces_nil_5068_test.go:11-67`: repository tests explicitly prove nil interface/unit slots are reachable on the tolerant/HA-sync path.
- #5068 added guards to show-interface presenters and completers, but this separate session-display builder was not included.

## Impact

A malformed but tolerated synchronized/loaded config turns a read-only operational command into a daemon crash. On an HA node this can trigger failover/restart and remove the operator's ability to inspect the sessions involved in the malformed configuration.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.

#5068 fixed the same representable nil class for `show interfaces` and completion only. Its tests and write scope do not exercise `buildSessionEgressIfacesWithLookup` or session display. No open/closed issue owns this remaining surface.

- Skip nil `InterfaceConfig` and nil `InterfaceUnit` values in the session-display map builder.
- Keep map resolution deterministic and preserve the first-wins `(ifindex,vlanID)` behavior for valid entries.
- Centralize tolerant config interface/unit walking in a nil-safe iterator/helper used by all read-only CLI presenters, rather than repeating guards indefinitely.
- Audit remote gRPC/REST session presentation and filter-map builders for the same raw config walk.

## Acceptance criteria

- A fixture containing a nil interface value, a nil unit on a valid interface, and valid sibling entries can run every local session show variant without panic.
- Valid siblings still map to the expected parent ifindex, VLAN/unit, and display name.
- A nil zone/interface reference does not turn into an empty/wrong filter match.
- Tests drive the real `handleShowSecurityFlowSession` path with a fake dataplane and deterministic ifindex lookup, not only the leaf helper.
- Remote CLI/gRPC/REST sibling builders are either proven nil-safe by tests or fixed in the same PR.
- `go test -race` covers concurrent read-only presentation against tolerant config publication semantics.

## #5814 — DHCP DDNS: update-server changes neither republish to the new endpoint nor clean the old endpoint [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Defect

The DHCP-lease DDNS reconciler (Surface B) defines record equality only by DNS content and does not include backend/update-server identity. It resolves the current updater each pass and overwrites its prior live-updater anchor before reconciliation. Changing an RFC 2136 server/zone/credentials while leases and records are otherwise unchanged therefore marks every owned record settled, performs no publish on the new server, and leaves the old server's record live indefinitely.

If DNS content also changes, Pass 1 attempts to delete the old owned tuple through the **new** updater, then publishes through the new endpoint. The old endpoint still retains the original record, but ownership can be removed/replaced locally, losing cleanup authority.

## Current-master evidence

Verified at `3821cd9d2fd12e1a3ab5aee6198efc8906d36824`:

- `pkg/ddns/manager.go:742-766`: each reconcile resolves current family updaters, then replaces the single `m.updater` live anchor before record reconciliation.
- `pkg/ddns/manager.go:1056-1072`: `stillWanted && recordsEqual(...)` treats the record as settled and skips both delete and upsert.
- `pkg/ddns/manager.go:1126`: changed/expired ownership is deleted through `env.updaterFor(owned.Family)`, which is the newly resolved backend, not necessarily the backend that published it.
- `pkg/ddns/manager.go:1478-1485`: `recordsEqual` compares FQDN/type/address/PTR/TTL only.
- `pkg/ddns/state.go:220+`: `ownedRecord` has a non-secret `BackendFingerprint`, but the lease reconciler's desired `ownedRecord` construction does not set or compare it; that protection is currently used by Surface A.

## Concrete traces

### Same record, endpoint A -> B

1. Endpoint A publishes A/AAAA/PTR/DHCID; ownership is stored without backend identity.
2. Config changes update-server to B with the same lease/FQDN/address/TTL.
3. Reconcile resolves B, `recordsEqual` is true, marks `seen`, and performs no wire operation.
4. B has no record; A retains the record permanently.

### Record and endpoint both change

1. A published old tuple.
2. Config moves to B and changes name/address/TTL.
3. Pass 1 sends the delete to B, where the old tuple never existed, and may count it successful.
4. Ownership is removed/replaced and B receives the new tuple; A's old tuple is orphaned.

## Impact

DNS can remain split across authoritative endpoints after an apparently successful config commit. Clients querying the new server miss current leases; clients querying the old server can receive stale addresses after lease reassignment, creating interception or traffic-blackhole risk. The appliance may no longer retain enough authority to clean the stale record.

Severity: **Medium**. Confidence: **High**.
