## #5842 — linksetup: positional NIC naming launders rename/persistence/reload failures and continues startup [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

**Severity:** High
**Confidence:** High
**Source:** codex-183 audit, current master `3821cd9d2`

## Problem

The default positional interface-naming path has no error channel for the operations that establish live and reboot-stable NIC identity:

- `renamePositional` returns only a `changed bool`; failed temp/final renames are logged and discarded (`pkg/daemon/linksetup.go:230-277,306-356`).
- `writeLinkFile` and `writeBootstrapFxp0Network` return `false` both for "unchanged" and "write failed" (`:404-460`).
- `enumerateAndRenameInterfaces` logs `networkctl reload` failure and always returns nil after successful enumeration (`:66-112`).
- `applyStartupNamingPolicy` propagates that nil, so normal startup/config-arrival naming proceeds toward VRF/networkd/dataplane work against logical names that may not exist or may name the wrong physical NIC (`pkg/daemon/device_map.go:95-107`).

The device-map path was made error-propagating in #4956, but the positional path still launders the same class of failures.

A failed final rename can also leave a newly written `.link` rule describing a state that is not live; a failed temp collision rename can cascade into EEXIST; a failed reload means next-boot persistence is unproven. Logs are not convergence.

## Required invariant

Startup naming must return a typed, per-interface convergence result. Dependent management, VRF, networkd, RSS/AF_XDP, and dataplane publication may proceed only after every required NIC is verified at its intended live name and persistence/reload state is known.

## Fix direction

- Replace bool-only helpers with a result/error structure covering temp rename, final rename, live-name verification, `.link`/bootstrap file publication, and networkd reload.
- Make the shared collision breaker return failures rather than only logging.
- Verify final name -> stable hardware identity after all renames; do not infer success from calls alone.
- Retain durable retry/recovery intent for partial renames and abort dependent startup phases.
- Unify positional and device-map orchestration around one transactional naming module instead of parallel helpers with different error semantics.

## Acceptance criteria / RED tests

- Inject failure in each temp rename, final rename, `.link` write, bootstrap `.network` write, final-name verification, and `networkctl reload`; startup returns non-nil and does not arm dataplane/RSS on the unconverged interfaces.
- Multiple failures are aggregated with exact from/to/interface identity.
- A partial rename retains enough state for idempotent restart/retry and never records a temp name as `OriginalName`.
- Existing `.link` file + failed live rename is reported as unconverged, not unchanged.
- Final inventory proves each logical name maps to the intended PCI/MAC identity and no `xpf-tmp-*` remains.
- Config-arrival retry markers are consumed only after verified convergence.
- Management-lifeline behavior is explicit: a naming failure cannot strand the protected interface without entering documented safe bootstrap.
- Device-map and positional paths share the same failure contract and tests.
- End-to-end boot fault injection proves no AF_XDP bind/config apply occurs after naming failure and a subsequent clean boot repairs the state.

## #5843 — HA posture: one VRRP MASTER masks partial/missing RETH ownership and prevents repair [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

**Severity:** High
**Confidence:** High
**Source:** codex-183 audit, current master `3821cd9d2`

## Problem

The periodic HA posture fixer treats **any** MASTER instance as complete primary posture:

`CheckVRRPPosture` computes `anyMaster` and reports `NeedsMaster` only when `clusterPri && !anyMaster` (`pkg/daemon/rg_state.go:318-343`). If an RG has two RETH VRRP instances and one is MASTER while the other remains BACKUP/stuck/missing, the state is classified OK, the mismatch timer is cleared, and `UpdateRGPriority` is never re-driven.

This contradicts the surrounding ownership model, which repeatedly says all VRRP instances must be MASTER to prevent partial ownership. In strict-VIP mode `rg_active` remains false; in default mode cluster-primary may activate forwarding, but traffic to VIPs on the non-MASTER interface still blackholes or remains owned by the peer.

There is a second inventory gap: `reconcileRGState` builds `rgVRRP` only from currently instantiated VRRP states (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:572-587`). The state machine replaces its map with that observed subset (`rg_state.go:144-157`). `allMasterLocked` therefore returns true when all **observed** instances are MASTER even if a configured RETH instance failed to build and is absent. Zero observed instances are silently posture-OK at `:322-327`.

## Required invariant

For a cluster-primary RG, posture is converged only when the complete expected configured RETH/VRRP instance set exists and every member is MASTER. For secondary, any MASTER member remains a resign condition.

## Fix direction

Carry expected per-RG VRRP inventory from the committed config/VRRP manager into posture evaluation. Compare expected vs observed explicitly:
- missing instance -> rebuild/rebind debt, not OK;
- present BACKUP/INIT/FAULT -> priority/election repair;
- all expected MASTER -> converged;
- unexpected stale instance -> removal/resign debt.

Do not infer completeness from the observed map length.

## Acceptance criteria / RED tests

- Two expected instances, one MASTER + one BACKUP: sustained primary posture returns `NeedsMaster` and re-drives the non-MASTER member.
- Two expected, one absent: posture remains degraded, triggers instance rebuild, and cannot report all-master/takeover-ready.
- Secondary with any MASTER still resigns every MASTER member.
- Strict and default VIP-ownership modes have explicit expected behavior; neither silently accepts partial VIP ownership.
- A dropped VRRP event is repaired from authoritative instance state.
- An interface reappearing after build failure joins expected inventory and converges without restart.
- Config removal updates expected inventory generation-safely; stale expected members do not block forever.
- Per-interface status/alarm names expected, observed, state, mismatch age, and last repair error.
- Repeated repair is rate-limited but retains debt until full convergence.
- Multi-RETH IPv4/IPv6 smoke forces one member BACKUP/missing and proves traffic does not report healthy/active until all configured VIP ownership is restored.

## #5846 — upgrade: stale STOPPED recovery ignores restart failure and starts a new cut with an unverified rollback target [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

When a stale upgrade journal is at `STOPPED` for target A but a newer staged target B is present, recovery tries to restart the still-current known-good daemon. If that restart fails, the error is only logged; recovery discards the stale journal in memory, removes partial evidence, and proceeds into a fresh cut to B. The new cut can therefore use a version that just failed to restart as its rollback target while the appliance control plane remains down.

**Severity:** High  
**Confidence:** High  
**Audit provenance:** codex-183 ledger row 203, reverified on `origin/master` `3821cd9d2`.

## Evidence

`pkg/upgrade/cutover.go:311-371` handles a journal whose target differs from the newly staged version. In the `STOPPED` arm:

```go
if j.State == StateStopped {
    if startErr := r.cfg.Sys.StartUnit(r.cfg.Unit); startErr != nil {
        r.logf("upgrade: WARN failed to restart unit after stale-stop recovery: %v", startErr)
    }
}
r.removeAllPartials()
j = &Journal{State: StateInit}
```

Execution then initializes a fresh journal from `versions/current` and may continue through preflight/copy/verify/stop/flip/start for B. The failed restart neither aborts nor remains durable recovery debt.

## Concrete failure trace

1. Upgrade A durably reaches `STOPPED`: the unit is down and `current` still points to old version O.
2. The process crashes, then apt stages newer B.
3. Resume detects A != B and calls `StartUnit` for O.
4. Start fails because O cannot execute/start or systemd is unhealthy.
5. The failure is warning-only; recovery erases partial evidence and resets the journal state in memory.
6. Fresh cut B records O as `PreviousVersion`, despite just proving O cannot restart.
7. If B later fails, rollback targets the known-bad/unstartable O. Even if B succeeds, the appliance remained without its control plane through an unacknowledged recovery mutation.

## Required invariants

- A stale `STOPPED` generation is recovered only after positive start and target-version health confirmation of the current version.
- A version that failed to restart cannot be accepted as a verified rollback target.
- Recovery evidence/journal state must remain durable until the unit is proven healthy.
- Failure must stop before deleting partial evidence or starting a newer cut.

5. The roll lease expires.
6. Self-recovery observes only the false `ARMED` journal and refuses to clear the drain forever.

1. calls `CompileCandidate` at `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:293`;

## #5849 — grpcapi: per-RPC cancellation destroys the connection's candidate configuration and releases its lock [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

The gRPC config-lock interceptor treats cancellation of any unary RPC as proof that the entire HTTP/2 connection disconnected. gRPC cancellation is per RPC/stream; the underlying connection can remain healthy and be reused. A deadline or Ctrl-C on one request therefore calls `ExitConfigureSession`, discards the connection’s candidate tree, clears dirty state/edit path, and releases its lock while the client is still connected.

```go
resp, err := handler(ctx, req)
if ctx.Err() != nil {
    sessionID := peerSessionID(ctx)
    if sessionID != "" {
        s.store.ExitConfigureSession(sessionID)
    }
}
```

`peerSessionID` is the peer address, intended to identify the connection. But `ctx` is the individual RPC context. A client deadline, explicit RPC cancellation, or server-side cancellation sets `ctx.Err()` without closing the gRPC connection.

`pkg/configstore/store_lock.go:227-242` shows that `ExitConfigureSession` does not merely unlock: it sets `candidate=nil`, `dirty=false`, clears config mode/holders, and drops the edit path.

The interceptor is installed on the loopback server and in the fabric unary chain.

## Concrete failure trace

1. One CLI/gRPC connection enters configure mode and stages uncommitted candidate edits.
2. Over the same HTTP/2 connection, an RPC is canceled or reaches its deadline. This can be a show/monitor-helper unary unrelated to configuration.
3. The handler returns with `ctx.Err()!=nil`.
4. The interceptor calls `ExitConfigureSession(peerAddr)`.
5. The candidate and edit state are destroyed.
6. The connection remains open; its next config RPC sees “not in configuration mode” and the operator’s edits are lost. Another session may acquire the lock immediately.

Multiplexed concurrent RPCs make the race stronger: one canceled stream can destroy state while another commit/edit stream on the same connection is still active.

## #5850 — gRPC MonitorPacketDrop bypasses event subscriber cap and permits unbounded fan-out [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

`MonitorPacketDrop` bypasses the event-buffer subscriber admission cap by calling `EventBuffer.Subscribe(256)` directly. Each live stream adds a buffered channel and expands the synchronous O(N) fan-out performed for every event. The primary gRPC listener is intentionally unauthenticated on loopback, so any local process can open an unbounded number of packet-drop streams and consume memory and event-production CPU.

This is distinct from #4484 L-2: that change capped REST SSE with `TrySubscribe`, while explicitly treating gRPC consumers as inherently bounded. `MonitorPacketDrop` is request-created and is not inherently bounded.

## Current-master evidence

- `pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_monitor.go:167-169`
  - every RPC allocates `eventBuf.Subscribe(256)`
  - `Subscribe` never rejects
- `pkg/logging/eventbuf.go:160-170,252-293`
  - `defaultMaxSubscribers = 64`
  - only `TrySubscribe` enforces it
  - every `Subscribe` caller still increments the shared subscriber set
- `pkg/logging/eventbuf.go:210-237`
  - every event walks and attempts delivery to every subscriber under `subMu.RLock`
- `pkg/grpcapi/server.go:351-371`
  - primary listener is loopback-clamped but unauthenticated
  - no `grpc.MaxConcurrentStreams` limit
- `pkg/grpcapi/server.go:484-492`
  - fabric server also has no server stream ceiling (the current allowlist denies MonitorPacketDrop there, but a server-wide limit is still defense in depth)

## Impact

A local unprivileged process can repeatedly open `MonitorPacketDrop` streams and hold them idle. Each stream retains a 256-record channel and adds per-event fan-out work. This can exhaust daemon memory and increase latency on security-event production. Because this is a router/security appliance control plane, local tenant/process compromise must not provide an unbounded daemon resource-amplification path.

## Required fix

1. Admit `MonitorPacketDrop` through `TrySubscribe` or a shared gRPC event-stream limiter.
2. Return `codes.ResourceExhausted` when the subscriber budget is full.
3. Ensure cancellation and send failure always release the slot.
4. Install a defensible `grpc.MaxConcurrentStreams` ceiling on both primary and fabric servers, or document and test why a shared interceptor-level stream budget is preferable.
5. Keep trusted, fixed-count internal subscriptions working without allowing request-created streams to bypass admission.

## Tests / acceptance criteria

- Exactly the configured number of packet-drop streams can subscribe.
- The next stream fails with `ResourceExhausted` before sending the start banner.
- Canceling or failing one admitted stream frees a slot.

## #5851 — Malformed cluster-failover node suffix executes untargeted RG failover [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

The loopback `SystemAction` handler parses `cluster-failover:<rgID>[:node<N>]` with a prefix search and treats an empty node suffix as if no target were supplied. Consequently, the malformed action `cluster-failover:1:node` passes validation and executes an untargeted `ManualFailover(1)` instead of returning `InvalidArgument`.

The fabric interceptor already rejects exactly this action through the stricter `parseProxiedFailoverAction` helper. The two parsers therefore disagree about the same destructive action grammar.

## Current-master evidence

- `pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_system_action.go:421-428`
  - finds the first `:node` substring
  - records an empty `nodeStr` for `cluster-failover:1:node`
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_system_action.go:435-478`
  - only enters targeted handling when `nodeStr != ""`
  - empty suffix falls through to `s.cluster.ManualFailover(rgID)`
- `pkg/grpcapi/server.go:642-695`
  - `parseProxiedFailoverAction` is documented as the single strict grammar
  - it rejects an empty suffix, unknown/trailing segments, and unsupported node IDs
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_fabric_allowlist_4122_test.go:105-111,169-181`
  - already pins `cluster-failover:1:node` as invalid at the fabric gate
- No handler-level test asserts that the malformed action cannot mutate cluster state.

## Impact

A typo in a destructive operator request changes semantics from “fail over RG 1 to a named node” to “toggle/fail over RG 1 without a target.” On an HA router this can move traffic ownership in the opposite direction from the operator's request and cause an avoidable outage. The action is local-loopback only, but operator mistakes and control-client bugs must fail closed.

## Required fix

1. Define one exact structured parser for all cluster-failover action forms.
2. Reuse it in both the fabric interceptor and `SystemAction` handler.
3. Distinguish valid local-only form `cluster-failover:<rgID>` from valid targeted form `cluster-failover:<rgID>:node<N>`.
4. Reject empty suffixes, duplicate/unknown segments, signs/whitespace not present in the documented grammar, trailing bytes, invalid RG IDs, and unsupported node IDs before any cluster method or peer proxy is called.
5. Prefer a typed protobuf request/action enum in a follow-up if wire compatibility prevents replacing the string grammar here.

## Tests / acceptance criteria

- Table-driven tests cover every accepted local and targeted form.
- `cluster-failover:1:node`, duplicate `:node`, trailing bytes, signed/whitespace IDs, empty RG IDs, negative IDs, and unsupported nodes return `InvalidArgument`.
- Invalid requests call neither `ManualFailover`, `RequestPeerFailover`, nor `proxyPeerSystemAction`.
- Handler and fabric-gate acceptance sets are mechanically compared so they cannot drift again.

## #5852 — rpm: StopAll cancellation is counted as path loss and can trigger route remediation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

RPM lifecycle cancellation is classified as probe loss. If `StopAll`, config replacement, or daemon shutdown cancels a probe while `runProbe` is in flight, `runSingleTest` treats the resulting `context.Canceled` as an ordinary path failure: it increments sent/failure counters, advances the successive-loss threshold, emits failure events, and may fire the route-remediation transition.

A control-plane lifecycle action must be neutral to path health.

## Current-master evidence

- `pkg/rpm/rpm.go:408-417`: `StopAll` cancels the shared probe context and waits for probe goroutines.
- `pkg/rpm/rpm.go:521-540`: after `runProbe(ctx,...)`, only `ErrProbeSetup` is held neutral; no `ctx.Err()` / cancellation classification exists.
- `pkg/rpm/rpm.go:542-568`: every other error increments `TotalSent`, `SuccFail`, failure counts, emits `ping_probe_failed`, and can cross the loss threshold.
- `pkg/rpm/rpm.go:606-627`: the resulting status change fires `ping_test_failed` and `fireTransition`; ip-monitoring can therefore change route preference during teardown/reconfigure.
- `pkg/rpm/icmp.go:216-230`: the ICMP path checks cancellation only before a blocking `ReadFrom`. With no context deadline, `StopAll` can wait for the fixed three-second socket deadline, after which the read error is also processed as loss.

## Impact

Stopping/reconfiguring RPM can generate false path-loss state and route-remediation actions exactly while the old configuration is being torn down. Depending on transition consumers, this can withdraw/retarget routes, emit misleading alarms, or race the replacement configuration. The single-probe default is enough to trigger this when the threshold is one.

## Required fix

1. Immediately after `runProbe`, if `ctx.Err() != nil`, return from the cycle without changing counters, timestamps, status, events, or transitions.
2. Alternatively define and consistently classify a dedicated neutral lifecycle-cancellation sentinel, preserving ordinary network timeouts as path failures.
3. Make ICMP cancellation interrupt a blocked read promptly, for example by advancing the socket deadline from a cancellation watcher with race-safe teardown, or by using a context-aware packet I/O abstraction.
4. Ensure `StopAll` cannot wait the full probe timeout solely because an ICMP read is blocked.
5. Keep genuine probe timeout, refused connection, and HTTP failure behavior unchanged.

## Tests / acceptance criteria

- Inject a `probeFn` that blocks on `ctx.Done()`; call `StopAll`; assert zero changes to `TotalSent`, `TotalRecv`, `SuccFail`, `LastProbeAt`, `LastStatus`, event stream, and transitions.
- Run the test for prior `unknown`, `pass`, and `fail` states, including the one-probe/threshold-one defaults.
- Exercise cancellation between probes and while the first immediate probe is running.
- A real/socket-seam ICMP test proves cancellation wakes the read promptly instead of waiting `icmpProbeTimeout`.
- Genuine timeout tests still increment loss and can transition to fail.
- Run focused tests under `-race`.

## Audit provenance

Current-master revalidation of codex-183 frozen-ledger item 245. Open/closed issue search found no owner for RPM lifecycle cancellation being treated as path loss.

## #5853 — event-options: same-policy bursts fill action queue and drop unrelated remediations [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

The event-options action queue claims to keep at most one pending action per policy, but deduplication only runs after the channel is already full. While the worker is blocked behind the configuration lock, a burst from one policy can occupy all 64 queue slots. The next remediation for an unrelated policy is then dropped even though 63 queued entries are redundant and will later be discarded by cooldown/staleness checks.

## Current-master evidence

- `pkg/eventengine/engine.go:94-98`: documented invariant says dedup-by-policy keeps at most one pending action per policy.
- `pkg/eventengine/engine.go:619-650`: `enqueue` first performs an unconditional channel send; same-policy replacement is attempted only in the `default` branch after the queue is full.
- `pkg/eventengine/engine.go:653-718`: `supersede` can replace duplicates, but is unreachable while any slot remains.
- `pkg/eventengine/engine_stale_revalidate_3750_test.go:132-166`: the existing test explicitly documents and relies on duplicates being queued while the channel is not full.
- `pkg/eventengine/engine_integration_test.go:636-671`: `TestQueue_DedupByPolicy` sends more than 64 same-policy events but never asserts the stated “at most one pending” invariant or that an unrelated policy remains admissible.

## Reproduction

1. Hold the config lock so the worker dequeues policy `p` and blocks retrying.
2. Send 64+ additional events matching `p`; the fast path fills every queue slot with `p`.
3. Send one event matching distinct policy `q`.
4. `supersede(q)` finds no queued `q`, cannot evict redundant `p` entries, and `enqueue` increments `DroppedQueueFull`.
5. After releasing the lock, `q` never executes.

## Impact

A noisy or attacker-influenced event source for one policy can starve unrelated remediation policies. On a router/security appliance this can suppress route failover, interface quarantine, configuration correction, or alerting actions at the exact time event volume is elevated. The bounded channel prevents memory growth but does not provide fairness or the documented per-policy bound.

## Required fix

1. Deduplicate by policy before every queue admission, not only after saturation.
2. Prefer keyed pending state plus an order queue:
   - one pending payload per policy;
   - a new trigger atomically replaces the pending payload/revision for that key;
   - distinct policy keys retain FIFO order;
   - the currently in-flight worker action is tracked separately from pending state.
3. Preserve the bounded count of distinct pending policies and nonblocking producer behavior.
4. Define metrics precisely: superseded same-policy payloads versus truly dropped distinct-policy actions should not share an ambiguous queue-full count.
5. Preserve stale-policy/cooldown revalidation immediately before commit.

## Tests / acceptance criteria

- Hold the config lock, send more than `actionQueueDepth` events for `p`, then one for `q`; after release, prove `q` commits and `p` occupied at most one pending slot.
- Concurrent producers for the same policy never create more than one pending key under `-race`.

## #5854 — config: strict commit accepts next-table/rib-group rules beyond live kernel windows [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Summary

Strict commit accepts next-table and rib-group configurations that exceed the kernel rule windows the runtime can program. The compiler emits only a warning. The reconciler then silently stops at the limit and returns success, so the committed generation and operational state claim routes that do not exist in the kernel.

## Current-master evidence

- `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go:1468-1474`: routing-rule window validation is appended through warning-only `ValidateConfig`.
- `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn_routing.go:166-222`:
  - counts next-table routes above 100 and rib-group connected-prefix rules above 1000;
  - explicitly says the runtime accepts the config and routes beyond the limit are ignored.
- `pkg/config/compiler_routing_rules_test.go:46-115`: tests require only warnings at 101/1001; no strict compile rejection is pinned.
- `pkg/routing/rules.go:117-151`: next-table programming stops at 100 with a warning and `break`.
- `pkg/routing/rules.go:169-172`: the truncation itself contributes no returned error.
- The same fixed-window/clear-range invariant exists for rib-group rules.

## Impact

An operator can successfully commit a generation containing more inter-VRF leak rules than the node realizes. Which routes work depends on compiler/runtime ordering; later routes silently disappear. This can blackhole traffic, create asymmetric routing, or leave only part of an intended VRF connectivity/security design active. The control plane must not acknowledge an unrealizable strict configuration.

## Required fix

Choose one explicit contract:

1. **Reject exact overflow on strict commit**
   - compute the exact effective rules the reconciler would program after unknown-target skips, deduplication, self-import elimination, family handling, and group expansion;
   - reject the first configuration exceeding the corresponding shared limit;
   - keep lenient load/HA sync fail-safe and visibly degraded.

or:

2. **Remove the artificial truncation**
   - allocate collision-free priority ranges large enough for the supported configuration bound;
   - keep stale-rule cleanup complete and bounded;
   - prove no overlap with PBR, rib-group, or other policy-rule bands.

Do not turn the existing conservative warning count directly into a hard reject because its comments admit false positives. Move the effective-rule planner and limits into a shared package/API consumed by both compiler and reconciler.

At runtime, reaching the limit despite validation must return an error rather than `break` and report success.

## #5855 — dhcpv6: DUID type changes restart the client but retain the old cached or persisted identity [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Problem

Changing an interface's configured DHCPv6 DUID type does not actually change the identity type used on the wire.

`Reconcile` includes `DUIDType` in the client fingerprint and restarts the client when it changes (`pkg/dhcp/reconcile.go:31-54,82-107`). It updates `m.duidTypes`, but it neither invalidates `m.duids[iface]` nor replaces the persisted DUID.

On restart, `getDUID` (`pkg/dhcp/dhcp.go:605-622`) returns the cached DUID first, or loads the persisted DUID next, without checking whether `DUIDType()` matches the newly requested `duid-ll` / `duid-llt` mode. The restarted client therefore keeps using the old type indefinitely. The configuration and operational state disagree, and an operator cannot deliberately rotate between LL and LLT through configuration.

## Impact

- A committed DUID-type change is acknowledged but has no wire effect.
- The old server identity/lease can persist unexpectedly after a requested identity rotation.
- Warm-cache and post-daemon-restart behavior differ only accidentally; both are wrong because neither validates type.
- A future fix that simply deletes the old identity must define and surface the resulting lease disruption rather than silently rotating it.

## Required design

Treat configured DUID type and resolved DUID as one lifecycle object. When the requested type differs from cached or persisted state, either:

1. atomically generate and durably persist the requested type before starting the replacement client, then retire the old identity; or
2. fail the commit with an explicit clear/rotation requirement.

Do not silently reuse a mismatched identity and do not expose a newly generated DUID-LLT unless persistence succeeds.

## Acceptance

- Warm-cache `duid-ll -> duid-llt` and `duid-llt -> duid-ll` tests prove the restarted client uses the requested type.
- Cold-cache tests seed each persisted old type and prove the mismatch is handled identically.
- Persistence failure leaves the previous identity and running client state coherent; no fallback identity is sent.
- Show/API output reports the actual active type and does not claim the newly configured type before successful rotation.
- README documents whether type change is automatic rotation or requires explicit clearing.

Re-verified on master `3821cd9d2`. This is distinct from #5711's acquisition/renew identity parity and #4909's persistence-error handling.

## #5856 — userspace-dp: process-global PTB and Time-Exceeded buckets let one zone starve ICMP errors for every zone [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Problem

The generated-error limiter isolates reasons but not security/tenant domains for ICMP Packet-Too-Big and Time-Exceeded.

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/icmp_ratelimit.rs` keeps `TIME_EXCEEDED_BUCKET` and `PACKET_TOO_BIG_BUCKET` as process-global statics. Every worker, interface, routing instance, redundancy group, and ingress zone consumes the same bucket for each reason. The file explicitly documents that only Reject was split per zone in #3618.

An attacker in one untrusted zone can continuously send TTL=1/hop-limit=1 traffic or oversized DF traffic, keep the corresponding global bucket empty, and suppress legitimate traceroute and PMTUD replies for unrelated zones. The forwarded data packet still fails closed, but cross-zone diagnostics and PMTUD convergence become attacker-controlled; suppressing PTB can turn unrelated large flows into persistent blackholes.

The generator call sites already carry ingress identity. PTB dispatch receives `ingress_ident`; Time-Exceeded is built from a polled ingress descriptor. The lack of a zone key is an API/design omission, not absence of attribution.

## Required design

Use bounded, configuration-keyed fairness domains for Time-Exceeded and PTB, analogous to #3618's sparse per-zone Reject buckets, while retaining a process/global ceiling so creating many zones cannot multiply reflection capacity without bound.

Recommended hierarchy:

1. per-ingress-zone bucket (fallback bucket for unzoned/unknown);
2. process-wide per-reason ceiling;
3. emit only when both gates admit.

Resolve the zone from the ingress ifindex at the generation site and preserve the same `Arc` state across forwarding snapshot refreshes. Keep cardinality configuration-bounded and counters observable at least by reason plus suppressed zone/interface. Define state/reset behavior across config publication.

## Acceptance

- Exhausting PTB or Time-Exceeded in zone A does not suppress the same reason in zone B.
- The process-wide ceiling still bounds aggregate replies across many zones.
- Unknown/unzoned ingress is rate-limited through a real fallback bucket.
- Repeated forwarding-state clone/publication does not reset live buckets into over-admission.
- Counter/status surfaces identify collateral suppression and do not require O(zone-count) work on the packet path.
- Concurrency tests prove no double-credit across workers.
- Packet captures demonstrate PMTUD/traceroute in a quiet zone while another zone floods the corresponding trigger.

Related but distinct from #3618, which fixed only active Reject and intentionally left these two reasons global. Re-verified on master `3821cd9d2`.

## #5857 — userspace-dp: lo0 firewall policers compile and report a match but never meter host-bound traffic [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Problem

Firewall filters attached to `lo0` can carry policers, and the Rust filter compiler preserves both the policer name and three-color runtime on the term. The userspace local-delivery path evaluates the lo0 filter with `evaluate_lo0_filter_counted`, but that evaluator only records counters and copies `policer_name` into `FilterResult`.

`apply_lo0_filter_action` then consumes only `result.action` and `result.log_match`. It never calls `apply_term_three_color_policer`, never meters a named policer, never applies policer drop/DSCP decisions, and never returns a policer outcome.

The metering implementation is used by interface TX-selection and cached flow paths, proving the runtime exists; it is simply absent from lo0/local delivery.

## Impact

A strict-valid control-plane firewall filter that appears to rate-limit SSH, BGP, routing protocols, ICMP, or other traffic to the router does not enforce the configured rate in the userspace local-delivery path. Counters/logs can make the term look active while every matching packet is delivered. An untrusted peer can therefore exceed the operator's control-plane protection envelope and consume kernel/listener/daemon CPU.

This is a security-appliance correctness issue, not just missing telemetry.

## Required design

- Evaluate lo0 terms through an API that meters every matched policer exactly once, including `then next term` chains.
- Pass a coherent monotonic timestamp and packet byte count from the poll iteration.
- Apply policer drop before local delivery and before synthesizing a reject that the policer did not authorize.
- Apply/document color-based DSCP behavior for host-bound packets; if unsupported, reject that action at strict commit rather than silently ignore it.
- Preserve counter/log attribution and expose policer conform/exceed/violate counters.
- Ensure nft/kernel host-inbound mirror semantics do not claim equivalent policer enforcement if it cannot meter.

The API should return a structured local-filter outcome (verdict, policer drop/color, rewrite, log), not continue discarding most of `FilterResult`.

## Acceptance

- Single-rate and three-color lo0 policer tests prove conforming packets deliver and exceeding/violating packets drop at the configured boundary.
- `next term` policers meter once per matching term and a later permit cannot erase an earlier policer drop.
- IPv4/IPv6, flow-backed/flowless local traffic, and cache-hit paths have identical enforcement.
- Concurrent workers share the intended policer state and do not multiply burst credit.
- No matched packet is double-metered.
- Live host-bound flood smoke demonstrates enforced pps/bps and observable counters.

Re-verified on master `3821cd9d2` at `userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/eval.rs` and `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/filter.rs`.

## #5858 — security: newly attached or tightened interface input filter does not revoke established transit sessions [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

An established userspace-dataplane transit session can bypass a newly attached or tightened interface input firewall filter. The normal session-hit path reuses the established forwarding decision and only re-evaluates input filters whose match semantics vary per packet (DSCP or selected L4 fields). A static address/protocol/port deny added after session creation is not rechecked and the session is not invalidated when the filter snapshot rotates.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:965+` resolves a session hit without normal cold-path input-filter evaluation.
- `poll_descriptor/filter.rs:334-379` re-evaluates only when `interface_input_filter_has_dscp_match` or `has_per_packet_l4_match` is true.
- `afxdp/worker/loop_body/mod.rs:369-393` detects only DSCP/per-packet-L4 filter family changes for purge.
- There is no commit-time invalidation keyed to newly attached, detached, or statically changed input filters.

Thus a flow admitted before `then discard/reject` is attached can continue until timeout, contrary to immediate firewall enforcement expectations.

## Required closeout

1. Fingerprint the effective input filter per logical interface and family.
2. On attach/detach or any verdict-relevant static match/action change, invalidate affected sessions/flow-cache entries before or atomically with snapshot publication.
3. Preserve the optimized per-packet re-evaluation only for fields that genuinely vary within a flow.
4. Propagate companion deletes to the HA peer and surface/retry partial invalidation.
5. Test address, protocol, port, except, term reorder, attach/detach, VLAN logical interfaces, IPv4/IPv6, flow cache, and HA failover.

Severity: High (security-policy revocation gap).

## #5859 — NAT64: accepted static-NAT `then static-nat inet` is emitted as literal `inet` and silently dropped [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

The compiler accepts the Junos static-NAT NAT64 target `then static-nat inet`, but the userspace snapshot sends the literal string `"inet"` to the same-family static-NAT table. Rust parses it as an IP prefix, fails, and skips the rule. Translation works only if the operator separately authors the native `security nat nat64` rule-set, which is a different configuration path.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- `pkg/config/compiler_nat_static.go:290-293` records `rule.Then = "inet"` and documents it as NAT64.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat_static.go:79-90` emits every non-NPT rule as `StaticNATRuleSnapshot{InternalIP: rule.Then}`; it has no `inet` branch.
- `userspace-dp/src/nat/static_nat.rs:348+` calls `parse_nat_prefix` for internal/external addresses; `"inet"` cannot parse and the rule is skipped.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat64.go:66+` builds NAT64 state only from `cfg.Security.NAT.NAT64`, not static-NAT `inet` rules.

## Impact

A strict-valid configuration claims NAT64 translation but is inert. Depending on following policy/defaults, IPv6 traffic is dropped or handled without the intended translation. This is silent feature incompleteness and vSRX parity failure.

## Required closeout

1. Define exact Junos `static-nat inet` semantics and lower it into the native NAT64 IR, including match scope, source pool, routing-instance target, counters, fragments, and reverse BIB.
2. Alternatively reject the syntax at strict commit until representable; tolerant/peer load must fail closed with a surfaced rule error.
3. Never send the sentinel string through the IP-address field.
4. Add end-to-end v6→v4 and reverse tests, scoped rules, collisions with native NAT64 rules, HA session sync/failover, and observability.

Severity: High (accepted security/NAT rule silently inert).

## #5860 — cluster: day-2 cluster-to-standalone transition leaves HA state machines and ownership producers alive [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Summary

Removing `chassis cluster` from a running system does not transactionally dismantle cluster mode. Transport change detection stops heartbeat/session-sync, but the daemon retains the cluster manager and long-lived watchers/ownership state. Subsequent apply/reconcile paths still branch on `d.cluster != nil`, so standalone runtime behavior can remain contaminated by stale RG/election state.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

Stale HA producers can keep blackholes/VIP/RA/DHCP/rg_active behavior, read-only posture, or ownership state after the operator commits standalone mode. Restart may appear to fix it, masking a day-2 convergence bug.

1. Introduce a declarative cluster lifecycle controller with explicit absent/present generations.

3. Make teardown errors fail the commit or retain observable retry debt; never publish standalone while old ownership remains.
4. Support absent→present day-2 construction symmetrically without restart.
5. Test both transitions, partial teardown, in-flight failover/config sync, retained VIPs/blackholes, RA/DHCP, userspace RG state, and restart.

Severity: High (HA/standalone ownership and forwarding correctness).

## #5861 — RA: config changes on a stable active cluster RG are never applied until an ownership transition [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

In cluster mode, a commit rebuilds router-advertisement configs but deliberately skips `ra.Apply`; RA is managed by ownership events. The periodic RG reconcile calls `applyRethServicesForRG` only when the RG active state changes. Therefore an RG that remains MASTER/active across a day-2 RA edit keeps advertising the old prefixes/lifetimes/options indefinitely.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:1361-1382` applies/withdraws RA only in standalone mode; cluster mode defers it to HA events.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:737-747` reconciles RA/DHCP only under `if tr.Changed`.

The primary can continue advertising removed prefixes, stale DNS/MTU/lifetimes, or fail to advertise added prefixes until failover/restart. Hosts may retain invalid routes for the advertised lifetime.

1. Reconcile per-RG RA desired hashes on every config apply and periodic safety pass.

3. On inactive owners, retain desired state without transmitting; removals must emit the correct lifetime-0 goodbye only from the current owner.

## #5862 — userspace-dp: dedicated session socket still contends on the snapshot-wide ServerState mutex [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

The Go manager uses a dedicated Unix socket and mutex for HA session synchronization, but the Rust server dispatches both sockets through one `Arc<Mutex<ServerState>>`. Session install/drain traffic therefore still serializes behind snapshot reconcile, status, forwarding/FIB updates, and other control handlers. A slow reconcile or large session operation can cause head-of-line blocking and HA loss/timeout despite transport separation.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- Go: `pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_control.go:146-184` states the dedicated socket prevents blocking behind snapshot publishes.
- Rust: `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/mod.rs:122-124` takes the global `state.lock()` before dispatching every request.
- `ServerState` owns the AF_XDP coordinator; snapshot reconcile can tear down/build workers and perform substantial work while this lock is held (`afxdp/coordinator/reconcile/mod.rs:167+`).
- Both listener paths receive the same shared state; the socket split does not split the critical section.

## Impact

Snapshot/FIB churn can delay correctness-critical HA session installs, deletes, barriers, and exports beyond socket deadlines. Conversely a burst of sync operations can delay forwarding-state publication. This creates latency tails and failover state loss exactly where the dedicated socket claims isolation.

## Required closeout

1. Decompose `ServerState` into independently synchronized snapshot/coordinator, session, telemetry, and persistence domains.
2. Keep session install/delete/barrier paths off the reconcile mutex; publish immutable forwarding/session dependencies through ArcSwap or generation-stamped handles.
3. Move all blocking worker waits, serialization, and file I/O outside locks.
4. Define lock ordering and bounded queues/backpressure.
5. Add contention benchmarks and tests with concurrent snapshot reconcile, 100k session sync operations, status polling, FIB bumps, worker stalls, and deadline assertions.

Severity: Medium/High (HA correctness under control-plane contention; latency scalability).

## #5863 — HA config sync: connect/role/uptime ordering can skip the only config push with no eventual reconciliation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

Config replication to a reconnecting peer is edge-triggered only by `OnPeerConnected`. That callback skips the push if the node is not RG0 primary at that instant or has been up less than 30 seconds. A later promotion or crossing the 30-second stability threshold does not re-evaluate the skipped work. Without another commit/reconnect, peers can remain indefinitely divergent.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:601-637` performs the only reconnect push and returns on not-primary or uptime <30s.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:349-378` handles later RG0 promotion but does not push/reconcile config.
- The 30-second threshold has no timer callback.
- Commit paths push only on a future commit; connection and role edges can arrive in either order.

## Concrete ordering

1. Session-sync connects while this node is secondary (or at uptime 10s); callback skips.
2. Node becomes RG0 primary (or uptime reaches 30s) while the connection remains up.
3. No new connect edge and no commit occurs.
4. The peer retains stale active config indefinitely.

## Required closeout

1. Model config sync as desired-generation reconciliation, not a one-shot edge.
2. Record pending push debt on any skipped/failed push.
3. Re-evaluate on peer connect, RG0 promotion, stability timer expiry, config-sync enable, and active-generation change; retry with bounded backoff until peer ACKs/applies the generation.
4. Prevent a newly booted stale node from pushing by requiring an explicit authority epoch/quorum invariant, not wall-clock alone.
5. Expose local/peer generation, pending reason, and last ACK/error.
6. Test every connect×role×uptime ordering, reconnect, simultaneous boot, apply rejection, stale generation, and failover.

Severity: High (HA configuration divergence).

## #5864 — userspace neighbor sync: authoritative empty replacement is omitted and leaves stale helper entries [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Summary

When the authoritative publishable neighbor set transitions to empty, Go sends `NeighborReplace=true` with an empty `Neighbors` slice. The field has `omitempty`, so JSON omits it. Rust decodes `neighbors=None` and returns before applying the replacement. Stale dynamic neighbors therefore remain installed.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol.go:41`: `Neighbors []NeighborSnapshot json:"neighbors,omitempty"`.
- `manager_neighbor.go:88-102` sends a filtered slice with `NeighborReplace: true`; it can be non-nil but length zero after the last usable entry disappears.
- JSON encodes both nil and empty slices as an absent field under `omitempty`.
- `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/neighbors.rs:13-15` returns immediately on `None`, before `apply_manager_neighbors(replace, ...)`.

## Impact

The helper continues forwarding to a stale MAC after kernel neighbor deletion/failure, causing blackholes or misdelivery until another non-empty snapshot happens to replace the table or restart clears it.

## Required closeout

1. Make authoritative replacement presence explicit: pointer/required array, replace-generation envelope, or decode absent vs present-empty distinctly.
2. An accepted replace generation with zero entries must clear the manager-neighbor table.
3. ACK the applied generation and retain retry debt on failure.
4. Add wire compatibility rules and tests for nil, absent, empty, filtered-to-empty, stale/reordered generations, v4/v6, and last-neighbor deletion.

Severity: High (forwarding convergence / stale L2 state).

## #5865 — HA session JSON fallback omits policy, timeout, and NAT64 state carried by the binary stream [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Summary

The helper's JSON/RPC session-delta fallback does not carry all state present in the binary event stream. In particular it omits admitting policy ID/counter, application inactivity timeout, and NAT64 marker/translated source. If the binary path is unavailable or falls back, the standby installs semantically degraded sessions that can be misattributed, aged incorrectly, or fail reverse NAT64 after promotion.

## Current evidence (master 3821cd9d2)

- Rust `SessionDeltaInfo` ends at per-policy log flags (`userspace-dp/src/protocol/binding.rs:1105-1184`); it has no policy ID, counter index, app timeout, NAT64 flag, or translated v4.
- `afxdp/session_delta.rs:100-175` constructs the JSON fallback and likewise emits only log flags from session metadata/NAT decision.
- Go's decoded `SessionDeltaInfo` expects `PolicyID`, `PolicyCounterIdx`, `AppTimeout`, `Nat64`, and `Nat64SnatV4` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol.go:2983-3005`), but they decode as zero/false.
- The binary open frame carries these fields, so the two supported transports are not semantically equivalent.

## Impact

Fallback HA is not a correctness-preserving transport:
- policy attribution/hit counters become zero;
- per-application timeouts fall back to globals;
- NAT64 reverse BIB cannot be reconstructed;
- promoted sessions may drop or translate incorrectly.

## Required closeout

1. Define one versioned canonical session-open schema and generate/convert both binary and JSON transports from it.
2. Add every correctness field to JSON or remove the fallback from HA admission.
3. Negotiate capabilities/version and fail closed rather than silently zeroing required fields.
4. Golden-test binary↔JSON semantic equality for every field and old/new rolling upgrades.
5. Run failover tests forced onto the fallback with policy counters, custom timeout, source/static NAT, NAT64, fabrics, and IPv4/IPv6.

Severity: High (HA failover correctness and cross-family NAT).

## #5866 — daemon: day-2 web-management commits do not replace the live listener or authentication snapshot [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Problem

The HTTP/HTTPS management server is constructed once during daemon startup. `daemon_run.go` resolves the web-management bind, TLS, port, and API-auth configuration, constructs `api.NewServer(apiCfg)`, and starts it. Later commits update the active config but no owner reconciles or atomically replaces the live listener/server.

A successful day-2 commit can therefore report the new management policy while the process continues enforcing the old bind address, TLS material, port, or authentication snapshot until restart.

## Evidence

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go:647-650`: management server startup is one-shot.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go:1377-1388`: bind/auth/TLS values are captured into a server instance.
- No apply-tail manager owns make-before-break listener replacement or auth snapshot publication.

## Impact

- revoked credentials or tightened authentication can remain usable;
- an interface/bind removal can leave the API exposed on the old address;
- port/TLS changes appear committed but are operationally absent;
- restart becomes an undocumented correctness/security requirement.

## Required invariants

- Add a dedicated `management/` lifecycle owner rather than another feature-suffixed daemon helper.
- Reconcile every active generation and publish authentication/TLS state atomically.
- Use make-before-break where endpoints differ; when a remote exposure is being removed or tightened, fail closed rather than retain a stale permissive listener.
- Return apply failure/degraded status and retain retry debt when replacement cannot converge.
- Ensure old listeners, connections, credentials, and TLS identities are retired under a bounded drain policy.
- Do not let an older apply complete after a newer generation.

## Validation

Add fail-on-revert tests for bind/port change, HTTPS certificate replacement, auth enable/disable and credential revocation, replacement bind failure, rollback, concurrent generations, and daemon shutdown during replacement. Include an integration test proving the old endpoint/credential stops working after commit.

## #5867 — daemon: failed management-VRF route replacement preserves a stale gateway/ifindex as desired [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Problem

The management-VRF route reconciler keys desired state only by destination/family and inserts that key into the desired set before `RouteReplace` succeeds. If a route keeps the same destination but changes gateway or output interface and replacement fails, cleanup treats the destination as desired and preserves the old route.

The commit can therefore leave management traffic pinned to a stale gateway/interface with no authoritative distinction between “desired” and “successfully applied.”

## Evidence

`pkg/daemon/daemon_flow.go:124-205` builds the desired-key set before applying replacements and later uses that set to protect routes from stale cleanup. The key omits route identity fields such as gateway, link index, table attributes, and protocol.

## Impact

A failed day-2 management route change can strand or misroute the management plane, including through a deauthorized tenant path, while subsequent cleanup refuses to remove the stale route.

## Required invariants

- Model desired and applied route identity separately using the full managed-route tuple.
- A failed replacement must not mark the new identity applied or protect an incompatible old identity as current.
- Preserve the last known working path only under an explicit rollback/degraded policy; do not silently call it converged.
- Retain retry debt for the newest active generation and expose management-route degraded status.
- Guard against removing the sole management path until replacement is confirmed, while still ensuring stale paths are eventually withdrawn.
- Prevent an older retry from overwriting a newer route generation.

## Validation

Cover same-destination gateway changes, interface changes, replacement failure, old-route delete failure, transient recovery, superseding commits, restart, and the single-management-path case with netlink seams that assert exact ordering and status.

## #5868 — daemon: confirmed-commit bootstrap rollback reports completion after teardown failures [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

The first-confirmed-commit rollback path enters bootstrap mode through a void, best-effort teardown routine. It sets bootstrap state and then discards failures removing generated state, reloading networkd, clearing FRR, and tearing down the dataplane before logging that rollback is complete.

## Evidence

- `pkg/daemon/bootstrap.go:313-382`: `enterBootstrapMode` returns no result and swallows multiple teardown errors.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:566-584`: confirmed-commit expiry invokes it as the terminal rollback action.

## Impact

After a failed initial commit, stale forwarding, routes, interfaces, credentials, or generated service state can remain active while the daemon declares factory/bootstrap state. This is especially dangerous when the expired candidate opened management or forwarding access.

## Required invariants

- Replace the void helper with a transactional bootstrap-reset coordinator returning a structured result.
- Fence newer applies and stop relevant managers before teardown.
- Define fail-closed ordering for dataplane, route, service, credential, and generated-file retirement.
- Record retry debt for every failed owner and keep readiness/degraded status until all critical cleanup converges.
- Never log or persist “rollback complete” while security-critical state remains.
- Make the operation idempotent and restart-recoverable.

## Validation

Inject failures at every teardown stage, including multiple simultaneous failures; prove all owners are attempted, errors remain attributable, retries converge, stale forwarding/auth state is not reported clean, and a restart resumes incomplete bootstrap cleanup.

## #5869 — security: asynchronous config archival can recreate prior-tenant secrets after zeroize [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

## Problem

Commit archival captures the active configuration and launches an untracked goroutine to write the archive. Factory reset/zeroize removes the archive directory but does not cancel or join in-flight archive writers. A writer that resumes after the wipe can recreate an archive containing the previous tenant's full configuration and secrets.

## Evidence

- `pkg/configstore/store_commit.go:227-240`: commit captures old/active config and starts `go writeArchive(...)`.
- `pkg/configstore/store_persist.go:462+`: the writer serializes the configuration to disk.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_zeroize.go:735-745`: zeroize removes the archive directory without fencing archive generations or waiting for writers.

## Security impact

A successful zeroize can leave newly recreated files containing IKE PSKs, WireGuard keys, SNMP communities, credentials, and other prior-tenant configuration material.

## Required invariants

- Give archival a supervised lifecycle with context cancellation, generation fencing, and a bounded join.
- Zeroize must block new archive work, cancel/join all existing work, then erase and fsync the archive root.
- A pre-zeroize generation must be unable to rename/write after the zeroize barrier.
- Preserve crash-safe atomic-write behavior without leaving secret-bearing temp files.
- Zeroize must fail closed and report incomplete erasure if quiescence/durability cannot be proven.

## Validation

Use deterministic barriers around capture, temp creation, write, rename, and directory fsync. Exercise zeroize at each point, concurrent commits, process shutdown, custom archive roots, and power-loss recovery. Assert no prior-generation archive or temp file exists after success.

## #5870 — api: REST candidate mutations bypass the configuration session holder [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

## Problem

The REST configuration endpoints call config-store operations with an empty session ID. In the store, an empty ID is an intentional internal/system bypass of the candidate lock. A remote stateless REST caller can therefore mutate the shared candidate while a CLI/gRPC configuration session owns it.

## Evidence

- `pkg/api/config.go:23-73`: REST enter/set/delete routes use the empty-session store APIs.
- `pkg/configstore/store_lock.go:31-61`: `sessionID == ""` bypasses holder enforcement.

## Impact

Concurrent operators can corrupt each other's candidate, smuggle changes into another session's commit, lose edits, or defeat exclusive configuration semantics. The remote API is accidentally using a privileged internal capability.

## Required invariants

- No remote path may use the empty/internal session capability.
- Introduce an opaque REST configuration lease/session token with authenticated ownership and expiry.
- Require the token for every mutation, compare/commit/rollback/exit operation.
- Bind the token to the authenticated principal and reject reuse across principals or daemon generations.
- Preserve a separate typed internal capability that cannot be supplied over HTTP.
- Define disconnect/expiry cleanup without silently committing or discarding another holder's candidate.

## Validation

Add concurrent REST vs CLI/gRPC tests, two REST principals, expired/stolen token tests, commit/rollback ownership tests, daemon restart, and explicit proof that empty IDs are rejected at the API boundary.

---

## #5871 — security: interactive CLI zeroize bypasses the daemon's complete reset transaction [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

## Problem

The in-process interactive CLI implements `request system zeroize` as its own partial sequence: wipe config state, remove BPF pins/networkd files, and best-effort stop xpfd. It does not enter the daemon's coordinated factory-reset transaction that fences applies/config sync, quiesces asynchronous secret writers, tears down every rendered service/runtime owner, and reports structured failures.

## Evidence

- `pkg/cli/cli_request_system.go:62-101`: independent CLI zeroize implementation with discarded removal/stop errors.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_zeroize.go` and `pkg/configstore/factory_reset.go`: separate, broader reset path and ownership.
- The CLI is constructed in-process from daemon startup, so this is not merely an offline recovery utility.

## Security impact

Depending on entry point, “zeroize” has different guarantees. The CLI path can leave rendered FRR/IPsec/Kea state, OS accounts/credentials, runtime managers, in-flight config archives, routes, and other prior-tenant artifacts while reporting success.

## Required invariants

- Define one daemon-owned `factoryreset/` coordinator and route CLI, gRPC, and future REST entry points through it.
- Fence config apply, config sync, commit-confirm timers, archival, and other asynchronous writers before erasure.
- Quiesce and teardown every rendered/runtime owner under explicit ordering and deadline.
- Return/journal a structured per-owner result; never print success after an ignored critical failure.
- Keep an explicit offline recovery mode separate and document its reduced guarantees.
- Make reset idempotent and restart-resumable.

## Validation

Run the same conformance matrix through CLI and gRPC: concurrent commit/archive/sync, injected owner failures, non-default config root, repeated zeroize, crash/restart, and assertions that all secret-bearing and forwarding state is gone before success.

## #5872 — frr: generated route-policy ACL names can collide or exceed FRR identifier limits [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-15)

## Problem

When a route-filter and same-family `from prefix-list` must coexist, the renderer derives an FRR access-list name by concatenating the external prefix-list name with `_rf`. There is no collision registry, namespace separation, or length bound.

## Evidence

`pkg/frr/policy_render.go:2056-2059` computes `aclName := fromPrefixList + "_rf"` and emits both the definition and route-map reference. The source identifier is operator/external configuration.

## Failure modes

1. A user prefix-list/ACL name can collide with another generated name, causing definitions to merge/replace and widening or narrowing routing policy.
2. A long valid Junos identifier can produce an FRR identifier beyond FRR's supported length (commonly 128 bytes), causing reload rejection or truncation/collision.
3. Sanitization alone cannot provide deterministic uniqueness.

## Required invariants

- Centralize generated FRR identifiers in a typed naming registry under a dedicated `frr/naming/` module.
- Use explicit namespace/type prefixes plus a deterministic hash suffix.
- Bound the final byte length below the strictest downstream limit while preserving stable output across restarts.
- Detect impossible collisions before render and fail the commit closed.
- Use the same registry for definitions and references; do not recompute ad hoc.
- Keep names independent of map iteration order.

## Validation

Cover exact user/generated collisions, two long names with identical prefixes, multibyte input, sanitization collisions, IPv4/IPv6 variants, deterministic restart output, and an FRR parse/reload fixture at the maximum supported length.

## #5873 — dataplane: standalone HA-state clear debt can be recorded before its only retry loop starts [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Problem

Standalone HA cleanup records `pendingHAStateClear` on a failed helper RPC and returns the apply error. The only consumer of that debt is the periodic status loop, but the normal apply path starts that loop only after the clear succeeds. On first startup or another path with no existing loop, the failure returns before `ensureStatusLoopLocked`, leaving debt with no worker to retry it.

## Evidence

- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_compile.go:365-379`: failed clear returns at line 374; status loop starts at line 379.
- Deferred-XSK path returns on failed clear at lines 267-280 and also does not ensure the loop.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_status.go:179-186`: retry occurs only on a status-loop tick.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go:98-126`: debt is purely in-memory.

## Impact

Stale helper HA groups can survive a cluster-to-standalone transition and keep owner-RG-0 transit in the HA-inactive drop path indefinitely, despite the code claiming eventual cleanup.

## Required invariants

- Start a lifecycle-owned debt worker independently of successful status publication, or synchronously ensure a retry owner before returning.
- Gate forwarding/readiness while stale HA state is unconfirmed.
- Reconstruct or deterministically re-derive cleanup debt after restart.
- Cancel the debt safely if the node becomes clustered again; never send an empty HA update into a live cluster generation.
- Use generation fencing so an old standalone retry cannot wipe newer clustered state.

## Validation

Test first-start failure with no status loop, deferred-XSK failure, repeated transient failures, restart, standalone-to-cluster transition while debt is pending, and successful convergence/readiness restoration.

## #5874 — security: post-cancel host-authorization closeout discards credential reconciliation failures and has no enforceable budget [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

## Problem

After a promoted apply is cancelled, the daemon runs a non-cancellable host-authorization closeout. NFT errors are returned, but login, sudoers, absent-user, SSH, and root-auth reconcilers are void/best-effort. The code also calls the sequence “bounded” without an enforced context/deadline or structured per-owner result.

## Evidence

`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:839-885` invokes:
- `applySystemLogin`
- `reconcileSudoers`
- `reconcileAbsentLoginUsers`
- `applySSHConfig`
- `applyRootAuth`

and returns only the two NFT errors. `closeoutHostAuthOnCancel` at lines 888-908 cannot know whether credential revocation completed.

## Security impact

A committed tightening can return from shutdown/cancellation with revoked users, sudo grants, root password/keys, or SSH policy still live, while no result or retry debt identifies the incomplete revocation.

## Required invariants

- Introduce one `hostauth/` closeout coordinator with typed owner results.
- Convert all security-critical reconcilers to return errors and completion state.
- Enforce a real bounded deadline while preserving non-cancellable cleanup semantics up to that deadline.
- Journal/emit degraded state and durable retry debt for incomplete revocations.
- Do not let multiple shutdown/apply writers race or allow an older generation to restore credentials.
- Define which failures block clean shutdown/readiness and which can continue asynchronously.

## Validation

Inject errors and hangs into every owner; verify all independent owners are attempted, failures remain attributable, the deadline is honored, the newest generation wins, retries converge after restart, and revoked authentication is never reported successfully applied while stale state remains.

## #5875 — nat: strict commit accepts zone-qualified IPv6 SNAT pool addresses that the Rust dataplane rejects [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Problem

The configuration grammar/strict source-NAT validation accepts scoped IPv6 literals such as `fe80::1%eth0` in source-NAT pool addresses. The userspace snapshot preserves the string, but Rust parses pool members as `std::net::IpAddr`, which does not accept a zone identifier.

A configuration can pass strict commit and then fail or drop the pool at dataplane apply.

## Evidence

- `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go:717+`: source-pool address validation.
- `pkg/config/lexer.go:336+`: tokenization permits percent-qualified address text.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat_source.go:80+`: pool address is serialized to userspace.
- `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs:467+`: Rust uses `IpAddr` parsing with no scope model.

The control plane and dataplane disagree on an accepted security/forwarding configuration. Link-local source NAT is also ambiguous without an interface scope in allocator keys and egress selection.

## Required invariants

Choose and enforce one behavior end to end:
- reject zone-qualified/scoped pool addresses at strict commit with an actionable error; or
- model scope explicitly in canonical config, snapshot protocol, allocator keys, route/egress validation, HA sync, and observability.

Do not strip `%zone` silently. Go and Rust validators must share parity fixtures.

## Validation

Cover IPv4, global IPv6, link-local IPv6 with and without scope, numeric/name scopes, mixed pools, tolerant load, peer sync, HA replay, snapshot protocol, and Rust allocator construction. A strict commit must never succeed if the applied dataplane cannot represent the address.

## #5876 — nat: strict SNAT validation omits the peer node's effective compiled view [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-17)

## Problem

Strict source-NAT validation is applied to the origin/local compiled configuration, but chassis-aware compilation and peer synchronization can rewrite or select a different effective view for the peer. Peer-only pool/interface/unit errors can therefore pass the originating commit and fail only when the standby applies the snapshot.

- strict source-NAT validation in `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go`;

## #5877 — nat: unbounded aggregate SNAT pool cardinality can exhaust memory and commit latency [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-18)

## Problem

Source-NAT validation bounds individual fields but not the aggregate number of pool addresses/ports/allocator instances across a configuration. A configuration-originated resource exhaustion can stall commits, watchdogs, HA convergence, or the Rust dataplane. Repeated applies magnify latency and transient memory pressure, undermining deterministic failover.

## Validation

## #5878 — config: peer-only numeric interface-unit aliases bypass strict canonical collision validation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

Numeric interface units can be expressed through aliases that normalize to the same effective unit. Strict validation checks the submitting/origin view, while peer-only groups and node-effective rewrites can introduce an alias collision only in the standby view.

The commit can therefore succeed even though the peer effective configuration contains two textual identities for one runtime unit or conflicting definitions selected by map/order behavior.

Node-specific compile results can diverge, with addresses/zones/NAT/policy bound to the wrong unit on standby. Failover can change forwarding or security behavior despite a green synchronized commit.

- Canonicalize every interface/unit identifier before map insertion or reference binding.
- Validate collisions over each node-effective compiled view, including peer-only groups and inherited/generated statements.

Cover `ge-0/0/0.01` vs `.1`, signed/zero-padded forms admitted by tolerant input, peer-only groups, group inheritance, node inversion, rollback/load, and references from zones/NAT/policies. Include a two-node compile parity test.

## #5879 — config: unsupported QinQ can bypass validation when outer/inner VLAN state is split across units or peer-only groups [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

## #5880 — control plane: session-scan admission is reentrant across REST fan-out and incomplete across scan surfaces [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

Session-table walks share a process-wide semaphore, but ownership is attached independently to handlers rather than propagated as one admission token through a request graph. REST list/summary endpoints acquire a slot and then invoke the in-process gRPC session service for `include_peer`; that service acquires the same limiter again. Nested fan-out double-charges one logical operation and can reject itself under load. Other scan surfaces remain easy to omit because admission is manually duplicated per handler.

- `pkg/api/sessions.go:99-118`: REST list acquires the shared limiter.
- `pkg/api/sessions.go:430-439`: while still holding it, REST calls `clusterSession().GetSessions`.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go`: the gRPC entry point independently acquires the same `diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter`.
- `pkg/diagcmd/limiter.go:80-101`: global raw semaphore has no request-scoped ownership/delegation model.

## Impact

A small number of `include_peer` requests can consume twice the intended budget, return false `ResourceExhausted`/HTTP failures, and make behavior depend on which API surface initiated the same scan. Conversely, an omitted handler can bypass the global bound entirely.

## Required invariants

- Acquire exactly once at the external trust boundary.
- Propagate an unforgeable in-process admission lease through local delegation and peer fan-out; child work must not reacquire the local token.
- Give peer-node work its own remote admission while preserving a global per-node bound.
- Inventory every list/summary/top/clear/session-export scan and make admission structural, not copied boilerplate.
- Support weighted cost for local+peer, cursor, and clear operations if their work differs.
- Keep fail-fast bounded behavior and cancellation-safe idempotent release.

## Validation

Cover REST→gRPC delegation at capacity 1, concurrent mixed REST/gRPC requests, include-peer fan-out, clear plus reads, cancellation/panic, and a source-level/registration test proving every full-table scan endpoint declares an admission policy.

## #5881 — dataplane: clear-all sessions reports success when authoritative Rust helper deletes fail [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-21)

In userspace mode, the Rust helper owns authoritative forwarding session state while BPF maps are mirrors. `Manager.ClearAllSessions` clears the mirrors and invokes per-chunk helper deletes, but helper IPC failures are only logged inside the sync path and cannot affect the returned error. ## Evidence

- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go:1146-1167`: clear returns the BPF shim's counts/error unchanged.
- `deleteHelperSessionsV4/V6` at lines 1170-1221 invoke a void sync operation.
- Comments explicitly state helper IPC errors are non-fatal.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go:1089-1111` treats nil error as authoritative success and may propagate the clear to a peer.

## Security impact

Operator/session-revocation actions can return success while traffic remains permitted. Mirror repopulation can make cleared entries reappear, and HA peers may disagree.

## Required invariants

- Treat the Rust helper as authoritative in userspace mode.
- Return a structured per-domain result for helper v4/v6, mirror v4/v6, DNAT companions, and peer propagation.
- Never claim success while an authoritative delete is unconfirmed.
- Retain bounded, idempotent retry debt or add an atomic helper bulk-clear verb with generation fencing.
- Order operations so mirror state cannot conceal still-forwarding helper state.
- Expose degraded/readiness state until convergence.

## Validation

Inject failure before, during, and after helper chunks; test partial v4/v6 progress, reverse/DNAT companions, helper restart, mirror republish, peer failure, retry, and idempotent repeated clear. Prove packets stop matching before success is returned.

## #5882 — api: clear-all session errors discard partial deletion counts and assume atomicity [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-16)

## Problem

The chunked clear implementation can delete part of IPv4 and/or IPv6 state before returning an error, and it explicitly returns partial counts. The gRPC clear-all handler treats any error as if nothing were reliably cleared, returns only a hard RPC error, and discards those counts. REST inherits the same ambiguity.

## Evidence

- `pkg/dataplane/maps_session.go:405-414`: `ClearAllSessionsChunked` returns partial `v4Deleted`/`v6Deleted` with errors.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go:1095-1101`: comment claims atomicity and returns no response on error.
- `pkg/api/sessions.go:782-785`: local fallback also drops returned counts when error is non-nil.

## Impact

Operators and automation cannot determine what was actually revoked, whether a retry is needed, or whether retrying may race newly created sessions. Cluster summaries can hide asymmetric partial progress.

## Required invariants

- Replace tuple/error semantics with a typed `ClearResult` carrying attempted, confirmed deleted, failed, remaining/unknown, domain/family, peer status, and a resumable generation/cursor where feasible.
- Never describe a multi-chunk operation as atomic unless the authoritative dataplane supplies an atomic primitive.
- Preserve partial results over gRPC and REST with an explicit incomplete status.
- Make retries idempotent and distinguish sessions created after the clear generation.
- Align helper, mirror, DNAT companion, and peer reporting.

## Validation

Inject iterator, batch-delete, helper, DNAT, and peer failures after deterministic partial progress. Assert exact counts/status survive through dataplane, gRPC, REST, and CLI, and that a retry converges without deleting post-generation sessions unexpectedly.

## #5883 — security: caller-controlled forwarded metadata suppresses HA peer actions and summaries [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

Several gRPC paths use incoming metadata such as `x-peer-forwarded` as an untrusted recursion guard. Any client able to reach the API can supply that key and be treated as an internal peer-forwarded request. In session clear, this suppresses propagation to the HA peer; in summary/list paths it suppresses peer fan-out or changes result completeness. Similar markers protect system-action proxying.

## Evidence

- `pkg/grpcapi/server_helpers.go:379`: forwarded detection checks only metadata presence.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go:1081-1087, 1103-1105, 1161-1163`: marker suppresses peer clear.
- Session summary/zone-pair and system-action paths stamp and trust the same class of caller-visible metadata.
- Tests construct ordinary incoming contexts with `metadata.Pairs("x-peer-forwarded", "1")`, demonstrating no authenticated peer identity is required by the predicate.

## Security impact

A caller can request a cluster clear that executes only locally, leaving sessions on the peer to survive/fail back. It can also obtain misleading local-only summaries or influence proxy routing while the API reports a normal response.

## Required invariants

- Strip reserved internal metadata at every external listener/interceptor.
- Derive peer-forwarded state from authenticated mTLS/Unix-socket peer identity plus an unforgeable in-process context capability, not a user header.
- Bind hop markers to method, request identity, and one hop; reject external attempts to set them.
- Return explicit peer completeness/failure status rather than silently suppressing work.
- Inventory all recursion/proxy markers across gRPC and REST bridges.

## Validation

Test external metadata injection over every transport, authenticated peer calls, proxied one-hop calls, replay to another method, mixed-version peers, and session clear/summary/system-action behavior. A non-peer client must never suppress mandatory HA work.
