## #6584 — cli: raw journalctl/tail and swanctl output reach the terminal unsanitized — the largest remaining #6468 escape-injection surface [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

#6468 established that device-originated text printed to an operator terminal
must be escaped: a DHCP lease hostname (option 12) is supplied by a device on a
served segment and can carry terminal escape sequences (OSC 52 clipboard write,
OSC 8 hyperlink, CSI cursor/erase) that the terminal **acts on** when the value
is displayed. #6468 covered the lease fields; PR #6579 covers the DDNS
`LastError` and the `vtysh` surfaces.

Two surfaces of the same class remain, both printing raw external-command stdout
to the terminal:

**A. `pkg/cli/cli_show_system.go:840,851` — raw `journalctl` / `tail` output.**
This is likely the **largest remaining surface of the whole class**, and the
most directly connected to #6468's own threat model: the syslog stream carries
the very DHCP hostnames #6468 was filed about. A device that sets its hostname
to an escape payload gets it logged, and then re-emitted verbatim the moment an
operator runs the log show command — the sanitized lease table is bypassed by
reading the log instead.

**B. `pkg/ipsec/ike.go:690` — raw `swanctl` SA output.** Carries peer-supplied
identity strings (IKE IDs).

## Why these are in the class

`pkg/termsafe` is a stdlib-only leaf package specifically so any renderer can
import it, and `pkg/cli/README.md` states the both-renderers rule as a contract.
Multi-line command output needs `SanitizeBlockForDisplay` (added in #6579),
which preserves LF/TAB so tables and log lines keep their shape while ESC, CR,
other C0, DEL, C1 and invalid UTF-8 are neutralized.

## Fix

Apply `termsafe.SanitizeBlockForDisplay` at both surfaces, and mirror to the
gRPC renderer if these commands have a remote-`cli` sibling (check
`pkg/grpcapi` — the #6579 review found all 12 `vtysh` sites had one, and the
remote `cli` is the more common operator posture).

and reintroduces the raw value.

and `:1958`. That text embeds the **provider's** response body for Cloudflare

via `%s`. So a hostile or compromised DDNS endpoint gets its bytes onto the
operator's remote syslog.

This is the same string PR #6579 sanitizes for the *terminal*; the syslog sink
was out of that PR's scope.

## #6587 — config/ra: prefix-length leaves take an unbounded Atoi (both preferred- and sub-prefix-length) and pkg/ra has no delegated-/0 floor [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Two related gaps found by the hostile review of PR #6581 (which fixed the WIRE
side of the same class — a DHCPv6 IA_PD prefix-length > 128 decoding to a `/0`
that was advertised on-link + autonomous to the LAN).

## A. Two config leaves take an unbounded prefix length

`preferred-prefix-length` and `sub-prefix-length` are BOTH parsed with an
unbounded `strconv.Atoi` at `pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go` (~:522), and
BOTH schema entries are untyped `<length>` placeholders — no range validator.

Current impact is **fail-closed, not fail-open**: a `sub-prefix-length` > 128
flows to `netip.PrefixFrom`, whose `Bits()` returns `-1`, and the existing
`IsValid()` check rejects it. So there is no live defect today. The problem is
that the guard is incidental — it depends on a downstream validity check
noticing, not on the value being rejected where the operator typed it. The
operator gets no commit-time error, just a silently absent delegation.

Both leaves should get typed range validators (0..128) at the schema, matching
how the sibling typed leaves in the same file are handled.

Note the review flagged that PR #6581's own out-of-scope report named only
`preferred-prefix-length`; the fix must cover **both** leaves.

## B. `pkg/ra` has no prefix-length floor of its own

`pkg/ra/sender.go` (~:886) marshals `uint8(prefix.Bits())` with no floor, and
there are zero `.Mask.Size()` sites in the package. End-to-end reachability was
traced: `DeriveSubPrefix` returns a `/0` unchanged when `subPrefLen == 0`, and a
`/0` passes `IsValid()`, so it clears the `pkg/daemon/daemon_ra.go` (~:34) guard.

This is **defense in depth, deliberately not fixed in #6581**. The reviewer's
reasoning for keeping the guard at the decoder is worth preserving here: at
`pkg/ra` a *delegated* `/0` is indistinguishable from an operator-authored
`::/0`, which is a legitimate configuration a naive floor would silently break.
So any floor added here must distinguish provenance (delegated vs configured)
rather than blanket-rejecting a `/0`.

## #6588 — config/cluster: packed-hierarchical interface-monitor compiles to ZERO monitors — link tracking silently never demotes the RG [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-01)

## Problem

A `interface-monitor` authored in the **packed hierarchical** spelling — one
statement directly under `redundancy-group`, no nested block — compiles to ZERO
monitors. The operator gets a monitor that silently never demotes the group on
link-down.

Verified by direct compile:

```
interface-monitor ge-0/0/0 weight 255;   (packed, directly under redundancy-group)
  -> rgs=1, monitors=0
```

This is a **fail-open**: the operator has configured link tracking, `commit`
succeeds with no error and no warning, `show` presumably reflects the intent,
and the redundancy group simply never demotes when the monitored interface goes
down. Failover does not happen when it should.

## Second-order consequence

Because the packed form compiles to zero monitors, an **out-of-range** packed
weight is also accepted at commit:

```
interface-monitor ge-0/0/0 weight -100;   (packed)
  -> accepted; the #6549 range gate never sees it
```

That is harmless *today* (no monitor means no debt is installed) but it makes the
range gate's coverage claim narrower than it reads.

## Scope note for the docs

`docs/config-schema.md` and the #6549 commit describe gating "the compiled int
rather than the AST" as covering "BOTH parser shapes at once". That is precise
for **flat-set** and **container-hierarchical**, but not for this third, packed
spelling — which never reaches the compiled struct at all. The doc deserves a
one-clause caveat naming the packed form explicitly.

## #6589 — cluster: a clamped (inert) interface-monitor weight is visible only in journald — no show surface or alarm distinguishes it from a working monitor [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

When an out-of-range `interface-monitor ... weight` arrives on the tolerant
path — a config persisted before the range gate existed, or one pushed over HA
config-sync — the runtime clamps it and emits a `slog.Warn`. That is the correct
runtime behavior (see the decision record below), but the **only** signal that a
configured failover monitor has been rendered inert is a log line.

An operator who configured `interface-monitor ge-0/0/0 weight -100` and had it
clamped to 0 now has a monitor that:

- appears in the configuration exactly as they wrote it,
- appears in `show chassis cluster` output as a configured monitor,
- and contributes **zero** debt, so the redundancy group never demotes when that
  link goes down.

Nothing in any operational show command distinguishes it from a working monitor.
The operator discovers it during a failover that does not happen.

## Why the clamp direction is not the fix

This was adjudicated during the review of PR #6586. Two reviewers disagreed:
one argued clamping a negative to 0 is fail-OPEN (the node keeps ownership behind
a failed link) and that 255 is the fail-closed choice.

Clamping to **0 was retained**, because:

- 0 is an already-legal, operator-reachable state — an `interface-monitor` with
  no `weight` token compiles to exactly 0, meaning "monitor this, contribute no
  debt". Clamping invalid input onto an existing semantic is less surprising than
  clamping it onto "maximally fatal", which the operator never asked for.
- Under clamp-to-255, a typo'd `-100` arriving over the **HA config-sync push**
  makes the receiving node instantly resign its redundancy group the moment that
  link flaps — turning the config-sync channel into a remote HA denial-of-service.
- The strict commit gate means the local authoring path can never produce an
  out-of-range weight at all; the clamp is reachable only from a pre-existing
  persisted config or a peer push.

So the residual risk is **not** the clamp value — it is that the clamp is
invisible outside the log.

## #6590 — frr: peer-advertised IS-IS hostname containing spaces shifts every column — a peer can forge State/Level/Interface in show isis adjacency [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`GetISISAdjacency` (`pkg/frr/status_parse.go`) parses `show isis neighbor` with
`strings.Fields`, which splits on whitespace and assigns tokens to columns
POSITIONALLY. The first column is the peer-advertised dynamic hostname
(RFC 5301), and FRR retains printable ASCII **spaces** when decoding that TLV.

A hostname containing a space therefore shifts every subsequent column:

```
wire row:  evil peer ge-0-0-1 2 Up 27
parsed as: SystemID=evil  Interface=peer  Level=ge-0-0-1  State=2  HoldTime=Up
```

With enough space-separated tokens the peer controls **all five displayed
cells**. The operator sees a well-formed adjacency table in which the values are
supplied by the adjacency's own remote end.

## This is NOT the #6468 escape-injection bug

PR #6579 sanitizes every cell of this row, which is correct and necessary — it
stops the peer putting ESC/CSI/OSC bytes on the operator's terminal. But
sanitizing preserves *plausible printable text*, so it cannot distinguish a
genuine `State=Up` from an attacker-supplied hostname token.

**The row can be terminal-safe and still materially false.** That is a display
INTEGRITY defect, and its fix is in the parser, not the display guard — which is
why it is filed here rather than folded into #6579.

## Blast radius

An operator running `show isis adjacency` to decide whether a neighbour is
healthy can be shown a fabricated `State`, `Level`, `Interface` or `HoldTime`
chosen by the neighbour itself. The obvious abuse is presenting `Up` for an
adjacency that is down, or attributing an adjacency to the wrong interface,
during exactly the troubleshooting session where the operator is trusting this
table.

Both renderers are affected — `pkg/cli/cli_show_routing.go` and
`pkg/grpcapi/server_routing.go` render the same parsed struct.

running the freshly pushed build:

## #6592 — userspace-dp: the surviving (new validation, old forwarding) pair is not drop-only — a new-stamped packet can be forwarded under stale policy/FIB [CLOSED] (closed 2026-07-31)

## Problem

PR #6333 (#6291) fixed the `(old validation, new forwarding)` torn window by
flipping the worker to acquire-load forwarding first and validation second, the
opposite of the coordinator's store order. That is correct and is a strict
improvement — **both** orientations were reachable before it.

But the surviving orientation, `(new validation, old forwarding)`, is **not
drop-only**, and #6333 documents it as benign. It permits a stale forward.

## The chain

1. A worker loads forwarding **before** the coordinator publishes, so
   `load_arc_if_changed` returns `None`.
2. The coordinator publishes new validation, then new forwarding.
3. The worker loads validation **after** the publish. In
   `worker/loop_body/mod.rs`, validation installs **unconditionally** when it
   differs, while forwarding updates **only** when the Arc rotated:

   ```go
   if live_validation != validation { validation = live_validation }   // always
   if let Some(new_forwarding) = new_forwarding_opt { ... }            // only on rotation
   ```

   So the worker now holds **new validation + old forwarding** for the rest of
   that iteration.
4. The coordinator returns the new generation to Go
   (`server/handlers/snapshot.rs`).
5. Go writes it to `userspace_ctrl`
   (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_compile.go`, `maps_sync.go`).
6. The XDP shim stamps subsequent packets with the **new** generation
   (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs`).
7. Those packets reach the worker's RX sweep, match the **new** validation, are
   classified `Valid` — and are forwarded using the **old** forwarding state.

Nothing orders step 5 after every worker's next forwarding load. There is no
per-worker generation acknowledgement, and a worker can simply be descheduled
between its validation refresh and its next poll.

## #6593 — userspace-dp: only 1 of 7 pre-forwarding publications has an ordering guard, and that one has a hoist bypass [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

The coordinator's snapshot publish (`refresh_runtime_snapshot`) relies on a
documented store ORDER: several shared structures must be published **before**
`ha.forwarding`, because `ha.forwarding` is the single worker-visible gate and
the worker reads it first. Reorder any of them after the forwarding store and a
worker can observe new forwarding paired with a stale sibling.

Only ONE of those publications is guarded by a test, and that guard has a bypass.

## Current state

**Guarded (with a bypass):** `cos_owner_at_forwarding_publish`
(`coordinator/snapshot_refresh.rs`) backs
`refresh_runtime_snapshot_publishes_cos_owner_map_before_forwarding`. Its RED
depends on the capture *sitting above* the forwarding store, so a reordering
done by **hoisting the `ha.forwarding` store above the capture** — rather than
exchanging the two lines in place — leaves the capture reading an
already-published value and the test passes vacuously.

PR #6333 closed exactly this bypass for its own new validation seam, by having
the seam also retain the worker-visible forwarding `Arc` from the same instant
and asserting it is not the post-refresh `Arc` — so the capture proves its own
position. (It retains an `Arc` rather than a raw pointer deliberately: dropping
it would let the next `Arc::new` reuse the freed address and fool `ptr_eq`.)
The same treatment applies here.

**Unguarded entirely** — no individual ordering assertion at all:

- CoS owner-live
- CoS root leases (`coordinator/cos_leases.rs`)
- CoS exact backlogs
- CoS queue leases
- CoS vtime floors
- `ha.fabrics`

Each is published before `ha.forwarding` by convention and comment only.

## #6597 — snmp: findNextOID is a linear MIB scan per varbind — sets the req/s floor for every operation on the serial agent goroutine [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`findNextOIDSnap` / `findNextOID` (`pkg/snmp/agent.go`) resolve each
lexicographic successor by a **linear scan** of the MIB snapshot — O(static +
interfaces x columns) per lookup — rather than a sorted/binary search.

That is a per-lookup cost multiplied by every varbind an operation emits, so it
sets the floor on how fast any walk can be.

## Measured

While fixing #6551 (GETBULK building varbinds before the size bound), a max-size
plain **GETNEXT** of 239 deep `ifXTable` OIDs was measured at **~33 ms**,
returning all 239 in a full 4095-byte `noError` response.

That ~33 ms is *not* unbounded expansion — it is `findNextOIDSnap` being linear.
GETNEXT is provably bounded: RFC 3416 §4.2.1/§4.2.2 bind it to one response
varbind per request varbind, so its walk is O(len(oids)) with no
max-repetitions multiplier, and built == returned. A pre-walk short-circuit is
provably useless there: the minimum response varbind is 6 bytes against a
minimum request varbind of 7, so `6 * len(oids)` can never exceed 4096 for any
datagram that fits on the wire.

So this is a distinct performance characteristic, correctly scoped OUT of #6551,
not a second instance of that defect.

## Why it still matters

The SNMP agent runs on a **single serial goroutine** (that serialization is what
made #6551 a denial-of-service rather than a slow query). Anything that raises
the per-lookup cost raises the ceiling on requests/second for every operation at
once. ~33 ms for one legitimate, well-formed GETNEXT is ~30 req/s for that shape
— fine in isolation, but it is the floor the whole agent shares, and it grows
with interface count.

## Fix

Make the successor lookup logarithmic: keep the snapshot's OIDs in sorted order
and binary-search for the successor, or maintain an index alongside the
snapshot. The snapshot is rebuilt on a known cadence, so the sort cost is paid

## #6598 — dataplane/fabric: buildFabricPeerMAC accepts NUD_FAILED and non-6-byte neighbour entries — the LIVE resolver is laxer than the one #6554 hardened [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`buildFabricPeerMAC` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/fabric.go:115-124`) selects the
fabric peer's MAC by taking the first neighbour entry whose IP equals the peer
address and whose `HardwareAddr` is non-nil.

It checks **neither**:

- the **NUD state** — so a `NUD_FAILED` or `NUD_INCOMPLETE` entry that still
  retains a stale link-layer address for the peer is accepted; nor
- `len(HardwareAddr) == 6` — so a malformed or non-Ethernet lladdr is accepted.

Every leg of `refreshFabricFwd` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_fabric.go`) checks both,
via `fabricNeighValidStates`.

## Why this matters more than it looks

This is the **live** resolver. PR #6595 (#6554) hardened the neighbour selection
in `refreshFabricFwd`, and its severity argument rests explicitly on
`buildFabricPeerMAC` being the trustworthy, address-matched path — the one whose
result actually reaches the dataplane as the cross-chassis redirect destination
MAC. `FabricFwdInfo.PeerMAC`, by contrast, is write-only post-#1476.

So the path that is *not* consulted got hardened, and the path that *is*
consulted remains measurably less strict than the one that was. That is not a
fail-open of the #6554 shape — this selection **is** address-matched, so an
unrelated host cannot be chosen — but a stale entry for the correct address can
be, and the consequence is cross-chassis frames sent to a MAC the peer no longer
owns.

## Realistic trigger

The peer's fabric NIC MAC changes and the neighbour entry goes `NUD_FAILED`

## #6599 — userspace-dp/HA: transient-purge re-entry emits identity-less Open that overwrites the peer's authoritative session (spoofed non-close first packet, translated-forward class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found during the #6461 research arc (round-92 Codex review of docs/research/6461-blind-rst/plan.md, branch research/6461-blind-rst).

## Summary

On the non-owner cluster node, a single spoofed NON-closing first packet (e.g. a SYN) carrying a peer-owned flow's translated 5-tuple drives master's transient-purge + miss re-entry path into installing an identity-less fresh ForwardFlow entry and emitting a latest-generation-wins Open delta that overwrites the peer's authoritative session family — destroying the victim's synced state and swapping the mid-flow SNAT translation (P1 to attacker-created P2).

## Trace (all master behavior today)

1. Non-owner node receives a packet matching a peer-synced translated-forward session key. should_keep_synced_hit_transient (userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/promote.rs:48) classifies it; purge_translated_synced_hit (promote.rs:167-207, driven from session_glue/mod.rs:1178-1188) removes the shared entry, the BPF/local row, the P1 reservation, and the shared NAT/wire aliases (shared_ops.rs:960).
2. The re-resolved miss installs a fresh ForwardFlow with a newly derived translation P2 (poll_descriptor/mod.rs:2449) and emits Open (userspace-dp/src/session/install.rs:234) stamped with a fresh #2170 install generation (pkg/cluster/sync_conn_write.go:53).
3. The peer's receiver applies latest-generation-wins: the fresh Open overwrites the victim's forward/reverse family (pkg/cluster/sync_conn_gen.go:435, pkg/dataplane/session_store.go:257).

No closing flags are involved, so the #6461 demote gate cannot see this class, and no sequence validation applies to a SYN (a SYN is the sequence bootstrap — the sender knows the state it seeded). The classical network-side mitigation is anti-spoof/ingress filtering; the sync-layer fix is identity-carrying Open/Close deltas (fenced provenance) or a provenance-aware purge, which is Phase-2 territory (docs/research/6461-blind-rst/phase2-brief.md).

## Why filed separately

This is pre-existing master behavior, plan-independent, and out of #6461's blind-close-demote blast radius. #6461's plan documents it in section 7 (coverage residuals) and section 10.6.2.

## #6600 — userspace-dp/HA: import publishes shared session before the worker reserves its NAT port (reservation refusal not propagated) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found during the #6461 research arc (round-92 Codex review of docs/research/6461-blind-rst/plan.md, branch research/6461-blind-rst).

## Summary

HA session import publishes the shared session entry BEFORE the worker-local upsert reserves the synced flow's translated NAT pool port (P1). In that window a local flow can allocate P1 first; the later reservation refuses to steal it and the failure is not propagated — the imported session's translation then references a port this node does not own.

## Trace

1. Initial HA import publishes the shared entry first (userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/session_import.rs:115, :215) and enqueues worker commands.
2. Workers can poll packets after observing an empty command queue (userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker/loop_body/mod.rs:682, :887).
3. The P1 reservation happens only inside the worker-local upsert (userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/commands/upsert_synced.rs:64, :80).
4. In the gap, another local flow's allocation can claim P1; the reservation refuses to steal (userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs:1636, :1682) and the failure is not propagated to the import outcome.

The exposure is packet-class-agnostic (any packet forwarded on a shared-backed decision during the window references the unreserved P1). Candidate fix: propagate the reservation failure into the import outcome (retry/reconcile), or reserve before publishing the shared entry.

## Why filed separately

Pre-existing master behavior, out of #6461's blast radius; documented in #6461's plan sections 7 and 10.6.2.

## #6606 — ddns: dyndns2 backend interpolates the raw provider server URL into errors (same credential-leak class as the checkip-url fix) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`pkg/ddns/backend_dyndns2.go:114` and `:122` interpolate the raw `server` value
into returned errors:

    provider %q server %q is not a valid URL: %w

Two distinct leaks in one statement:

1. `%q` on the raw `server` echoes any credential carried in userinfo
   (`https://user:PASS@host/`) or in the query string.
2. `%w` wraps `url.Parse`'s error. `(*url.Error).Error()` **re-embeds the full
   raw input including the query**, so redacting the `%q` argument alone would
   not close it — the wrapped error reintroduces the raw string.

These errors reach the daemon's logging path the same way the checkip ones did.

## Relationship to #6545 / PR #6594

Identical leak class, different file. PR #6594 closed the `checkip-url` instance
(`pkg/ddns/checkip.go`) by rendering `config.RedactURL(u)` in every branch and
**dropping the `%w`** in favour of a `urlParseCause` helper that extracts only
the parse cause. This site was deliberately left out of scope: different file,
not touched by that PR.

Note that the package's existing `scrubURLError` helper is **not** a usable fix
here, for the same reason it was not usable in #6594 — it recovers a safe URL by
re-parsing `ue.URL`, and this is precisely the URL that failed to parse, so it
falls through to the raw value.

## Severity — Low

Narrower than the checkip case: a dyndns2 `server` is less commonly
credentialed than a `checkip-url` (which frequently carries an API key in the
query), and reaching it requires a malformed server URL in the committed
config. Bounded to journal/log exposure — no remote trigger, no
privilege-boundary break. It is a real cleartext-secret-to-journald path, so it
should not stay open.

## Problem

`ForwardBeacon` (Gate 4 of the kernel promote gate chain,
`pkg/upgrade/kernel_linux.go:661-663`) probes:

    systemctl is-active xpfd-userspace-dp

That unit name appears **nowhere else in the repository**. The managed binary is
`xpf-userspace-dp` (see `pkg/upgrade/manifest`), and it is **not a systemd unit
at all** — xpfd spawns the userspace dataplane helper as a child process.

So the probe can never report active, and the gate's `A != nil && B != nil`
shape collapses to "xpfd must be active". The dataplane half of the beacon is
dead weight.

## Why it matters

Gate 4 is the post-reboot forward-progress beacon in the A/B kernel
promote/rollback chain (#1930). Its purpose is to confirm the new kernel
actually carries a working forwarding path before the promotion is made
permanent. Confirming only that `xpfd` is active is a materially weaker
statement than confirming the dataplane is up: xpfd can be running with a
dataplane that failed to load, which is exactly the condition a kernel change is
most likely to cause (AF_XDP shim vs. new kernel, verifier, driver).

Fail direction: this makes the beacon **more permissive** than intended, so a
bad kernel is more likely to be promoted rather than rolled back.

## Severity — Medium

Not remotely triggerable and not a policy fail-open, but it silently weakens a
safety gate whose entire job is to catch a kernel that breaks forwarding. The
bounding factor is that other gates in the chain (Gate 3 `verify-dataplane`)
still exercise the dataplane directly, so this is a defence-in-depth loss rather
than the only check. It should not be left as a probe that cannot ever succeed.

## #6609 — config: RedactURL is authority-@-based and does NOT redact a credential that lands in the host:port slot — every caller that renders an UNPARSEABLE operator-authored URL leaks it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`config.RedactURL` (`pkg/config/secret.go:93`) is a purely string-based redactor.
It finds userinfo by locating `@` within the authority and drops the query after
`?`. It never parses the URL.

That is sound for a URL that parses. It is NOT sound for a malformed one. The
commonest credentialed operator typo — **omitting the `@`** — defeats it
completely:

    RedactURL("http://user:s3cr3t-PASSWORD.example/")
      => "http://user:s3cr3t-PASSWORD.example/"        // UNCHANGED

There is no `@` in the authority, so nothing is redacted, and the password is
rendered in full.

## Why this is more than a corner case

That exact input is *also* what `url.Parse` rejects with an unbounded raw
substring — `invalid port ":s3cr3t-PASSWORD.example" after host`. So one
realistic mistake hits two surfaces at once, and any code path that reports "this
URL is malformed" while rendering `RedactURL(input)` leaks the credential twice
over.

This was found while fixing the `checkip-url` instance (#6545 / PR #6594). The
fix there was to print **no part of the input** on the parse-failure branch and
apply `RedactURL` only *after* `url.Parse` succeeds — where it is provably sound,
since a successfully-parsed URL cannot hide a credential in `host:port`
(`http://h:abc/x` is itself a parse error).

The same parse-first split has NOT been applied to the other callers.

## Affected callers (non-test, on origin/master)

Highest concern — these render a URL specifically *because* it is malformed, so
the input is unparseable by construction:

- `pkg/ddns/backend_generic.go:128` — `url-template %q must be an http(s) URL (no scheme)`
- `pkg/ddns/backend_generic.go:132` — `url-template %q must be an http(s) URL`
- `pkg/ddns/backend_generic.go:157` — `url-template %q has no host`

## #6610 — userspace-dp: the snat_allocator bench panics with 'attempt to add with overflow' in debug — off the make test-rust gate, and the arithmetic may be wrong rather than merely unguarded [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`cargo test --all-targets` builds and runs benches. The `snat_allocator` bench
panics in debug:

    attempt to add with overflow
    userspace-dp/benches/snat_allocator.rs:503

This is **pre-existing on master** and does not surface under the project's
normal Rust gate: `make test-rust` runs `cargo test --release --bins --tests`,
which excludes benches. So anyone who runs `--all-targets` — a reasonable thing
to do — hits a panic that looks like their own change broke something.

## Why this may be more than an unguarded bench

An `attempt to add with overflow` at a port-accounting site is not obviously a
debug-only artifact. There are two readings:

1. **Benign:** the bench deliberately drives values past a realistic range and
   the addition simply needs a `wrapping_add`/`saturating_add` or a larger type.
2. **Not benign:** the bench's port-accounting arithmetic is genuinely wrong. In
   release, integer overflow wraps silently instead of panicking — so the same
   bug would produce a WRONG accumulator rather than a crash, and the bench's
   published contention/throughput numbers would be quietly incorrect.

Reading 2 matters because those numbers have been cited when reasoning about
SNAT allocator contention. A bench that is wrong in release and loud in debug is
worse than one that is simply broken, because its output has been trusted.

Determine which reading applies before choosing a fix. If it is reading 1, guard
the arithmetic and say so. If it is reading 2, the fix is the accounting, and any
previously-published numbers from this bench should be re-measured.

## Severity — Low (as a defect), but worth resolving deliberately

No production code path is involved; `benches/` is not shipped. The impact is
developer-facing (a confusing panic on `--all-targets`) plus the credibility of
the bench's own measurements. It is not a dataplane correctness issue.

## #6617 — pkg/refactoraudit: TestHeatmapNotStale fails on clean origin/master — the suite is red in the default branch [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-01)

## Problem

`go test ./pkg/refactoraudit/ -run TestHeatmapNotStale` **FAILS on a clean
checkout of `origin/master`**, with no local modifications.

Verified firsthand in a throwaway detached worktree at master `1aa1d38c2`:

```
--- FAIL: TestHeatmapNotStale (2.25s)
FAIL    github.com/psaab/xpf/pkg/refactoraudit   2.253s
```

## Why it matters more than a single red test

The heatmap is a generated artifact (`docs/refactoring-audit-current.txt` and
friends) and this test exists to assert it has been regenerated. A test that is
permanently red in the default branch has three costs:

1. **It stops being a signal.** Every contributor who runs `go test ./...` sees
   a failure that is not theirs, learns to ignore this package, and will ignore
   it when it fails for a real reason.
2. **It weakens the merge gate.** This project's discipline is "never dismiss a
   failing test" and "prove a pre-existing failure at the master SHA before
   attributing it". Every PR that touches a refactor-audited file now has to
   burn that verification, and each one is an opportunity to wave through a real
   failure as "the known one".
3. **It hides staleness.** If the heatmap is genuinely stale, the audit data
   informing refactor prioritisation is wrong — which is the thing the test was
   written to prevent.

## Fix

Determine which of these applies and act accordingly:

- **The artifact is stale** → regenerate it and commit, in its own commit (the
  project convention keeps generated-artifact regen separate from logic).
- **The generator is non-deterministic** → the test cannot pass reliably;
  make the generator deterministic (sorted iteration, no timestamps, no map
  ordering) before re-enabling.
- **The test's staleness criterion is wrong** → fix the criterion.

## Problem

xpf treats `host-inbound-traffic system-services any-service` as admitting
**every IP protocol**. Junos defines it as *"all system services on an entire
port range including the system services that are not defined"* — i.e. it widens
the PORT range across TCP/UDP, not the protocol space.

So under xpf, `any-service` currently admits GRE, ESP, AH, OSPF, PIM, VRRP and
any future protocol number; under Junos it does not.

#3226 / PR #6616 fixed the sibling defect: `system-services all` was
packet-wide-admitting with no catch-all drop, so an `all` zone accepted raw IP
protocols. That fix scopes `all` to the defined system-service list (which
contains no raw IP protocol) and **relies on `any-service` remaining broad as
the documented migration path** for an operator who genuinely needs
protocol-wide admission.

Narrowing `any-service` in the same change would have removed that escape hatch
in the same release that took the old behaviour away. It is a second, separate
behaviour decision — and now cleanly isolated to one token, which is why it is
worth tracking rather than leaving implicit.

## Severity — Low/Medium

It is over-permissive relative to Junos, so it is a fail-OPEN in parity terms.
But it is explicitly opt-in: an operator must write `any-service`, and the token
exists precisely to say "be broad". The risk is an operator who reads the Junos
documentation, expects port-range semantics, and gets protocol-wide admission.

Decide deliberately, because this one has a real migration cost:

1. **Narrow to Junos semantics** — `any-service` widens the TCP/UDP port range
   only; raw IP protocols require an explicit protocol-bearing service or a
   filter. Needs a commit-time warning for configs relying on the current

## #6620 — upgrade: the INNER promote hop still infers xpfd from filesystem leftovers — same class the outer hop just closed [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`resolveVerifyGateBin` (`pkg/upgrade/kernel_linux.go`) falls back to
`<SbinDir>/xpfd` and then `<VersionsDir>/current/xpfd` when `os.Executable()`
fails or its path no longer resolves.

That is the same defect class PR #6601 just eliminated from the OUTER shell hop
(`scripts/image/xpf-kernel-promote`): selecting a binary by inference from
filesystem evidence, where a leftover from a relocated runtime is
indistinguishable from a healthy layout. #6601 took four review rounds precisely
because each fix closed one ambiguous case and the next reviewer found another —
and it converged only when the fallback was deleted outright in favour of
"unambiguous or refuse".

The outer hop's authority order is now `/proc/<MainPID>/exe` → strictly-parsed
`ExecStart` → loud refusal. The inner hop should follow the same rule.

## Why it is lower severity than the outer hop was

- Its PRIMARY source is `os.Executable()`, i.e. the kernel's answer for the
  RUNNING process — that is already authoritative, not an inference.
- By the time it runs, the outer hop has already resolved authoritatively, so
  the process executing it is the right one.
- The fallback engages only when `os.Executable()` fails or its path no longer
  resolves, which is rare.

So this is a latent inference path, not a live selection bug. It has not been
shown to mis-select.

## Why it is still worth closing

The failure mode if it ever does engage is the expensive one: verifying a
candidate kernel against the WRONG dataplane, silently, and then authorizing a
promotion on that result. "Rare and latent" is how the outer hop's version
looked too, until someone constructed the relocated-roots case.

## Fix

Apply the same rule: if `os.Executable()` cannot be resolved and validated,
REFUSE rather than guessing from `SbinDir`/`VersionsDir`. A Gate-3 error already

to that PR: the source under test is unchanged by that fold, and the failure
reproduces independently of it.

A reproducible red in the Rust suite has the same corrosive effect as the
permanently-red Go test filed as #6617: `make test` runs BOTH legs
(`make test-rust` is gated on this suite), so every subsequent PR that touches
`userspace-dp` now has to establish that this failure is "the known one" before
it can trust its own result. That is exactly the reasoning-load that lets a real
regression through as a known failure.

It also degrades the mutation-proof discipline this campaign relies on: a
revert-probe whose red set includes an unrelated pre-existing failure is harder
to read, and a probe that reports a clean red may simply have not reached this
test.

- Does it fail on clean `origin/master`? (Verify in a detached worktree at the

  a namespace restriction, an AF_XDP/UMEM resource cap) or a genuine defect in
  the stop-path drop accounting the test exercises?
- Does it fail deterministically or only under `--test-threads=1` / only under
  load / only after other tests have run?

If it is environmental, the test should SKIP with a stated reason rather than
fail, so the suite's red genuinely means a regression. If it is a real defect in
the #5165 stop-path behaviour, fix it — a batch received after stop being
mis-accounted is a correctness question, not a test-harness one.

`pkg/refactoraudit`'s heatmap gate compares the committed artifact against the audited

crossing — which is correct, and is the whole point of that PR — but it means a stale cached
pass can now survive for many commits instead of one. The mechanism is identical on master;
the exposure is not.

1. Add `-count=1` to the `make test-go` invocation for this package (or generally). Cheapest,

   covers what the test reads. Heavier and arguably fights the tool.
3. Have the test itself detect a cached run and fail loudly. Fragile.

Option 1 unless someone objects.

## #6627 — refactoraudit: a duplicated heatmap row is invisible to every check [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by the hostile review of #6623. Pre-existing, low severity, filed so it is not lost.

## Defect

A duplicated row in `docs/refactoring-audit-current.txt` passes every check:

- the staleness comparison builds a `tierByPath` map, so a second row for the same path
  collapses onto the first and compares equal;
- the sort-order check permits equal-adjacent rows, so the duplicate does not break ordering;
- the band check passes because the duplicate carries the same (valid) LOC and tier.

So the artifact can carry the same file twice and nothing notices.

## Why it is LOW

No wrong decision follows from it. The tier and membership — the things the project's rules
act on — are unchanged by a duplicate, and the generator does not produce one. This is a
hand-edit detector gap, not a live defect: it matters only if someone edits the artifact by
hand, which the surrounding tests already discourage for every other shape (retagging,
deletion, phantom rows and reordering are all caught).

Filed rather than fixed inside #6623 because it is pre-existing and nothing in that PR makes
it more reachable.

## Fix

In the well-formed check, assert each path appears at most once — a single `map[string]bool`
pass over the parsed rows, erroring on the second sighting with the offending path.

## Gate for a fix

- Duplicate a row in a scratch artifact and confirm the new check REDs as an assertion with
  `go vet` clean.
- Confirm the unmutated artifact stays green, so the check is not rejecting valid input.

Related: the same review also filed the `go test` caching gap. Provenance: hostile review of
PR #6623, verified firsthand.

## #6628 — cluster: session-sync never re-handshakes on an authentication-key change — an unkeyed stream stays unkeyed forever [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by the Codex review of #6624. **Pre-existing on `origin/master`** — dormant only because
no shipped config sets `authentication-key`, so every stream is unkeyed today and the bug has
had nothing to expose. It becomes load-bearing the moment anyone enables the key.

## Defect

`performSyncHandshake` selects authentication **once, when the TCP connection is created**
(`pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go:329`). `wrapSyncConn` then permanently fixes that connection's
authentication state and derived key (`sync_auth.go:415`), and frame sealing only checks the
already-fixed state (`sync_protocol.go:59`).

Applying a new configuration updates the manager's key, but the restart decision compares only
`clusterTransportKey`, which **excludes** the authentication key
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:221`, `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:1421`). So committing a
key does not tear down or re-handshake the existing connection.

## Consequences

- An unkeyed session-sync stream stays unkeyed **indefinitely** after the key is committed.
- A hostile stream admitted before the commit keeps injecting frames afterwards.
- Legitimate traffic also stays unauthenticated until an incidental disconnect or a daemon
  restart — so the security posture depends on luck.
- Rotation never revokes an existing connection's old derived frame key.

The practical effect: a commit-time gate that requires a key can be fully satisfied while the
runtime path it exists to protect is still failing open.

## Why there is no test

Codex checked and there is **no test that changes the key while a session-sync connection is
already open**. That is precisely why this escaped — the existing coverage builds keyed
connections and unkeyed connections, never a connection that outlives a key change.

## Fix

Include the authentication key in the restart/re-handshake decision, so an auth-key change
forces the connection down and back up through `performSyncHandshake`. Consider whether a
graceful in-band re-handshake is preferable to a drop, given HA sensitivity to session-sync
gaps — a drop mid-bulk-sync has its own cost.

## #6629 — cluster: config-sync ships the control-channel PSK in cleartext over an HMAC-only (and initially unauthenticated) link [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by the Codex review of #6624. Filed separately because it makes the *prescribed rollout*
of a control-channel PSK leak that PSK.

## Defect

Config synchronization takes raw `ShowActive()` configuration
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:355`), serializes it, and writes it over session-sync
(`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_config.go:234`).

Session-sync authentication is **HMAC-only — it does not encrypt frames**. So any secret in the
configuration crosses the control link in cleartext to anyone who can observe it.

## Why this is worse than it sounds

The documented rollout for enabling the control-channel key relies on config-sync to propagate
that key to the peer. Combine with the fact that the pre-existing session-sync stream is
**completely unauthenticated** until it is re-established (filed separately — session-sync
never re-handshakes on a key change), and the sequence is:

1. Operator commits the PSK on node A.
2. Config-sync carries the PSK, in cleartext, over a link that is at that moment neither
   authenticated nor encrypted.
3. A passive observer on the control link learns the PSK that was just introduced to secure
   that very link.

The rollout procedure defeats itself on first use. This is not a residual risk to note in a doc;
it is the bootstrap problem the mechanism has to solve.

## Fix

Secret provisioning has to be out-of-band, or config-sync needs confidentiality. Options:

1. Provision the PSK out-of-band (operator sets it independently on both nodes; config-sync
   never carries it). Simplest and probably correct — it also matches how a shared secret is
   normally bootstrapped.
2. Give config-sync confidentiality (encrypt frames, not just HMAC them), which is a real
   protocol change with its own review.
3. Redact `Secret` leaves from the config-sync payload and require out-of-band provisioning for
   all of them — a generalisation of (1) that also covers future secrets.

## #6630 — cluster: control-channel key rotation has no overlap protocol — rotating one node breaks heartbeat liveness [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by the Codex review of #6624. Pre-existing design gap in the control-channel auth
mechanism, exposed as soon as anyone actually uses a key.

## Defect

Once both peers have authenticated with key A, rotating one node to key B makes each receive a
**present-but-invalid** heartbeat HMAC. Such frames are unconditionally rejected
(`pkg/cluster/heartbeat.go:605`).

Bidirectional heartbeat liveness is therefore lost for the whole window between the first
commit and the second — risking a false failover, fencing, or a split-brain election, on a
mechanism whose detection threshold is ~1s.

## Why the documented workaround does not work

`pkg/cluster/README.md:469` suggests clearing both keys first and then setting the new one. The
strict validator introduced alongside this mechanism **expressly forbids** committing a cluster
with no key (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_cluster_auth.go:43`). So the documented
rotation path is rejected by the very gate that requires the key.

## What is missing

There is no previous/current key overlap, no key identifier on the wire, no coordinated rekey,
and no explicit finalize step. "Dual-accept" closes only through runtime sticky evidence, so
there is no operator-controlled rollout boundary — the operator cannot tell when it is safe to
remove the old key.

## Fix

A standard two-key overlap:

- Accept frames sealed under EITHER the current or the previous key during rotation.
- Put a key identifier on the wire so a receiver knows which to verify against, rather than
  trying both blindly.
- Provide an explicit finalize operation that retires the previous key, and a `show` that tells
  the operator which keys are currently accepted on each node — so "is it safe to finalize?"
  has an answer.

## #6631 — upgrade: a non-default --journal path can never be promoted — the boot gate hardcodes /var/lib/xpf [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found while gating #6601, confirmed independently by that PR's hostile review by running the
real Go writer and the real shell gate end to end. **Pre-existing on `origin/master`** — master's
gate also read only the default journal and no-op'd identically, so #6601 does not regress it.

## Defect

`xpfd upgrade kernel arm --journal <path>` is production-reachable — `--journal` is accepted by
every verb including `arm` (`cmd/xpfd/upgrade_kernel.go:35`). The Go side honours it: the journal
goes to `<path>`, and with #6601 the arm-record sidecar is derived from it via
`ArmRecordPath(cfg.JournalPath)`, so it lands beside the journal.

The boot-time gate hardcodes both locations:

- `scripts/image/xpf-kernel-promote:51` — `ARM_RECORD="/var/lib/xpf/kernel-promote-binary"`
- `scripts/image/xpf-kernel-promote:61` — `KERNEL_JOURNAL="/var/lib/xpf/kernel-upgrade.state"`

So arming with a non-default journal path puts BOTH files somewhere the gate never looks. The
gate sees both absent, takes the benign "nothing to promote" branch, and exits quiet. The armed
candidate is never verified, never promoted, and reverts on the next boot.

Verified both halves firsthand: the real Go writer with a non-default `JournalPath` (journal and
sidecar both land elsewhere), then the real script with both hardcoded paths absent → quiet
"nothing to promote".

## Why it is not louder

#6601 adds a loud refusal for the ARMED-without-record divergence, but that branch needs the
journal to be readable at the DEFAULT path and say `ARMED`. Here the journal is elsewhere too,
so the gate takes the quiet branch instead. The failure direction is safe (no promotion, revert)
but silent, which is the benign-skip laundering #6601 otherwise works hard to eliminate.

There is no way to close this by teaching the gate the path: the boot unit hardcodes its
`ExecStart` and has no channel to pass one.

## Fix

Recommended: **arming REFUSES a non-default journal path** for the kernel channel specifically,
with an error saying the boot gate can only read the default location. That converts a silent
never-promote into an immediate, actionable refusal at the moment the operator asks for it.

## #6632 — kernel channel: arming with a non-default --journal produces a structurally unpromotable candidate [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-07)

Advances #6541 hardening (found during the #6601 r8 hostile review).

## Problem

`cmd/xpfd/upgrade_kernel.go` defines `--journal` on every `upgrade kernel`
verb, including `arm`. Arming with a non-default value writes both the
journal and the arm-record sidecar under that directory
(`ArmRecordPath` derives from `filepath.Dir(journalPath)`).

The boot-time promotion gate cannot follow. `xpf-kernel-promote.service`
hardcodes `ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/xpf-kernel-promote`, and the script
hardcodes `/var/lib/xpf/kernel-upgrade.state` +
`/var/lib/xpf/kernel-promote-binary` — there is no way to pass it a
journal path.

So a candidate armed against a non-default journal is **structurally
unpromotable**: it boots, runs unverified, the gate finds neither file
and takes the benign "nothing to promote" branch, and the next plain
reboot reverts it. The operator gets no signal.

Verified during the #6601 review: on `origin/master` the gate ran
`xpfd upgrade kernel promote` with no `--journal`, read the default
journal, found nothing and no-op'd identically. This is a pre-existing
hole in the flag's design, not something #6601 introduced. #6601 r8
corrected the three places that wrongly cited `--journal` as a desync
the ARMED-without-record check catches (it does not — that flag moves
both files together, so the gate takes the quiet branch) and documented
the flag as diagnostic-only for `arm`.

## Proposed fix

`Arm` should REFUSE a non-default `JournalPath`. Arming is a preflight
and is retryable; the honest place to fail is the operator's terminal,
not a silent non-promotion at the next boot. This matches the pattern
the kernel channel already uses elsewhere (`recordPromoteBinary` fails
closed rather than arming something that cannot be verified).

## Problem

`afxdp::wg::engine::engine_internal_tests` has two load-sensitive defects that
surface only in a full parallel `cargo test --release` run on a loaded machine.
Both were found while diagnosing #6621; neither is caused by it.

### 1. `install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal` fails under load

```
thread '...install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal' (4130867)
  panicked at src/afxdp/wg/engine_tests.rs:872:5:
reconcile loop must have completed at least one full add/remove cycle
```

Observed once in 21 full-suite runs (load average ~25, many concurrent agents).

The test spawns two threads:

- **installer** — a BOUNDED loop of `iterations` install attempts.
- **reconciler** — `while !stop { reconcile_peers(&[]); reconcile_peers(&cfg); }`

The main thread does `installer.join()`, THEN `stop.store(true)`, THEN
`reconciler.join()`. Nothing guarantees the reconciler is ever scheduled before
the installer finishes, so under CPU oversubscription it can complete **zero**
cycles and the `reconcile_iters >= 1` assertion trips.

That assertion is correct in intent — it exists (per the r7 Codex hostile
finding recorded in the file) to reject a tautological pass where the
reconciler always wins the lock. The problem is that it asserts a scheduling
outcome the harness does not actually arrange. The fix is synchronisation, not
relaxing the bound: the main thread should not signal `stop` until the
reconciler has published at least one completed cycle (e.g. the reconciler
bumps an `AtomicU32` and the installer/main waits for it to reach 1 before
`stop.store(true)`), so the "made progress on both sides" precondition is
established rather than hoped for.

## #6634 — ddns: provider RESPONSE TEXT is rendered verbatim into errors — a hostile provider can echo the credential URL into the log [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by the Codex review of #6594. **Pre-existing on `origin/master`** — verified: the render
sites below are all present on master and #6594 neither introduced nor regressed them. It is a
DIFFERENT class from what #6594 fixes (that PR bounds error VALUES that carry a request URL;
this is provider-supplied response TEXT).

## Defect

Four backends render text taken from the provider's HTTP response body straight into a returned
error, which the daemon logs:

- Cloudflare: `Errors[].Message` (`pkg/ddns/backend_cloudflare.go`, `cfErrors`)
- Route 53: decoded `Code` and `Message` on non-2xx (`backend_route53.go`)
- dyndns2: the unrecognized first response line — `unrecognized response %q`
  (`backend_dyndns2.go:270` on master)
- DuckDNS: the same shape (`backend_duckdns.go`)

The provider is the untrusted party here. A scratch response containing
`https://user:SUPERSECRET@example.test/update` reached the returned error **unchanged through all
four paths**. No hostile transport is needed — only a provider that echoes (or is induced to
echo) our own update URL back in an error message, which is exactly what a "your request was
invalid: <the request>" style API does.

Also unbounded: three Cloudflare `json.Unmarshal` sites render the decoder error with `%w`
(`backend_cloudflare.go:162/180/220` on master). Go's JSON decoder quotes offending input back —
a scratch response with an overflowing numeric `result_info.page` produced
`json: cannot unmarshal number 9876543210...` with the complete provider-selected number in the
error. `json.Unmarshal` is absent from `urlErrorProducers`, so the structural gate does not see
these.

## Why it is not simply "scrub it"

Provider error text is the *most useful* diagnostic the operator gets — "token invalid",
"zone not found", "rate limited". Withholding it wholesale trades a real operational capability
for the fix, which is why this needs a decision rather than a one-line change. Options:

1. **Bound the shape**: render provider text through a filter that strips anything URL-shaped or
   userinfo-shaped, keeping ordinary prose. Preserves the diagnostic; needs care that the filter
   cannot be evaded by encoding.
2. **Cap and classify**: map known provider error codes to our own constants (the
   `transportReason` discipline #6594 established) and render only the code, not the message.

Not reachable in production. `CheckIP` and the backends take a caller-supplied `*http.Client`,
and this is the same adversary model rounds 7-8 of #6594 were built for — but no production
caller supplies a hostile transport, and errors reaching these paths come from `net/http` and the
stdlib. This is a robustness/model-consistency gap, not a live DoS.

traversal is covered, so nothing currently misleads a reader into assuming totality.

## #6639 — upgrade: flip/cut does not re-stamp the kernel arm record — an in-place binary upgrade mid-candidate refuses the promotion [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by the hostile review of #6601 r8. **Not a defect of that PR** — it is a consequence of the
arm-record design that PR introduces, in the safe direction, and strictly better than the master
behaviour it replaces. Filed so it is not lost.

## The sequence

1. `xpfd upgrade kernel arm` records the CURRENT binary's resolved path (`os.Executable()`) into
   the kernel journal and its sidecar. That record is the authority the boot gate reads.
2. An ordinary in-place xpfd upgrade (`flip` / `cut`) then swaps the running binary to a new
   version.
3. The candidate kernel boots. The gate compares the recorded path against what the unit now
   names, they genuinely differ, and it REFUSES loudly. The candidate is never promoted and
   reverts.

`flip` and `cut` never consult the kernel journal (grep-confirmed over `pkg/upgrade/`), so
nothing re-stamps the record when the binary underneath it moves.

## Why this is not a regression

The refusal is the SAFE direction: no promotion, revert to the known-good kernel. And on master
the same sequence would have run whatever `command -v xpfd` resolved to — i.e. it would have let
an arbitrary binary authorize the promotion, which is exactly the hazard #6601 exists to close.
The behaviour is documented at `pkg/upgrade/kernel_arm_record.go:43-47`.

So: an operator who upgrades xpfd while a kernel candidate is armed loses that candidate and has
to re-arm. Annoying, discoverable (the refusal is loud and names the disagreement), and safe.

## Fix options

1. **Re-stamp on flip/cut**: if the kernel journal is ARMED, rewrite `PromoteBinary` and the
   sidecar to the new binary as part of the flip. Keeps the candidate alive across an xpfd
   upgrade. Needs care that the re-stamp is as fail-closed as the original write — a flip that
   half-updates the record is worse than one that leaves it alone.
2. **Refuse the flip while a kernel candidate is armed**, telling the operator to let the
   candidate settle or disarm first. Simplest and most explicit; costs the operator a wait.
3. **Leave it**, now that the behaviour is documented and the refusal is loud.

(1) is the better operator experience, (2) the easier thing to get right. Either needs a decision
about whether an xpfd upgrade should be able to invalidate an in-flight kernel trial.

## #6648 — userspace: required-protocol gates key on the shared ProtocolVersion, so any wire bump retroactively disarms helpers for unrelated features [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

Every per-feature required-protocol gate compares the helper's reported version
against the single shared `ProtocolVersion` constant rather than against an
immutable minimum for that feature. So bumping `ProtocolVersion` for ANY new
wire feature retroactively raises the bar for every previously-gated feature.

Found by Codex reviewing PR #6644. The coupling is **pre-existing on
`origin/master`**; #6644 is simply the first bump that makes it bite.

```go
	if m.lastStatus.ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion >= ProtocolVersion {   // :675

```

`ensurePersistentSourceNATProtocolLocked` is identical at `:697`. Neither pins
the version at which its own feature became representable.

Policy-scheduler snapshots became representable at version 3. A helper at
version 3 runs a scheduled-policy config correctly today, because the gate
evaluates `3 >= 3`.

## #6649 — userspace: control plane gates on >= snapshot protocol while the helper requires ==, so a newer helper slips the required-protocol gate [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

The Go control plane admits a helper whose snapshot protocol is `>=` the
required version, but the Rust helper accepts a snapshot only on **exact**
equality. A helper NEWER than the control plane therefore passes the
required-protocol gate and then rejects the snapshot — so the fail-closed
sentinel the gate exists to raise never fires.

Found by Codex reviewing PR #6644. **Pre-existing on `origin/master`.**

## Evidence (re-verified at `39f1f8b93`)

**Graded REAL.** The asymmetry is exactly as filed and is present at every gate.

**Go side — `>=`, 8 sites in `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_compile.go`:**
```
870:  if m.lastStatus.ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion >= ProtocolVersion {
876:      if status.ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion >= ProtocolVersion {
938:  / 944: / 992: / 998: / 1014: / 1020:   ... same predicate
```

**Rust side — exact equality, `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/snapshot.rs`:**
```rust
if snapshot.version != CONFIG_SNAPSHOT_PROTOCOL_VERSION {
    ... "unsupported snapshot protocol version {} (want {})",
        snapshot.version, CONFIG_SNAPSHOT_PROTOCOL_VERSION
```
(two sites: the `apply` handler and the preflight at `:446`).

So a helper NEWER than the control plane reports a higher `ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion` in status, satisfies `>=`, and passes the required-protocol gate — after which Go stamps its own (lower) `ProtocolVersion` into every snapshot and the helper rejects each one on `!=`. The fail-closed sentinel the gate exists to raise never fires; the failure surfaces instead as a stream of rejected snapshots.

Note `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go` uses the inverse form (`< ProtocolVersion`) for its own guard, so the `>=` family is not universal in the package — worth checking both directions when fixing.

This issue already carried real inline evidence and a correct diagnosis; only the base sha and line numbers needed re-pinning.

## Failure scenario

Control plane at `ProtocolVersion = 4`, helper at 5 (helper upgraded first, or
rolled forward independently).

## #6650 — cluster: HA config-sync pushes a multi-zone scoped policy to a pre-v4 peer that narrows it — #5488 fail-open relocated to the cross-chassis skew [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

The #5488 snapshot-protocol gate protects the daemon↔local-helper skew. It does
NOT protect the cross-chassis skew, where the same fail-open reappears — a
multi-zone scoped global deny narrows to its first zone on a peer node running a
pre-v4 daemon. On this product "rolling upgrade" most often means exactly that:
a chassis cluster upgraded one node at a time.

Found by the hostile review of PR #6644 (finding F5). Not a defect in shipped
code — an old binary cannot be fixed from a new one — but it is the hazard #6644
claims to close, in the topology its own framing points at.

## Trace (two-node cluster, node A upgraded, node B not yet)

1. A runs a v4 daemon + v4 helper. B runs a v3 daemon + v3 helper.
2. Operator commits on A:
   `set security policies global policy g match from-zone [ dmz trust ]`,
   `match to-zone untrust`, `then deny`.
3. **A's gate does not fire.** `m.lastStatus.ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion` is 4,
   so `4 >= ProtocolVersion` short-circuits at `manager_compile.go:750`. The
   commit succeeds and `pushCommittedConfigToPeer`
   (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go:275`) ships the config **text** to B.
   `applyErrSkipsPeerSync` suppresses the push only when A's own gate fired,
   which it did not.
4. B compiles that text with its own v3 daemon and publishes to its own v3
   helper. `3 == 3` — accepted. B's helper reads only `match_from_zone` and
   installs the deny scoped to `dmz` alone.
5. Traffic sourced from `trust` toward `untrust` is denied on A and falls through
   to lower-precedence rules on B. On failover to B, or for any flow B already
   owns, the operator's deny is not enforced.

## Why A cannot currently detect it

The config-snapshot protocol version is deliberately node-local and is never
exchanged between chassis. The heartbeat carries only `HAProtocolVersion`
(`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:270`, `:325`), and `xpfd protocol-versions`
explicitly excludes the local one — `cmd/xpfd/main.go:197-199` says so in a
comment: "NOT the daemon↔helper local control socket
(`userspace.ProtocolVersion`)".

## #6652 — userspace-dp: reconcile snapshot reads the synced-session map non-recovering, so a poisoned mutex replays ZERO sessions after a contained worker panic [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`snapshot_shared_session_entries` reads the shared synced-session map with
`.lock().map(...).unwrap_or_default()`. On a poisoned mutex that yields an
**empty vector**, which the reconcile path then preserves as the set of sessions
to replay — so a reconcile that crosses a contained worker panic silently
replays nothing.

The module's stated policy is to RECOVER from poison (`lock_shared_recover`:
keep the committed map, clear the poison, count and log). This read applies the
opposite policy.

Found by Codex reviewing PR #6643. **Pre-existing** — the file is untouched by
that PR, which repaired three sibling reads in `ha/session_import.rs`.

## Evidence (origin/master)

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/mod.rs:802`:

```rust
.lock().map(...).unwrap_or_default()
```

## Failure scenario

1. A worker panics while holding `sessions.synced`; the #925 supervisor contains
   it and the process keeps running. The mutex is now poisoned.
2. Reconcile teardown calls `snapshot_shared_session_entries` before any other
   recovering path has touched that mutex.
3. The read yields `None` → `unwrap_or_default()` → an empty vector, which is
   preserved as "the sessions to bring back".
4. `stop_inner(false)` replaces the workers.
5. Bring-up replays no sessions. The shared map still holds them, but the new
   worker tables and the immediate replay path do not.

The window is real but interleaving-dependent: any other shared-session path
(publish, lookup, remove, prewarm) that locks first CLEARS the poison, after
which this read behaves correctly. That nondeterminism is the point — whether a
reconcile preserves state depends on which thread happened to lock first.

## #6653 — userspace-dp: full teardown skips poisoned session maps and indexes, leaving torn state that resolves stale sessions and consumes the #5674 ceiling [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

Full teardown skips clearing the shared session maps when their mutex is
poisoned, and the owner-RG indexes independently do the same. A subsequent start
can then resolve stale sessions, and stale entries count toward the #5674
aggregate admission ceiling — refusing legitimate imports.

Found by Codex reviewing PR #6643. **Pre-existing** — both files are untouched
by that PR.

## Evidence (origin/master)

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/mod.rs:756` — teardown skips clearing
  poisoned `synced`, `nat`, and `forward_wire` maps.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types/mod.rs:65` — independently skips any poisoned
  owner-RG index.

## Failure scenario

1. A worker panics while holding `synced`; the supervisor contains it.
2. `stop_inner(true)` runs a full teardown. It leaves `synced`'s entries intact
   because the mutex is poisoned, while clearing some or all of the sibling maps
   and indexes whose mutexes are not.
3. The result is a torn state: entries present in one map, absent from its
   siblings and from the indexes that are supposed to mirror it.
4. On the next start, lookups can resolve stale sessions, and the stale entries
   count toward the #5674 ceiling, so legitimate imports are refused.

The asymmetry is what makes this worse than a plain leak: teardown is supposed
to leave every surface empty, and poison makes it leave them **inconsistently**
empty, which no later code is written to expect.

## Fix

Centralize teardown clearing through recovering locks for all three maps and all
four indexes, so a poisoned surface is cleared like any other rather than
skipped. Add a test per poisoned surface asserting teardown leaves it empty.

## #6654 — userspace-dp: HA bulk export refuses on a poisoned mutex instead of recovering, so the refusal fires nondeterministically by lock order [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`ha/export.rs:107` returns the error `"shared sessions lock poisoned"` instead of
recovering, so whether event-stream bulk session export is REFUSED depends on
which thread happened to lock the mutex first.

Found by Codex reviewing PR #6643. **Pre-existing** — the file is untouched by
that PR.

## Evidence (origin/master)

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/export.rs:107` returns `"shared sessions lock
poisoned"` rather than going through `lock_shared_recover`.

## Why the nondeterminism is the defect

`lock_shared_recover` CLEARS the poison. Every other shared-session path —
publish, lookup, remove, prewarm — uses it. So after a contained worker panic
the poisoned window closes the instant any of those paths touches the mutex.

That means this refusal fires or does not fire purely on interleaving: if a
lookup got there first, export succeeds; if export got there first, it fails.
A guard whose firing depends on thread scheduling is not a guard.

This is precisely the reasoning PR #6643 used to justify RECOVERING rather than
refusing on its three reads. The same argument applies here and was not carried
across.

## Bounding factor (why MINOR, not MAJOR)

End-to-end correctness is bounded: `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:289` falls back
to the authoritative `BulkSync` when the event-stream export fails. So a refused
export degrades to a slower path rather than losing session state. The defect is
the nondeterministic refusal itself, not a loss of sync.

## Fix

Use `lock_shared_recover` and add a test that poisons the mutex and asserts bulk
snapshot export still succeeds.

## #6657 — userspace-dp: full-suite runs intermittently HANG or fail across MULTIPLE concurrency tests (wg-engine install/reconcile, CoS-lease seqlock) — reproduced on master [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-08)

## Summary

`afxdp::wg::engine::engine_internal_tests::install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal`
intermittently HANGS when the cargo suite runs at full concurrency. In isolation
it passes reliably; under a full-suite run it can wedge indefinitely.

Reproduced on `origin/master` in a detached worktree, so this is not caused by
any in-flight branch.

## Evidence

Verified at `origin/master` in a detached worktree:

- In isolation: **10/10 passes**.
- Full-suite run: **hung on this test for 21+ minutes** before being killed.

Observed independently on a feature branch during PR #6655 work: failed once in
6 full-suite runs, passed the other 5. The branch's only compiled addition there
was a `#[cfg(test)]` module, which is why the master reproduction was run — and
it reproduced.

## Why this matters more than a flaky test

1. **It can burn 20+ minutes of a gate run and looks like a hang, not a
   failure.** An agent or CI job watching for a result gets neither.

## #6660 — api: the REST READ surface is still unauthenticated — any local uid reads GET /api/v1/config after the #5561 mutation gate [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

#5561 / PR #6645 authorizes the **mutating** REST surface per principal. The
**read** surface is unchanged: any local process can still `GET /api/v1/config`
and `POST /api/v1/show-text` without being identified, and no login-class `view`
permission is consulted.

Raised as INFO by the hostile review of PR #6645 and stated as an explicit
residual by that PR's author in `pkg/api/README.md`. Filing it so it is tracked
rather than living only in a README paragraph.

## What is and is not covered after #6645

Covered: the 19 mutating routes — `/config/set`, `/config/load`, the commit
family, the clear verbs, diagnostics, `/system/action`. Each resolves the caller
from the kernel socket table at accept time and checks a login-class permission.

Not covered: every read route. `GET /api/v1/config` returns the full running
configuration. On a box with no `api-auth` configured — the default posture on a
loopback bind, since #4047 only *requires* a credential off-loopback — any local
uid reads it, including a uid with no `system login user` entry at all, and
including one whose configured class is `view`-less.

## Why it is worth its own issue rather than folding into #5561

The blast radius is genuinely different, which is why #6645 scoped it out and
why that was the right call:

- A mutating-route denial can only cost an operator an action they retry after
  being added to the login model. A read-route denial can break monitoring,
  automation, or a support workflow that has never needed an identity before.
- The running config contains secrets in redacted-but-present form and the full
  topology; the correct answer may be "gate it" or may be "redact by class",
  which is a design question, not a mechanical extension of the same middleware.
- #6645 verified by grep that nothing in-tree performs REST mutations
  (`cli` speaks gRPC; the deploy, day-0 and image scripts never touch REST; the
  incus harnesses read `/metrics` only). The same sweep has NOT been done for
  reads, and `/metrics` at minimum IS read by the harnesses — so a naive
  extension of the mutation gate to reads would break in-tree tooling.

## Summary

The packed-instance-body defect fixed for `redundancy-group` in #6588/#6658 is
present in other `namedInstances` stanzas. A statement written on the instance
line — rather than in a nested block — is silently dropped, and the commit
succeeds.

Measured by direct compile through the real `NewParser` → `CompileConfig` path,
not by inspection:

|---|---|
| `system login class ops permissions view;` | class with **EMPTY permissions** |
| `system login user bob class ops;` | user with **NO class** |
| `system syslog host 10.0.0.9 any;` | host with **ZERO facilities** |

Each produces the named instance with an empty body and returns no error.

## Root cause

`namedInstances` returns `{name: Keys[1], node: child}` whenever
`len(child.Keys) >= 2` — i.e. for a packed statement it hands back the node with
the whole statement still on `Keys` — and each caller's body loop then iterates

`user` (`:119`), `host` (`:309`), `file` (`:350`), `provider` (`:579`),
`scheduler` (`:1664`) and others.

This is the same shape as #6588 one level up, in different stanzas.

**Distinct from #6659.** That issue is the `nodeVal`/multi-value-leaf class —
reading one side of a leaf that carries a LIST. This is an instance BODY being
invisible because the body is on `Keys` rather than in `Children`. Same family,
different mechanism, and they do not share a fix.

`system login user bob class ops;` compiling a user with no class is the one to
look at first: the class is what carries the permission set, so what a class-less
user is authorized to do becomes an implicit-default question rather than the
operator's stated one. Worth confirming which way that defaults before rating it —

## #6666 — cluster: the displayed session id changes at promotion — decide whether the standby mirror should adopt the cross-node RTFlowSessionID [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

Split out of #6198 as an explicit deferral (PR #6661, merged `a93bb5aa2`).

The control plane writes a **node-local** session id into the standby's
conntrack mirror, while the helper — once it owns the session — stamps the
**adopted cross-node** id into the same field. So the id an operator sees for a
given flow can CHANGE at promotion.

## Why it is a real operator-facing wrinkle

`show security flow session` renders the dataplane id (#5213), and RT_FLOW log
records carry a session id too (#4915). After a failover the same flow can be
displayed under a different id than it had before, which breaks correlation for
anyone stitching pre- and post-failover records together — exactly the SIEM use
case the #3337 additive forensic fields exist to serve.

## Why it was not bundled into #6198

#6198 was a truncation bug: the HA-synced SessionID masked the session slot to
16 bits (`delta.Slot & 0xffff`) and collided at scale. #6661 fixed that by
minting a real 48-bit identity in a reserved `0xFFFF << 48` namespace.

Whether the mirror should instead carry the cross-node `RTFlowSessionID` is a
**behaviour choice** in the #5212/#5213 lineage, not a bug in the truncation
fix. Bundling it would have mixed a design decision into a defect fix.

## The decision to make

1. **Status quo** — the mirror keeps a node-local id and the displayed id may
   change at promotion. Document it so operators know not to correlate across a
   failover on this field.
2. **Adopt `RTFlowSessionID` in the mirror** — the displayed id is stable across
   promotion. Needs care: the control plane would be writing a value it does not
   own, and the two ids have different uniqueness domains (node-local unique vs
   originating-node stable).
3. **Surface both** — render the node-local id and the cross-node id as separate
   fields so neither claim is overloaded.

## #6675 — test: userspace route-rule enumeration test discards a permission error and nil-derefs the snapshot [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

A userspace-dataplane test discards an error from route-rule enumeration and then
dereferences the resulting nil snapshot, so in any environment where the netlink
route-rule dump is not permitted the test panics on a nil dereference instead of
skipping or failing with the real cause.

Surfaced by a Codex hostile review of PR #6670, whose sandbox returned
`operation not permitted` for route-rule enumeration. The panic masked the actual
environment limitation and made an unrelated PR's review run look like a failure.

## Why it matters

This is test robustness, not a product defect — but it has a real cost: it turns
"this environment cannot enumerate route rules" into a nil-pointer panic with no
diagnostic, which is exactly the failure mode that makes a reviewer or CI run
chase a phantom regression in whatever PR happens to be under test.

It also means the test provides no coverage at all in any sandboxed or
reduced-capability environment, silently, since the panic is indistinguishable
from a genuine break.

## Fix

Handle the enumeration error: `t.Skipf` when the failure is a permission error
(the capability genuinely is not available), and `t.Fatalf` with the wrapped
error otherwise. Do not dereference the snapshot before checking the error.

## Repro

Run the userspace-dataplane test suite in an environment without
`CAP_NET_ADMIN` (or otherwise unable to dump `ip rule`).

## Provenance

Codex hostile review of PR #6670 (host-inbound multi-member scoping). Unrelated
to that PR's change — filed separately so it is not carried as a caveat on
review runs of other work.

## #6678 — daemon/device-map: deviceMapOriginalNameFor falls back to the LOGICAL name on an empty derivation, persisting an OriginalName= udev never presents [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`deviceMapOriginalNameFor` (`pkg/daemon/device_map.go:121`) calls
`deriveKernelNameFn` and, when that returns `""`, falls through and returns
`currentNIC`. In the branch that matters — the "NIC already wearing its logical
name but missing its `.link`" recovery case — `currentNIC == logical`, so the
**logical** name is persisted as `OriginalName=` through the mapped-name apply
path (`device_map.go:209`).

The function's own documentation states that udev will never present that logical
name. So the written `.link` cannot match on the next boot, and boot-time
persistence silently fails.

## Why it is a latent rather than live bug

An empty derivation is currently hard to produce from a genuine kernel sysfs
address: `pciAddrToEnp` returns `""` only for a malformed address, and real
addresses are well-formed. Every other consumer treats `""` as a clean skip —
`ensureRethLinkOriginalName` (`daemon_reth.go:39`) returns immediately without
rewriting the RETH `.link`, which is the correct posture.

So this is the one non-skip fallback in the call graph, and it converts "I could
not derive a name" into "here is a name" rather than "do nothing". Whenever a
future change widens the set of inputs that fail to derive, this turns into a
silent boot-persistence failure rather than a loud one.

## Why it is worth fixing now rather than when it bites

The failure is silent and deferred: the bad `.link` is written at apply time, and
the consequence appears at the *next boot*, on a machine the operator is not
watching, as a NIC that did not get its name. Correlating that back to an empty
derivation hours earlier is expensive.

Declining to write a `.link` at all is strictly better — it leaves the NIC under
its kernel name, which is at least a state the rest of the daemon understands.

Return an explicit "no name derivable" signal rather than `currentNIC`, and have
the apply path skip writing `OriginalName=` for that NIC — matching what
